chapters.title: Inferno, Canto I
paragraphs: Halfway through the journey of my life, I found myself lost in a dark forest, for the straight path ahead had vanished.
How hard it is to describe that forest — savage, dense, and forbidding — the very memory of it revives my terror.
It was so bitter that death itself is hardly worse. But to tell of the good I found there, I will speak of the other things I witnessed.
I cannot clearly recall how I entered that place, so heavy with sleep was I at the moment I strayed from the true path.
But when I reached the foot of a hill, at the point where the valley that had pierced my heart with dread came to an end,
I looked up and saw its slopes already clothed in the rays of that planet which guides all travelers on their way.
Then the fear that had pooled in the lake of my heart through that dreadful night began, at last, to ease.
And like a man who, gasping for breath, has dragged himself from the sea onto the shore and turns back to stare at the dangerous waters,
So my soul, still fleeing in terror, turned back to gaze upon the pass that no living person had ever survived.
After resting my exhausted body, I resumed my climb up the barren slope, always keeping my lower foot firmly planted.
And there, almost at the very start of the ascent, a leopard appeared — swift, light, and covered in spotted fur!
It would not move from my path. In fact, it blocked my way so thoroughly that I turned back again and again.
It was the break of dawn, and the sun was rising with those same stars that accompanied it when divine Love first set all beautiful things in motion.
The early hour and the sweet season gave me reason to hope, despite the beast's dappled hide.
But that hope was short-lived, for a lion appeared before me.
It seemed to be charging straight at me, head held high, ravenous with hunger — the very air seemed to tremble before it.
And then a she-wolf, gaunt and wasted, yet seemingly burdened with every craving — she had driven countless souls to ruin!
She weighed on me with such heaviness, with the dread that poured from her very appearance, that I abandoned all hope of reaching the summit.
Like a man who revels in his winnings until the moment of loss arrives, and then weeps and despairs with every thought,
That is what the restless beast made of me, as she advanced upon me step by step, driving me back to where the sun falls silent.
As I was stumbling back down into the darkness, a figure appeared before my eyes — one who seemed faint from a long silence.
When I saw him in that vast wilderness, I cried out, "Have mercy on me, whoever you are — whether shade or living man!"
He answered me: "Not a man — though I was one once. My parents were both from Lombardy, both Mantuans by birth.
I was born under Julius Caesar, though late in his time, and I lived in Rome under the good Augustus, in the age of false and lying gods.
I was a poet, and I sang of the righteous son of Anchises who sailed from Troy after proud Ilion was burned.
But you — why are you turning back toward such misery? Why not climb the Delectable Mountain, the source and cause of all joy?"
"Are you truly that Virgil, that wellspring from which such a broad river of eloquence flows?" I replied, my face flushing with awe.
"O glory and light of all other poets, may the long devotion and deep love that drove me to study your work now serve me well!
You are my master and my author. You alone are the one from whom I learned the beautiful style that has brought me honor.
Look at the beast that turned me back. Save me from her, famous sage, for she makes my very blood tremble in my veins."
"You must take a different road," he answered, seeing my tears, "if you wish to escape this savage place.
For this beast you cry out against lets no one pass her way. She harasses every traveler until she destroys them.
Her nature is so vicious and insatiable that she is never satisfied — after feeding, she is hungrier than before.
She mates with many beasts, and will mate with more still, until the Greyhound comes to make her die in agony.
He will feed not on land or wealth, but on wisdom, love, and virtue. His homeland will lie between Feltro and Feltro.
He will be the salvation of humbled Italy, for whose sake the maiden Camilla died, and Euryalus, Turnus, and Nisus fell from their wounds.
Through every city he will hunt her down, until he drives her back into Hell, from where Envy first let her loose.
Therefore I judge it best that you follow me. I will be your guide and lead you through an eternal place,
Where you will hear the desperate cries of lamentation and see the ancient spirits in their anguish, each one screaming for a second death.
And you will see those who are content within the fire, because they hope one day to join the blessed.
Then, if you wish to ascend to them, a soul worthier than I will take you further. I will leave you in her care when I depart.
For the Emperor who reigns above, because I was a rebel against His law, will not allow anyone to enter His city through me.
He rules everywhere, but there He reigns. There is His city and His throne. Oh, blessed is the one He chooses!"
And I said to him: "Poet, I beg you, by that God you never knew, help me escape this evil and worse —
Lead me to the place you have described, so that I may see the gate of Saint Peter and those souls you say are so full of grief."
Then he set off, and I followed behind him.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto II
paragraphs: Day was fading, and the darkening air released all living creatures on earth from their labors. I alone
Was preparing myself to endure the struggle ahead — both the hardship of the journey and the grief of what I would witness, which unerring memory will now retrace.
O Muses! O great genius! Help me now! O memory, that recorded all I saw — here your true worth will be revealed!
I began: "Poet, you who guide me, consider whether I am strong enough before you entrust me to this daunting passage.
You say that the father of Silvius, while still alive and in his mortal body, traveled to the immortal world.
But if the Adversary of all evil was gracious to him, considering the great things that would come from him — who he was and what he would become —
It seems fitting to any reasonable mind. For he was destined to be the father of great Rome and her empire, both chosen for the highest heaven.
Rome and her empire, to speak the truth, were established as the holy place where the successor of the greatest Peter sits.
On that journey you praise him for, he learned things that led both to his victory and to the papal mantle.
Later, the Chosen Vessel went there too, to bring back strength for that Faith which is the gateway to salvation.
But why should I go there? Who permits it? I am not Aeneas. I am not Paul. Neither I nor anyone else would think me worthy.
So if I agree to come, I fear the journey may be foolish. You are wise — you understand better than I can say."
And like a man who changes his mind, whose new doubts undo his former resolve so completely that he abandons his purpose,
That is what I became on that dark hillside — overthinking destroyed the boldness that had come so quickly at the start.
"If I have understood you correctly," replied that shade of the Great-Souled One, "your spirit has been seized by cowardice,
Which so often burdens a man that it turns him away from noble endeavors, like a false vision that startles a skittish animal.
To free you from this fear, I will tell you why I came and what I heard at the first moment I felt grief for you.
I was among the souls in Limbo when a beautiful, blessed Lady called to me, and I begged her to command me.
Her eyes shone brighter than the stars. She began to speak, gentle and low, in an angelic voice and in her own tongue:
'O courteous spirit of Mantua, whose fame still endures in the world and will endure as long as the world lasts,
A friend of mine — and not a friend of Fortune — is so blocked upon the desert slope that he has turned back in terror.
I fear he may already be so lost that I have risen too late to help him, from what I have heard of him in Heaven.
Go now, and with your eloquent speech and whatever else is needed to save him, help him so that I may be consoled.
I am Beatrice, and I bid you go. I come from the place where I long to return. Love moved me — love compels me to speak.
When I stand before my Lord, I will praise you to Him often.' Then she fell silent, and I began:
'O Lady of virtue, through whom alone the human race surpasses all that is contained within the smallest circling heaven,
Your command so pleases me that to obey, even if already done, would still feel late. You need say no more of your wish.
But tell me: why do you not shrink from descending here into this depths, away from the vast place you burn to return to?'
'Since you wish to understand so deeply,' she answered me, 'I will tell you briefly why I am not afraid to enter here.
One should fear only those things that have the power to do harm. Nothing else is frightening — nothing else deserves fear.
God in His mercy made me such that your suffering cannot touch me, nor can any flame of this burning reach me.
A gentle Lady in Heaven grieves at this obstacle I am sending you to remove, and her grief breaks the strict judgment above.
She called upon Lucia and said, "Your faithful one now needs you, and I commend him to your care."
Lucia, enemy of all cruelty, hurried away and came to the place where I was sitting with the ancient Rachel.
She said, "Beatrice, true praise of God, why do you not help the one who loved you so much? For your sake he rose above the common crowd.
Do you not hear the anguish in his weeping? Do you not see the death that threatens him beside that flood where the ocean has no power?"
Never in all the world were people so quick to seek their good and flee their harm as I was after hearing those words.
I came down from my blessed seat, trusting in your noble speech, which honors both you and all who have heard it.'
After she had spoken these words to me, she turned away her shining eyes, weeping — which made me come even faster.
And so I came to you, as she wished. I rescued you from that wild beast that blocked the short path up the beautiful mountain.
So what is this? Why, why do you hesitate? Why does such cowardice lodge in your heart? Why do you lack boldness and daring,
When three such blessed Ladies are watching over you in the court of Heaven, and my words promise you so much good?"
As little flowers, bent and closed by the night's chill, straighten and open on their stems when the sun touches them,
So I revived from my exhaustion, and such good courage rushed into my heart that I spoke like a man emboldened:
"O compassionate one who came to my aid, and you who obeyed so quickly the true words she spoke to you!
Your words have filled my heart with such eager desire for this journey that I have returned to my original resolve.
Now lead on, for we share a single will. You are my leader, my lord, my master." I said this to him, and when he moved forward,
I entered upon the deep and savage way.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto III
paragraphs: "Through me you enter the city of suffering. Through me you enter into eternal pain. Through me you enter among the lost.
Justice moved my great Maker. I was shaped by divine Power, by the highest Wisdom, and by primal Love.
Before me, nothing was created except eternal things — and I will last forever. Abandon all hope, you who enter here."
These words, written in a dark color, I saw inscribed above a gate. "Master," I said, "their meaning is hard for me."
And he, speaking like one who knows: "Here you must leave all hesitation behind. Here all cowardice must die.
We have come to the place I told you of, where you will see the wretched souls who have lost the good of the intellect."
Then he took my hand in his, and with a reassuring look he led me into the hidden world beyond.
Sighs, cries, and piercing wails echoed through the starless air, and at first I wept to hear them.
Strange languages, horrible accents, words of agony, shouts of rage, voices shrill and hoarse, and the slapping of hands —
All of it merged into a roar that whirled ceaselessly through that forever-darkened air, like sand spinning in a whirlwind.
And I, my head reeling with horror, said: "Master, what is this I hear? Who are these people, so overwhelmed by pain?"
He replied: "This miserable fate belongs to the pathetic souls of those who lived without either shame or praise.
They are mixed in with that worthless choir of angels who were neither rebellious against God nor faithful to Him — they chose only themselves.
Heaven expelled them to preserve its beauty, and the depths of Hell refuse them too, for even the damned would gain glory by comparison."
"Master," I said, "what torments them so terribly that they cry out like this?" He answered: "I will tell you very briefly.
These souls have no hope of death. Their blind, degraded existence is so base that they envy every other fate.
The world allows no trace of their fame to survive. Mercy and Justice both despise them. Let us not speak of them — just look, and move on."
When I looked again, I saw a banner whirling and racing forward so fast that it seemed furious at any pause.
Behind it trailed such an endless procession of people that I would never have believed death had undone so many.
After I recognized a few of them, I spotted the shade of the one who, through cowardice, made the great refusal.
At once I understood with certainty that this was the company of wretches despised by God and by His enemies alike.
These miserable souls, who were never truly alive, were naked, stung relentlessly by wasps and hornets.
Blood streamed down their faces, mingled with their tears, and was lapped up at their feet by disgusting worms.
When I looked further, I saw crowds gathered on the bank of a great river. "Master," I said, "tell me, please —
Who are these people, and what law makes them so eager to cross, as I can see through this murky light?"
He replied: "All this will become clear to you when we halt on the grim shore of the Acheron."
Then, my eyes cast down in shame, fearing my questions might annoy him, I held my tongue until we reached the river.
And there, coming toward us in a boat, was an old man with white hair, shouting: "Woe to you, depraved souls!
Give up all hope of ever seeing the sky again. I come to ferry you to the other shore, into eternal darkness, fire, and ice.
And you there — you, the living soul — step away from these dead!" But when he saw that I did not move,
He said: "By other routes, by other ports you will reach the shore — not here. A lighter vessel must carry you."
My Guide replied: "Charon, do not torment yourself. It is willed where the power exists to do what is willed. Ask nothing more."
At that, the ferryman of the livid marsh fell silent, his fleecy cheeks still, though wheels of flame burned around his eyes.
But all those weary, naked souls changed color and gnashed their teeth the moment they heard his cruel words.
They cursed God, their parents, the human race, the place, the time, the seed that made them, and the wombs that bore them.
Then, weeping bitterly, they drew together toward the accursed shore that awaits every soul who does not fear God.
Charon the demon, with eyes like glowing coals, beckoned them all together, striking with his oar anyone who lingered.
As autumn leaves fall from a branch one by one, until the bough has surrendered all its covering to the earth,
In the same way, the evil seed of Adam hurled themselves from that bank one after another, each answering the signal like a falcon to the lure.
So they departed across the dark water, and before they had landed on the far side, a new crowd had already gathered on this one.
"My son," said my courteous Master, "all who die under the wrath of God assemble here from every land.
They are eager to cross the river because divine Justice spurs them on, transforming their fear into desire.
No good soul ever passes this way. So if Charon complains about you, now you understand what his words mean."
When he had finished, the dark plain trembled so violently that the memory of that terror still drenches me in sweat.
The land of tears released a blast of wind that flashed with crimson light, overwhelming all my senses,
And I fell like a man overtaken by sleep.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto IV
paragraphs: A crash of heavy thunder broke through the deep sleep in my head, and I jolted awake like someone shaken by force.
I moved my rested eyes around and stood up, staring hard, trying to make out where I was.
I found myself on the very brink of the abyss of grief — a valley so deep it gathered an infinity of thundering cries.
It was dark, deep, and thick with mist. No matter how hard I fixed my gaze into its depths, I could see nothing at all.
"Let us descend into the blind world below," the Poet began, his face utterly pale. "I will go first, and you will follow."
Noticing how pale he was, I said: "How can I come if even you are afraid — you who usually comfort me in my fears?"
He replied: "It is the anguish of the people below that paints this pity on my face — which you have mistaken for fear.
Let us go, for the long road demands it." And with that he entered, and led me into the first circle surrounding the abyss.
From what I could hear, there were no screams of agony — only sighs, which made the eternal air tremble.
This came from a sorrow without torment, felt by great crowds of men, women, and children.
My good Master said: "You do not ask who these spirits are? I want you to know, before you go further,
That they did not sin. Yet their virtues were not enough, for they lacked baptism — the gateway to the faith you hold.
And those who lived before Christianity did not worship God in the proper way. I myself am among them.
For this failing, and no other guilt, we are lost — punished only in this: that we live without hope, sustained only by desire."
Great grief seized my heart when I heard this, for I knew that people of immense worth were suspended in that Limbo.
"Tell me, Master — tell me, my Lord," I began, eager for certainty about the faith that conquers every error,
"Did anyone ever leave this place through their own merit, or another's, and go on to blessedness?" He understood my veiled question,
And replied: "I was new to this place when I saw a Mighty One descend, crowned with the sign of victory.
He drew out the shade of the First Father, and of Abel his son, and Noah, and Moses the lawgiver, and obedient
Abraham the patriarch, and King David, and Israel with his father and his children, and Rachel, for whose sake he labored so long,
And many others — and He made them blessed. You should know that before these, no human soul had ever been saved."
We did not stop walking as he spoke but kept passing through the forest — I mean the forest of thronging ghosts.
We had not gone far from where I woke when I saw a fire that conquered a hemisphere of darkness.
We were still some distance away, but close enough that I could partly make out distinguished figures gathered there.
"O you who honor every art and science, who are these people who hold such honor that it sets them apart from all the rest?"
He answered: "The glorious fame that echoes above in your world wins grace in Heaven, which advances them to this place."
Just then a voice called out: "All honor to the supreme Poet! His shade, which had departed, now returns."
After the voice fell silent, I saw four mighty shades approaching us, their expressions neither sad nor joyful.
My gracious Master began: "Look at the one with the sword in his hand, who walks before the other three as their lord.
That is Homer, the sovereign poet. Next comes Horace the satirist, Ovid is third, and Lucan is last.
Because the name 'poet' applies to each of them as it does to me — the name that lone voice proclaimed — they do me honor, and rightly so."
And so I watched the noble school of that lord of the highest song gather together — he who soars above the others like an eagle.
After they had spoken among themselves for a time, they turned to me with gestures of welcome, and at this my Master smiled.
And they honored me even further — they made me one of their company, so that I was the sixth among such minds.
We walked on together toward the light, speaking of things it is right to pass over in silence, just as it was right to speak of them there.
We reached the foot of a noble castle, encircled seven times by high walls and protected by a beautiful stream.
This we crossed over as if on solid ground. Through seven gates I entered with those Sages, and we came into a meadow of fresh green.
The people there had grave, unhurried eyes and faces of great authority. They spoke rarely, and in gentle voices.
We withdrew to one side, to an open, luminous, elevated place, from which all of them could be seen.
There, on the green below, the mighty spirits were pointed out to me — and I feel exalted to have seen them.
I saw Electra with many companions, among whom I recognized Hector and Aeneas, and Caesar in armor with his falcon eyes.
I saw Camilla and Penthesilea on the other side, and King Latinus seated with his daughter Lavinia.
I saw the Brutus who drove out Tarquin, Lucretia, Julia, Marcia, and Cornelia, and sitting alone and apart, the Saladin.
When I raised my eyes a little higher, I saw the Master of those who know, seated among his philosophical family.
Everyone gazed at him with reverence. I recognized Socrates and Plato, standing closest to him, ahead of the rest.
Democritus, who attributes the world to chance, Diogenes, Anaxagoras, Thales, Zeno, Empedocles, and Heraclitus.
I saw the great collector of natural properties, Dioscorides, and I saw Orpheus, Cicero, Livy, and the moralist Seneca.
Euclid the geometer, Ptolemy, Galen, Hippocrates, Avicenna, and Averroes, who wrote the great Commentary.
I cannot describe them all in full, for my long subject drives me forward so relentlessly that words often fall short of the reality.
The company of six divided into two. My wise Guide led me by another path, out of that stillness into air that trembled.
And I came to a place where nothing shines.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto V
paragraphs: So I descended from the first circle down to the second, which encompasses less space but holds far greater anguish, goading souls to wail.
There stands Minos, snarling hideously. He examines each soul's sins at the entrance, judges them, and assigns their depth by the coils of his tail.
When an evil-born spirit comes before him, it confesses everything. And this great judge of sins
Sees which level of Hell is right for it. He wraps his tail around himself as many times as the number of circles the soul must descend.
A multitude always stands before him. They step forward one by one to be judged, confess, hear their sentence, and are hurled below.
"You there, coming to this house of pain," Minos said to me, interrupting his great office when he noticed me,
"Watch how you enter and whom you trust. Do not let the wide-open gate deceive you." My Guide replied: "Why do you protest?
Do not block his fated journey. It is willed where the power exists to do what is willed. Question it no further."
And now the sounds of suffering began to reach me. I had arrived where a great torrent of weeping struck my ears.
I came into a place stripped of all light, bellowing like the sea in a storm when it is battered by warring winds.
The hellish hurricane, which never rests, snatches the spirits up in its fury, spinning and battering them without mercy.
When they reach the edge of the precipice, the shrieks and weeping and lamentation erupt — and there they curse God's power.
I understood that this punishment was for the lustful — those who surrendered reason to desire.
And as starlings are carried on their wings in the cold season, in great, dense flocks, so that blast drives these cursed spirits.
It whips them here, there, up, and down. No hope consoles them — not of rest, not even of lesser pain.
And as cranes fly in long lines, chanting their mournful songs, so I saw approaching, uttering cries of grief,
Shadows carried by that violent wind. "Master," I said, "who are these people punished by the black air?"
"The first of those you wish to know about," he told me, "was an empress who ruled over many lands and tongues.
She was so enslaved to lust that she made depravity legal, to remove the shame she had brought upon herself.
She is Semiramis, who, as we read, succeeded Ninus and was his wife. She held the land the Sultan now rules.
The next killed herself for love and broke faith with the ashes of Sychaeus. Then comes voluptuous Cleopatra."
I saw Helen, for whom so many years of bloodshed turned, and I saw great Achilles, who at the end fought against Love.
I saw Paris, Tristan — and he pointed out more than a thousand shades, naming each one whom Love had torn from life.
After I had listened to my Teacher naming those ancient ladies and knights, pity overwhelmed me and I felt lost.
I began: "Poet, I would gladly speak to those two who move together and seem so light upon the wind."
He replied: "Watch for when they drift near us, then call to them by the love that carries them — and they will come."
As soon as the wind bent them toward us, I raised my voice: "O weary souls! Come speak to us, if no one forbids it."
Like doves called by desire, gliding with open, steady wings through the air to their sweet nest, carried by their longing,
So they came from the group where Dido dwells, moving toward us through the poisonous air — so powerful was my compassionate call.
"O gracious living creature, kind and good, who comes through this dark air to visit us, who stained the world red with blood,
If the King of the Universe were our friend, we would pray to Him for your peace, since you take pity on our twisted suffering.
Whatever you wish to hear or say, we will listen and speak with you, while the wind is still, as it is now.
The city where I was born sits on the coast where the Po descends to find its final peace with all its tributaries.
Love, which takes hold so swiftly of a noble heart, seized this man for the beautiful body that was torn from me — and the manner of it still wounds me.
Love, which demands that every beloved return that love, seized me so fiercely with desire for him that, as you see, it has not left me even here.
Love led us both to one death. Caina awaits the one who took our lives." These words drifted from them to us.
When I heard those tormented souls, I bowed my head and held it down so long that the Poet finally said: "What are you thinking?"
When I answered, I began: "Alas! How many sweet thoughts, how much longing, led them to this devastating moment!"
Then I turned to them and spoke: "Francesca, your suffering makes me weep with sadness and compassion.
But tell me: in the time of those sweet sighs, how and by what sign did Love allow you to recognize your hidden desires?"
She said to me: "There is no greater sorrow than to remember happiness in a time of misery — and your Teacher knows this well.
But if you so deeply wish to know the first root of our love, I will do as one who weeps and speaks at the same time.
One day, for pleasure, we were reading about Lancelot and how love seized him. We were alone, and unsuspecting.
Again and again that reading made our eyes meet and drained the color from our faces. But it was one single moment that undid us.
When we read of how that longed-for smile was kissed by so noble a lover, this man, who will never be parted from me,
Kissed me on the mouth, trembling all over. The book was our Gallehaut, and so was its author. That day, we read no further."
While one spirit spoke, the other wept so bitterly that pity overwhelmed me like death itself,
And I fell, as a dead body falls.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto VI
paragraphs: When I regained consciousness — which had shut down before the pity I felt for those two lovers, overwhelming me with grief —
I saw new torments and new tormented souls all around me, wherever I moved, wherever I turned my gaze.
I was in the third circle, the circle of rain — eternal, accursed, cold, and heavy — its nature and its force never changing.
Enormous hailstones, foul dark water, and snow poured down through the murky air. The ground that received this deluge reeked.
Cerberus, that monstrous, hideous beast, barked from three throats like a rabid dog over the souls submerged in the muck.
His eyes were red, his beard greasy and black, his belly swollen, and his hands armed with claws. He ripped the spirits apart, flayed them, and tore them to pieces.
The rain made them howl like dogs. They tried to shield one side of their bodies with the other, constantly writhing — those wretched sinners.
When Cerberus, that great worm, spotted us, he opened his three mouths wide and bared his fangs, every limb of his body quivering.
My Guide spread his hands wide, scooped up fistfuls of earth, and hurled them into those ravenous gullets.
Like a dog that barks and craves food, then falls quiet the moment it has something to chew, absorbed entirely in devouring it,
So too fell silent those filth-encrusted muzzles of the demon Cerberus, who thundered so terribly over the souls that they wished they were deaf.
We walked across the shades, pressed down by the heavy rain, placing our feet upon their empty, ghostly forms.
They all lay flat on the ground, except for one who sat upright the moment he saw us passing before him.
"O you who are being led through this Hell," he said to me, "recognize me if you can. You were made before I was unmade."
I replied: "The anguish that distorts you may have erased you from my memory. I don't think I have ever seen you.
But tell me who you are, placed in such a miserable spot and such foul punishment — for if others are worse, none is more revolting."
He said: "Your city, so gorged with envy that the sack is already overflowing, held me within it during the bright life above.
Your citizens used to call me Ciacco. For the ruinous sin of gluttony, I am battered by this rain, as you can see.
And I, wretched soul, am not alone — all these others suffer the same penalty for the same sin." And he said no more.
I answered him: "Ciacco, your wretchedness weighs on me so heavily it makes me want to weep. But tell me, if you know — what will become
Of the citizens of our divided city? Is anyone there just? And tell me why such discord has torn it apart."
He replied: "After long strife, they will come to bloodshed, and the rural faction will drive the other out with great brutality.
Then within three years that faction must fall, and the other will rise again through the power of one who now plays both sides.
It will hold its head high for a long time, keeping the other under heavy burdens, no matter how much they weep and rage.
Two men are just, but no one listens to them. Envy, Arrogance, and Avarice — these are the three sparks that have set every heart on fire."
Here he ended his tearful speech. I said to him: "I wish you to teach me more. Grant me the gift of further words.
Farinata and Tegghiaio, who were once so worthy, Jacopo Rusticucci, Arrigo, and Mosca, and the others who set their minds on doing good —
Tell me where they are and let me know their fate, for a great desire compels me to learn whether Heaven sweetens them or Hell poisons them."
He answered: "They are among the blacker souls, dragged down by different sins to deeper levels. If you descend far enough, you will see them.
But when you return to the sweet world above, I beg you — bring me to the memory of others. I will say no more, and answer no more."
Then his steady eyes turned aside. He looked at me briefly, then bowed his head and fell face down like the other blind souls.
My Guide said to me: "He will not wake again until the angel's trumpet sounds, when the hostile Judge arrives.
Each soul will find its grim tomb again, take back its flesh and form, and hear the sentence that echoes through eternity."
So we passed onward over the foul mixture of shades and rain, stepping slowly, touching briefly on the subject of the afterlife.
I asked: "Master, will these torments increase after the great judgment, or grow less, or remain as fierce as they are now?"
He replied: "Return to your philosophy, which teaches that the more perfect a thing is, the more it feels both pleasure and pain.
Although these accursed people can never attain true perfection, they expect to be more complete after the judgment than they are now."
We followed the curving road around the circle, speaking of much more than I will repeat, until we reached the point of descent.
There we found Plutus, the great enemy.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto VII
paragraphs: "Pape Satan, pape Satan, aleppe!" Plutus clucked in his garbled voice. And the gentle Sage, who understood all things,
Said, to encourage me: "Don't let your fear harm you. Whatever power he has, he cannot stop us from descending this cliff."
Then he turned to that bloated creature and said: "Silence, accursed wolf! Consume yourself with your own rage.
This journey to the abyss is not without cause. It is willed on high, where Michael took vengeance on the proud rebellion."
Like sails swollen with wind that collapse and tangle when the mast snaps, so that cruel monster crumpled to the ground.
We descended into the fourth chasm, pushing further along the grief-stricken shore that holds all the sorrow of the universe.
Justice of God! Who piles up so many strange new torments as I witnessed there? And why does our sin waste us so?
As the waves crash and break above Charybdis, colliding with those that rush to meet them, so here the souls must dance their endless round.
Here I saw more people than anywhere else, on both sides, howling as they shoved enormous weights forward with their chests.
They crashed into each other, and at that point each turned around, rolling their burden backward, shouting, "Why do you hoard?" and "Why do you waste?"
Then they rolled back along the gloomy circle to the opposite point, screaming their shameful refrain all the while.
When each arrived there, he wheeled through his half-circle to clash again. And I, my heart pierced by what I saw,
Exclaimed: "Master, tell me — who are these people? And were all those with shaved heads on the left side of us clergymen?"
He replied: "Every one of them was so skewed in judgment during their first life that they could not spend with any measure.
Their voices bark it out clearly enough whenever they reach the two collision points where opposite faults divide them.
Those with tonsured heads were clerics — popes and cardinals — in whom Avarice ran to its worst excess."
I said: "Master, among such a crowd I should surely recognize a few who were infected with these vices."
He replied: "That is a vain thought. The same undiscerning life that made them sordid now makes them impossible to tell apart.
Forever they will charge at each other from opposite sides. On Judgment Day, some will rise from the grave with fists clenched tight, and others with their hair shorn off.
Hoarding and squandering stole the beautiful world from them and placed them in this brawl. I will not waste fine words describing it.
Now, my son, you can see for yourself the brief farce of the goods entrusted to Fortune, for which the human race tears itself apart.
For all the gold that lies beneath the moon, or ever has, could not give a single one of these weary souls a moment's rest."
"Master," I said, "tell me more. What is this Fortune you speak of, that holds the world's wealth so tightly in her grip?"
He replied: "O foolish creatures, what ignorance afflicts you! Listen, and learn my judgment of her.
The One whose knowledge surpasses all things created the heavens and assigned guides to govern them, so that every region shines equally,
With light distributed in perfect balance. In the same way, He ordained a general minister and guide for worldly splendors,
So that she might, from time to time, shift hollow riches from one people to another, from one bloodline to another, beyond all human resistance.
That is why one nation rises while another falls, following her judgment, which is hidden like a serpent in the grass.
Your understanding cannot counter her. She provides, judges, and pursues her governance, just as the other heavenly powers pursue theirs.
Her changes never pause. Necessity drives her swiftly, so that people's turns come thick and fast.
This is the one so often crucified even by those who should praise her — blaming her wrongly, giving her a bad name.
But she is blessed and does not hear them. Among the other primal creatures, she turns her sphere in joy and happiness.
Now let us descend to greater suffering. Every star that was rising when I set out is now sinking, and we must not linger."
We crossed the circle to the far bank, near a spring that boiled and poured its waters down a channel running from it.
The water was far darker than any purple dye. We followed the murky waves downward along an ugly path.
This grim brook flows down to the base of the malignant gray shores, where it forms a marsh called the Styx.
I stood staring intently and saw people plastered in mud in that swamp, all naked, all with furious expressions.
They struck each other not just with their hands but with their heads, their chests, their feet, tearing each other apart with their teeth.
My good Master said: "Son, you now behold the souls of those who were conquered by anger. And I want you to know for certain
That beneath the water there are others who sigh, making the surface bubble everywhere you look.
Stuck in the mud they say: 'We were sullen in the sweet air that is gladdened by the sun, carrying within us a smoldering gloom.
Now we are sullen in this black mire.' They gurgle this hymn in their throats, for they cannot form the words clearly."
So we circled around the filthy marsh in a wide arc between the dry bank and the swamp, our eyes on those who gorged themselves on mud,
Until we came at last to the foot of a tower.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto VIII
paragraphs: Continuing my account: long before we reached the foot of that high tower, our eyes were drawn upward to its summit,
Because two small flames had been placed there, and from far away another flame answered them — so distant the eye could barely reach it.
Turning to the sea of all wisdom, I asked: "What do those signals mean? What does the other fire answer? And who made them?"
He said to me: "Across those turbid waves you can already make out what is expected, unless the swamp's fumes hide it from you."
No bowstring ever launched an arrow that cut through the air as swiftly as the little boat I saw racing toward us across the water,
Guided by a single helmsman who shouted: "Now I have you, wicked soul!"
"Phlegyas, Phlegyas, you cry out in vain this time," said my Lord. "You will have us only for the time it takes to cross this slough."
Like a man who hears of some great wrong done to him and seethes with resentment — that is how Phlegyas looked, swelling with contained rage.
My Guide stepped down into the boat, then had me board after him. Only when I climbed in did it seem to bear any weight.
Once my Guide and I were aboard, the ancient prow moved forward, cutting deeper through the water than it did with other passengers.
While we were crossing that dead canal, a mud-caked figure rose before me and demanded: "Who are you, coming before your time?"
I answered: "I come, but I am not staying. But who are you, so covered in filth?" He replied: "You can see I am one who weeps."
I said to him: "Then stay here and weep and wail, you cursed spirit. I know you, even under all that grime."
He reached both hands toward the boat, but my alert Master shoved him back, saying: "Away with you — go join the other dogs!"
Then Virgil embraced my neck, kissed my face, and said: "Proud soul! Blessed is the woman who carried you in her womb.
That one was an arrogant man in the world above. Nothing good adorns his memory, and so his shade is furious here too.
How many who think themselves great kings up there will wallow like pigs in this mud, leaving behind them nothing but horrible contempt!"
I said: "Master, I would be very pleased to see him plunged deep into this filth before we leave this lake."
He replied: "Before the far shore comes into view, you will be satisfied. It is only right that you should enjoy such a wish."
Shortly after, I saw the other muddy souls tear into him so savagely that I still praise and thank God for the sight.
They all screamed: "Get Filippo Argenti!" And that enraged Florentine spirit turned on himself, biting his own flesh with his teeth.
We left him there, and I will say no more of him. But a sound of wailing struck my ears, and I strained my eyes forward.
The good Master said: "Now, my son, the city called Dis draws near, with its grave citizens and its great throng."
I said: "Master, I can already clearly make out its towers in the valley below, glowing red as if they were emerging from fire."
He replied: "The eternal fire that burns inside them makes them glow red, as you can see in this lower Hell."
Then we arrived within the deep moats that encircle that desolate city. Its walls appeared to me to be made of iron.
After making a wide circuit, we reached a place where the pilot shouted: "Get out! Here is the entrance."
At the gates I saw more than a thousand of the angels cast down from Heaven, who cried angrily: "Who is this that, without death,
Walks through the kingdom of the dead?" My wise Master made a gesture, signaling that he wished to speak with them privately.
They restrained their scorn a little and said: "You come alone. Let the other one go — the one who so boldly entered these domains.
Let him find his way back alone on his mad road — try, if he can. For you will stay here, having escorted him through these dark regions."
Imagine, reader, how shaken I was at those accursed words. I believed I would never return.
"O my dear Guide, who has brought me to safety more than seven times and pulled me from terrible danger,
Do not abandon me," I begged, "so helpless. If we cannot go forward, let us at least retrace our steps together."
The Lord who had led me this far said: "Do not be afraid. No one can take our passage from us — it has been granted by such authority.
But wait for me here. Feed your weary spirit with better hope, for I will not leave you in this netherworld."
And so my sweet Father walked on, leaving me there. I stood in doubt, as Yes and No battled inside my head.
I could not hear what he proposed to them, but he was not with them long before they all rushed back inside, competing with each other.
Our adversaries slammed the gates shut, right in my Master's face. He stood outside, then turned and walked slowly back to me,
His eyes downcast, his brow stripped of all boldness. He sighed and said: "Who has denied me the houses of sorrow?"
Then he said to me: "Do not be alarmed by my anger, for I will win this contest, no matter what defense they mount inside.
This insolence of theirs is nothing new. They showed it once before, at a less secret gate, which still stands open, without a lock.
Above it you saw the inscription of death. And already, on this side of it, descending the steep slope,
Passing through the circles without an escort, one is coming whose power will open this city to us."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto IX
paragraphs: The color that cowardice had painted on my face when I saw my Guide turned back made him quickly hide his own new pallor.
He stopped, listening intently, like a man straining to hear, for his eyes could not carry far through that black air and heavy fog.
"Still, we must win this fight," he began, "otherwise... But such help was offered to us. How long it seems before anyone arrives!"
I saw clearly how he had covered his opening words with what followed, words that were different from the first. But his speech still frightened me,
Because I drew a worse meaning from his broken sentence than perhaps he intended.
"Does anyone from the first circle, where the only punishment is severed hope, ever descend this deep into the pit?"
I asked this question. He answered: "It seldom happens that any of us makes this journey.
It is true that once before I was summoned down here, conjured by that cruel sorceress Erichtho, who called shades back into their bodies.
My flesh had been stripped from me only briefly when she made me enter within that wall, to draw out a spirit from the circle of Judas.
That is the deepest place, the darkest, and the farthest from the heaven that turns all things. I know the way well — so set your mind at ease.
This marsh, breathing its enormous stench, encircles the grieving city on every side, and now we cannot enter without wrath."
He said more, but I cannot recall it, because my eyes had been seized entirely by the sight atop the glowing tower,
Where, in an instant, three blood-stained Furies had risen up — they had the forms and bearing of women,
Girded with the greenest of water-serpents. Instead of hair, small vipers and horned snakes wreathed their savage temples.
He who well knew the handmaids of the queen of endless weeping said to me: "Look — the fierce Erinyes.
That is Megaera on the left. The one weeping on the right is Alecto. Tisiphone is in the middle." And with that, he fell silent.
Each one was clawing at her own breast with her nails. They struck themselves with their palms and shrieked so loudly that I pressed close to the Poet in terror.
"Let Medusa come! We will turn him to stone!" they screamed together, looking down. "We should have punished Theseus when he came."
"Turn around and keep your eyes shut! If the Gorgon shows herself and you see her, there will be no returning to the world above."
So said my Master, and he himself turned me around, not trusting my hands alone — he covered my eyes with his own.
O you who have sound understanding, look beneath the veil of these strange verses and see the hidden doctrine!
And now, across the turbid waves, there came a crash of sound, terrible and full of dread, that made both shores tremble.
It sounded like a wind, made violent by opposing waves of heat, that strikes a forest and without restraint snaps and tears branches down,
Sweeps them away in a cloud of dust, drives forward in its pride, and sends beasts and shepherds fleeing before it.
He uncovered my eyes and said: "Now aim your gaze across that ancient scum, there where the fumes are thickest."
As frogs scatter before a hostile snake, diving through the water until each one squats on the bottom,
So I saw more than a thousand ruined souls fleeing before one who crossed the Styx with dry feet.
He waved the thick air from before his face with his left hand, and that seemed to be the only effort that wearied him.
I knew at once that he was sent from Heaven, and I turned to my Master, who signaled me to be still and bow before him.
How full of scorn he looked! He reached the gate and opened it with a small wand — there was no resistance.
"O outcasts of Heaven, despised race," he began, standing on that dreadful threshold, "why does this insolence still lodge in you?
Why do you kick against that Will which can never be thwarted, and which has more than once added to your suffering?
What good does it do to butt against fate? Your Cerberus, if you remember, still bears the scars on his chin and throat for trying."
Then he turned back along the filthy road without a word to us, looking like a man consumed by other cares
Than by whatever stands before him. And we moved our feet toward the city, made confident by his holy words.
We entered without any resistance, and I, eager to learn what punishments such a fortress held,
Looked all around as soon as I was inside. I saw a vast plain on every side, full of anguish and cruel torment.
Just as at Arles, where the Rhone spreads into marshland, or at Pola, near the Gulf of Quarnero which closes Italy and bathes its borders,
The ground is made uneven everywhere by tombs — so it was here on every side, except far worse.
For among these tombs, flames were scattered everywhere, heating them until they glowed white-hot — hotter than any craft requires of iron.
All the tomb lids were raised open, and from within came such bitter wailing that the sound could only belong to souls in true torment.
I asked: "Master, who are these people buried in the burning chests, making themselves known by their agonized groans?"
He replied: "Here lie the heresiarchs, with their followers, of every sect. The tombs are far more crowded than you might think.
Like is buried with like, and the sepulchers burn with more or less heat." Then, turning to the right, we passed onward
Between the torments and the high parapets.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto X
paragraphs: Now we walked along a narrow path between the torments and the city wall, my Master ahead and I following at his back.
"O supreme power who leads me through these impious circles as you see fit," I began, "speak to me and satisfy my longing.
The people lying in these tombs — can they be seen? All the lids are raised, and no one seems to stand guard."
He said to me: "They will all be sealed shut when the souls return from Jehoshaphat with the bodies they left behind above.
On this side lies the cemetery of Epicurus and all his followers — those who held that the soul dies with the body.
But the question you have asked will soon be answered here inside, along with that other wish you are keeping silent."
I said: "Good Guide, I only keep my thoughts hidden to speak less. You yourself have encouraged this in me before."
"O Tuscan, you who walk through the city of fire still alive, speaking so modestly — be pleased to stop here a moment.
Your way of speaking reveals you as a native of that noble city to which I was, perhaps, too harmful."
This voice erupted suddenly from one of the tombs, and I pressed closer to my Guide in fear.
He said to me: "Turn around. What are you doing? Look — Farinata has risen. You can see him from the waist up."
I had already fixed my eyes on his. He rose upright, chest and head held high, as though he held Hell itself in utter contempt.
My Guide pushed me toward him boldly, threading between the tombs, and said: "Choose your words carefully."
As soon as I stood at the foot of his tomb, he studied me with a look of disdain and asked: "Who were your ancestors?"
I, wanting to obey, held nothing back and told him everything. At this he raised his eyebrows slightly.
He said: "They were fiercely opposed to me, to my forefathers, and to my party — so much so that twice I scattered them."
"If they were driven out, they came back both times from every side," I answered. "But yours have not mastered that art so well."
Then another shade rose into view beside him, visible from the chin up. I think he had risen to his knees.
He looked around me, as if hoping to see someone else with me. When his expectation was spent,
He said, weeping: "If you walk through this blind prison by the height of your genius, where is my son? Why is he not with you?"
I replied: "I do not come here on my own. The one waiting over there leads me through — the one your Guido, perhaps, held in disdain."
His words and the nature of his punishment had already told me his name, which is why my answer was so direct.
He sprang up suddenly and cried: "What did you say — 'held'? Is he no longer alive? Does the sweet light no longer strike his eyes?"
When he noticed my brief hesitation before answering, he fell back and did not appear again.
But the other one — the great-spirited one at whose request I had stopped — did not change his expression, did not turn his neck, did not shift his body.
"And if," he continued his earlier train of thought, "my people have not learned that art of return, that torments me more than this bed.
But the face of the Lady who rules here will not be rekindled fifty times before you yourself will learn how heavy that art is.
And as you hope to return to the sweet world above, tell me — why is that people so merciless against my family in every one of its laws?"
I answered: "The slaughter and the great carnage that stained the Arbia red — that is what causes such prayers to be made in our city's churches."
He shook his head with a sigh and said: "I was not alone in that, and certainly I would not have acted without cause.
But I was alone — the only one — when everyone else agreed to destroy Florence. I was the one who defended her openly."
"May your descendants find peace," I begged him. "Untangle for me the knot that has entangled my thinking here.
It seems, if I hear correctly, that you can see what the future brings, but have a different relationship to the present."
"We see like people with bad eyesight," he said. "We can make out things that are far off — the Sovereign Ruler still grants us that much light.
But when events draw close, or are happening now, our minds go completely blank. Unless someone brings us news, we know nothing of your human world.
So you can understand that all our knowledge will die entirely the moment the door of the future is shut forever."
Then, as if stung by guilt, I said: "Please tell that fallen one that his son is still among the living.
And if I was silent when he asked, tell him it was because I was already puzzling over the difficulty you have just resolved for me."
My Master was already calling me back. So I hurried to ask the spirit to tell me who else lay with him.
He said: "I lie here with more than a thousand. The second Frederick is within, and the Cardinal too. Of the rest, I will not speak."
With that he hid himself. I turned back toward the ancient Poet, reflecting on those words that seemed so hostile to me.
He walked on, and as we went, he asked: "Why are you so bewildered?" I answered his question fully.
"Keep in your memory what you have heard against yourself," that Sage commanded me, "and now pay attention." He raised his finger.
"When you stand before the sweet radiance of the one whose beautiful eyes see all things, from her you will learn the journey of your life."
Then he turned his steps to the left. We left the wall and headed toward the center along a path that led to a valley
Whose stench was nauseating even from above.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XI
paragraphs: On the rim of a high bank made jagged by a circle of great broken rocks, we came upon an even more savage crowd.
There, because of the horrible, overwhelming stench thrown up by the deep abyss, we drew back behind the shelter
Of a great tomb, on which I saw an inscription reading: "I hold Pope Anastasius, whom Photinus led from the true path."
"We should slow our descent so that our senses can adjust to this foul air. After that, we will not even notice it."
So said the Master. I replied: "Find some way to use the time, so it does not pass in idleness." He said: "That is exactly what I intend.
My son," he then began, "within these rocks are three smaller circles, descending by degrees, like the ones you are leaving.
All are filled with cursed spirits. But so that the sight alone will be enough for you later, hear now how and why they are imprisoned.
The aim of every malice that earns the hatred of Heaven is to cause injury, and every such aim afflicts others through either force or fraud.
But because fraud is a sin unique to humans, it offends God more. Therefore the fraudulent are placed lowest, and greater suffering assails them.
The entire first of the three circles holds the violent. But since violence can be directed against three targets, it is divided into three rings.
Against God, against oneself, and against one's neighbor — violence can be done to any of these, as you will hear with clear reasoning.
Violent death and painful wounds are inflicted on our neighbors, and their possessions suffer ruin, arson, and extortion.
Therefore murderers and all who strike unjustly, plunderers and robbers — the first ring torments them all in separate groups.
A man may lay violent hands on himself and on his own goods. Therefore in the second ring, those must repent in vain
Who rob themselves of your world, who gamble away and waste their wealth, and weep where they should have found joy.
Violence can also be committed against God — by denying and blaspheming Him in one's heart, and by scorning Nature and her gifts.
For this reason the smallest ring brands with its seal both Sodom and Cahors, and those who speak against God from the depths of their hearts.
Fraud, which gnaws at every conscience, can be practiced against those who trust and against those who place no special confidence.
This latter kind seems to break only the general bond of love that Nature creates. Therefore within the second circle nest
Hypocrites, flatterers, sorcerers, forgers, thieves, simonists, panders, corrupt officials, and similar filth.
The other kind forgets not only that general love, but also the special trust that was added to it, creating a deeper bond of loyalty.
Therefore in the smallest circle, at the very center of the universe where Dis sits enthroned, whoever betrays is consumed forever."
I said: "Master, your explanation proceeds with perfect clarity. It draws sharp distinctions between this cavern and the people who fill it.
But tell me — the ones in the fetid marsh, the ones driven by wind, the ones beaten by rain, and those who clash with such bitter tongues —
Why are they not punished inside the red city, if God holds them in His wrath? And if He does not, why do they suffer as they do?"
He replied: "Why does your mind wander so far from its usual sharpness? Or where else is your attention looking?
Have you forgotten the words with which your Ethics discusses the three dispositions that Heaven will not tolerate:
Incontinence, Malice, and insane Bestiality? And how Incontinence offends God less and draws less blame?
If you think carefully on this conclusion, and recall who those souls are up above, suffering their penalties outside,
You will clearly see why they are kept separate from these criminals, and why divine Justice strikes them with a lighter hammer."
"O Sun who heals all clouded vision, you satisfy me so completely when you explain that even doubt itself becomes a pleasure!
But go back a little," I said, "to where you said that usury offends divine Goodness, and untangle that knot for me."
"Philosophy," he said, "teaches those who study it — and not in one place only — how Nature takes her course
From the divine Intellect and its art. And if you note your Physics carefully, you will find after only a few pages
That human art follows Nature as far as it can, as a student follows a master. So your art is, in a sense, God's grandchild.
From these two — Nature and human art — if you recall how Genesis begins, humanity must earn its living and advance.
The usurer takes a different path. He scorns both Nature herself and Nature's follower, human labor, placing his hope elsewhere.
But follow me now, for I am ready to move on. The Fishes are trembling on the horizon, and the Great Bear lies entirely over the northwest,
And the cliff we must descend lies far ahead."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XII
paragraphs: The place where we came to descend the bank was alpine, and what else was there made it a sight that every eye would turn from.
Like the landslide that struck the flank of the Adige this side of Trent — whether caused by earthquake or by crumbling supports —
Where from the mountaintop to the plain below, the cliff is so shattered that it offers some kind of path to anyone above,
Such was the descent of that ravine. And stretched along the edge of the broken chasm lay the shame of Crete —
The one conceived inside the fake cow. When it saw us, it bit itself, like a creature consumed by its own inner fury.
My Sage shouted at it: "Perhaps you think the Duke of Athens is here — the one who dealt you death in the world above?
Get away, beast! This man does not come instructed by your sister. He comes to witness your punishments."
Like a bull that breaks free at the instant of the killing blow and cannot walk, only staggers this way and that,
So the Minotaur thrashed about. My alert Guide cried: "Run to the passage! While he is in a fury, now is the time to descend."
We picked our way down over that rubble of stones, which often shifted under my feet from the unfamiliar weight.
I walked deep in thought. He said: "You are thinking about this rockslide, guarded by that bestial rage I just quenched.
I want you to know that the last time I descended to lower Hell, this cliff had not yet collapsed.
But shortly before His coming — the One who carried off the great spoil from Dis, from the highest circle —
The deep, loathsome valley trembled on all sides so violently that I thought the universe was thrilled with love, by which, some believe,
The world has been several times reduced to chaos. At that moment, this ancient rock broke apart, both here and elsewhere.
But look below, for the river of blood is near — the one in which all those who injured others through violence are boiling."
O blind greed! O insane rage! You spur us so fiercely in our short lives, and then steep us so horribly in the eternal one!
I saw a wide moat curving like a bow, encompassing the entire plain, just as my Guide had described.
Between the moat and the foot of the embankment, centaurs were running in single file, armed with arrows, as they once hunted in the world above.
Seeing us descend, each one stopped. Three separated from the group, advancing with bows and arrows already drawn.
One called from afar: "What torment do you come for, you who descend the hillside? Tell us from there, or I draw the bow."
My Master replied: "We will give our answer to Chiron, close beside you. As usual, that hasty temper of yours serves you badly."
Then he nudged me and said: "That one is Nessus, who died for the beautiful Deianira and took vengeance for his own death.
The one in the middle, gazing down at his own chest, is the great Chiron, who raised Achilles. The other is Pholus, who was so full of wrath.
Thousands upon thousands patrol the moat, shooting arrows at any soul that rises out of the blood higher than its sin permits."
We drew near those swift monsters. Chiron took an arrow and used the notch to push his beard back from his jaw.
When he had uncovered his great mouth, he said to his companions: "Have you noticed that the one behind moves whatever he touches?
The feet of the dead do not do that." And my good Guide, who now stood at Chiron's chest, where the two natures are joined,
Replied: "He is indeed alive, and I alone must show him the dark valley. Necessity drives us, not pleasure.
A soul withdrew from singing Hallelujah to give me this task. He is no thief, and I am no criminal spirit.
But by the power through which I walk this savage road, give us one of your company to travel with us,
To show us where the ford can be crossed, and to carry this one on his back — for he is no spirit who can walk on air."
Chiron turned on his right flank and said to Nessus: "Turn around and guide them. If another band crosses your path, warn them off."
We moved forward with our faithful escort along the rim of the boiling red river, from which the scalded souls shrieked their agony.
I saw people plunged up to their eyebrows. The great Centaur said: "These are tyrants who dealt in bloodshed and plunder.
Here they weep for their merciless crimes. Here is Alexander, and fierce Dionysius, who brought years of misery to Sicily.
That head with the jet-black hair is Azzolino. The blond one is Obizzo d'Este, who was, in truth,
Murdered by his stepson in the world above." I turned to the Poet, and he said: "Let Nessus be your first guide now, and I will be second."
A little farther on, the Centaur stopped beside souls who emerged from the boiling stream as far as their throats.
He pointed out a shade, alone on one side: "That one split open, in God's very bosom, the heart that is still honored on the Thames."
Then I saw people who lifted their heads and their entire chests above the river, and I recognized many of them.
The blood grew shallower and shallower, until it covered only the feet, and there we found a place to cross the moat.
"Just as you see the boiling stream getting shallower on this side," the Centaur said, "I want you to know
That on the other side its bed sinks deeper and deeper, until it rejoins the place where tyranny must groan.
There, divine Justice goads Attila, who was a scourge upon the earth, and Pyrrhus, and Sextus. And forever it milks
The tears, unlocked by the boiling blood, of Rinier da Corneto and Rinier Pazzo, who waged such war upon the roads."
Then he turned back and crossed the ford again.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XIII
paragraphs: Nessus had not yet reached the other side when we entered a wood that was unmarked by any path.
The foliage was not green but dark. The branches were not smooth but gnarled and tangled. There were no fruit trees — only thorns dripping with poison.
Not even the wild beasts that shun the cultivated land between Cecina and Corneto inhabit thickets so dense and tangled.
There the hideous Harpies built their nests — the creatures that drove the Trojans from the Strophades with dire warnings of disaster to come.
They had broad wings, human necks and faces, clawed feet, and great feathered bellies. They sat in the strange trees, wailing.
My good Master began: "Before you go further, know that you are in the second ring, and will be until
You come out upon the horrible sand. So look carefully, and you will see things that would make my words hard to believe."
I heard wailing on every side but could see no one who might be making those sounds. Completely bewildered, I stopped.
I think he thought I might be thinking that all those voices came from people hiding among the trunks.
So the Master said: "If you break off a small twig from any of these trees, your assumptions will be shattered."
I reached out and snapped a branchlet from a large thorn — and the trunk cried: "Why are you tearing me?"
As dark blood oozed from the break, it cried again: "Why do you rip me apart? Have you no pity at all?
We were men once, and now we are changed into trees. Your hand should show more mercy, even if we had been the souls of serpents."
Like a green log burning at one end, which drips and hisses with escaping steam from the other,
So from that broken splinter both words and blood flowed together. I dropped the twig and stood frozen, like a man struck with terror.
"If he had been able to believe beforehand," my Sage replied, "O wounded soul, what he had only read in my verses,
He would never have raised his hand against you. But the incredible nature of the thing forced me to urge him to an act that grieves me.
Tell him who you were, so that by way of amends he may refresh your fame in the world above, to which he can return."
The trunk replied: "Your sweet words draw me out. I cannot stay silent — and do not be annoyed that I am tempted to speak at length.
I am the one who held both keys to Frederick's heart, and I turned them so softly in locking and unlocking
That I kept almost everyone from his secrets. I was so faithful to that glorious office that I lost my sleep and my health.
The harlot who never turned her wanton eyes from Caesar's court — that common death, that vice of all courts —
Inflamed every other mind against me. And they, once inflamed, so inflamed Augustus that my joyful honors turned to bitter grief.
My spirit, in disdainful exultation, thinking to escape disdain through death, made me unjust against my just self.
By the strange roots of this wood, I swear to you that I never broke faith with my lord, who was so worthy of honor.
If either of you returns to the world, comfort my memory, which still lies crushed beneath the blow that Envy dealt it."
The Poet waited a moment, then said: "Since he is silent, do not waste the time. Speak to him, and ask whatever you wish."
I said to him: "You ask him whatever you think will satisfy me. I cannot — such pity fills my heart."
So he began again: "May this man do freely for you what your words implore, imprisoned spirit. Please,
Tell us how the soul becomes bound in these knots. And tell us, if you can, whether any soul is ever freed from such limbs."
Then the trunk blew out a great breath, and the wind transformed itself into a voice: "I will answer you briefly.
When the enraged soul abandons the body from which it has torn itself away, Minos sends it down to the seventh pit.
It falls into the forest, and no spot is chosen for it. Wherever Fortune flings it, there it sprouts like a grain of wheat.
It grows into a sapling, then a forest tree. The Harpies, feeding on its leaves, create pain and an outlet for that pain.
Like the other dead, we will come to reclaim our bodies. But we will not put them on again — it is not just to have what one has thrown away.
Here we will drag them, and through this mournful forest our bodies will hang — each one on the thorn of the shade that tormented it."
We were still listening to the trunk, thinking it might say more, when a tumult overtook us,
Like a hunter at his post who hears the boar and the chase crashing toward him through the beasts and branches.
And there, on our left, came two naked, scratched figures, running so wildly that they shattered every branch in their path.
The one in front screamed: "Come quick, Death, come quick!" The other, who seemed to be falling behind, shouted: "Lano, your legs weren't this fast
At the jousts of the Toppo!" And then, perhaps because his breath was failing, he threw himself into a bush.
Behind them the forest was full of black mastiffs, ravenous and swift as greyhounds slipping from their chains.
They sank their teeth into the one who had crouched down, tore him apart piece by piece, and carried off those aching limbs.
My escort then took me by the hand and led me to the bush, which was weeping in vain through its bloody wounds.
"O Jacopo da Sant'Andrea," it said, "what good did it do you to make a shield of me? What blame do I bear for your wicked life?"
When my Master had stopped beside it, he said: "Who were you, who through so many wounds blows out your sorrowful speech with blood?"
It answered us: "O souls who have come to witness the shameful destruction that has stripped my leaves from me,
Gather them up beneath this wretched bush. I was from the city that changed its patron saint to the Baptist — and for this its first patron
Will forever torment it with his art. And were it not that some trace of him still remains on the bridge over the Arno,
Those citizens who rebuilt the city on the ashes left by Attila would have labored in vain.
I made a gallows of my own house."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XIV
paragraphs: Because love of my native city compelled me, I gathered the scattered leaves and gave them back to the one whose voice was already growing hoarse.
Then we came to the boundary where the second ring meets the third, and where a terrible form of Justice is revealed.
To make these strange new sights clear, I should say that we arrived at a plain that rejects every plant from its bed.
The sorrowful forest rings it like a garland, just as the sad moat rings the forest. There, right at the edge, we halted.
The ground was thick, dry sand — no different from the sand once pressed beneath the feet of Cato.
O vengeance of God, how greatly you should be feared by everyone who reads what was revealed before my eyes!
I saw many herds of naked souls, all weeping miserably, and each group seemed subject to a different law.
Some lay flat on their backs. Others sat hunched together. Still others wandered ceaselessly.
Those who walked about were far more numerous. Those who lay in torment were fewer, but their tongues were freer to cry out in pain.
Over the entire sand, great flakes of fire drifted slowly down, like snow falling in the Alps on a windless day.
Like Alexander in those scorching lands of India, who watched flames fall unbroken on his army until they reached the ground,
And had his soldiers trample the soil, because the embers were easier to extinguish one by one,
So the eternal heat descended here, igniting the sand like tinder under flint, doubling the torment.
Without rest, the dance of wretched hands never stopped — here, there, everywhere — brushing away the fresh-fallen sparks.
"Master," I began, "you who overcome everything except the stubborn demons who blocked us at the gate,
Who is that great figure who seems to ignore the fire, lying there scowling and contemptuous, as if the rain does not ripen him at all?"
The figure himself, realizing I was asking my Guide about him, shouted: "What I was alive, I am in death!
Even if Jove should exhaust his blacksmith — the one from whom he seized in anger the sharp thunderbolt that struck me on my last day —
And even if he should wear out all the others, one by one, in the dark forge of Mongibello, crying, 'Help, good Vulcan, help!'
As he did at the battle of Phlegra, and hurl his bolts at me with all his might — he would still not have his joyful vengeance."
Then my Leader spoke with a force I had never heard before: "O Capaneus, the very fact that your pride remains unquenched
Is your greatest punishment. No torment except your own rage would be agony enough for your fury."
Then he turned to me with a gentler expression: "He was one of the seven kings who besieged Thebes. He held God in contempt then, and seems to hold Him in contempt still.
But as I told him, his own defiance is the fittest ornament for his chest.
Now follow me, and be careful not to set your feet on the burning sand. Keep close to the edge of the forest."
Without speaking, we reached a place where a small stream gushes out of the woods. Its redness still makes my hair stand on end.
Like the hot brook that flows from the Bulicame and is shared among the sinful women downstream, so this rivulet wound its way across the sand.
Its bed and both its sloping banks were made of stone, as were the margins on either side, and I realized that our path lay there.
"In everything I have shown you since we entered through the gate whose threshold is denied to no one,
Nothing your eyes have discovered is as remarkable as this stream, which quenches all the flames above it."
These were my Leader's words, and I begged him to give me the knowledge my appetite now craved.
"In the middle of the sea," he said, "there lies a ruined land called Crete, whose king once ruled over a world of innocence.
A mountain stands there that was once green with water and leaves — it was called Ida. Now it is abandoned, like a thing worn out.
Rhea chose it as the safe cradle for her son, and to keep him hidden, she had her attendants raise a clamor whenever he cried.
Inside the mountain stands a great Old Man, his back turned toward Egypt, his face turned toward Rome as if gazing into a mirror.
His head is made of refined gold. His arms and chest are pure silver. Then he is brass down to the fork of his legs.
From there down, he is made of chosen iron, except that his right foot is baked clay — and he rests more weight on that foot than on the other.
Every part except the gold is cracked with a fissure that weeps with tears, and these tears, collecting together, bore through the cavern.
They drip from rock to rock into this valley, forming the Acheron, the Styx, and the Phlegethon. Then they flow down this narrow channel
To the very bottom, where there is no more descent. There they form Cocytus — and what that pool is, you will see for yourself. I will not describe it now."
I said: "If this stream originates from our world in this way, why does it appear to us only at this edge?"
He replied: "You know the place is round. And though you have traveled far, always descending to the left toward the bottom,
You have not yet completed the full circle. So if something new appears, it should not surprise you."
I asked again: "Master, where can Lethe and Phlegethon be found? You do not mention one, and say the other is formed by this rain."
"Your questions truly please me," he answered. "But the boiling of the red water should answer one of them for you.
You will see Lethe — but outside this moat, in the place where souls go to wash themselves when their repented sin has been removed."
Then he said: "Now it is time to leave the wood. Follow close behind me. The stone margins make a path that does not burn,
And above them all the fire is extinguished."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XV
paragraphs: Now one of the hard stone margins carries us forward, and the steam from the brook creates a canopy overhead that shields both the water and the banks from the fire.
Just as the Flemings, between Wissant and Bruges, fearing the flood that hurls itself toward them, build their bulwarks to hold back the sea,
And as the Paduans build theirs along the Brenta to protect their towns and villages before the snows of Carentana begin to melt,
In just that fashion these banks had been constructed — though neither as high nor as thick, whoever the master builder was.
We were already so far from the forest that I could not have seen where it was, even if I had turned back to look,
When we encountered a company of souls walking beside the bank. Each one stared at us the way people peer at each other
Under a new moon at dusk, squinting at us the way an old tailor squints at the eye of his needle.
Scrutinized by this group, I was recognized by one who seized the hem of my garment and cried out: "What a marvel!"
When he stretched his arm toward me, I fixed my eyes on his scorched face — and despite the burned features that disguised him,
My mind recognized him. Leaning down toward his face, I replied: "Are you here, Ser Brunetto?"
He said: "My son, may it not displease you if Brunetto Latini turns back a little to walk with you, letting his company go on."
I said: "I beg you with all my heart. And if you wish me to sit with you, I will, if my companion permits — for I go with him."
"O son," he said, "whoever in this herd stops for even a moment must then lie a hundred years without fanning away the fire.
So walk on, and I will follow at your side. Afterward I will rejoin my band, who go lamenting their eternal doom."
I did not dare step down from the raised path to walk level with him. But I kept my head bowed, as one who walks with reverence.
He began: "What fortune or what fate brings you down here before your final day? And who is this showing you the way?"
I answered: "Up above, in the bright life, I lost my way in a valley before my years were complete.
Just yesterday morning I turned my back on it. This one appeared as I was falling back and is leading me home by this road."
He said: "If you follow your star, you cannot fail to reach a glorious harbor — if I judged rightly in the beautiful life above.
And if I had not died so soon, seeing Heaven so generous to you, I would have given you encouragement in your work.
But that ungrateful, malicious people, descended long ago from Fiesole, who still smack of the mountain and the granite,
Will make themselves your enemy because of your good deeds. And rightly so — among bitter crab apples, it is not fitting for the sweet fig to bear fruit.
An old saying in the world calls them blind: a people avaricious, envious, and proud. Make sure you cleanse yourself of their habits.
