Your fortune holds such honor in store for you that both factions will hunger for you — but the grass will be far from the goat.
Let the beasts of Fiesole make fodder of themselves, and let them not touch the plant — if any still springs up on their dunghill —
In which the sacred seed of those Romans lives on, who stayed behind when that nest of wickedness was built."
I replied: "If my prayer were fully answered, you would not yet be banished from human nature.
For the dear, kind, fatherly image of you is fixed in my mind and touches my heart — the image of you in the world, hour after hour,
Teaching me how a man makes himself eternal. And how deeply grateful I am must be shown in my words, as long as I live.
What you say about my future I write down and keep, to be explained together with another text by a Lady who will know how, if I reach her.
This much I want you to know: as long as my conscience does not reproach me, I am ready for whatever Fortune brings.
This kind of prophecy is not new to my ears. So let Fortune turn her wheel however she pleases, and the peasant turn his hoe."
At this, my Master turned his head to the right, looked back at me, and said: "He listens well who takes note of it."
Still, I continued walking and talking with Ser Brunetto. I asked him which of his companions were the most notable and distinguished.
He replied: "It is well to know of some. Of the rest, silence is more fitting — the time is too short for so many names.
Know, in sum, that all of them were scholars and men of great literary fame, tainted in the world by the same sin.
Priscian walks among that miserable crowd, and Francesco d'Accorso. And if you had any appetite for such scurf, you could have seen
The one who was transferred by the Servant of Servants from the Arno to the Bacchiglione, where he left behind his sin-strained body.
I would say more, but my walk and my talk can go no further, for I see new dust rising over there from the sand.
A group is coming with whom I must not be. Let my Tesoro, in which I still live, be commended to you. I ask nothing more."
Then he turned and ran, and looked like one of those who race for the green cloth at Verona across the open field — and he looked like
The one who wins, not the one who loses.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XVI
paragraphs: I had reached a place where I could hear the roar of water cascading into the next circle, a sound like the humming of beehives,
When three shades broke away from a group passing beneath the rain of sharp punishment and came running toward us.
Each one cried out: "Stop! By your clothing, you seem to be someone from our corrupt city."
What wounds I saw on their bodies — both fresh and old, seared in by the flames! It pains me still just to remember it.
My Teacher listened to their cries and paused. He turned to me and said: "Wait now. To these we should be courteous.
Were it not for the fire that the nature of this place rains down, I would say that haste is more fitting for you than for them."
When we stopped, they resumed their old lament. When they reached us, the three of them formed themselves into a wheel.
Like naked, oiled wrestlers watching for their advantage and their grip before they trade blows and holds,
Each one wheeled around, keeping his face turned toward me, so that his neck and feet moved continuously in opposite directions.
One began: "If the misery of this place, and our blistered, blackened appearance, bring scorn upon us and our pleas,
Let our reputation move your mind to tell us who you are, walking so securely on living feet through Hell.
The one in whose footsteps you see me treading, naked and skinless as he is now, was of higher rank than you might think.
He was the grandson of the good Gualdrada. His name was Guido Guerra, and in life he accomplished much with both his wisdom and his sword.
The other treading the sand beside me is Tegghiaio Aldobrandi, whose fame should be welcome in the world above.
And I, placed on the cross with them, am Jacopo Rusticucci. My savage wife, more than anything, drove me to this."
If I could have been shielded from the fire, I would have thrown myself among them, and I believe my Teacher would have allowed it.
But since I would have been scorched and baked, my fear overcame the good will that made me hungry to embrace them.
I began: "Your condition planted in me not contempt but sorrow — sorrow so deep that it will take a long time to shed,
As soon as my Lord said words that made me realize people of your kind were approaching.
I am from your city. I have always rehearsed and listened to your deeds and honorable names with affection.
I leave the bitter gall behind and go toward the sweet fruit promised to me by my truthful Guide — but first I must plunge to the very center."
"May your soul long guide those limbs of yours," he replied, "and may your fame shine after you.
Tell us: do courage and courtesy still dwell in our city as they used to, or have they gone from it entirely?
For Guglielmo Borsiere, who joined our torment only recently and walks there with our companions, has been tormenting us with his words."
"New arrivals and sudden wealth have bred pride and excess in you, Florence, and already you weep for it!"
I cried this out with my face raised high. The three took it for my answer, and looked at each other the way people look when they hear the truth.
"If it costs you so little at other times to satisfy people's curiosity," they all replied, "happy are you, speaking so freely!
Therefore, if you escape these dark places and return to see the beautiful stars, when it pleases you to say 'I was there,'
Make sure you speak of us to the world." Then they broke up their wheel, and in their flight their swift legs seemed like wings.
An Amen could not have been said as fast as they vanished. And so my Master decided it was time to leave.
I followed him, and we had gone only a short way before the roar of water was so close that we could barely hear each other speak.
Like the river that holds its own course — the first from Monte Viso to flow eastward on the left slope of the Apennines,
Called Acquacheta above before it drops to its lower bed, and at Forli loses that name,
Thundering above San Benedetto dell'Alpe as it plunges in a single waterfall where a thousand could shelter,
So, plummeting from a steep bank, we found that dark water roaring so loudly it would have quickly hurt our ears.
I had a cord wrapped around my waist — the same cord with which I had once hoped to snare the leopard with the painted skin.
After I had completely unwound it, as my Guide had ordered, I handed it to him, gathered and coiled.
He turned to his right, and at a little distance from the edge, he hurled it down into that deep abyss.
"Something extraordinary must rise in answer to this new signal," I thought to myself, "which my Master follows so intently with his eye."
How careful people should be around those who can read not just their actions, but their very thoughts!
He said to me: "What I am waiting for will come up soon — and what your mind is imagining must soon reveal itself to your sight."
When it comes to a truth that wears the face of a lie, a man should seal his lips, because without any fault of his, it brings him shame.
But here I cannot stay silent. Reader, I swear to you by the verses of this Comedy — may they not lack lasting favor —
That through that thick, dark air I saw a figure swimming upward, astonishing to even the steadiest heart,
Like a diver who goes down to free an anchor snagged on a reef or some other hidden thing in the sea,
Who stretches upward and draws in his feet.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XVII
paragraphs: "Behold the monster with the pointed tail, who smashes through mountains, shatters walls and weapons. Behold the one who poisons the whole world."
So my Guide began, and beckoned the creature to come to shore, near the edge of the stone path we had walked.
That foul image of deceit swam up and brought its head and torso onto the bank, but did not drag its tail ashore.
Its face was the face of a just man, outwardly kind and gentle in appearance. But the rest of its body was entirely a serpent's.
It had two hairy paws reaching to the armpits. Its back, chest, and both flanks were painted over with knots and circles.
No Turk or Tatar ever wove cloth with more colors, more elaborate patterns — nor did Arachne ever lay such webs.
Like boats that sometimes rest on shore, half in the water and half on land, or like the beaver among the heavy-drinking Germans
That positions itself to wage its hunt, so that vile creature lay on the border of stone and sand.
Its tail quivered entirely in the void, twisting upward the venomous fork that armed its tip like a scorpion's sting.
My Guide said: "Now we must turn aside a little, toward that malevolent beast crouching over there."
We descended on the right and took ten steps along the outer edge, carefully avoiding the sand and the flames.
When we reached the creature, I noticed a group of people sitting on the sand a little farther off, near the edge of the abyss.
The Master said to me: "So that you may carry away a full experience of this round, go now and see their condition.
Keep your conversation brief. While you are gone, I will speak with this beast, so it will lend us its strong shoulders."
So I went on alone, further along the outermost rim of the seventh circle, to where the sorrowful souls sat.
Their grief was gushing from their eyes. They kept swatting with their hands — now at the flames, now at the scorching ground.
They were just like dogs in summer, snapping now with their muzzles, now with their paws, when bitten by fleas or flies or gadflies.
When I looked at the faces of some on whom the painful fire was falling, I recognized none. But I noticed
That from each one's neck hung a pouch of a particular color and design — and their eyes seemed to feast on these.
As I looked around among them, I saw on a yellow pouch an azure shape that had the face and posture of a lion.
Then, as my gaze swept on, I saw another pouch, blood-red, displaying a goose whiter than butter.
And one, whose little white pouch bore the image of a fat blue sow, said to me: "What are you doing in this ditch?
Get out of here. And since you are still alive, know that my neighbor Vitaliano will come to sit at my left side.
I am a Paduan among these Florentines. Time and again they thunder in my ears, shouting: 'Let the sovereign knight come,
The one who will bring the pouch with three goats!'" Then he twisted his mouth and stuck out his tongue, like an ox licking its nose.
Fearing that staying longer might annoy the one who had warned me to be brief, I turned back from those exhausted souls.
I found my Guide already mounted on the back of that savage animal. He said to me: "Now be strong and bold.
From now on, we descend by stairways like these. Climb on in front. I will sit in the middle, so the tail cannot reach you."
Like someone so close to a quartan fever that his nails have already turned blue, who trembles all over just looking at a shady spot,
That is what I became at his words. But the shame his warning produced in me made me brave — the shame a good servant feels before a worthy master.
I seated myself on those monstrous shoulders. I wanted to say, "Hold me tight" — but my voice would not come out as I intended.
But he who had rescued me before in other dangers, the moment I was mounted, wrapped his arms around me and held me steady.
He said: "Now move, Geryon. Make the circles wide and the descent gradual. Remember the strange new burden you carry."
As a small vessel backs away from shore, slowly, slowly — so Geryon withdrew. And when he felt himself entirely afloat,
He swung his tail around to where his chest had been, and stretched it out like an eel, drawing the air toward him with his paws.
I do not think there was greater fear when Phaethon dropped the reins and the heavens were scorched — as the sky still shows —
Or when poor Icarus felt the feathers melting from his sides, his father crying, "You are going the wrong way!"
Than my own fear, when I found myself surrounded on all sides by nothing but air, with every sight extinguished except the monster itself.
On he swam, slowly, slowly, wheeling and descending. I could feel it only by the wind striking my face and rising from below.
I heard already on the right the whirlpool making a horrible crash beneath us. I thrust my head out and looked down.
The abyss made me even more terrified — I saw fires below and heard cries of pain, and I clung tighter, trembling.
Then I saw what I had not noticed before: the spiraling descent, as horrors loomed up from all directions.
Like a falcon that has been long on the wing and, seeing neither lure nor prey, makes the falconer cry, "You are coming down!"
And descends wearily through a hundred spirals to land far from its master, sullen and resentful,
Just so Geryon set us down at the very bottom, close to the base of the jagged cliff. And freed of our weight,
He shot away like an arrow from a bowstring.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XVIII
paragraphs: There is a place in Hell called Malebolge — entirely of stone and iron-colored, like the cliff that encircles it.
Right in the middle of that malignant field yawns a well, enormously wide and deep, whose structure I will describe in its place.
The belt that remains between the well and the foot of the high, hard bank is round, and its floor is divided into ten separate valleys.
Like the pattern formed when many moats surround a castle to protect its walls,
Just such an image those concentric valleys presented. And as bridges cross from the gates of such fortresses to the outer bank,
So rocky ridges projected from the base of the cliff, crossing over the ditches and embankments all the way to the central well.
This was the place we found ourselves after being shaken from Geryon's back. The Poet turned left, and I followed behind.
On my right I saw new anguish, new torments, and new torturers with whips, filling the first ditch to the brim.
At the bottom the sinners were naked. On our side of the middle they walked toward us; on the far side they moved in the same direction as we did, but with longer strides.
It was like the system the Romans devised for the great crowds during the Jubilee year, to manage the flow across the bridge:
On one side, everyone faces toward the Castel Sant'Angelo and walks to Saint Peter's. On the other side, they walk toward the Mount.
On both sides, along the livid stone, I saw horned demons with great whips, cruelly lashing them from behind.
How they made them lift their legs at the first blow! Not a single one waited for a second, let alone a third.
As I walked, my eyes locked on one of them. I said at once: "I have seen this one before — I have not been starved of this sight."
So I stopped to get a better look. My gentle Guide stopped with me and allowed me to go back a few steps.
The scourged soul tried to hide by lowering his face, but it did him little good. I said: "You, with your eyes cast down —
Unless your features deceive me, you are Venedico Caccianemico. What brings you to such stinging sauces?"
He replied: "I tell this unwillingly, but your clear speech forces me to remember the old world.
I was the one who persuaded the fair Ghisola to satisfy the Marquis's desires — however the shameful story may be told.
I am not the only Bolognese weeping here. In fact, this place is so packed with them that not as many tongues today are taught
To say 'sipa' between the Reno and the Savena. If you want proof, just recall our greedy hearts."
While he was speaking, a demon struck him with a whip and said: "Move along, pimp! There are no women here for your coin."
I rejoined my Guide, and after a few steps we came to a point where a rocky ridge jutted out from the bank.
We climbed it easily and, turning right along its crest, we left those eternal circles behind.
When we reached the place where the ridge arches over the ditch to let the scourged pass underneath, my Guide said: "Stop, and let the sight
Of those other evil-born souls strike you — those whose faces you have not yet seen, because they were walking in our same direction."
From the old bridge we watched the line coming toward us on the other side, driven forward by the same whips.
Without my asking, the good Master said: "Look at that tall one coming this way — he sheds no tear for all his pain.
What a regal bearing he still has! That is Jason, who by his courage and cunning stripped the Colchians of the Golden Fleece.
He passed by the island of Lemnos, after those pitiless, daring women had put all their menfolk to death.
There, with his charming words and fine gestures, he seduced young Hypsipyle — the maiden who had first deceived all the rest.
He left her there, pregnant and abandoned. Such sin condemns him to such punishment, and vengeance is also taken for Medea.
All who deceive in that way go with him. And let this suffice for the first valley and those caught in its jaws."
We had already reached the place where the narrow ridge crosses the second ditch and forms a buttress for the next arch.
From there we heard people moaning in the next trench, snorting through their nostrils and slapping themselves with their palms.
The banks were crusted with a mold from the vapors rising below, which clung to the stone and waged war against both eyes and nose.
The bottom was so deep that we could not see it without climbing to the highest point of the arch, where the ridge is steepest.
We went there, and from that vantage point I looked down into the ditch and saw people smothered in a filth that seemed to flow from human latrines.
While I searched the depths with my eyes, I spotted one whose head was so caked with excrement that it was impossible to tell if he was a cleric or a layman.
He screamed at me: "Why are you so eager to stare at me rather than the other foul ones?" I replied: "Because, if I remember correctly,
I have seen you before, when your hair was dry. You are Alessio Interminei of Lucca. That is why I study you more than the others."
He beat his own skull with his fists and said: "Flattery has sunk me here — my tongue could never get enough of it."
Then my Guide said: "Lean out a little farther, so your eyes can fully reach the face
Of that filthy, disheveled woman over there, who scratches herself with her grimy nails, and now squats, now stands upright.
That is Thais the harlot, who, when her lover asked, 'Do I have your deep gratitude?' replied, 'Marvelous gratitude!'
And with that, let us be satisfied with what we have seen."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XIX
paragraphs: O Simon Magus! O you miserable disciples who take the things of God — things that should be the brides of holiness —
And prostitute them for silver and gold! Now the trumpet must sound for you, for you dwell in the third ditch.
We had already climbed to the next tomb — to that part of the ridge that hangs directly over the middle of the trench.
O supreme Wisdom, what great art you display in heaven, on earth, and in the evil world! How justly your power distributes!
I saw on the sides and at the bottom that the livid stone was pierced with holes, all the same size, and each one round.
They seemed no wider and no narrower than the baptismal fonts in my beautiful San Giovanni,
One of which, not many years ago, I broke to save someone who was drowning in it. Let this be the seal that sets all minds straight.
From the mouth of each hole the feet and legs of a sinner protruded up to the calves. The rest of the body remained inside.
Both soles of every sinner were on fire, which made the joints twitch so violently they would have snapped ropes and chains.
Just as flame on oily things skims along the outer surface only, so it was here, flickering from heel to toe.
"Master, who is that one who writhes more than the rest, and whose feet are sucked by a redder flame?"
He replied: "If you wish, I will carry you down along the lower bank, and from him you will learn his sins and who he is."
I said: "Whatever pleases you pleases me. You are my lord. You know I do not stray from your will — and you know what I leave unspoken."
We descended to the fourth embankment, turned, and climbed down to the left, to the narrow, hole-pierced bottom.
My good Master did not set me down from his hip until he brought me to the hole of the one who wept so hard with his kicking legs.
"Whoever you are, sorrowful soul, planted upside-down like a stake," I began, "speak, if you can."
I stood there like a friar who confesses a treacherous assassin, who, once wedged in the hole, calls the friar back to delay the moment of death.
He cried out: "Is that you already? Are you standing there already, Boniface? The record lied to me by many years.
Have you so soon grown tired of the wealth for which you did not fear to seize the beautiful Lady by fraud and then do her harm?"
I stood there like someone hearing words he does not understand, feeling mocked, not knowing how to respond.
Virgil said: "Tell him quickly: 'I am not the one, I am not the one you think.'" And I replied as I was told.
The spirit twisted both feet violently. Then, with a sigh and a voice of lamentation, he said: "Then what do you want from me?
If you care so much to know who I am that you crossed the bank for it, know that I wore the great papal mantle.
I was truly a son of the She-Bear, so eager to advance my cubs that I pocketed wealth up above and pocketed myself down here.
Beneath my head, all those who preceded me in simony are dragged down, flattened along the crevice of the rock.
I too will fall down there when the one arrives whom I mistook you for, the moment I asked my hasty question.
But already I have roasted my feet and hung here upside-down longer than he will be planted with reddened feet.
For after him will come, from the west, a shepherd even more lawless — one fit to cover both him and me.
He will be a new Jason, like the one we read of in Maccabees — and as that king was compliant to him, so the ruler of France will be to this one."
I do not know if I was too bold here, but I answered him in this measure: "Tell me — how much treasure
Did our Lord demand from Saint Peter before He placed the keys in his keeping? Surely He asked nothing except 'Follow me.'
Nor did Peter or the others demand silver or gold from Matthias when he was chosen by lot to fill the place the guilty soul had lost.
So stay right where you are, for you are justly punished. And guard well the ill-gotten money that made you so bold against Charles.
Were it not that I am still restrained by the reverence I owe the supreme keys that you held in the happy life above,
I would use even harsher words. For your greed afflicts the world, trampling the good and lifting up the wicked.
It was you shepherds that the Evangelist had in mind when he saw the one who sits upon many waters fornicating with kings —
The one who was born with seven heads, and drew strength and power from her ten horns, as long as virtue pleased her spouse.
You have made a god of gold and silver! How do you differ from the idolater, except that he worships one and you worship a hundred?
Ah, Constantine! What evil was mothered not by your conversion, but by that dowry the first wealthy Father accepted from you!"
While I sang these words to him, whether stung by anger or by conscience, he kicked both feet furiously.
I truly believe it pleased my Guide, for he listened the whole time with a look of deep contentment to the sound of those true words.
Then he lifted me up with both arms, and when he had me fully on his chest, he climbed back the way he had come down.
He did not tire of holding me clasped to him, but carried me to the top of the arch that bridges the fourth and fifth ditches.
There he gently laid his burden down — gently, on a crag so steep and rough that even goats would find it treacherous.
From there, another valley was revealed to me.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XX
paragraphs: Now I must turn new pain into verses and give substance to the twentieth canto of the first canticle, which is about the submerged.
I was already positioned to peer down into the exposed depth, which was bathed in tears of anguish.
Through the circular valley I saw people coming, silent and weeping, walking at the slow pace of a litany procession in our world.
As my gaze descended lower upon them, I saw that each one was grotesquely twisted from the chin down to the beginning of the chest.
Their faces were turned toward their backs, and they were forced to walk backward, since they could no longer look ahead.
Perhaps palsy has twisted someone this completely, but I have never seen it, and I do not believe it possible.
Reader, so may God let you gather fruit from your reading — think now for yourself how I could have kept my face dry,
When I saw our own human form distorted so terribly, the tears from their eyes running down the cleft and bathing their backsides.
Truly, I wept, leaning against a jutting point of the hard crag. My Guide said: "Are you still as foolish as the rest?
Here, pity lives only when it is completely dead. Who is a greater scoundrel than the one who feels sorrow at God's judgment?
Lift up your head. See the one for whom the earth opened before the Thebans' eyes, and they all cried: 'Where are you rushing,
Amphiaraus? Why do you abandon the battle?' And he did not stop falling until he reached Minos, who seizes everyone.
See how he has made a chest of his shoulders! Because he wished to see too far ahead, he now looks behind and walks backward.
Look at Tiresias, who changed his form from male to female, every part of his body transformed.
Afterward he was forced to strike the two entwined serpents with his rod once more before he could regain his masculine features.
That one backing against the other's belly is Aruns, who in the hills of Luni, where the people of Carrara dig below,
Had a cave among the white marble for his dwelling, from which the view of stars and sea was unobstructed.
And the one who covers her breasts — which you cannot see — with her loosened hair, and has all her hairy skin on that far side,
Was Manto, who searched through many lands, then settled in the place where I was born. Let me tell you a little about this.
After her father departed from life and the city of Bacchus fell into bondage, she wandered the world for a long time.
High up in beautiful Italy, at the foot of the Alps that border Germany above Tyrol, lies a lake called Benaco.
By a thousand springs and more, I think, the area between Garda, Val Camonica, and the Pennine heights is bathed with water that collects in that lake.
In the middle is a place where the bishops of Trent, Brescia, and Verona could each give their blessing, if they passed that way.
Peschiera, that fine, strong fortress, sits facing the Brescians and Bergamasques, at the point where the shore descends lowest.
There, everything that cannot stay within Benaco's basin must overflow, becoming a river that flows through green meadows.
As soon as the water begins to run, it is no longer called Benaco but Mincio, all the way to Governo, where it empties into the Po.
Before it flows far, it finds flat land where it spreads out into a marsh that in summer often turns foul and sickly.
Passing through there, the pitiless virgin found land in the middle of the swamp — uncultivated and uninhabited.
There, to escape all human contact, she stayed with her servants, practiced her arts, lived out her life, and left her empty body behind.
Afterward, the people scattered around that region gathered at that spot, which was made strong by the marshes on every side.
They built their city over her dead bones and named it Mantua after her, the one who first chose the place, without any other omen.
Its population was once denser, before the stupidity of Casalodi was deceived by Pinamonte.
So I warn you: if you ever hear a different story of my city's origin, do not let any falsehood corrupt the truth."
I said: "Master, your words are so certain and so command my belief that any other account would be dead coals to me.
But tell me about the people passing by. If you see anyone noteworthy, my mind keeps turning back to that alone."
He said: "That one who stretches his beard from his cheek across his dark shoulders was an augur when Greece was so emptied of men
That scarcely any remained in their cradles. He, along with Calchas, gave the signal at Aulis to cut the first cable.
His name was Eurypylus, and my own noble Tragedy sings of him somewhere — as you know well, since you know the whole work.
The next one, so thin in the flanks, was Michael Scot, who truly knew every trick of magical illusion.
Look at Guido Bonatti. Look at Asdente, who now wishes he had stuck to his leather and his thread — but he repents too late.
Look at the wretched women who gave up the needle, the spindle, and the distaff to become fortune-tellers. They worked their spells with herbs and wax images.
But come now, for Cain with his bundle of thorns already holds the border of both hemispheres and touches the ocean beneath Seville.
Last night the moon was already full — you should remember that well, since it did you no harm at times deep in the forest."
So he spoke, and we walked on.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXI
paragraphs: From bridge to bridge we traveled, speaking of things my Comedy does not care to record, and we held the top of the ridge when
We stopped to see the next fissure of Malebolge and its next round of pointless wailing. I found it marvelously dark.
As in the Arsenal at Venice, where tenacious pitch boils all winter long, used to coat the ships that cannot sail,
So that instead one man builds a new hull, another recaulks the ribs of one that has made many voyages,
One hammers at the bow, another at the stern, one makes oars, another twists rope, another mends the mainsail and the jib —
Just so, not by fire but by divine craft, a thick pitch boiled below, coating the banks on every side.
I could see it, but nothing in it except the bubbles the boiling raised — swelling up and sinking back, compressed.
While I stared fixedly downward, my Leader cried "Watch out! Watch out!" and pulled me toward him from where I stood.
I spun around like someone desperate to see what he must flee from, who is seized by sudden terror and does not delay his escape even while looking —
And I saw behind us a black devil running along the ridge toward us.
How savage he looked! How ruthless in his movements, with wings spread wide and feet light on the stone!
His sharp, high shoulders carried a sinner draped across both haunches, gripped by the tendons of his feet.
From our bridge he called: "Hey, Malebranche! Here is one of the elders of Santa Zita! Plunge him under — I am going back for more
From that city, which is well stocked with them. Everyone there is a grafter, except Bonturo. There, 'No' becomes 'Yes' for money."
He hurled the sinner down and turned back over the hard cliff. No mastiff ever chased a thief with such speed.
The sinner sank and bobbed back up, curled in a ball. But the demons sheltering under the bridge shouted: "Here the Holy Face has no place!
Swimming is different here than in the Serchio! If you don't want to feel our hooks, don't rise above the pitch."
They jabbed him with over a hundred prongs and said: "Here you dance under cover. Skim what you can in secret, if you are able."
It was just like cooks who make their kitchen boys push meat down into the pot with their forks to keep it from floating.
My good Master said to me: "So they don't see you're here, squat behind a jutting rock that will give you cover.
And no matter what violence is done to me, do not be afraid. I know these matters well — I have been in a scuffle like this before."
Then he crossed to the far side of the bridge. When he stepped onto the sixth embankment, he needed every ounce of composure.
With the same fury and uproar that dogs unleash on a beggar who suddenly stops to plead at the spot where he stands,
Out rushed the demons from beneath the bridge, turning all their hooks toward him. But he cried: "None of you be savage!
Before those prongs of yours touch me, let one of you step forward to hear what I say. Then decide whether to hook me."
They all cried: "Let Malacoda go!" So one advanced while the rest stood still, and he came saying: "What good will this do him?"
"Do you think, Malacoda, that you see me here," said my Master, "safe from all your defenses,
Without divine will and favorable fate? Let us pass, for it is willed in Heaven that I show another this savage road."
At that, Malacoda's pride collapsed. He let his hook drop to his feet and said to the others: "Then do not strike him."
My Guide called to me: "You there, crouching among the broken rocks of the bridge — you can come back safely now."
I moved and came to him quickly. The devils all pressed forward, and I feared they would not keep the agreement.
I once saw soldiers, under a treaty of surrender, file out of Caprona looking terrified as they walked among the enemy —
In the same way, I pressed my whole body close to my Guide, never taking my eyes off their faces, which did not look friendly.
They lowered their hooks and said to each other: "Want me to touch his backside?" And the answer came: "Sure, give him a nick."
But the demon who was speaking with my Leader turned around sharply and said: "Hold it, hold it, Scarmiglione!"
Then he said to us: "Going further along this ridge is impossible. The sixth arch lies shattered at the bottom.
But if you still wish to continue, walk along this embankment. Nearby there is another ridge that provides a crossing.
Yesterday, five hours later than this very hour, it was one thousand two hundred and sixty-six years since the road here was broken.
I am sending some of my men that way to see if anyone is airing themselves above the pitch. Go with them — they will not harm you."
"Step forward, Alichino and Calcabrina," he began, "and you, Cagnazzo. Let Barbariccia lead the squad of ten.
Let Libicocco come too, and Draghignazzo, the tusked Ciriatto, Graffiacane, Farfarello, and the mad Rubicante.
Search around the boiling glue. Keep these two safe as far as the next ridge that crosses all the ditches unbroken."
I said: "Master, what is this I see? If you know the way, let us go alone, without an escort. I do not want one.
If you are as observant as usual, do you not see how they grind their teeth and threaten us with their eyes?"
He replied: "I do not want you to be afraid. Let them grind their teeth as much as they please — they do it for the wretches boiling in the pitch."
They turned along the left-hand bank. But first, each one pressed his tongue between his teeth as a signal to their leader,
And he made a trumpet of his rear.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXII
paragraphs: I have seen horsemen breaking camp, launching attacks, holding musters, and sometimes retreating to save themselves.
I have seen scouts ride through your lands, O Aretines, and raiding parties go forth, and tournaments clashed, and jousts run —
Now with trumpets, now with bells, now with drums, now with castle signals, now with things native and foreign —
But never to so bizarre a bugle have I seen cavalry or infantry move, or a ship steer by star or shore.
We walked with the ten demons. Terrible company — but in church with the saints, and in the tavern with the drunks.
My attention was fixed on the pitch, to observe everything about this ditch and the people burning in it.
Like dolphins, when they arch their backs above the water, signaling to sailors to start securing their ship,
So now and then, to relieve their pain, a sinner would show his back above the surface and then duck down again, quick as lightning.
And like frogs that squat at the edge of a ditch with only their muzzles poking out, hiding their feet and the rest of their bodies,
So the sinners squatted on every side. But the instant Barbariccia drew near, they pulled back under the boiling.
I saw — and my heart still shudders at the memory — one who lingered, the way one frog sometimes stays while another dives.
Graffiacane, who was nearest, hooked him by his pitch-matted hair and hauled him up. He looked to me like an otter.
I already knew every demon's name — I had noted them when they were chosen, and listened when they called to each other.
"O Rubicante, sink your claws into him! Flay him!" all the cursed ones screamed together.
I said: "Master, find out who that wretched one is, if you can, who has fallen into his enemies' hands."
My Guide drew close and asked him where he was from. He replied: "I was born in the kingdom of Navarre.
My mother placed me in the service of a lord, for she had borne me to a wastrel who destroyed himself and his fortune.
Then I served the good King Thibaut as a household official. There I took up grafting — and here, in this heat, I pay the reckoning."
And Ciriatto, from whose snout on either side a tusk protruded like a boar's, made him feel how one of them could rip.
The mouse had fallen among cruel cats. But Barbariccia locked his arms around the sinner and said: "Stand back while I have him prong-locked."
Then he turned to my Master: "Ask him more, if there is anything else you wish to learn, before the others tear him apart."
My Guide asked: "Tell us — among the other sinners under the pitch, do you know any who are Italian?" He answered: "I just now
Left one who came from nearby. I wish I were still under cover with him — I would not fear these hooks and claws."
Libicocco said: "We have endured too much!" and seized his arm with his hook and tore out a sinew.
Draghignazzo also wanted a go at his legs. But their sergeant wheeled around and glared at them all.
When they had calmed a little, my Guide quickly asked the sinner — who was still staring at his wound —
"Who was the one you say you were unfortunate to leave when you came to shore?" He replied: "It was Fra Gomita,
Of Gallura — a vessel of every fraud — who held his master's enemies in hand and dealt with them so that all praise him.
He took their money and let them off easy, as he himself says. And in his other offices he was no petty grafter but a sovereign one.
With him keeps company Don Michel Zanche of Logodoro, and their tongues never tire of talking about Sardinia.
But look at that one grinding his teeth! I would say more, but I fear he is getting ready to scratch my scab."
The great provost turned to Farfarello, whose eyes were rolling with eagerness to strike, and said: "Get back, you filthy bird!"
The frightened soul continued: "If you wish to see or hear Tuscans or Lombards, I can bring them out.
Let the Malebranche stand back a little, so those souls won't fear their vengeance. I, sitting in this very spot,
For one that I am, will whistle seven of them up — that is our signal when any of us pokes out of the pitch."
Cagnazzo raised his snout at this and shook his head, saying: "Listen to the trick he has cooked up to dive back under!"
The sinner, who had plenty of tricks, answered: "I am indeed a trickster, when I arrange worse suffering for my companions."
Alichino could not resist. Against the others' opinion he said to the sinner: "If you dive, I will not gallop after you —
I have wings to beat above the pitch. We will leave this ridge and use the bank for cover. Let us see if you alone can beat all of us."
Now hear a new sport, reader! They all turned their eyes to the other side — he first who had been most opposed to the plan.
The Navarrese timed his moment perfectly. He planted his feet on the ground, and in an instant leaped and freed himself from their leader's grip.
Each demon stung with guilt — but most of all the one who had caused the blunder. He launched himself, screaming: "You are caught!"
But it did no good. Wings could not outrace terror. The sinner plunged under, and the demon pulled up from the dive, chest high —
Exactly like a duck that dives when a falcon swoops, and the falcon rises again, frustrated and beaten.
Calcabrina, furious at the trick, flew after Alichino, eager for the sinner to escape so he would have a fight.
When the grafter vanished, Calcabrina turned his claws on his companion, and they grappled above the ditch.
But the other was a fully armed hawk and clawed him right back. Together they tumbled down into the boiling pitch.
The heat instantly separated them, but their wings were so gummed with pitch that they could not lift themselves out.
Barbariccia, groaning with the rest, had four of them fly to the far side with all their hooks.
They scrambled down quickly to their posts on both banks, stretched their hooks toward the two who were already cooked beneath the crust,
And we left them struggling in that mess.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXIII
paragraphs: Silent, alone, without escort, we walked — one before the other — like Franciscan friars on the road.
The recent brawl had turned my thoughts to Aesop's fable of the frog and the mouse — the one in which he tells of the frog and mouse.
For 'now' and 'just then' are no more alike than those two tales, if you match their beginnings and endings carefully.
And as one thought springs from another, so from that one was born a new idea that doubled my first fear.
I thought: these demons have been tricked and humiliated because of us, and that must anger them greatly.
If rage is added to their malice, they will come after us more savagely than a dog snaps at a hare.
Already I could feel my hair bristling with terror. I was staring intently behind us when I said: "Master, if you do not hide us both quickly,
I am terrified of the Malebranche. They are already behind us — I imagine them so vividly I can practically hear them."
He replied: "If I were a silvered mirror, I could not capture your outward reflection more quickly than I catch your inner thought.
Your thoughts just now entered mine — identical in both their appearance and their meaning — and from the two I have formed a single plan.
If the right bank slopes gently enough for us to descend into the next ditch, we will escape the chase you fear."
He had barely finished explaining this plan when I saw them coming, not far off, wings spread wide, intent on seizing us.
My Guide grabbed me instantly — like a mother woken by noise who sees flames around her and seizes her child and runs,
Caring more for the child than for herself, not even stopping to throw on a shift.
Down from the top of the hard embankment he slid on his back along the sloping rock that walls one side of the next ditch.
Water never ran so fast through a millrace, not even at the point where it strikes the paddles, as my Master shot down that bank,
Carrying me on his chest as if I were his own son, not merely a companion.
His feet had barely touched the bottom of the bed below when the demons appeared on the ridge above us. But there was nothing to fear:
The high Providence that made them guardians of the fifth ditch strips from them all power to leave it.
Down below, we found a painted people who circled with incredibly slow steps, weeping, and looking exhausted and defeated.
They wore cloaks with cowls pulled low over their eyes, cut in the style of the monks at Cluny.
On the outside, the cloaks were gilded so brilliantly they dazzled. But on the inside, they were all lead — so heavy that Frederick's capes were straw by comparison.
O weary mantle for eternity! We turned again to the left and walked with them, absorbed in their mournful weeping.
But the people moved so slowly under their crushing weight that with every step we took, we found new company beside us.
I said to my Guide: "Find someone here whose name or deeds I might recognize. Cast your eyes around as we walk."
One who caught my Tuscan speech cried out behind us: "Stay your feet, you who run so fast through this dark air!
Perhaps I can give you what you ask." My Guide turned to me and said: "Wait, then walk at his pace."
I stopped, and saw two whose faces showed great urgency to join me, but their burden and the narrow path slowed them.
When they arrived, they stared at me a long time with sidelong glances, without speaking.
Then they turned to each other and said: "This one seems alive, by the movement of his throat.
And if they are dead, by what privilege do they walk without the heavy stole?"
Then they said to me: "O Tuscan, who has come to the college of these wretched hypocrites, do not scorn telling us who you are."
I replied: "I was born and raised in the great city on the beautiful river Arno, and I wear the body I have always worn.
But who are you, from whom such grief distills down your cheeks? And what punishment is this that glitters so?"
One answered: "The orange-colored cloaks are made of lead so thick that the weight makes us, their scales, creak.
We were Jovial Friars, both Bolognese — I was Catalano and he was Loderingo. Together we were chosen by your city,
To keep the peace, as normally a single man is chosen. And what we made of it can still be seen around the Gardingo district."
I began: "Friars, your evil —" but I stopped short, for my eye fell on one crucified on the ground with three stakes.
When he saw me, he writhed all over, blowing sighs into his beard. Friar Catalano noticed and said:
"That one pinned there, whom you are looking at, counseled the Pharisees that it was expedient to put one man to torture for the sake of the people.
He lies naked and crosswise in the path, as you see, and must feel the weight of everyone who passes.
His father-in-law is stretched in the same fashion in this ditch, and so are the others of that council that sowed such evil seed for the Jews."
I saw Virgil standing amazed above the one who lay there stretched out in eternal exile, like a cross.
Then he addressed the friar: "If it is permitted, may it please you to tell us whether any opening on the right leads out of here,
So that we can leave without having to summon any of the black angels to come and pull us from this pit."
He answered: "Closer than you hope, there is a ridge that extends from the great encircling wall and spans all the savage valleys,
Except that in this one it is broken and does not cross. You can climb up over its ruins, which slope along the bank and pile up at the bottom."
My Guide stood with his head bowed for a moment, then said: "The one up there who hooks sinners gave us a false account of this."
The friar replied: "In Bologna I once heard many of the Devil's vices recounted — among them, that he is a liar and the father of lies."
Then my Guide moved off with long, angry strides. I left the burdened souls behind and followed the prints of his beloved feet.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXIV
paragraphs: In that part of the young year when the sun warms his locks beneath Aquarius, and the nights are already growing shorter toward the equinox,
When the frost paints a copy of her white sister on the ground — though her pen's edge lasts only a short while —
The farmer, running low on fodder, gets up, looks out, and sees the fields all white, slaps his thigh,
Goes back inside and paces like a wretch who does not know what to do. Then he goes outside again and gathers hope,
Seeing that the world has changed its face in just a little while, and takes his staff and drives his sheep out to pasture.
In the same way, my Master filled me with alarm when I saw how troubled his brow looked. But just as quickly the remedy came for my distress.
When we reached the ruined bridge, my Guide turned to me with that same sweet look I first saw at the foot of the mountain.
He opened his arms — first studying the rubble carefully and forming a plan — then took hold of me and lifted me up.
Like someone who works things out as he goes, always thinking ahead, he boosted me up toward the top of one boulder and then pointed out the next,
Saying: "Now grab hold of that one — but test it first to make sure it will bear your weight."
It was no path for someone wearing a leaden cloak. Even we — he weightless, I pushed from behind — could barely make it from rock to rock.
If the slope on that side had not been shorter than on the other, I cannot speak for him, but I would certainly have been defeated.
But since all of Malebolge tilts toward the mouth of the lowest well, the structure of each valley means
That one side stands higher and the other lower. We did reach the top at last, the point where the last stone breaks away.
My lungs were so wrung of breath by the climb that I could go no farther. The moment I reached the top, I sat down.
"From now on you must shake off laziness," my Master said. "Sitting on cushions or lying under blankets does not lead to fame.
Without fame, the man who consumes his life leaves no more trace in the world than smoke in air or foam on water.
So get up! Conquer your panting with the spirit that wins every battle, unless the body drags it down.
There is a longer stairway to climb. It is not enough to have left those others behind. If you understand me, act so that it matters."
I stood up, showing myself better supplied with breath than I felt, and said: "Go on — I am strong and ready."
We took our way along the ridge, which was rugged, narrow, and difficult, and far steeper than the one before.
I walked and talked, so as not to seem winded, when a voice rose from the next ditch — a voice ill-suited for forming words.
I do not know what it said, though I was already on the arch that spans the ditch. But whoever was speaking seemed to be in motion.
I had bent down to look, but my living eyes could not reach the bottom through the darkness. So I said: "Master, let us get to the next bank,
For from here I can hear but not understand, and I look but cannot make anything out."
"The only answer I give you," he said, "is the deed itself. A fair request should be met with the act, in silence."
We descended from the bridge at the point where it meets the eighth embankment, and then the ditch lay open to my view.
I saw a terrible swarm of serpents inside — so strange in variety that the memory still freezes my blood.
Let Libya with its sands boast no more! Though it breeds chelydri, jaculi, phareans, cenchres, and amphisbaena,
Never did it display plagues so many or so monstrous, not even with all of Ethiopia and the land above the Red Sea.
Among this cruel and dismal swarm, naked people ran in terror, with no hope of a hiding-hole or heliotrope to make them invisible.
Their hands were bound behind them with serpents, which thrust their heads and tails through the loins and knotted themselves in front.
And look — one sinner near our bank was struck by a serpent that pierced him right where the neck meets the shoulders.
No O or I was ever written as fast as he caught fire and burned, and as he fell, he was reduced entirely to ashes.
After he lay there on the ground, destroyed, the dust gathered itself together and instantly reformed into the same shape.
Just so, the great sages confirm, the Phoenix dies and is reborn when it approaches its five-hundredth year.
In life it feeds on neither grass nor grain, but only on tears of incense and cardamom, and nard and myrrh are its final shroud.
Like someone who falls — he does not know how, whether by a demon's force that pulls him down or by some blockage that binds him —
Who, when he rises, stares all around, bewildered by the great anguish he has suffered, sighing as he looks,
Such was that sinner after he had risen. O how severe the power of God, which rains down blows of such vengeance!
My Guide asked who he was. He answered: "I rained down from Tuscany into this savage throat not long ago.
Bestial life, not human, pleased me — mule that I was. I am Vanni Fucci, the beast, and Pistoia was a fitting den for me."
I said to my Guide: "Tell him not to slip away, and ask what sin thrust him down here. I knew him as a man of blood and rage."
The sinner heard, and did not pretend otherwise. He turned his face toward me, coloring with wretched shame.
He said: "It pains me more that you have caught me in this misery than the moment I was torn from the other life.
I cannot refuse what you ask. I am placed this deep because I stole the beautiful ornaments from the sacristy — a crime falsely blamed on others.
But so that you do not enjoy this sight, if you ever escape these dark regions, open your ears to what I announce, and hear it well:
Pistoia first strips itself of the Blacks. Then Florence renews her people and her ways.
Mars draws a lightning bolt from the Val di Magra, wrapped in turbid clouds. And with a fierce and bitter storm
Battle will be joined on the fields of Piceno — where it will suddenly rip through the fog, so that every White shall be struck.
And I have said this so that it may grieve you."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXV
paragraphs: At the end of his speech, the thief raised both hands with the fingers formed in an obscene gesture, shouting: "Take that, God — I aim them at you!"
From that moment on, the serpents became my friends. One coiled around his neck as if to say: "I will not let you speak another word."
Another wound around his arms and bound them tight, clinching itself together in front so he could not make a single movement.
Pistoia, Pistoia! Why not burn yourself to ashes and vanish, since you surpass your own seed in wickedness?
Through all the dark circles of Hell, I saw no spirit so proud against God — not even the one who fell from the walls at Thebes.
He fled without another word. Then I saw a centaur full of rage come galloping up, shouting: "Where is he? Where is the blasphemer?"
I do not think the Maremma has as many serpents as he carried along his back, all the way up to where the human features begin.
On his shoulders, just behind the nape, a dragon crouched with spread wings, breathing fire on everything it encountered.
My Master said: "That is Cacus, who beneath the rock of the Aventine Hill often created a lake of blood.
He does not walk the same road as his brother centaurs, because of the fraudulent theft he committed against the great herd pastured near him.
That crooked career ended under the club of Hercules, who may have given him a hundred blows — though he barely felt ten."
While he was still speaking, the centaur had passed. Below us, three spirits had arrived, which neither my Guide nor I had noticed
Until they shouted: "Who are you?" Our conversation stopped, and we turned our attention entirely to them.
I did not know them. But it happened, as chance often arranges, that one was forced to name another,
Exclaiming: "Where has Cianfa got to?" At that, I laid my finger from chin to nose to signal my Guide to pay close attention.
If you are slow to believe what I am about to say, reader, it will be no wonder — for I who saw it can scarcely accept it myself.
As I was watching them with raised brows, a six-footed serpent shot out and fastened itself entirely onto one of them.
With its middle feet it gripped his belly. With its front feet it seized his arms. Then it drove its fangs through both his cheeks.
Its hind legs it stretched along his thighs, threading its tail between them and spreading it up along his back.
Ivy never clung to a tree with its hooks as tightly as that hideous reptile wrapped its limbs around the other's.
Then they fused together, as if they had been made of heated wax, and their colors blended — neither one looked like what it had been.
Just as a brown hue creeps up paper ahead of a flame — not yet black, but the white already dying.
The other two watched and cried: "Oh, Agnello, how you are changing! Look — you are already neither two nor one!"
The two heads had already merged into one. Two shapes had melted into a single face, in which both were lost.
From the four arms, two were fashioned. The thighs, the legs, the belly, the chest — all became limbs never seen before.
Every original feature was cancelled. The perverted image appeared two and yet none, and it shuffled away at a slow pace.
Just as a lizard, darting from hedge to hedge under the scorching heat of the dog days, flashes like lightning if it crosses the road,
So a small, fiery serpent came darting toward the bellies of the other two — livid and black as a peppercorn.
It pierced one of them in the navel — the place where we first receive nourishment — then fell stretched out before him.
The pierced one stared at the serpent but said nothing. Instead, with feet planted, he yawned, as though overtaken by sleep or fever.
He gazed at the serpent, and it gazed at him. Smoke poured violently from his wound and from the serpent's mouth, and the two smokes mingled.
Let Lucan be silent from now on, where he tells of wretched Sabellus and Nasidius. Let him wait and hear what comes next.
Let Ovid too be silent about Cadmus and Arethusa. If his poetry transforms one into a snake and the other into a fountain, I do not begrudge him,
For he never transformed two natures face to face, so that both forms were ready to exchange their matter.
They answered each other in such a way that the serpent split its tail into a fork, and the wounded man drew his feet together.
His legs and thighs pressed together so tightly that in a short time the seam was completely invisible.
The cloven tail took on the shape the other was losing. Its skin grew soft while the other's hardened.
I saw the arms withdraw into the armpits, and the reptile's short feet lengthen by exactly the amount that the man's arms shortened.
The hind feet, twisting together, became the organ a man conceals, while from his own the wretch had sprouted two new feet.
While the smoke veiled both of them in a new color, growing hair on one and stripping it from the other,
One rose up and the other fell down, though neither turned away those unholy lamps beneath which each one's muzzle was transforming.
The standing one drew his face toward his temples, and from the surplus flesh that gathered there, ears sprouted from the smooth cheeks.
What did not retreat — the excess that remained — formed a nose on the face, and thickened the lips to their proper size.
The one lying flat thrust his muzzle forward and pulled his ears back into his head, the way a snail retracts its horns.
The tongue, which had been whole and fit for speech, split in two. The forked tongue of the other fused shut. And the smoke ceased.
The soul that had been changed into a reptile hissed off along the valley. The other spat and sputtered after it.
Then the newly changed one turned his fresh shoulders and said to the other: "I will have Buoso crawl along this road as I have done."
In this way I saw the seventh cargo shift and re-shift. Let the strangeness of the thing excuse me if my pen has wandered.
Although my eyes were somewhat bewildered and my mind stunned, the sinners could not flee so secretly
That I did not clearly recognize Puccio Sciancato — the only one of the three who arrived at first that was not changed.
The other was the one for whom you weep, Gaville.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXVI
paragraphs: Rejoice, Florence, for you are so great that you beat your wings over sea and land, and your name is spread through all of Hell!
Among the thieves I found five of your citizens — which brings me shame, and you no great honor.
But if our dreams near morning are prophetic, you will feel before long what Prato, among others, craves for you.
And if it were already happening, it would not be too soon. Let it come, since come it must — for the older I grow, the more it will weigh on me.
We left that place, and climbed back up the stone ridges that had served as our stairway down. My Guide remounted the crag and pulled me after him.
Following the solitary path among the boulders and broken rocks, my feet made no progress without the help of my hands.
I grieved then, and I grieve again now, when I turn my mind to what I saw. I rein in my talent more than usual,
Lest it run where virtue does not guide it — so that if a good star, or something better, has given me a gift, I may not squander it.
As many as the fireflies a farmer sees, resting on a hillside at the hour when the sun hides its face least from us,
At the time when flies give way to gnats — he sees them glimmering down in the valley where he plows and tends his vines —
With that many flames the eighth ditch blazed, as I discovered the moment the bottom came into view.
Like Elisha, who watched the chariot of Elijah depart — when the horses reared upward toward heaven,
And could not follow it with his eyes, seeing nothing but the flame rising upward like a small cloud —
So each flame moved along the throat of the trench. None revealed the theft inside, but every flame concealed a stolen sinner.
I stood on the bridge, risen on tiptoe to see, and if I had not gripped a jutting rock, I would have fallen in without being pushed.
My Guide, seeing me so intent, said: "Inside the fires are the spirits. Each one wraps himself in the flame that burns him."
"Master," I replied, "hearing you confirms what I had already guessed. But I was about to ask:
Who is inside that flame which comes so forked at the top that it seems to rise from the pyre where Eteocles was laid with his brother?"
He answered: "Within it, Ulysses and Diomedes are tormented together. They rush toward vengeance as once they rushed toward wrath.
There within their flame they grieve for the stratagem of the wooden horse — the door through which the noble Roman bloodline emerged.
There they weep for the cunning by which the dead Deidamia still mourns for Achilles, and there they bear the penalty for stealing the Palladium."
"If they have the power to speak from within those flames," I said, "Master, I pray you urgently — and let my prayer be worth a thousand —
Do not refuse to wait until the twin-horned flame comes near. You can see how I lean toward it with desire."
He replied: "Your request is worthy of great praise, and I grant it. But restrain your tongue.
Let me do the speaking. I know what you wish to ask. But since they were Greeks, they might scorn your words."
When the flame had arrived at the point where my Guide judged the time and place were right, I heard him speak like this:
"O you who are two within a single fire, if I earned anything from you while I was alive, if I deserved anything from you, great or small,
When in the world I wrote my lofty verses — do not move on. Let one of you tell where, having lost his way, he went to die."
The greater horn of that ancient flame began to murmur and sway, like a flame struggling against the wind.
Then, tipping its peak back and forth as if it were the tongue that spoke, it uttered a voice that said: "When I
Departed from Circe, who had hidden me near Gaeta for more than a year, before Aeneas gave it that name,
Neither fondness for my son, nor devotion to my aging father, nor the love that should have made Penelope happy,
Could overcome in me the burning desire to gain experience of the world and to understand human vice and worth.
I put out on the deep open sea with a single ship and the small band of men who had never deserted me.
I saw both shores — as far as Spain, as far as Morocco, the island of Sardinia, and the other islands washed by that sea.
My crew and I were old and slow when we arrived at that narrow strait where Hercules set up his pillars
To warn that man should venture no farther. On my right I left Seville behind; on the left, I had already passed Ceuta.
'O brothers,' I said, 'who through a hundred thousand dangers have reached the West, do not deny, to this brief remaining vigil
Of your senses, the experience of the unpeopled world that lies beyond the sun.',
Consider the seed from which you spring. You were not made to live like animals, but to pursue knowledge and excellence.'
With this brief speech I made my companions so eager for the voyage that I could hardly have held them back.
Turning our stern to the morning, we made wings of our oars for the mad flight, always gaining to the left.
Night had already seen all the stars of the other pole, and our own sky was so low it did not rise above the ocean floor.
Five times the light beneath the moon had kindled and gone out since we had entered that deep passage,
When a mountain appeared to us, dim with distance, and it seemed higher to me than any I had ever seen.
We rejoiced — but our joy quickly turned to weeping. From that new land a whirlwind rose and struck the bow of the ship.
Three times it spun us around with all the waters. On the fourth, it drove the stern upward and the prow down, as pleased Another,
Until the sea closed over us again."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXVII
paragraphs: The flame was already standing straight and still, done with its speech, and moving away from us with the gentle Poet's permission,
When another flame behind it drew our eyes to its tip by the confused sound issuing from within.
Like the Sicilian bull — which first bellowed with the cries of the man (and rightly so) who had shaped it with his file —
That bellowed with the voice of the tormented, so that, although it was made of brass, it seemed pierced with agony,
So, having at first no way or opening to escape the fire, the wretched words were converted into the fire's own language.
But afterward, when they found their way up through the tip, giving it the vibration the tongue had given them as they passed,
We heard it say: "O you at whom I aim my voice — you who were just speaking Lombard, saying, 'Go your way, I urge you no more' —
Though I may have come a little late, do not mind stopping to speak with me. You can see it does not bother me, and I am burning.
If you have only recently fallen into this blind world from that sweet Italian land from which I bring all my guilt,
Tell me — do the people of Romagna have peace or war? For I was from the mountains between Urbino and the ridge from which the Tiber springs."
I was still bent forward, listening, when my Guide nudged me and said: "You speak — this one is Italian."
I had my answer already prepared and began without delay: "O soul hidden down there in the flame,
Your Romagna is not now and never has been without war in the hearts of its tyrants. But no open war did I leave there just now.
Ravenna stands as it has for many years. The Eagle of Polenta broods there, covering Cervia with its wings.
The city that once endured a long siege and made a bloody heap of Frenchmen now finds itself under the Green Paws.
The old Mastiff of Verrucchio and the new one, who made such cruel use of Montagna, still bore their teeth where they always do.
The cities of Lamone and Santerno are governed by the young Lion of the white den, who switches sides between summer and winter.
And the city whose flank the Savio bathes, just as it lies between plain and mountain, lives between tyranny and freedom.
Now I beg you, tell us who you are. Be no more stubborn than the others have been, so that your name may hold its place in the world."
After the fire had roared a little more in its own fashion, the sharp point swayed back and forth, and then released this breath:
"If I believed my reply were being made to someone who would ever return to the world, this flame would stop flickering.
But since no one has ever returned alive from this depth, if what I hear is true, I answer without fear of infamy.
I was a man of arms, then a Franciscan friar, believing that the cord would make amends. And truly my belief would have been fulfilled,
Were it not for the High Priest — may evil befall him — who dragged me back into my former sins. How and why, I will have you hear.
While I was still in the form of bone and flesh my mother gave me, my deeds were not those of a lion but of a fox.
I knew every stratagem and covert trick, and practiced the art so well that my fame reached the ends of the earth.
When I saw myself arriving at that stage of life when everyone ought to lower the sails and coil up the ropes,
What had pleased me before now disgusted me. Repentant and confessing, I surrendered myself. And it would have saved me!
But the Prince of the new Pharisees, waging war near the Lateran — and not against Saracens or Jews,
For every one of his enemies was Christian, and none of them had gone to conquer Acre or to trade in the Sultan's land —
Regarded neither his high office nor his sacred orders, nor in me the cord that used to make those who wore it leaner.
But just as Constantine sought out Sylvester inside Soracte to cure his leprosy, so this one sought me out as a doctor
To cure the fever of his pride. He asked my counsel, and I stayed silent, because his words seemed like those of a madman.
Then he said: 'Let your heart not be afraid. From this moment I absolve you in advance. Now instruct me how to raze Palestrina to the ground.
I have the power to lock and unlock Heaven, as you know. The keys are two — which my predecessor did not hold dear.'
Then his heavy arguments pushed me to the point where silence seemed the worst advice. I said: 'Father, since you wash me clean
Of the sin I am about to commit — promise much and deliver little: that will give you triumph on your lofty throne.'
When I died, Saint Francis came for me. But one of the black Cherubim said: 'Do not take him! Do not wrong me!
He must come down among my servants, because he gave the fraudulent counsel. Since then I have been at his hair.
For one who does not repent cannot be absolved, and one cannot both repent and will the sin at the same time — the contradiction will not allow it.'
Oh, wretched me! How I shuddered when he seized me, saying: 'Perhaps you did not think I was a logician!'
He carried me to Minos, who wound his tail eight times around his rigid back, and in a fury of rage bit it,
And said: 'This one belongs to the thievish fire.' And so here where you see me, I am lost, and dressed in this flame I grieve."
When it had finished its account, the flame departed with cries of lamentation, writhing and flapping its sharp horn.
We passed onward, both my Guide and I, up over the crag to the arch that spans the next moat — where those who earn their burden
By sowing discord pay the fee.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXVIII
paragraphs: Who could ever find words — even in the freest prose — to tell fully of the blood and wounds I now saw, no matter how many times the telling were repeated?
Every tongue would surely fall short, because our speech and memory lack the capacity to hold so much.
If all the people who once bled on the fateful soil of Puglia were assembled again, mourning their blood
Shed by the Romans in that long war which yielded such a famous harvest of rings, as Livy records without error,
Together with those who suffered the agony of blows by resisting Robert Guiscard, and all the rest whose bones are still gathered
At Ceperano, where every Apulian was a traitor, and at Tagliacozzo, where old Alardo won without weapons —
And if each showed their pierced and severed limbs, it would be nothing compared to the revolting spectacle of the ninth ditch.
No barrel, even one that has lost its center-piece or a stave, was ever so shattered as the one I saw, split from chin to the place where one breaks wind.
His entrails hung between his legs. His vital organs were visible, along with the wretched sack that turns what we swallow into filth.
While I stood completely absorbed in staring at him, he looked at me, pulled open his chest with his hands, and said: "See how I tear myself apart!
See how mangled Muhammad is! Before me walks Ali, weeping, his face cleft from forehead to chin.
And all the others you see here were sowers of scandal and schism when alive, and so they are split open like this.
A devil stands behind us who cleaves us cruelly with his sword, hacking each one of our group anew
Every time we complete the circuit of this miserable road, because our wounds close up again before any of us passes in front of him again.
But who are you, standing there on the bridge — perhaps postponing the punishment assigned for your own sins?"
"Neither death nor guilt brings him here to be tormented," my Master answered. "To give him full experience,
I, who am dead, must lead him down through Hell, from circle to circle. And this is as true as the fact that I am speaking to you."
More than a hundred stopped in the trench to stare at me when they heard him, their torment forgotten in their amazement.
"Then tell Fra Dolcino — you who may soon see the sun — to arm himself with provisions if he does not wish to follow me here soon.
Let him stock up so deeply that a siege of snow does not hand victory to the Novarese, which otherwise would not be easy to win."
Muhammad said these words to me, then lifted one foot to walk away and planted it on the ground to depart.
Another one, whose throat was pierced through and whose nose was cut off just below the brows, leaving only a single ear,
Paused to stare with the others. Before the rest, he opened his gullet — which was red with blood on every side —
And said: "O you whom guilt does not condemn, and whom I once saw up in Italian land — unless a strong resemblance deceives me —
Remember Pier da Medicina, if you ever see again the lovely plain that slopes from Vercelli down to Marcabo.
And make it known to the two best men of Fano — Messer Guido and Angiolello — that unless our foresight here is useless,
They will be thrown from their vessel and drowned near Cattolica, through the treachery of a vicious tyrant.
Between the isles of Cyprus and Majorca, Neptune never witnessed so great a crime — neither by pirates nor by Greeks.
That traitor with one eye, who rules the city that one of my companions here wishes he had never seen,
Will summon them to a parley, then deal with them so that they will need neither vow nor prayer against the wind of Focara."
I said: "Show me and point out — if you want me to carry news of you above — who is this one with the bitter sight?"
He laid his hand on the jaw of one of his companions, pried open his mouth, and cried: "This is the one — and he does not speak.
This exile, this man, silenced every doubt in Caesar by declaring that the one who is prepared always suffers from delay."
How stunned he looked to me — Curio, with his tongue slit inside his throat — Curio, who in life had been so bold in speech!
And one whose hands had both been chopped off raised the stumps through the murky air, so that the blood made his face horrible,
And cried: "You will remember Mosca too — who said, 'A thing done has an end!' — which was a seed of evil for the Tuscan people."
"And death to your whole line!" I added. At this, grief piled upon grief, he went away like a man driven mad with sorrow.
But I stayed to watch the crowd, and I saw something that I would be afraid to tell even now, without more proof,
Were it not that my conscience reassures me — that good companion which emboldens a man beneath the armor of its purity.
I truly saw, and I still seem to see, a trunk walking without a head, just like the others in that mournful procession.
It held the severed head by the hair, dangling from its hand like a lantern. The head stared at us and said: "Oh, me!"
It made a lamp of itself for itself. They were two in one, and one in two. How that can be, He knows who so ordains it.
When it reached the foot of our bridge, it raised its arm high, holding the head aloft to bring its words closer to us.
The words were: "Now behold this terrible punishment, you who breathe and go among the dead to view them. See if any is as great as this.
And so that you may carry news of me, know that I am Bertran de Born — the one who gave the Young King evil counsel.
I made father and son rebel against each other. Ahithophel did no worse with Absalom and David, with all his wicked goading.
Because I severed persons so united, I now carry my brain — alas! — severed from its root, which is here in this trunk.
Thus the law of retribution is observed in me."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXIX
paragraphs: The sheer number of people and their astonishing wounds had made my eyes so drunk that they wanted to linger and weep.
But Virgil said: "What are you still staring at? Why do you keep your gaze fixed down there among the sad, mutilated shades?
You did not do this at the other ditches. Consider that this valley winds for twenty-two miles, if you intend to count them all.
The moon is already beneath our feet. The time allotted to us is short, and there is more to see than what lies before you."
I replied: "If you had understood the reason I was looking, you might have allowed me to stay longer."
Meanwhile my Guide walked on, and I followed, making my answer as I went, adding: "Inside that cavity
Where I fixed my eyes so intently, I think a spirit of my own blood weeps for the sin that costs so dearly down there."
My Master said: "Do not break your thoughts upon him any longer. Turn your mind elsewhere and let him stay.
I saw him below the little bridge, pointing at you with his finger and threatening fiercely. I heard them call him Geri del Bello.
You were so completely absorbed at that moment by the one who once held Hautefort that you did not look that way, and so he departed."
"O my Guide," I said, "his violent death, which has not yet been avenged by anyone who shares in the shame,
Made him scornful. That is why he left, I imagine, without speaking to me — and it makes me pity him all the more."
We spoke of this until we reached the first point on the ridge from which the next valley would be visible, all the way to the bottom, if there were more light.
When we were directly above the last cloister of Malebolge, so that its lay-brothers became visible to us,
Piercing cries of lamentation struck me from every side — arrows tipped with compassion — and I covered my ears with my hands.
If all the diseases from the hospitals of Valdichiana between July and September, and from the Maremma and Sardinia,
Were gathered into a single ditch, the suffering and stench would be like what we found here — the reek of putrefying limbs.
We had descended to the furthest bank along the long ridge, still keeping to the left, and my sight grew sharper
As I peered toward the bottom, where the minister of the Almighty — infallible Justice — punishes the forgers she has registered here.
I do not think it was a sadder sight when all the people of Aegina fell sick, when the air was so thick with pestilence
That every animal, down to the smallest worm, perished, and afterward the ancient race, as the poets affirm,
Was restored from the seed of ants — than it was to see the spirits languishing in heaps through that dark valley.
Some lay on their bellies, some on their backs. Others crawled along the wretched road, shifting themselves as best they could.
We moved forward step by step in silence, watching and listening to the sick, who lacked the strength to raise their bodies.
I saw two leaning against each other, the way plates lean together when set to warm, covered from head to foot with scabs.
I never saw a stable boy — hurrying because his master waits, or because he is fighting sleep — ply a currycomb as fast
As each of those two raked his own skin with his nails, driven by the ferocious itch that nothing else could relieve.
Their nails dragged the scabs off like a knife scraping the scales from a bream or any other fish with large scales.
"You there, peeling yourself with your fingers and using them as pincers," my Guide said to one of them,
"Tell me whether any Italian is among the souls in here — and may your nails last for all eternity at this work."
"We are both Italians, wasted as you see us," one replied, weeping. "But who are you, asking about us?"
