My Guide said: "I am one who descends with this living man from ledge to ledge, and my purpose is to show him Hell."
Their mutual support broke apart. Trembling, each turned toward me, along with others who had overheard.
The good Master drew close to me and said: "Tell them whatever you wish." And since he wanted me to, I began:
"So may your memory not be stolen from the minds of men in the first world, but survive beneath many suns,
Tell me who you are and of what people. Do not let your loathsome, foul punishment make you afraid to reveal yourselves to me."
One answered: "I was from Arezzo. Alberto of Siena had me burned, but what I died for is not what brought me here.
It is true that I said to him, joking, that I could fly through the air. And he, full of vanity but short on sense,
Wanted me to show him the art. Just because I could not make him a Daedalus, he had me burned by the one who treated him like a son.
But to this last of the ten ditches, Minos — who cannot err — condemned me for the alchemy I practiced in the world."
I said to the Poet: "Was there ever a people as vain as the Sienese? Certainly not even the French come close."
The other leper, hearing me, replied: "Except for Stricca, who knew how to spend in moderation,
And Niccolo, who first discovered the costly cult of the clove in the garden where such seed takes root,
And except for the company in which Caccia d'Asciano squandered his vineyard and his woods, and the Blockhead showed his wit.
But so that you know who supports you against the Sienese, sharpen your eye and look at me closely,
So you will see that I am the shade of Capocchio, who falsified metals through alchemy. And you must remember, if I recognize you rightly,
How skilled an ape of nature I once was."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXX
paragraphs: In the time when Juno was enraged against the Theban royal blood, because of Semele — as she showed more than once —
Athamas was driven to such madness that, seeing his wife approach carrying their two sons, one on each arm,
He cried: "Spread the nets so I can catch the lioness and cubs as they pass!" Then he stretched out his pitiless claws
And seized the one called Learchus, swung him around, and dashed him against a rock. She drowned herself with her other burden.
And when Fortune brought down the all-daring pride of the Trojans, so that both king and kingdom were destroyed,
Hecuba — wretched, captive, and enslaved — after she saw Polyxena slaughtered, and then discovered
Her Polydorus dead on the seashore, went mad with grief and howled like a dog — so completely had sorrow wrenched her mind.
But neither the furies of Thebes nor those of Troy were ever seen to be so cruel — not in goading beasts, much less human limbs —
As the two pale, naked shades I saw running and biting, the way a pig does when it bursts from its pen.
One fell upon Capocchio and sank its fangs into his neck, dragging him so that his belly scraped along the hard bottom.
The Aretine who remained, trembling, said to me: "That goblin is Gianni Schicchi, and he goes around in a frenzy, savaging others like that."
I said: "Oh — so may the other one not sink its teeth in you — please, before it runs off, tell me who it is."
He replied: "That is the ancient soul of wicked Myrrha, who became her own father's lover, in defiance of all right.
She came to sin with him by disguising herself in another's form, just as the other one who runs off over there
Dared to impersonate Buoso Donati, making a will and giving the testament proper legal form, so he could win the prize mare of the herd."
After those two raging souls, on whom I had kept my eyes fixed, had passed, I turned to look at the other ill-born spirits.
I saw one who would have looked like a lute, if only his groin had been cut off at the point where the body forks.
The heavy dropsy, which distorts the limbs so grotesquely with its badly processed fluids that the face no longer matches the belly,
Forced him to hold his lips apart like a man sick with fever, who from thirst curls one lip toward the chin and the other upward.
"O you who are in this terrible world without any punishment — and I do not know why," he said to us, "look and take note
Of the misery of Master Adam. While alive, I had everything I wanted. Now, alas, I crave a single drop of water.
The little streams that from the green hills of the Casentino flow down into the Arno, making their channels cool and moist,
Stand always before me — and not in vain, for the image of them parches me far more than the disease that wastes my face.
The rigid Justice that probes me uses the very place where I sinned to drive my sighs faster.
There is Romena, where I counterfeited the currency stamped with the Baptist's image — for which I left my body burned above.
But if I could see the miserable soul of Guido, or Alessandro, or their brother here inside this ditch, I would not trade the sight for the fountain of Branda.
One of them is already here, if the raging shades who circle this place speak true. But what good is that to me, since my limbs are bound?
If only I were light enough to move just one inch in a hundred years, I would already have set out on the path,
Searching for him among these disfigured people, even though the ditch circles eleven miles around and is no less than half a mile across.
Because of them I am in this family. They induced me to stamp the florins that contained three carats of alloy."
I said: "Who are those two wretched souls steaming like wet hands in winter, lying close together on your right side?"
He answered: "I found them here when I rained down into this ditch, and they have not stirred since, and I doubt they ever will.
One is the false woman who accused Joseph. The other is the lying Sinon, the Greek from Troy. The burning fever makes them reek like that."
One of them, offended perhaps at being named so contemptuously, struck Adam on his taut, drum-like belly with his fist.
It boomed like a drum. Master Adam struck him in the face with his arm, which was no less hard,
Saying: "Though I am too heavy to move, I have an arm free for occasions like this."
The other answered: "It was not so free when you walked to the fire. But it was ready enough when you were counterfeiting coins."
The dropsied one replied: "Now you speak truth. But you were not so truthful a witness when you were asked for the truth at Troy."
"If I spoke falsely, you falsified the coin," said Sinon. "I am here for a single sin — but you for more than any other demon."
"Remember the horse, perjurer," replied the one with the swollen belly, "and let it torment you that the whole world knows."
"Let the thirst that cracks your tongue torment you," said the Greek, "and the foul water that makes your belly a hedge before your eyes."
The counterfeiter answered: "Your mouth gapes open for its own harm, as always. If I am thirsty and swollen with fluid,
You burn with fever and your head aches. You would not need much invitation to lick the mirror of Narcissus."
I was standing there completely absorbed in listening when my Master said: "Go on, keep staring! A little more and I will quarrel with you."
When I heard anger in his voice, I turned to him with such shame that even now the memory of it makes me blush.
Like a man who dreams he is in trouble, and while dreaming wishes it were only a dream, longing for what already is as if it were not,
So I became — unable to speak, wanting to apologize, and already apologizing, though I did not realize it.
"Less shame would wash away a greater fault than yours," my Master said. "So unburden yourself of all this sadness.
And remember that I am always at your side, should it happen again that fortune places you where people are locked in quarrels like this.
The wish to listen to such things is a base desire."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXXI
paragraphs: One and the same tongue first stung me, making both cheeks burn with its rebuke, and then offered me the medicine.
So I hear that the spear of Achilles — inherited from his father — was the cause first of a grievous wound and then of a healing gift.
We turned our backs on that wretched valley and climbed the embankment that rings it, crossing it without a word.
There it was neither night nor day, so that my sight reached only a short distance ahead. But I heard the blast of a horn so loud
That it would have made any thunder seem faint. My eyes, following its sound backward, were drawn to a single point.
After the disastrous rout in which Charlemagne lost his holy campaign, Roland's horn did not sound so terrible.
I had barely turned my head that way when I seemed to see many tall towers. I said: "Master, what city is this?"
He replied: "Because you are peering through the darkness at too great a distance, your imagination is deceiving you.
When you arrive there, you will see clearly how much the senses are tricked by distance. So push yourself a little faster."
Then he took me tenderly by the hand and said: "Before we go further, so that the reality may seem less strange to you,
Know that those are not towers but giants. They stand in the well, around the rim, each one visible from the navel up."
As when fog is lifting, little by little the eye begins to make out what the mist had hidden,
So, as I pierced through that dense, dark air, approaching the edge step by step, my error fled and fear took its place.
For just as Montereggione crowns itself with towers on its circular walls, so the rim surrounding this well
Was turreted with the upper halves of terrible giants — the ones Jove still threatens from heaven whenever he thunders.
Already I could make out the face, shoulders, chest, a large part of the belly, and both arms hanging at the sides of one of them.
Nature certainly did well when she stopped creating animals like these, depriving Mars of such executors.
And if she does not repent of making elephants and whales, whoever looks at the matter carefully will find her all the more wise and just for it.
For where intellect is added to malice and power, human beings have no defense.
His face appeared as long and wide as the pine cone at Saint Peter's in Rome. The rest of his bones were proportional.
The bank, which served as an apron from his waist down, left so much of him exposed above that three men from Friesland, stacked on top of each other, would not have reached his hair.
For I could see thirty great spans of him below the place where a man buckles his cloak.
"Raphel mai amech izabi almi!" the savage mouth began to bellow — an utterance for which sweeter psalms would not have been fitting.
My Guide called to him: "Stupid soul! Stick to your horn and vent yourself with that when rage or passion seizes you.
Feel around your neck and you will find the belt that holds it. See it there, strapped across your enormous chest, you confused creature."
Then he said to me: "He condemns himself with his own gibberish. That is Nimrod, whose wicked idea is the reason the world no longer shares a single language.
Let us leave him and not waste our breath. Every language is as meaningless to him as his is to everyone else."
So we traveled on further, turning left, and a crossbow-shot away we found another giant, far more fierce and enormous.
What master had bound him I cannot say, but his right arm was pinned behind him and his left in front,
Lashed with chains that wound around his exposed upper body from the neck down five full turns.
"This proud one tried to test his strength against almighty Jove," my Guide said, "and this is his reward.
His name is Ephialtes. He showed his great might when the giants rose against the gods. The arms he wielded then he will never move again."
I said: "If possible, I would like these eyes of mine to experience the immeasurable Briareus."
He replied: "You will see Antaeus nearby — he can speak and is unbound, and he will set us at the bottom of all sin.
The one you wish to see is much farther off. He is bound and made like this one, except that he looks even more ferocious."
No earthquake ever shook a tower so violently as Ephialtes suddenly shook himself.
Then I feared death more than ever, and the fear alone would have been enough to kill me, had I not seen the chains holding him fast.
We went further and came to Antaeus, who rose five full ells above the well's edge, not counting his head.
"O you who, in the fortunate valley where Scipio became the heir of glory by routing Hannibal and all his forces,
Once brought a thousand lions as your prey, and who — had you been present at the great war alongside your brothers —
Some still believe the sons of Earth would have won the victory: set us down below, there where the cold locks up Cocytus.
Do not send us to Tityus or Typhoeus. This living man can give what is longed for here. So stoop down, and do not curl your lip.
He can still restore your fame in the world above, for he lives, and expects a long life yet — unless Grace calls him home early."
So spoke my Master. And in haste the giant stretched out his hands — the hands whose crushing grip Hercules once felt — and seized my Guide.
When Virgil felt himself gripped, he called to me: "Come close, so I can hold you." Then he made one bundle of himself and me.
As the leaning tower of the Garisenda appears to someone standing beneath its tilted side when a cloud passes above it, making the tower seem to topple,
So Antaeus appeared to me as I watched him bend — and in that moment I could have wished to take some other route.
But gently he set us down in the abyss that swallows Judas along with Lucifer. He did not linger in that stooped position,
But rose up straight again, like a mast in a ship.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXXII
paragraphs: If I had verses as rough and grating as would befit this dismal pit, on which all the other rocks press their weight,
I would squeeze out the essence of my vision more fully. But since I do not have them, it is not without fear that I bring myself to speak.
For to describe the very bottom of the universe is no joke — not a task for a tongue that still cries 'Mama' and 'Papa.'
But may those Ladies aid my verse who aided Amphion in walling Thebes, so that the words do not fall short of the reality.
O you wretched rabble above all others, in a place so hard to describe — it would have been better for you to have been born sheep or goats!
When we were down in the dark well, far below the giant's feet, and I was still gazing up at the towering wall above,
I heard a voice say: "Watch where you step! Be careful not to trample the heads of these tired, miserable brothers!"
I turned around and saw beneath me and before me a lake that looked like glass from the frost — not like water at all.
Never did the Danube in Austria make so thick a cover of ice in winter, nor the Don beneath its frigid sky,
As there was here. If the mountains of Tambernich or Pietrapana had fallen on it, the edge would not even have creaked.
And as a frog sits with its muzzle poking above the water to croak, at the season when the peasant girl often dreams of gleaning,
So the wretched shades were frozen in the ice up to the point where shame shows on the face, their teeth chattering with a sound like storks.
Every face was turned downward. The cold from their mouths and the grief from their eyes bore witness to their suffering.
After I had looked around a little, I glanced down and saw two pressed so close together that the hair on their heads was tangled.
"Tell me, you who press your chests together so tightly — who are you?" I said. They craned their necks upward, and when they raised their faces to me,
Their eyes, which had been merely damp inside, spilled tears over the lids — and the frost instantly froze those tears, locking them shut again.
No clamp ever bound wood to wood so tightly. They butted each other like rams, such fury overcame them.
And another one, who had lost both ears to the cold, still looking down, said: "Why do you stare at us so intently?
If you want to know who these two are, the valley down which the Bisenzio flows belonged to them and to their father, Albert.
They came from one body. You can search all of Caina and you will not find a shade more worthy of being set in ice —
Not the one whose breast and shadow were pierced by a single blow from Arthur's hand, not Focaccia, and not this one who blocks my view
With his head so that I cannot see past him — whose name was Sassol Mascheroni. If you are Tuscan, you know well who he was.
And so you do not make me talk any longer, know that I was Camicione de' Pazzi, and I am waiting for Carlino to come and make me look better by comparison."
Then I saw a thousand faces turned purple with cold — and the memory still makes me shudder, and always will, at frozen pools.
As we made our way toward the center, where all weight converges, and I was shivering in the eternal shadow,
Whether it was will, fate, or chance, I do not know, but as I walked among the heads, I kicked one hard in the face.
He wailed: "Why are you trampling me? Unless you have come to add to the vengeance of Montaperti, why do you assault me?"
I said: "Master, wait here for me. I need to clear up a doubt through this one. Then you can hurry me along as fast as you like."
My Leader stopped. I spoke to the one who was still cursing violently: "Who are you, rebuking others so harshly?"
"And who are you," he shot back, "walking through Antenora, kicking people's faces? If you were alive, that would be too much."
I replied: "I am alive. And it could be valuable to you, if you want fame — for me to place your name among my other notes."
He answered: "I want the opposite. Get away from me and stop pestering me. You flatter badly in this frozen hollow."
Then I grabbed him by the hair at the back of his skull and said: "Either you name yourself, or I will not leave a hair on your head."
He replied: "Even if you strip me bald, I will not tell you who I am or show you my face, not if you stomp on my head a thousand times."
I already had his hair twisted in my hand and had pulled out more than one clump, while he barked with his eyes fixed downward,
When another one shouted: "What is the matter with you, Bocca? Is it not enough to chatter with your jaws? Now you have to bark too? What devil has got into you?"
"Now," I said, "I do not need you to speak, accursed traitor. To your shame, I will carry true news of you to the world."
"Go away," he replied, "and tell whatever you like. But do not be silent, if you get out of here, about the one who just now had his tongue so ready.
He weeps here for the silver of the French. 'I saw,' you can say, 'the one from Duera, down where sinners shiver in the cold.'
If you are asked who else was there, you have beside you the one from Beccaria, whose throat Florence cut open.
Gianni del Soldanieri is over there, I think, along with Ganelon and Tebaldello, who opened Faenza's gates while the city slept."
We had already moved on from him when I saw two frozen in a single hole, one head fitted over the other like a hood.
Just as a starving man devours bread, the upper one had set his teeth on the other at the place where the brain meets the nape of the neck.
Not otherwise did Tydeus gnaw the temples of Menalippus in fury than this one gnawed the skull and everything beneath.
"O you who show by such a bestial sign your hatred for the one you are eating," I said, "tell me why, with this agreement:
That if your complaint against him is just, knowing who you both are and what he did to you, I will repay you for it in the world above,
If the tongue with which I speak does not go dry."

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXXIII
paragraphs: That sinner raised his mouth from his grim meal, wiping it on the hair of the head he had been devouring from behind.
Then he began: "You ask me to renew a desperate grief that wrings my heart even to think of, before I speak of it.
But if my words can be seeds that bear fruit of infamy for the traitor I gnaw, then you will see me speak and weep together.
I do not know who you are, or how you came down here, but when I hear you, you seem truly Florentine.
You should know that I was Count Ugolino, and this one is Archbishop Ruggieri. Now I will tell you why I am such a neighbor to him.
That through his treacherous scheming I was taken prisoner and then put to death — that much I need not say.
But what you cannot have heard — how cruel my death was — you will hear now, and judge whether he has wronged me.
A narrow slot in the tower that now bears the name of Hunger because of me — where others must yet be locked away —
Had already shown me several moons through its opening when I had the evil dream that tore the veil of the future for me.
This man appeared as lord and master, hunting the wolf and its cubs on the mountain that blocks the Pisans' view of Lucca.
He had sent Gualandi, Sismondi, and Lanfranchi ahead with lean, eager, well-trained hounds.
After a short chase, both the father wolf and its young seemed exhausted to me, and I thought I saw their flanks ripped open by sharp fangs.
When I woke before dawn, I heard my sons — who were with me — moaning in their sleep and crying for bread.
You are cruel indeed if you do not grieve already, thinking of what my heart foresaw. And if you do not weep now, what do you ever weep at?
They were awake now, and the hour was approaching when food was usually brought to us. But each was filled with dread because of his dream.
I heard the lower door of the horrible tower being nailed shut. Without a word, I stared into the faces of my sons.
I did not weep. I turned to stone inside. They wept. And my little Anselm said: 'Father, you stare so — what is wrong?'
Still I shed no tear, nor did I answer — all that day, nor the night that followed, until another sun rose on the world.
When a thin sliver of light crept into that agonizing prison, and I saw my own haggard face reflected in their four faces,
I bit both my hands in anguish. And they, thinking I did it from hunger, suddenly stood up
And said: 'Father, it would cause us far less pain if you ate us. You clothed us in this poor flesh — now strip it off.'
I calmed myself then, so as not to make them sadder. That day we were all silent, and the next. O hard earth, why did you not open?
When the fourth day came, Gaddo threw himself at my feet, crying: 'Father, why don't you help me?'
There he died. And as you see me here, I watched the other three fall, one by one, between the fifth day and the sixth. Then I,
Already blind, began groping over each of them, calling their names for three days after they were dead. Then hunger did what grief could not."
When he had said this, with his eyes rolling wildly, he seized the wretched skull again with his teeth, which gnawed the bone as strong as a dog's.
O Pisa, disgrace of the peoples of the fair land where 'si' is heard! Since your neighbors are slow to punish you,
Let the islands of Capraia and Gorgona shift and dam the mouth of the Arno, so that every soul in you may drown!
For even if Count Ugolino had the reputation of betraying your castles, you had no right to put his sons on such a cross.
Their youth made them innocent — you modern Thebes! — young Uguccione and Brigata, and the other two my song has already named.
We went further on, to where the ice roughly encases a different group of people — not turned facedown, but all of them reversed, facing upward.
The very act of weeping prevents them from weeping. Grief, blocked by a barrier at the eyes, turns inward to deepen the anguish.
Because the first tears form a cluster and fill the hollow beneath the brow like a visor of crystal,
And although all feeling had abandoned my face from the cold, as if it were callused over,
I still thought I felt some wind. I said: "Master, what causes this? Is not every vapor extinguished down here?"
He answered: "Soon you will be where your own eyes will answer that question, when you see what sends this blast downward."
One of the wretches encased in the frozen crust cried out to us: "O souls so merciless that you have been given this last outpost,
Lift the hard veils from my eyes so that I may vent the grief that fills my heart a little, before the tears freeze again."
I said: "If you want my help, tell me who you were. And if I do not free you, may I go to the very bottom of the ice."
He answered: "I am Friar Alberigo — the one of the evil fruit from the evil garden. Here I receive a date for my fig."
"Oh," I said, "are you dead already?" He replied: "How my body fares up in the world, I have no knowledge.
This Ptolomaea has such a privilege that the soul often falls here before Atropos cuts its thread.
And so that you may more willingly peel these glassy tears from my face, know that the moment any soul commits betrayal,
As I did, a demon takes possession of the body and rules it for the remainder of its natural life.
The soul plunges down into this cistern. The body above may still seem to be alive — as perhaps is the case with the shade who winters here behind me.
You should know this, if you have just come down. He is Ser Branca d'Oria, and many years have passed since he was locked up here."
I said: "I think you are deceiving me. Branca d'Oria is not dead yet. He eats, and drinks, and sleeps, and puts on clothes."
He replied: "In the ditch above, where the sticky pitch boils in the Malebranche's domain, Michel Zanche had not yet arrived
When this one left a devil in his place in his own body, and so did one of his relatives, who committed the betrayal with him.
But now, reach out your hand. Open my eyes." And I did not open them. To be rude to him was courtesy.
O Genoese — people at odds with every virtue and filled with every vice — why have you not been swept from the world?
For alongside the vilest spirit of Romagna, I found one of yours whose soul, for his deeds, already bathes in Cocytus,
While his body still appears alive above.

chapters.title: Inferno, Canto XXXIV
paragraphs: "'The banners of the King of Hell advance toward us.' Look ahead," said my Master, "and see if you can make him out."
As when a thick fog settles, or when our hemisphere darkens into night, and far off a windmill appears, its arms turning,
Something like that I thought I saw. Then, for shelter from the wind, I drew behind my Guide — there was no other cover.
I was now — and I put it into verse with dread — where the shades were entirely covered by the ice, showing through it like straws in glass.
Some lie flat, others stand upright — this one head-up, that one soles-up. Another bends like a bow, face to feet.
When we had gone far enough forward that it pleased my Master to show me the creature who was once the most beautiful of all beings,
He stepped aside and stopped me, saying: "Behold Dis. Behold the place where you must arm yourself with courage."
How frozen and faint I became — do not ask, reader, for I will not write it. All language would be inadequate.
I did not die, and yet I did not remain alive. Think for yourself, if you have any wit, what I became, deprived of both.
The emperor of the kingdom of grief jutted from the ice from mid-chest up. I would compare better with a giant
Than giants compare with his arms alone. Consider how vast the whole must be, if it is proportional to such a limb.
If he was once as beautiful as he is now hideous, and still raised his brow against his Maker, well may all sorrow proceed from him.
What a marvel it was to me when I saw three faces on his head! The one in front was crimson red.
The other two were joined to it above the middle of each shoulder, and all three met at the crest.
The right face seemed between white and yellow. The left was the color of those who come from where the Nile flows down into its valley.
Beneath each face two enormous wings spread out — wings befitting such a monstrous bird. I never saw sails at sea so large.
They had no feathers but were fashioned like a bat's. He flapped them constantly, generating three winds.
Those three winds kept all of Cocytus frozen solid. From six eyes he wept, and down three chins tears and bloody drool trickled.
In each mouth he crunched a sinner between his teeth, like a flax-brake, so that he tormented three at once.
For the one in front, the biting was nothing compared to the clawing — at times his back was stripped entirely of skin.
"The soul up there suffering the greatest punishment," said my Master, "is Judas Iscariot. His head is inside, and he kicks his legs outside.
Of the other two, who hang head downward, the one dangling from the black jowl is Brutus — see how he writhes without a word.
The other, who looks so powerfully built, is Cassius. But night is rising again, and it is time for us to leave. We have seen everything."
As he wished, I clasped my arms around his neck. He seized the right moment and place, and when the wings were spread wide apart,
He caught hold of the shaggy sides and descended from tuft to tuft of hair, between the matted fur and the frozen crust.
When we reached the point where the thigh turns, right at the thickest part of the haunch, my Guide, with labor and hard-drawn breath,
Swung his head around to where his feet had been, and clung to the hair like a man climbing — so that I thought we were heading back into Hell.
"Hold tight," panted the Master, exhausted, "for by stairs like these we must depart from so much evil."
Then he emerged through an opening in the rock, sat me down on the rim, and carefully picked his way toward me.
I raised my eyes, expecting to see Lucifer as I had left him. Instead I saw his legs held upward.
If I was bewildered then, let the dull-witted judge — those who cannot see what the point was that I had passed beyond.
"Stand up," said my Master. "The road is long, the way is hard, and the sun has already returned to mid-morning."
The place where we stood was no palace hallway, but a natural dungeon with an uneven floor and almost no light.
"Before I tear myself from the abyss, Master," I said, standing up, "speak a little to free me from my confusion.
Where is the ice? And why is he fixed upside down? And how has the sun traveled from evening to morning in so short a time?"
He replied: "You still imagine you are on the other side of the center, where I grasped the hair of the evil worm that bores through the world.
You were on that side as long as I descended. When I turned around, you passed through the point toward which all weight is drawn from every direction.
Now you are beneath the hemisphere opposite the one that covers the great dry land — under whose sky
The Man who was born and lived without sin was put to death. Your feet rest on the small sphere that forms the other face of Judecca.
Here it is morning when it is evening there. And the one whose hair made a stairway for us remains fixed just as he was before.
On this side he fell from Heaven. All the land that once extended here fled from him in terror, veiled itself beneath the sea,
And came to our hemisphere. And perhaps the land on this side, to escape him, rushed upward and left this empty space behind."
There is a place below, as far from Beelzebub as his tomb extends, known not by sight but by the sound
Of a small stream that trickles down through a channel it has carved in the rock, winding gently and falling gradually.
My Guide and I entered that hidden path to make our way back to the bright world. Without stopping to rest,
We climbed, he first and I second, until through a round opening I saw some of the beautiful things that Heaven bears.
And from there we emerged to see the stars again.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto I
paragraphs: To sail over better waters, the small vessel of my genius now hoists its sail, leaving behind a sea so cruel.
And of that second kingdom I will sing, where the human spirit purges itself and becomes worthy to ascend to Heaven.
But here let dead poetry rise again. O sacred Muses, since I am yours, and here let Calliope rise somewhat higher,
Accompanying my song with the sound that struck the wretched magpies so hard that they despaired of pardon.
A sweet sapphire color was gathering in the cloudless face of the pure sky, from horizon to the first circle of stars,
And brought delight back to my eyes the moment I emerged from the dead air that had filled both my eyes and chest with sadness.
The beautiful planet that inspires love was making the whole east smile, veiling the constellation of the Fishes in her escort.
I turned to the right and fixed my gaze on the southern pole. I saw four stars never seen before except by the first people who lived.
The sky seemed to rejoice in their flames. O widowed northern hemisphere, deprived forever of that sight!
When I withdrew my eyes from them and turned a little toward the northern pole, where the Wain had already disappeared,
I saw beside me an old man standing alone, his face worthy of such reverence that no son owes more to his father.
He wore a long beard, streaked with white, like the hair that fell in two strands on his chest.
The rays of those four sacred stars so adorned his face with light that I saw him as if the sun were shining directly on him.
"Who are you, who have fled the eternal prison, traveling against the blind river?" he said, shaking those venerable locks.
"Who guided you? Who was your lamp, leading you out of the deep night that keeps the infernal valley forever black?
Are the laws of the abyss broken? Or has some new decree been issued in Heaven, that you, though damned, come to my cliffs?"
My Guide seized me and, with words, hands, and gestures, made my knees and brow bow in reverence.
Then he answered: "I did not come on my own. A Lady descended from Heaven, and at her prayers I gave this man my company.
But since you wish our true condition to be more fully revealed, my will cannot refuse you.
This man has not yet seen his final evening. But through his folly he came so close to it that very little time remained to turn him around.
As I said, I was sent to rescue him, and there was no other way than the one I have taken.
I have shown him all the souls of perdition. Now I intend to show him those spirits who purge themselves under your guardianship.
How I brought him here would be long to tell. A power descends from on high that helps me lead him to see and hear you.
Now may it please you to grant his coming. He seeks Liberty, which is so precious — as he knows who gives his life for her.
You know it well. For her sake, death in Utica was not bitter to you, where you left behind the garment that will shine so brightly on the great day.
The eternal decrees are not broken by us. This man is alive, and Minos does not bind me. I come from the circle where the chaste
Eyes of your Marcia still silently pray you, O holy breast, to hold her as your own. For love of her, then, be gracious to us.
Allow us to pass through your seven realms. I will carry your kindness back to her, if you think it worthy to be mentioned there below."
"Marcia was so pleasing to my eyes while I was on the other side," he said, "that every grace she asked of me, I granted.
Now that she dwells beyond the evil river, she can no longer move me, by the law that was made when I was brought forth from there.
But if a Lady of Heaven moves and directs you, as you say, no flattery is needed. It is enough that you ask me for her sake.
Go, then, and make sure you gird this man with a smooth rush and wash his face, cleansing every stain from it.
For it would not be fitting for eyes clouded by any mist to approach the first Angel of Paradise.
This little island bears rushes on its muddy shore below, down where the waves beat against it.
No other plant that puts forth leaf or hardens can survive there, because it does not yield to the blows.
Do not return this way afterward. The rising sun will show you where to take the mountain by an easier ascent."
With that he vanished. I rose without a word, drew close to my Guide, and fixed my eyes on him.
He began: "Son, follow my steps. Let us turn back, for this plain slopes downward toward its lower edge."
Dawn was conquering the last hour of darkness, which fled before it. In the distance I could make out the trembling of the sea.
We walked along the lonely plain like a man who returns to a lost road and feels he is walking in vain until he finds it.
When we reached the place where the dew still resists the sun — in a spot where shadow keeps it from evaporating quickly —
My Master gently spread both his hands upon the dewy grass. And I, understanding his intent,
Held out my tear-stained cheeks to him. There he uncovered the true color that Hell had hidden beneath its grime.
Then we came down to the deserted shore, which has never seen anyone navigate its waters and return.
There he girded me as the other had instructed. And — wonder of wonders! — the humble plant, the very instant he plucked it,
Sprang up again at once in the same spot where he had pulled it out.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto II
paragraphs: The sun had already reached the horizon whose meridian circle passes over Jerusalem at its highest point,
And Night, revolving opposite to him, was rising from the Ganges with the Scales — which fall from her hand when she grows too long —
So that the white and rosy cheeks of beautiful Aurora were, where I stood, turning to orange with advancing age.
We were still standing on the shore, like travelers who think about the road ahead — their hearts already journeying while their bodies stay.
And look — just as Mars glows fiery red through the thick vapors near the ocean floor at the approach of dawn,
A light appeared to me — may I see it again! — coming across the sea so swiftly that no wing could match its speed.
When I had briefly turned my eyes away to question my Guide, I saw it again, brighter and larger.
Then on each side something white appeared — I could not tell what — and beneath it, gradually, another shape emerged.
My Master had not yet spoken when the first whiteness unfolded into wings. But the moment he clearly recognized the pilot,
He cried: "Quick, down on your knees! Behold the Angel of God! Fold your hands! From now on you will see such ministers!
See how he scorns human tools — needing neither oar nor any sail but his own wings between such distant shores.
See how he holds them pointed toward heaven, fanning the air with those eternal pinions that never shed or change like mortal hair!"
As the divine Bird drew nearer and nearer, he grew more radiant — so bright that up close the eye could not bear it.
I looked down. He reached shore in a small, swift vessel, so light that it drew no water at all.
The celestial Pilot stood at the stern. Blessedness seemed written on his face. More than a hundred spirits sat within.
"In exitu Israel de Aegypto!" they all chanted together in one voice, along with everything else in that psalm.
Then he made the sign of the holy cross over them. They all cast themselves onto the shore, and he departed as swiftly as he had come.
The crowd that remained seemed unfamiliar with the place, gazing around on every side like people encountering something entirely new.
Daylight was streaming forth everywhere. The sun had chased Capricorn from the mid-heaven with his bright arrows,
When the newly arrived souls raised their faces to us and said: "If you know the way, show us the path up to the mountain."
Virgil answered: "You may think we know this place, but we are strangers here just as you are.
We arrived only a little while before you, by a different way — one so rough and steep that climbing from here will feel like play."
The souls who had noticed from my breathing that I was still alive turned pale with astonishment.
Like people crowding around a messenger who carries an olive branch, eager to hear the news and not shy about pressing close,
So all those fortunate spirits stood fixed on me, as if they had forgotten to go and make themselves fair.
One of them came forward to embrace me with such great affection that it moved me to do the same.
O empty shades, solid only in appearance! Three times I clasped my hands behind him, and three times they returned to my own chest.
I must have shown my bewilderment in my face, for the shade smiled and drew back — and I, pursuing him, pressed forward.
Gently he told me to stop. Then I recognized who it was, and I begged him to pause awhile and speak with me.
He replied: "Just as I loved you in my mortal body, so I love you free of it. That is why I stop. But why are you making this journey?"
"My own Casella! I make this journey so that I may return to this place again," I said. "But why has so much time been taken from you?"
He answered: "No wrong has been done to me. If the one who takes whom he will and when he will has many times refused me passage,
His will is made from a just will. Indeed, for the past three months he has taken everyone who wished to board, in perfect peace.
So when I turned toward that shore where the waters of the Tiber grow salty, he graciously received me.
His wing is now directed toward that outlet, because those who are not bound for Acheron always gather there."
I said: "If no new law strips from you the memory or practice of the love-songs that used to calm all my desires,
May it please you to comfort my soul with them, which has grown so weary traveling here in its body."
"Love that speaks within my mind" — he began so melodiously that the sweetness still sounds within me.
My Master, and I, and all the people with him seemed as contented as if nothing else could touch our minds.
We stood motionless, rapt in his music, when suddenly the stern old man appeared, crying: "What is this, you laggard spirits?
What negligence, what loitering is this? Run to the mountain and strip off the scales that keep God from being manifest to you!"
Like doves gathered together at their feeding, quiet and showing none of their usual skittishness,
Who, if something appears that frightens them, suddenly abandon the food, seized by a greater care —
So I saw that new company drop the song and head toward the hillside, like people going without knowing where.
And our own departure was no less hurried.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto III
paragraphs: Although their sudden flight had scattered them across the plain, all turning toward the mountain where reason spurs us,
I pressed close to my faithful companion. How could I have kept my course without him? Who would have led me up the mountain?
He seemed stung by self-reproach. O noble conscience, clean of stain! How sharp a thorn is even a small fault to you!
When his feet had shed the haste that strips dignity from every act, my mind, which until then had been held tight,
Released its powers as if in delight, and I raised my eyes to the hill that lifts itself highest toward heaven.
The sun, blazing red behind us, was broken before me into the shape formed by my body blocking its rays.
I turned to one side in fear of being abandoned when I saw the ground darkened only in front of me.
My Comforter turned fully around and said: "Why do you still distrust? Do you not believe I am with you, guiding you?
It is already evening there where the body in which I once cast a shadow is buried. Naples holds it, taken from Brindisi.
Now, if no shadow falls before me, do not marvel at it any more than at the heavens, where one ray does not block another.
To endure torments of heat and cold, bodies like mine are provided by a Power that wills its workings not to be unveiled to us.
He is insane who hopes that our reason can travel the limitless path traced by one Substance in three Persons.
Mortals, be content with the 'because.' For if you had been able to see everything, there would have been no need for Mary to give birth.
And you have seen the fruitless longing of those whose desire would otherwise have been satisfied — but instead is given to them as eternal grief.
I speak of Aristotle, and Plato, and many others." Here he bowed his head, said no more, and remained troubled.
Meanwhile we came to the foot of the mountain. There we found the rock so steep that the nimblest legs would have been useless.
The most remote, most desolate path between Lerici and Turbia is a wide, easy stairway compared to that.
"Who knows which side the mountain slopes gently enough," my Master said, halting, "for someone without wings to climb?"
While he stood with his eyes on the ground, studying the nature of the path, and I looked up around the rock,
On our left appeared a crowd of souls moving their feet in our direction — yet so slowly they seemed not to move at all.
I said to my Master: "Raise your eyes. Over here are people who can advise us, if you cannot find the way yourself."
He looked at them and replied with an open expression: "Let us go to them, for they come slowly. And you, sweet son, hold fast to your hope."
After we had walked a thousand steps, those people were still as far from us as a good thrower could hurl a stone.
Then they all pressed together against the hard face of the high bank, standing motionless and close, like someone who stops in doubt to look around.
"O blessed dead! O spirits already chosen," Virgil began, "by that peace which I believe awaits you all,
Tell us where the mountain slopes gently enough to make the ascent possible. The one who knows most finds it most painful to waste time."
Like sheep coming out of their fold, one, then two, then three — while the others stand timidly with their eyes and noses lowered —
And what the first one does, the others do, pressing against her if she stops, simple and quiet, not knowing why —
Just so I saw the leader of that blessed flock begin to move toward us, modest in face and dignified in step.
As soon as the ones in front saw the light broken on the ground at my right side — my shadow reaching the rock —
They stopped and shrank back a little. All the rest who followed them did the same, without knowing why.
"Without your asking, I will tell you: this is a human body that you see, which is why the sunlight is split on the ground.
Do not be amazed. But believe that not without heavenly power does he attempt to scale this wall."
So said my Master. Those worthy souls replied: "Turn back, then, and enter before us," motioning with the backs of their hands.
And one of them began: "Whoever you are, as you walk turn your eyes this way. Consider whether you ever saw me in the other world."
I turned and looked at him closely. He was blond, handsome, and noble in appearance — but a blow had split one of his eyebrows.
When I humbly denied ever having seen him, he said: "Now look!" and showed me a wound high on his chest.
Then he said with a smile: "I am Manfredi, grandson of the Empress Constance. Therefore I beg you, when you return,
Go to my beautiful daughter — the mother of the honor of Sicily and Aragon — and tell her the truth, if other stories are told.
After my body had been pierced by these two mortal wounds, I gave myself, weeping, to the One who pardons willingly.
My sins had been horrible. But Infinite Goodness has arms so wide that it embraces everyone who turns to it.
If only the pastor of Cosenza, who was sent to hunt me down by Clement, had read this page of God's book with understanding,
My bones would still be at the bridgehead near Benevento, under the protection of a heavy cairn.
Now the rain soaks them and the wind moves them, outside the kingdom, near the Verde, where he transported them with extinguished candles.
But the curse of men cannot destroy Eternal Love — it can always return, as long as hope retains anything green.
It is true that whoever dies in defiance of Holy Church, even if repentant at the last, must wait outside this bank
For thirty times the length of his presumption — unless such a sentence is shortened by righteous prayers.
See now if you can make me happy by telling my good Constance how you have seen me, and about this banishment —
For those on earth can do much to advance us here."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto IV
paragraphs: Whenever delight or pain seizes any one of our faculties, the soul gathers itself entirely into that one,
And seems to neglect every other power. This disproves the error of those who believe that one soul kindles above another inside us.
And so, whenever something is seen or heard that holds the soul intensely focused upon it, time passes and we do not notice,
Because the faculty that listens is one thing, and the faculty that keeps the soul whole is another — the first is bound, the second is free.
I had direct proof of this in listening to and gazing at that spirit. For the sun had climbed a full fifty degrees
Without my noticing it, when we arrived at a place where those souls cried out together: "Here is what you are looking for!"
A farmer often seals a wider gap in his hedge with a single forkful of thorns when the grapes turn dark
Than was the narrow passage through which only my Guide and I climbed, after that company left us.
One climbs San Leo, descends to Noli, and reaches the summit of Bismantova with feet alone. But here a man must fly —
With the swift wings and feathers of great desire, I mean — following the one who gave me hope and lit the way.
We scrambled up through the split rock, the walls pressing us on both sides. Both feet and hands were needed on the ground below.
When we reached the upper rim of the high bank, out on the open slope, I said: "Master, which way do we go?"
He replied: "Do not take a single step downward. Keep climbing the mountain behind me until some wise escort appears."
The summit was so high it defeated the eye. The slope was far steeper than a line drawn from the midpoint of a quadrant to its center.
I was spent with exhaustion when I cried: "O sweet Father, turn and see — I will be left alone if you do not stop!"
"Son, drag yourself up to there," he said, pointing to a ledge a little higher that circled the whole hillside.
His words spurred me so hard that I strained every nerve, scrambling after him until the ledge was beneath my feet.
There we both sat down, facing east — the direction from which we had climbed — for looking back delights everyone.
I first looked down at the low shores, then raised my eyes to the sun, marveling that its light struck us from the left.
The Poet saw I was completely bewildered by the chariot of light entering between us and the north.
He said: "If Castor and Pollux were in the company of that mirror that conducts its light both up and down,
You would see the zodiac's reddish wheel revolving even closer to the Bears — unless it strayed from its ancient path.
If you want to think about how this can be, imagine, concentrating within yourself, Mount Zion and this mountain standing on the earth
So that they share one horizon but opposite hemispheres. That means the road which Phaethon, to his sorrow, could not drive
Must pass on one side of this mountain when it passes on the other side of that — if your mind sees clearly."
"Truly, Master," I said, "I have never seen as clearly as I do now — where my understanding seemed inadequate —
That the middle circle of the heavens' motion, called the Equator in one science, which always lies between the Sun and winter,
Lies as far north of here, for the reason you explain, as the Hebrews used to see it toward the south."
"But if it pleases you, I would gladly know how far we still must go. The hill rises higher than my eyes can reach."
He replied: "This mountain is such that climbing is always hardest at the beginning. The higher you go, the less it hurts.
Therefore, when it feels so pleasant to you that climbing upward is as easy as floating downstream in a boat,
You will have reached the end of this path. There you can expect to rest your panting breath. I will say no more. This much I know for certain."
Just as he finished, a voice nearby said: "Maybe you will need to sit down before that."
At the sound of it we both turned and saw, on our left, a large rock that neither of us had noticed before.
We went over to it. There were people sitting in the shade behind the rock, lounging the way people do when they are being lazy.
One of them, who looked especially worn out, was sitting with his arms around his knees, his head hanging low between them.
"O my sweet Lord," I said, "look at that one — he shows himself more negligent than if Sloth herself were his sister."
He turned toward us and gave us a look, merely lifting his eyes above his thigh, and said: "Well, go on up then, since you are so energetic."
Then I knew who he was. The breathlessness that still quickened my lungs did not stop me from going to him. When I reached him,
He barely raised his head and said: "Did you notice how the sun drives his chariot over your left shoulder?"
His lazy posture and his curt words moved my lips to a slight smile. I said: "Belacqua, I no longer worry
About you. But tell me, why are you sitting here? Are you waiting for an escort, or has your old habit of laziness simply taken hold again?"
He replied: "Brother, what is the use of climbing? God's Angel, who sits at the gate, would not let me through to my torments.
First the heavens must circle around me outside that gate for as long as they did in my lifetime, since I put off my good sighs until the end,
Unless, before that, a prayer from a heart that lives in grace comes to help me. What good are prayers that Heaven does not hear?"
Meanwhile the Poet was already climbing ahead of me, saying: "Come now. See, the sun has touched the meridian, and from the western shore
Night already covers Morocco with her foot."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto V
paragraphs: I had already left those shades behind and was following in the footsteps of my Guide, when from behind, one pointed his finger at me
And shouted: "Look — the sunshine does not seem to strike the ground to the left of that one below, and he walks like a living man!"
I turned at these words and saw them staring in astonishment — at me, at me alone, and at the light that was broken.
"Why does your mind get so caught up," my Master said, "that you slow your pace? What does it matter what they whisper here?
Follow me, and let the people talk. Stand like a solid tower that never sways its top no matter how hard the wind blows.
For the man in whom thought piles upon thought always pushes himself farther from the goal, because the force of one weakens the other."
What could I say but "I am coming"? I said it, coloring slightly with the kind of flush that sometimes makes a man worthy of forgiveness.
Meanwhile, across the mountainside, a group of people came a little ahead of us, singing the Miserere verse by verse.
When they realized that I gave no passage for the sunshine through my body, they changed their song to a long, hoarse "Oh!"
Two of them ran forward like messengers to meet us and demanded: "Tell us about your condition."
My Master said: "You may go back and report to those who sent you that this man's body is real flesh.
If they stopped because they saw his shadow, as I suppose, that is answer enough. Let them honor him — it may benefit them."
I never saw shooting stars streak so fast through clear air at early nightfall, nor August lightning flash through the clouds at sunset,
As these two raced back to the group. Once there, they all wheeled toward us, like a troop charging with loose reins.
"These people pressing toward us are many, and they come to make a request of you," said the Poet. "But keep walking, and listen as you go."
"O soul traveling toward happiness in the same limbs you were born with," they cried as they came, "pause your steps a moment!
Look and see if you recognize any of us, so you can carry news of one of us back to the world. Why are you still walking? Why don't you stop?
We all died by violence, and we were sinners until our final hour. Then light from Heaven made us wise,
So that, repenting and forgiving, we left life at peace with God, who fills our hearts with longing to see Him."
I said: "Though I look at your faces, I do not recognize any of you. But if there is something I can do for you, well-born spirits,
Speak, and I will do it — by that peace which makes me seek it from world to world, following the steps of such a Guide."
One began: "Each of us trusts in your good will without your swearing it, unless inability cuts short your will.
So I, who speak before the others, beg you — if ever you see the land between Romagna and Charles's kingdom —
Be gracious to me with your prayers in Fano, so that worthy intercessions are made for me to purge my heavy sins.
From there I came. But the deep wounds from which the blood poured that held my life were dealt to me in the bosom of the Antenori,
Where I believed myself most safe. The one from Este had it done — he who held me in wrath far beyond what justice warranted.
But if I had fled toward La Mira when I was overtaken at Oriago, I would still be there where people breathe.
I ran to the marshes, and the reeds and mud entangled me. I fell, and there I watched a pool form on the ground from my own veins."
Then another said: "May that desire be fulfilled which draws you up the high mountain! With loving pity, help me with mine.
I was of Montefeltro, I am Buonconte. Neither Giovanna nor any other cares for me, which is why I walk among these with bowed head."
I said: "What force or chance carried you so far from Campaldino that your burial place was never found?"
He answered: "At the foot of the Casentino, a stream called the Archiano crosses, born in the Apennines above the Hermitage.
There, at the place where its name is lost in the Arno, I arrived with a wound in my throat, fleeing on foot, bloodying the ground.
There I lost sight and speech. I ended on the name of Mary, and there I fell — and only my flesh remained.
I will tell the truth, and you repeat it among the living: God's Angel took me, and the one from Hell cried: 'O you from Heaven, why do you rob me?
You carry off the eternal part of him for one little tear! But the other part I will deal with differently!'
You know how moisture gathers in the air and turns to rain the moment it reaches the cold. That evil will, which seeks only evil,
Joined with intellect, and stirred the mist and wind by the power that its nature gave it.
Then, when the day was spent, he covered the valley from Pratomagno to the great ridge with cloud, and made the sky above so heavy
That the saturated air turned to water. Rain fell, and whatever the ground could not absorb rushed into gullies,
Merging into great torrents that raced toward the royal river with such speed that nothing could hold them back.
The raging Archiano found my frozen body at its mouth and swept it into the Arno, undoing the cross my arms had made on my chest
When pain had conquered me. It tumbled me along its banks and over its bed, then buried and covered me with the debris it had carried."
"Please," said a third spirit, following on from the second, "when you have returned to the world, and rested from your long journey,
Remember me — I am La Pia. Siena made me; the Maremma unmade me. He knows it well, the one who,
Having first pledged himself to me, wed me with his ring."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto VI
paragraphs: When the game of dice breaks up, the loser stays behind, sadly replaying the throws, and learns through his grief.
The crowd goes off with the winner. One tugs at him from the front, another from behind, a third presses from the side to be remembered.
He does not stop. He listens to this one and that. Whoever he stretches his hand to stops pressing. And so he fends off the crush.
That is what I was like in that thick crowd — turning my face this way and that, making promises to free myself from them.
There was the Aretine who met his death at the brutal hands of Ghin di Tacco, and the other who drowned while chasing his enemy.
There, with outstretched hands, prayed Federigo Novello, and the Pisan who made the good Marzucco show such fortitude.
I saw Count Orso, and the soul torn from its body by spite and envy, as it said — not for any fault committed:
Pierre de la Brosse, I mean. And let the Lady of Brabant take heed while she is still in this world, lest she end up in a worse flock.
When I was free of every one of those shades, who prayed only that others pray for them to speed their way to blessedness,
I began: "It seems to me, O light of mine, that you explicitly deny in one passage that prayer can bend heaven's decree.
Yet these people pray for exactly that. Is their hope, then, empty? Or am I not understanding your words correctly?"
He replied: "My writing is clear, and the hope of these souls is not deceived, if you look at it with a sound mind.
The height of justice is not brought low because the fire of love fulfills in a single moment what those who dwell here owe.
And in the place where I affirmed that point, prayer could not mend a fault, because the prayer was disconnected from God.
But do not settle such a deep question on your own. Wait until she tells you — she who will be a light between truth and intellect.
I do not know if you understand me: I mean Beatrice. You will see her above, smiling and happy, on the summit of this mountain."
I said: "Good Guide, let us go faster. I am no longer as tired as before. And look — the hillside already casts its shadow."
"We will go as far as we can today," he answered. "But the reality is different from what you imagine.
Before you reach the top, you will see the sun return — the one now hidden by the slope so that you no longer break its light.
But look — over there is a soul stationed all alone, looking toward us. It will point us to the quickest way."
We came to it. O Lombard soul, how proud and disdainful you held yourself! How stately and slow the movement of your eyes!
It said nothing to us but let us approach, watching us only the way a lion watches when it is at rest.
Still, Virgil drew near and asked it to show us the best ascent. It did not answer his question,
But asked us instead about our country and our lives. My gentle Guide began: "Mantua..." And the shade, which had been so withdrawn into itself,
Leapt toward him from where it stood, crying: "O Mantuan, I am Sordello, from your own land!" And they embraced each other.
O Italy, you slave! Ship without a pilot in a great storm! No longer a mistress of provinces, but a brothel!
That noble soul was so quick, at the mere sweet sound of his city's name, to welcome his fellow citizen there.
Yet now your living inhabitants cannot exist without war — and those enclosed by the same wall and moat gnaw at each other!
Search, wretched one, around your shores and then look into your own heart — is there a single part of you that enjoys peace?
What good does it do that Justinian repaired the bridle, if the saddle is empty? Without it, the shame would be less.
You people who should be devout and let Caesar sit in the saddle, if you understood what God prescribes for you —
Look how wild this beast has become from lack of spurs, since you seized the reins instead of letting them be corrected!
O German Albert, who abandon her — this beast that has grown wild and unmanageable — when you should bestride her saddle-bow,
May a just judgment fall from the stars upon your blood! One so strange and so plain that your successor will be terrified.
For you and your father, held back there by greed, have allowed the garden of the Empire to be laid waste.
Come and see the Montagues and the Capulets, the Monaldi and Filippeschi — those already grieving and these full of dread!
Come, cruel one, come and see the oppression of your nobles. Cure their wounds — and you will see how dark Santafiora has become.
Come and see your Rome, who weeps, widowed and alone, crying day and night: "My Caesar, why do you not keep me company?"
Come and see how the people love each other! And if no pity for us moves you, come and feel shame for your own reputation.
And if it is permitted, O highest Jove, who were crucified on earth for us — are Your just eyes turned elsewhere?
Or is this preparation, in the depths of Your counsel, for some good entirely beyond our understanding?
For the cities of Italy are full of tyrants, and every peasant who plays the partisan becomes a Marcellus.
My Florence, you may well be happy with this digression, which does not touch you — thanks to your people, who are so resourceful!
Many have justice in their hearts but are slow to let the arrow fly, because they do not loose it without deliberation. But your people have it on their lips!
Many refuse public office. But your people eagerly answer the call without being asked, crying: "I'll take it on!"
Be happy now, for you have good reason! You are rich, at peace, and full of wisdom! The facts prove whether I speak the truth.
Athens and Sparta, which made the ancient laws and were so civilized — gave only the faintest hint of good living
Compared to you, who spin such fine-threaded provisions that what you make in October does not last to mid-November.
How many times, within living memory, have you changed laws, currency, offices, and customs, and renewed your very members!
And if you remember well and see clearly, you will see that you resemble a sick woman who cannot find rest on her feathered bed,
But turns and turns to escape her pain.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto VII
paragraphs: After the joyful, gracious greetings had been exchanged three and four times over, Sordello drew back and asked, "Who are you?"
"Before the souls worthy of ascending to God were ever directed to this mountain, my bones were buried by Octavian.
I am Virgil, and I lost heaven for no other crime than lacking faith." Such was my guide's reply.
Like someone who suddenly sees something before him that fills him with wonder — half believing, half doubting, saying "It is! It can't be!" —
just so Sordello appeared. Then he bowed his head and returned to Virgil with humility, embracing him as an inferior embraces a superior.
"O glory of the Latin people," he said, "you through whom our language showed its full power — O eternal pride of the place where I was born —
what merit or what grace reveals you to me? If I am worthy to hear your words, tell me — do you come from Hell, and from which circle?"
"Through all the circles of that sorrowful realm," Virgil replied, "I have come here. Heaven's power drove me, and with that power I come.
Not by doing, but by failing to do, I lost the sight of that high Sun you long for — the one I recognized too late.
There is a place below not tormented with suffering, but only darkness, where the laments are not wailing cries but sighs.
There I dwell with the little innocents snatched away by the teeth of Death before they could be freed from human sinfulness.
There I dwell among those who never wore the three holy virtues, but who knew and followed all the rest without vice.
But if you know and can, give us some direction by which we may more quickly reach the place where Purgatory truly begins."
He answered: "No fixed place has been assigned to us. I'm free to go up and around. As far as I can go, I'll join you as a guide.
But see how the day is already declining. To go up by night is impossible, so it would be wise to think of a good place to rest.
There are souls withdrawn to the right over here. If you allow me, I'll lead you to them, and you'll find delight in knowing them."
"How is that?" came the reply. "Would someone who wished to climb by night be prevented by others, or would he simply lack the power?"
The good Sordello drew his finger along the ground and said, "See — you could not cross even this line once the sun has gone.
Not that anything else would stop you from going up, except the darkness of night. That robs you of the will by robbing you of the power.
We could, of course, go back down and wander around the hillside while the horizon holds the day prisoner."
At this my Lord said, as if in wonder, "Lead us then to the place you mention, where we can take pleasure in lingering."
We had barely withdrawn from that spot when I noticed the mountain was hollowed out, shaped the way valleys are hollowed here on earth.
"Over there," said the shade, "is where we'll go — where the hillside makes a natural lap. There we'll wait for the new day."
Between the hill and the plain, a winding path led us to the rim of that dell, where the border dies away more than halfway.
Gold and fine silver, scarlet and pearl-white, Indian wood bright and clear, fresh emerald the moment it is broken —
each would be surpassed in color by the flowers and grasses planted within that hollow, as the lesser is surpassed by the greater.
And nature had not only painted there, but from the sweetness of a thousand scents had made a mingled, unknown fragrance.
"Salve Regina" — seated on the green and the flowers, I saw spirits singing, spirits not visible from outside the valley.
"Before the fading sun seeks its nest," began the Mantuan who had led us there, "do not ask me to take you down among them.
From this ledge you will better see the faces and gestures of them all than if you went down to join them on the plain below.
The one who sits highest, and looks as though he neglected what he should have done, and does not move his lips to the others' song —
that was the Emperor Rudolf, who had the power to heal the wounds that have killed Italy, so that she now revives only slowly through others.
The other, who seems to comfort him, governed the land where the waters spring that the Moldau carries to the Elbe, and the Elbe to the sea.
His name was Ottocar. Even in swaddling clothes he was far better than his bearded son Wenceslaus, who feeds on luxury and ease.
And that small-nosed one, who seems deep in counsel with the one who has such a kind face — he died fleeing and deflowering the lily.
Look there — see how he beats his breast! And see the other, who has made a bed for his cheek with the palm of his hand, sighing.
They are the father and father-in-law of the Plague of France. They know his vicious and depraved life, and that is the grief that pierces them so deeply.
The one who appears so robust, singing in harmony with the large-nosed one, wore the belt of every virtue.
And if the young man sitting behind him had remained as king after him, that valor would have poured well from vessel to vessel —
which cannot be said of the other heirs. Frederick and James possess the kingdoms, but neither possesses the better heritage.
Rarely does human worth rise through the branches of a family tree. This is God's will — so that we may ask it of Him.
My words reach the large-nosed one no less than the other, Peter, who sings beside him — and Provence and Apulia already grieve for it.
The plant is as inferior to its seed as, more than Beatrice and Margaret, Constance still boasts of her husband.
See the monarch of the simple life, Henry of England, sitting there alone. He has a better harvest in his descendants.
The one who sits lowest among them, looking upward, is the Marquis William, on whose account Alessandria and its war
make Monferrato and Canavese weep."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto VIII
paragraphs: It was now that hour which turns back the longing in sailors' hearts and melts them with tenderness — the day they've said goodbye to their dear friends.
It is the hour when the new traveler is pierced with love if he hears a distant bell that seems to mourn the dying day.
That was when I stopped listening and began to watch one of the souls who had risen, begging for attention with an upraised hand.
It joined both palms together and lifted them upward, fixing its eyes on the east, as if saying to God, "I care for nothing else."
"Te lucis ante" poured from its mouth so devoutly, with such sweet notes, that it carried me out of myself entirely.
Then the others joined in, sweetly and devoutly accompanying the whole hymn through to the end, their eyes fixed on the heavenly wheels.
Sharpen your eyes on the truth here, Reader, for now the veil is so fine that seeing through it is easy.
I saw that noble company afterward gaze upward in silence, as if waiting for something — pale and humble.
And from on high I saw two angels descend, bearing two flaming swords with their points broken off.
Green as freshly sprouted leaves were their garments, which billowed and trailed behind them, beaten and blown by their green wings.
One took his station just above us, and the other descended to the opposite bank, so that the people were enclosed between them.
I could clearly make out their golden hair, but their faces overwhelmed the eye, like a faculty confounded by excess.
"Both of them come from Mary's bosom," Sordello said, "as guardians of the valley against the serpent that will come soon."
At that, not knowing by what path, I turned around and pressed myself, utterly frozen, against the trustworthy shoulders of my guide.
And Sordello said again: "Now let us go down among the great shades. We will speak with them. They'll be glad to see you."
I think I had gone down only three steps when I was below, and I saw one who was looking only at me, as if he wanted to recognize me.
The air was growing dark by now, but not so dark that what it had hidden before was not revealed between his eyes and mine.
He moved toward me, and I toward him. Noble Judge Nino! How it delighted me to see you not among the damned!
No warm greeting was left unsaid between us. Then he asked: "How long has it been since you crossed the far waters to the foot of the mountain?"
"Oh," I told him, "I came through the dismal places this morning. I am still in the first life, though by going this way, I seek to gain the other."
The instant they heard my reply, both he and Sordello shrank back from me like people who are suddenly bewildered.
One turned to Virgil, the other to someone seated there, crying, "Rise, Currado! Come see what God in His grace has willed!"
Then, turning to me: "By that special grace you owe to Him who hides His own first purpose so deeply that it has no crossing —
when you are beyond the wide waters, tell my Giovanna to pray for me, there where the prayers of the innocent are answered.
I don't think her mother loves me anymore, since she has set aside her white mourning veil — which she, poor woman, will wish back again.
Through her one can easily see how long the fire of love lasts in a woman if sight and touch do not keep relighting it.
The Viper that leads the Milanese into battle will not make as fine a tomb banner for her as Gallura's Rooster would have."
He spoke this way, his face bearing the stamp of that righteous zeal which burns measuredly in the heart.
My eager eyes kept wandering up to heaven, to the point where the stars move most slowly, just as a wheel is slowest nearest its axle.
My guide said: "Son, what are you gazing at up there?" And I answered: "At those three torches that set this whole pole ablaze."
And he to me: "The four brilliant stars you saw this morning have sunk low over there, and these three have risen to where those were."
As he was speaking, Sordello drew close to him and said, "Look! There is our Adversary!" And he pointed his finger to show where.
On the side of the little valley that has no barrier, there was a serpent — perhaps the very one that gave Eve the bitter fruit.
Through grass and flowers the evil streak came gliding, turning its head from time to time and licking its back the way a beast grooms itself.
I did not see — and so I cannot say — how the two celestial hawks began to move, but I clearly saw that both were in motion.
Hearing the air split by their green wings, the serpent fled. The angels wheeled around and flew back to their stations in perfect unison.
The shade who had drawn close to the Judge when he called never once let go of me with his gaze during the whole encounter.
"So may the light that leads you upward find in your free will as much wax as is needed to reach the highest azure," he began.
"If you know any true report of Valdimagra or its neighborhood, tell it to me — I was once a great man there.
I was called Currado Malaspina. Not the elder, but his descendant. I bore my family the love which is here refined."
"Oh," I said to him, "I have never passed through your lands. But where in all of Europe is there a place that does not know of them?
The fame that honors your house proclaims its lords and proclaims its land, so that even one who has never been there knows of them.
And I swear to you, as I hope for heaven, that your honored family does not at all diminish the glory of either purse or sword.
It is so privileged by nature and custom that though a guilty leader misdirects the world, yours alone walks straight and scorns the evil path."
And he replied: "Now go. For the sun will not lie seven times upon the pillow that the Ram covers and bestrides with all four feet
before this courteous opinion of yours will be nailed into the center of your head with greater nails than any other's words can drive —
unless the course of justice stands still."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto IX
paragraphs: The old concubine of Tithonus was already gleaming white on the eastern balcony, risen from the arms of her sweet lover.
Her forehead was ablaze with gems set in the shape of that cold creature which strikes the nations with its tail.
And Night, in the place where we were, had already climbed two of its steps, and the third was folding its wings downward.
When I — who had something of Adam in me — sank down on the grass, overcome by sleep, there where all five of us were already seated.
At just the hour when the little swallow begins her sad song near the dawn — perhaps in memory of her former sorrows —
and when the human mind, more free from the flesh and less imprisoned by thought, becomes almost prophetic in its visions —
I dreamed I saw an eagle suspended in the sky with feathers of gold, its wings spread wide, poised to swoop.
And this seemed to be the very place where Ganymede was snatched from his kin, when he was carried up to the high assembly of the gods.
I thought to myself: perhaps it only strikes here out of habit, and from other places it disdains to carry anyone in its talons.
Then, wheeling a little more, it seemed to me it plunged down terrible as lightning and snatched me upward all the way to the sphere of fire.
There it seemed that both the eagle and I were burning, and the imagined fire scorched me so fiercely that my sleep was shattered.
No differently did Achilles start awake, turning his roused eyes all around him, not knowing where he was —
when his mother stealthily carried him sleeping in her arms from Chiron to Scyros, from which place the Greeks later drew him away —
than I leaped up when sleep fled from my face. I went pale, like a man who freezes with fright.
Only my Comforter was beside me. The sun was already more than two hours high, and my face was turned toward the sea.
"Do not be afraid," said my Lord. "Be reassured — all is well with us. Do not hold back, but put forth all your strength.
You have at last arrived at Purgatory. See the cliff that closes it all around. See the entrance there, where it appears to split open.
Earlier, at dawn before the day, while your spirit slept within you upon the flowers that adorn the land below,
a lady came and said: 'I am Lucia. Let me take this sleeping one. I will make his journey easier.'
Sordello and the other noble shapes remained behind. She took you, and as day brightened she came upward, and I followed in her steps.
She set you down here. First her beautiful eyes showed me that open entrance. Then she and sleep departed together."
Like someone whose doubts are resolved and whose fear turns to confidence once the truth is revealed to him —
