so I changed. And when my guide saw me free of worry, he moved up along the cliff, and I followed him toward the heights.
Reader, you can see how I am raising my subject. So do not be surprised if I fortify it with greater art.
We drew nearer, and we reached a place where what had first appeared to me as a crack — like a fissure splitting a wall —
I now saw was a portal, with three stairs of different colors leading up to it, and a gatekeeper who had not yet spoken a word.
As I opened my eyes wider, I saw him seated on the highest step, his face so brilliant I could not endure it.
In his hand he held a naked sword that reflected the sunlight back at us so brightly that I lifted my eyes to it in vain.
"Tell me from where you stand — what is it you want?" he called out. "Where is your escort? Be careful that coming here does not harm you."
"A lady from heaven, who knows about these things," my master answered him, "just now told us, 'Go there — there is the entrance.'"
"And may she speed your steps toward every good," the courteous gatekeeper replied. "Come forward then, to our stairs."
We approached. The first step was white marble, so polished and smooth that I saw myself mirrored in it just as I am.
The second was dark — deeper than purple — a scorched, rough stone, cracked lengthwise and across.
The third, which rested massively on top, appeared to me like porphyry, as flaming red as blood spurting from a vein.
On this the Angel of God rested both feet, sitting on the threshold, which seemed to me a stone of diamond.
Up the three stairs my guide drew me willingly, saying, "Ask humbly that he undo the lock."
I threw myself devoutly at his holy feet and begged for mercy, asking him to open. But first I struck my breast three times.
Seven P's he traced on my forehead with the point of his sword, and said, "See that you wash these wounds away when you are inside."
Ashes or dry-dug earth matched the color of his robes, and from beneath them he drew forth two keys.
One was gold and the other silver. First with the white key, then with the yellow, he worked the door, and I was satisfied.
"Whenever either of these keys fails to turn properly in the lock," he told us, "this entrance does not open.
One is more precious, but the other requires more skill and intellect before it will unlock, for it is the one that unties the knot.
I hold them from Peter, and he told me to err on the side of opening rather than keeping shut, so long as people fall down at my feet."
Then he pushed open the panels of the sacred door, saying, "Enter — but I warn you: whoever looks back must return outside."
And when the hinges of that consecrated gate turned on their swivels — which are massive metal and deeply resonant —
the Tarpeian Rock did not roar so loudly or sound so harsh when good Metellus was torn from it, leaving it stripped bare.
At the first thunderous sound I turned my ear attentively, and I seemed to hear "Te Deum laudamus" in voices mingled with sweet melody.
What I heard gave me exactly the same impression one gets when people stand singing with an organ —
where now you catch the words and now you cannot.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto X
paragraphs: When we had crossed the threshold of the door that the corrupted love of souls leaves unused — because it makes the crooked way seem straight —
I heard it close again with a resounding echo. And if I had turned my eyes back toward it, what excuse could there have been for such a failing?
We climbed upward through a cleft in the rock that undulated to one side and then the other, like a wave advancing and retreating.
"Here we need to use a little skill," my guide began, "adjusting ourselves now to this side, now to that, as the path curves away."
This made our steps so infrequent that the waning moon had reached its bed and set again before we came out through that needle's eye.
But when we were free and in the open, there where the mountain rises steeply back —
I was exhausted. Both of us were uncertain of our way, and we stopped on a ledge more desolate than desert roads.
From the edge that borders the void to the foot of the high bank that continues to rise, a human body measured three times over would span the width.
And as far as my eye could range, both to the left and to the right, this cornice appeared the same to me.
We had not yet moved our feet when I noticed that the inner embankment — which was too steep to climb —
was white marble, adorned with sculptures so perfect that not only Polycletus but Nature herself would have been put to shame.
The Angel who came down to earth with tidings of the peace that had been wept for through so many years, and who opened heaven from its long ban —
he appeared before us there, sculptured so truthfully in a gracious pose that he did not seem a silent image.
You would have sworn he was saying "Ave" — for she was also portrayed there, the woman who turned the key to open the highest love.
And in her bearing, these words were stamped as clearly as any figure pressed in wax: "Ecce ancilla Dei."
"Don't fix your mind on only one place," said the gentle Master, who had me standing on the side where people carry their hearts.
So I moved my eyes and saw, behind Mary and on the side where my guide was standing, another story carved into the rock.
I passed by Virgil and drew close so that it lay directly before my eyes.
There, sculptured in the same marble, were the cart and oxen drawing the holy Ark — a warning against taking on duties not appointed to you.
People appeared in front of it, divided into seven choirs. Two of my senses disagreed: one said "No, they are not singing," the other said "Yes, they are."
In the same way, the smoke of the incense depicted there made my eyes and nose argue: one said yes, the other no.
There before the blessed vessel danced the humble Psalmist, his robes girded up — and in that moment he was both more and less than a king.
Opposite him, looking out from the window of a great palace, Michal gazed down at him like a woman full of scorn and sorrow.
I moved from where I stood to examine up close another scene that gleamed white beyond Michal.
There the great glory of the Roman Prince was chronicled — the Emperor Trajan, whose magnificent generosity moved Pope Gregory to his great victory.
I am speaking of the Emperor Trajan. A poor widow stood at his bridle, her posture one of weeping and grief.
Around him the scene was thronged with cavalry, and eagles in gold above them visibly stirred in the wind.
The wretched woman in their midst seemed to be saying: "Lord, give me vengeance for my dead son — my heart is breaking."
And he seemed to answer her: "Wait until I return." And she, like one made impatient by grief: "My lord, what if you do not return?"
And he: "Whoever takes my place will do it for you." And she: "What good is another's deed to you if you neglect your own?"
At which he replied: "Take comfort now. I must fulfill my duty before I go. Justice demands it, and compassion holds me here."
He who never looked upon anything new was the creator of this visible language, which is astonishing to us because it is not found on earth.
While I was delighting in studying these images of deep humility, precious to behold for their Maker's sake —
"Look — on this side," the Poet murmured, "many people are coming, though they move with rare, slow steps. They will point us to the stairway above."
My eyes, which had been intent on seeing new things (as they are always eager for novelty), were not slow to turn toward him.
But I don't want you, Reader, to be discouraged from your good intentions because you hear how God decrees the debt be paid.
Don't dwell on the form of the torment. Think about what follows. Think that at worst it cannot last beyond the final judgment.
"Master," I began, "what I see moving toward us does not look like people to me. I can't tell what it is — my sight wavers."
And he to me: "The crushing nature of their torment bends them so low to the ground that my own eyes at first struggled with it too.
But look steadily and untangle with your sight what comes beneath those stones. You can already see how each one is stricken."
O proud Christians, wretched and exhausted! You whose inner vision is so weak that you place your confidence in backward steps —
do you not realize that we are worms, born to bring forth the angelic butterfly that flies to judgment without any screen?
Why does your spirit float so high in the air? You are like undeveloped insects, like worms in which formation has failed!
Just as a figure is sometimes seen in place of a corbel, joining its knees to its chest to support a ceiling or a roof —
a figure which, though not real, creates real anguish in the one who sees it — so I saw those souls, when I looked carefully.
True, they were more or less bent down according to how much they carried. And the one who showed the most patience in his face
seemed to say through his tears: "I can bear no more!"

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XI
paragraphs: "Our Father, who dwells in the heavens — not confined there, but out of the greater love you bear for your first creations on high —
praised be your name and your omnipotence by every creature, as it is right to give thanks for your sweet outpouring.
May the peace of your kingdom come to us, for we cannot reach it by ourselves, with all our intellect, unless it comes to us.
Just as your own angels sacrifice their will to you, singing Hosanna, so may all people sacrifice theirs.
Give us this day our daily manna, without which he who toils hardest to advance goes backward in this harsh wilderness.
And as we pardon in one another the trespasses we have suffered, so may you pardon us with kindness, and not look at what we deserve.
Our strength, which is so easily overcome, do not put to the test with the old Adversary, but deliver us from him who goads it so.
This last petition, dear Lord, is made not for ourselves — we have no need of it — but for those we have left behind."
Praying thus for themselves and for us, those shades moved under a weight like the kind that oppresses us in nightmares.
Unequally burdened and weary, they circled round and round that first cornice, purging away the stains of the world.
If good words are always spoken there on our behalf, what can we not do and say for them here, we who have good roots to our will?
We should certainly help them wash away the marks they carried from life, so that clean and light they may ascend to the starry spheres!
"Ah, so may pity and justice relieve you soon, that you may spread the wing that lifts you according to your desire —
show us which way to the stairs is shortest. And if there is more than one passage, point out the one that is least steep.
For the one who comes with me, weighed down by the flesh of Adam he still wears, finds the climbing hard despite his will."
The words they returned in answer to what my guide had said — it was not clear from whom they came.
But this was spoken: "Come with us to the right, along the bank, and you will find a gap that a living person can climb.
And were I not hindered by this stone that subdues my proud neck and forces me to keep my face down,
I would look at this one who still lives and does not name himself, to see if I know him and can make him pity me under this burden.
I was an Italian, born of a great Tuscan family. Guglielmo Aldobrandeschi was my father — I don't know if his name ever reached you.
The ancient blood and gallant deeds of my ancestors made me so arrogant that, forgetting our common mother the earth,
I held all men in contempt to such an extent that I died for it, as the Sienese know, and every child in Campagnatico.
I am Omberto. And pride has done harm not only to me — it has dragged all my kindred into ruin.
And here I must carry this weight until God is satisfied — since I did not do it among the living, I do it among the dead."
Listening, I bowed my face downward. And one of them — not the one who was speaking — twisted himself under the weight that cramped him,
and looked at me and recognized me, and called out, keeping his eyes laboriously fixed on me as I walked along, bowed down with them.
"Oh!" I asked him, "Are you not Oderisi, the honor of Gubbio and the honor of that art which in Paris they call illuminating?"
"Brother," he said, "the pages touched by the brush of Franco Bolognese smile more brightly now. The honor is all his, and only partly mine.
Truly I would not have been so gracious while I was alive, because of the great desire for excellence that consumed my heart.
Here the penalty for such pride is paid. And I would not even be here yet, had it not been that while I still had the power to sin, I turned to God.
O vain glory of human powers! How briefly green lingers at your summit, unless it is followed by an age of dullness!
In painting, Cimabue thought he held the field. Now Giotto has the acclaim, so that the other's fame grows dim.
So one Guido has taken the glory of our language from the other — and perhaps he is already born who will chase both from the nest.
Worldly fame is nothing but a gust of wind that blows now from one direction, now from another, and changes its name as it changes its side.
What greater fame will you have if you shed your flesh in old age than if you had died before outgrowing baby talk —
once a thousand years have passed? And that span is shorter compared to eternity than the blink of an eye compared to the slowest turning circle in heaven.
The one who takes such tiny steps ahead of me — all Tuscany once rang with his name. And now he is barely whispered of in Siena,
where he was lord at the time when the Florentine frenzy was overthrown — that city which was as proud then as it is degraded now.
Your reputation is the color of grass, which comes and goes — and the same power that drew it green from the earth turns it brown again."
And I said: "Your true words fill my heart with good humility and deflate a great swelling in me. But who is the one you just spoke of?"
"That," he replied, "is Provenzan Salvani. He is here because he presumed to seize all of Siena in his hands.
He has gone like this, and goes without rest, ever since he died. Such is the payment rendered by one who was too daring on earth."
And I: "If every spirit who waits until the brink of life before repenting must remain below and not climb here
until as much time as he lived has passed — unless good prayers come to his aid — how was he granted early passage?"
"When he lived in his greatest splendor," he said, "he freely placed himself in the Campo of Siena, setting all shame aside.
And there, to free his friend from the prison where he suffered under Charles, he brought himself to tremble in every vein.
I say no more, and I know I speak darkly. But before long, your neighbors will act in such a way that you'll be able to explain it.
This act of his released him from those waiting bounds."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XII
paragraphs: Side by side, like oxen yoked together, I walked with that burdened soul, for as long as the gentle teacher allowed it.
But when he said, "Leave him and push on — here each one does well to drive his vessel forward with all sail and oar" —
I straightened myself upright, as walking requires, even though my thoughts remained downcast and humbled within me.
I had moved on and was gladly following my Master's footsteps — we were both showing how light on our feet we were —
when he said to me: "Cast your eyes downward. To ease your way, it would be good to look at the ground beneath your feet."
As the tombs above the buried dead bear carved images of what they were in life, so that memory of them may survive —
and often there we weep for them afresh, pricked by remembrance, which spurs only those who feel compassion —
so I saw there, but sculpted with a finer art, the entire path projecting from the mountainside covered with carved figures.
I saw the one who was created nobler than any other creature — Lucifer — plunging down from heaven, blazing with lightning, on one side.
I saw Briareus on the other side, struck by the celestial bolt, lying heavy on the earth in the frost of death.
I saw Thymbraeus, Pallas, and Mars, still clad in armor around their father, gazing at the scattered limbs of the giants.
I saw Nimrod at the foot of his great labor, looking bewildered at the people who had been proud with him in Shinar.
O Niobe! With what anguished eyes I saw you traced upon the pavement, between your seven slain sons and seven slain daughters!
O Saul! How you appeared there, fallen upon your own sword, lifeless on Gilboa — which afterward felt neither rain nor dew!
O mad Arachne! I saw you there, already half-spider, wretched upon the shreds of the web you wove to your own destruction!
O Rehoboam! Your image there no longer seems to threaten. Instead, a chariot carries it away in terror, though no one pursues!
The adamantine pavement also showed how Alcmaeon made his mother pay dearly for the cursed ornament.
It showed how Sennacherib's own sons threw themselves upon him in the temple, and left him there dead.
It showed the ruin and the cruel slaughter that Tomyris wrought, when she said to Cyrus: "You thirsted for blood — with blood I glut you!"
It showed how the Assyrians fled in rout after Holofernes was slain, and the remnants of that massacre.
I saw Troy in ashes and in ruins. O Ilion, how debased and abject the image that was carved there showed you to be!
What master of brush or stylus could portray the shadings and outlines that would make even the most subtle mind marvel there?
The dead seemed truly dead, the living truly alive. No one who saw the real events could have seen them better than I, walking bent over, treading on them.
Now be proud! Go with your looks lifted high, you children of Eve — and do not bow your heads to see the evil of your ways!
We had now circled more of the mountain, and the sun had spent far more of its course, than my preoccupied mind had realized.
When my guide, who was always watchfully ahead, said: "Lift your head. This is no time for such deep meditation.
Look — an Angel is hurrying toward us. See, the sixth handmaiden of the day is now returning from her service.
Adorn your bearing and your looks with reverence, so that he may be pleased to send us upward. Remember — this day will never dawn again."
I was well used to his warnings never to waste time, so on that subject he could not speak to me obscurely.
Toward us came the beautiful being, clothed in white, with a face like the trembling morning star.
He opened his arms and then his wings. "Come," he said. "The steps are close at hand, and from now on the ascent is easy."
How few come at this invitation! O human beings, born to soar aloft — why do you fall before such a little wind?
He led us to where the rock was split. There he struck my forehead with his wings, then promised me safe passage.
As on the right-hand side, climbing the hill where stands the church that overlooks well-governed Florence above the Rubaconte bridge,
the steep ascent is broken by staircases built in an age when ledgers and measures were still honest —
just so the bank is eased that drops sheer from the next circle, though the high rock grazes us on either side.
As we were turning that way, voices sang "Beati pauperes spiritu" with a sweetness beyond what words could tell.
How different these entrances are from Hell's! For here one enters with hymns, and there below with savage cries of grief.
We were now climbing the sacred stairs, and it seemed to me far easier than it had on the flat terrace below.
So I asked: "Master, tell me — what heavy thing has been lifted from me, that I hardly feel any effort in walking?"
He answered: "When the P's that still remain on your face, now almost invisible, are completely erased like the first one —
your feet will be so mastered by good will that they will not only feel no fatigue, but the urging upward will be a delight."
Then I did what people do who walk along with something on their head that they don't know about, until others' reactions make them wonder.
The hand goes up to check, and searches, and finds, and does the job that the eyes cannot manage on their own.
With the fingers of my right hand spread wide, I found only six of the letters that the key-bearing angel had carved on my temples.
Seeing which, my guide smiled.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XIII
paragraphs: We had reached the top of the stairs, where the mountain is cut back a second time as it purges those who climb.
There a cornice encircles the hill in the same way as the first, except that its arc curves more sharply.
There is no shade here, no sculpture to be seen. The bank and the road appear equally smooth, with nothing but the livid color of bare stone.
"If we wait here for people to ask directions," the Poet said, "I'm afraid our choice will be too long delayed."
Then he fixed his eyes steadily on the sun, made his right side the pivot of his motion, and swung his left side around.
"O sweet light, trusting in you I enter this new path — lead us," he said, "as one needs to be led within this place.
You warm the world and shine over it. Unless some other reason says otherwise, your rays should always be our guide."
As much as we would call a mile on earth, we had already covered in that short time, driven by eager will.
And toward us we heard spirits flying — though they were not visible — uttering courteous invitations to the table of Love.
The first voice that passed overhead in flight cried loudly, "Vinum non habent" — and went on repeating it behind us.
And before it had entirely faded with distance, another passed, crying, "I am Orestes!" — and it too did not linger.
"Father, what are these voices?" I asked. And even as I spoke, the third came, saying: "Love those who have done you evil!"
The good Master said: "This circle scourges the sin of envy, and for that reason the lashes of the whip are drawn from love.
The curb will be of a different sound. I expect you will hear it before you reach the Pass of Pardon.
But fix your gaze steadily through the air, and you will see people sitting before us, each one pressed close against the cliff."
Then I opened my eyes wider than before. I looked ahead and saw shades wearing mantles that were no different in color from the stone.
When we had gone a little farther, I heard a cry of "Mary, pray for us!" and a cry of "Michael, Peter, and all the Saints!"
I don't think there walks on earth a man so hard-hearted that he would not be pierced with pity at what I saw next.
For when I had come close enough that their condition was clear to me, heavy grief was wrung from my eyes.
They appeared to me covered in coarse sackcloth, and each one leaned on another's shoulder, and all of them were supported by the bank.
It is the same way the blind stand at church doors begging for alms — one resting his head against the next,
so that pity may rise quickly in others, not only from the sound of their words but from their very appearance, which pleads no less.
And just as the sun does not reach the blind, so to these shades I have been speaking of, heaven's light does not give itself freely.
For an iron wire pierces through all their eyelids and sews them shut, as is done to a wild sparrowhawk that will not stay still.
It seemed to me, as I passed, that I was committing an outrage — seeing others without being seen. So I turned to my wise counselor.
He knew well what the silent one wished to say, and did not wait for my question but said: "Speak — and be brief and to the point."
I had Virgil on that side of the embankment where one might fall, since it has no railing.
On my other side were the devout shades, who through the horrible seam pressed out tears that bathed their cheeks.
I turned to them and began: "O people who are certain of beholding the high light that is your desire's only care —
so may grace quickly dissolve the scum upon your consciences, so that the stream of your mind may flow clearly through them —
tell me, for I will hold it dear and precious, whether any soul among you here is Italian. It may benefit that person if I learn of it."
"O my brother, each one of us is a citizen of the one true city. But you mean to ask who lived as a pilgrim in Italy."
This I seemed to hear as an answer, from a little farther on than where I stood. So I moved closer to make myself better heard.
Among the rest I saw a shade that seemed expectant. And if anyone asks how — it was lifting its chin upward the way a blind person does.
"Spirit," I said, "you who bow yourself to rise — if you are the one who answered me, make yourself known to me by your place or name."
"I was Sienese," it replied, "and with the others here I cleanse my guilty life, weeping to Him that He lend Himself to us.
Wise I was not, though I was called Sapia. And I took far more joy in the harm of others than in my own good fortune.
And lest you think I'm deceiving you, hear whether I was as foolish as I say. The arc of my years was already descending.
My fellow citizens were joined in battle near Colle with their adversaries, and I was praying to God for whatever He willed.
They were routed and driven into the bitter straits of flight. And I, watching the chase, felt a joy unmatched by any other —
so much that I lifted my brazen face to heaven, crying to God, 'Now I no longer fear You!' — like a blackbird emboldened by a moment of sunshine.
I wanted peace with God at the very end of my life, and my debt of penance would not yet have been paid
had it not been that Pier Pettignano remembered me in his holy prayers, and out of charity grieved for me.
But who are you, who go asking about our condition and have your eyes unbound, as I believe, and speak while breathing?"
"My eyes," I said, "will yet be taken from me here, but only for a short time — the offense they committed through envy was small.
Far greater is the fear that holds my soul in suspense — the torment of the circle below. Even now the weight of it presses down on me."
And she said to me: "Then who led you up here among us, if you think you will return below?" And I: "He who is with me and does not speak.
And I am alive. So ask of me, chosen spirit, if you would have me take some steps for you over there, with my mortal feet."
"Oh, this is something so extraordinary to hear!" she answered. "It is a great sign that God loves you. So help me sometimes with your prayers.
And I beg you, by whatever you most desire — if you ever set foot on the soil of Tuscany, restore my good name among my kindred.
You will find them among that foolish people who pin their hopes on Talamone, and will lose more hope there than in finding the underground Diana.
But the admirals will lose even more."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XIV
paragraphs: "Who is this one going around our mountain before Death has given him the power of flight, opening and closing his eyes at will?"
"I don't know who he is, but I know he's not alone. Ask him yourself — you're nearer to him. And do it gently, so he'll answer."
Two spirits, leaning toward each other, were discussing me there on my right. Then they tilted their faces upward to address me.
One said: "O soul still fastened within the body, making your way toward heaven — for charity's sake, comfort us and tell us:
where do you come from and who are you? Your being granted this grace makes us marvel as much as anything never seen before must."
And I replied: "Through the heart of Tuscany there wanders a little stream born in Falterona, and a hundred miles are not enough for its course.
From its banks I bring this body. Telling you my name would be pointless, because it has not yet made much noise."
"If I correctly penetrate your meaning with my mind," the one who had first spoken then answered, "you are speaking of the Arno."
And the other said to him: "Why did he hide the name of that river, as one does with something horrible?"
The shade who had been questioned answered: "I don't know. But truly, the name of such a valley deserves to perish.
For from its source — where the Alpine mountain from which Peloro is cleft teems so abundantly that few places surpass it —
to where it surrenders itself, replenishing what the sky draws up from the sea, giving rivers what flows through them —
virtue is shunned by everyone like an enemy, like a snake, whether through the bad luck of the place or through the bad habits that drive them.
The inhabitants of that wretched valley have so transformed their natures that it seems Circe had them in her pasture.
Among ugly swine, fit more for acorns than for food made for human use, the river first directs its meager way.
Coming downstream, it then finds curs more snarling than their strength warrants, and turns its muzzle from them with disdain.
On it goes, falling, and the bigger it grows the more it finds the dogs becoming wolves — this accursed, ill-fated ditch.
Descending then through many a deep gorge, it finds foxes so full of fraud that they fear no cleverness that might outwit them.
Nor will I stop because someone hears me. And it will be well for him if he takes to heart what a truthful spirit is revealing to me.
I see your grandson becoming a hunter of those wolves on the bank of the savage river, and he terrifies them all.
He sells their flesh while they are still alive, then slaughters them like worn-out cattle. He robs many of life, and himself of honor.
Blood-stained he comes out of the dismal forest. He leaves it in such a state that a thousand years from now it will not be reforested."
As the face of someone hearing news of coming disaster is disturbed, from whichever direction the danger may threaten —
so I saw the other soul, who had turned to listen, grow troubled and sad when it had taken in those words.
The speech of one and the look of the other made me eager to know their names, and I asked with prayers mixed into my question.
At which the spirit who had spoken first began again: "You want me to do for you what you won't do for me.
But since God wills that such grace shines forth in you, I won't hold back. Know then that I am Guido del Duca.
My blood was so set on fire by envy that if I had seen anyone happy, you would have seen me turn pale with spite.
This is the straw I reap from my own sowing! O human race, why do you set your hearts where sharing is forbidden?
This is Renier. This is the pride and honor of the house of Calboli, from which no one since has inherited his worth.
And not his bloodline alone, between the Po and the mountains, the sea and the Reno, has been stripped of the good required for truth and joy.
For within those borders everything is choked with poisonous roots, so rank that cultivation would be too late to thin them now.
Where is good Lizio? Where is Arrigo Manardi, Pier Traversaro, Guido di Carpigna? O Romagnoles, turned into bastards!
When will a Fabbro arise in Bologna? When in Faenza a Bernardin di Fosco — that noble shoot from a humble root?
Don't wonder, Tuscan, if I weep, remembering Guido da Prata and Ugolin d'Azzo, who lived among us,
and Federigo Tignoso and his circle, the house of Traversara and the Anastagi — both families now extinct.
The ladies and the cavaliers, the toils and pleasures that filled our hearts with love and courtesy, there where hearts have grown so malicious!
O Brettinoro, why don't you simply vanish, since your whole family is gone, and so many good people have left to avoid corruption?
Bagnacaval does well in not producing heirs. Castrocaro does badly, and Conio worse, in bothering to breed such counts.
The Pagani will do well once their Devil departs. But even so, no pure testimony of them will ever remain.
O Ugolin de' Fantoli, your name is safe, since no one is expected who could darken it by falling short!
But go now, Tuscan. It pleases me now far more to weep than to speak. Our conversation has weighed too heavily on my mind."
We knew those beloved souls heard us leave. By keeping silent, they confirmed the direction of our path.
When we had walked on and were alone, a voice came crashing toward us like thunder splitting the air, crying:
"Whoever finds me shall slay me!" And it fled like the echo of thunder that dies away as the cloud bursts apart.
As soon as our hearing had a moment's truce from this, another came with such a crash it sounded like thunderclap following thunderclap:
"I am Aglaurus, who was turned to stone!" And then, to press close to the Poet, I took a step backward, not forward.
By now the air was quiet on all sides. And he said to me: "That was the hard curb meant to keep mankind within bounds.
But you swallow the bait so greedily that the hook of the old Adversary reels you in, and neither curb nor calling avails much.
The heavens call to you and wheel around you, showing you their eternal beauties — yet your eye stays fixed on the ground.
And so He who sees all things chastises you."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XV
paragraphs: As much time as passes between the close of the third hour and sunrise — that much appeared to remain of the sun's course before nightfall.
It was evening there and midnight here.
The rays were striking us full in the face, because we had circled the mountain far enough that we were now heading straight toward the west.
When I felt my forehead overwhelmed by a brilliance far greater than before, and the unfamiliar strangeness of it stupefied me.
So I raised my hands above my brow and made myself a visor to reduce the blinding glare.
As when a sunbeam bounces off water or a mirror and leaps to the opposite side, rising at the same angle it descended —
deviating equally from the straight fall of a stone, as both experiment and theory demonstrate —
just so it seemed to me that I was struck by a light reflected from ahead of me, and my sight was quick to flee from it.
"What is that, sweet Father, that I cannot shield my sight from well enough?" I said. "It seems to be moving toward us."
"Don't be surprised if the family of heaven still dazzles you," he answered. "It is an angel who comes to invite us upward.
Soon it will no longer be painful but delightful for you to see such things, as much as nature has fitted you to feel."
When we reached the blessed Angel, he said in a joyful voice: "Enter here — onto a stairway far less steep than the others."
We were already climbing, having left that place behind, and "Beati misericordes" was sung behind us, and "Rejoice, you who overcome!"
My Master and I were going up alone, just the two of us, and I thought to profit from his words as we walked.
So I turned to him and asked: "What did the spirit from Romagna mean when he mentioned 'forbidden sharing'?"
He replied: "He knows the harm of his own greatest fault, so don't wonder if he reproaches it, hoping we suffer it less.
Because your desires are aimed where sharing diminishes each person's portion, envy works the bellows to your sighs.
But if the love of the highest sphere drew your aspirations upward, that fear would not be in your breast.
For there, the more people say 'ours,' the more good each one possesses, and the more charity burns in that cloister."
"I am hungrier to be satisfied now," I said, "than if I had kept quiet before. And more doubt gathers in my mind.
How can it be that a good thing, shared among more people, can make each one richer than if it were held by a few?"
And he to me: "Because you fix your mind entirely on earthly things, you draw darkness from the very source of light.
That infinite, ineffable Goodness above runs toward love the way a sunbeam runs toward a shining surface.
It gives as much of itself as it finds warmth to receive, so that as far as charity extends, the eternal power grows over it.
And the more people aspire toward it, the more there are to love well, and the more they love, each reflecting the other like a mirror.
And if my reasoning does not satisfy you, you shall see Beatrice, and she will fully take from you this and every other longing.
Just strive to quickly erase the remaining five wounds, as the two already have been — they close themselves by causing pain."
Just as I was about to say "You satisfy me," I saw that I had reached the next circle, and my eager eyes silenced my tongue.
There I seemed to be suddenly caught up in an ecstatic vision, and in a temple I saw many people.
And at the door, a woman with the gentle manner of a mother, saying: "My son, why have you treated us this way?
Look — your father and I have been searching for you in sorrow." And as she fell silent, the vision vanished.
Then I saw another woman, her cheeks streaming with the tears that grief distills from great indignation.
She was saying: "If you are lord of that city over whose naming the gods so quarreled, and from which all knowledge shines —
avenge yourself on those brazen arms that embraced our daughter, O Pisistratus!" And the lord seemed mild and gentle
as he answered her with a measured look: "What shall we do to those who wish us harm, if we condemn the one who loves us?"
Then I saw people burning with rage, stoning a young man to death, shouting at each other ceaselessly: "Kill him! Kill him!"
And I saw him sink to the earth under the weight of death already pressing on him, but his eyes were still open gates to heaven,
pleading with the Lord Most High, in the midst of that terrible assault, to forgive his persecutors — with a look that unlocks compassion.
As soon as my soul returned outward to the things that are truly external to it, I recognized my errors, which were not false but visionary.
My guide, who could see me behaving like a man waking from sleep, said: "What's wrong with you? You can barely stand!
You've been stumbling along for more than half a league, your eyes glazed over and your legs tangling — like someone overcome by wine or sleep!"
"O my sweet Father, if you listen, I'll tell you," I said, "what appeared to me when my legs were taken from under me."
And he said: "Even if you wore a hundred masks on your face, your thoughts, however small, would not be hidden from me.
What you saw was shown so that you would not fail to open your heart to the waters of peace that pour from the eternal fountain.
I did not ask 'What's wrong?' the way someone does who only looks with eyes that cannot see when the soul has left the body.
I asked it to give strength to your feet. That is how sluggards must be urged on — slow to make use of their wakefulness when it returns."
We walked on through the twilight, peering forward as far as the eye could reach against the late, bright rays of the setting sun.
And gradually a smoke approached us, dark as night, with no place to hide from it.
It stripped us of both sight and the pure air.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XVI
paragraphs: The darkness of Hell and a night stripped of every star, under a sky as clouded and black as possible —
never made so thick a veil for my eyes, or so rough a texture for my skin, as the smoke that enveloped us there.
It would not let an eye stay open. So my faithful and wise escort moved close and offered me his shoulder.
Just as a blind man walks behind his guide, to keep from straying or striking something that might hurt or kill him —
so I went through the bitter, foul air, listening to my guide, who said nothing but "Make sure you don't get separated from me."
I heard voices, and each one seemed to plead for peace and mercy from the Lamb of God who takes away our sins.
"Agnus Dei" was always their opening. One word, one meter for all of them, so that there seemed to be perfect harmony among them.
"Master, are those spirits I hear?" I asked. And he: "You perceive correctly. They are untying the knot of anger."
"Now who are you, cleaving through our smoke and speaking of us as though you still divided time by calendar months?"
So spoke a voice. My Master said to me: "Answer him, and ask if the way upward lies on this side."
And I: "O soul who cleanse yourself to return beautiful to your Maker — you will hear wonders if you follow me."
"I will follow you as far as I am allowed," he answered. "And if the smoke prevents our seeing, hearing will keep us joined instead."
So I began: "I am climbing upward still wrapped in the binding that death unwinds, and I came here through the anguish of Hell.
And if God has enfolded me in such grace that He wills I behold His court by a method entirely outside modern custom —
do not hide from me who you were before death, but tell me, and tell me if I'm going right for the pass. Let your words be our escort."
"I was a Lombard, and my name was Marco. I knew the world and loved that excellence at which everyone today has stopped aiming their bow.
You are going the right way for climbing." He added: "I pray you to pray for me when you are above."
And I to him: "I pledge my faith to do what you ask. But I am bursting inwardly with a doubt, unless I can rid myself of it.
First it was simple, and now your words have made it double, confirming for me here what I was already coupling it with elsewhere.
The world is indeed utterly deserted of every virtue, as you tell me — heavy with wickedness and covered in it.
But I beg you, point out the cause, so that I can see it and show it to others. For some place it in the stars, and some here below."
A deep sigh, forced by grief into a groan, he first let out, and then he began: "Brother, the world is blind, and you truly come from it!
You who are living still refer every cause upward to the heavens, as if they moved all things by necessity.
If that were so, free will would be destroyed in you, and there would be no justice in feeling joy for good or grief for evil.
The heavens set your impulses in motion, I grant — I will not say all of them — but even granting that, you have been given light to know good from evil,
and free will, which, if it suffers some fatigue in its first battles with the heavens, will afterward conquer all, if it is nurtured well.
You are subject to a greater power and a better nature, though free — and that creates the mind in you, which the heavens do not have in their charge.
Therefore, if the present world goes astray, the cause is in you. Seek it in yourselves. And I will now be your faithful spy in this matter.
From the hand of Him who delights in it before it exists, like a little girl who laughs and cries in childish play,
comes forth the simple soul that knows nothing, except that, proceeding from a joyful Maker, it gladly turns to whatever gives it pleasure.
First it tastes the flavor of some trivial good. It is deceived and runs after it, unless a guide or rein turns its love aside.
That is why laws were needed as a rein, and a ruler was needed who could at least discern the tower of the true city.
The laws exist — but who enforces them? No one. Because the shepherd who leads can ruminate but does not have cloven hooves.
And so the people, seeing their guide strike only at the goods they themselves crave, feed on those and seek nothing further.
You can clearly see that bad leadership is the cause that has corrupted the world — not that your nature is rotten.
Rome, which made the world good, once had two suns, which lit one road and the other — the road of God and the road of the world.
One has put out the other. The sword is joined to the shepherd's staff, and it goes badly when they are forced together by brute strength —
because joined together, neither fears the other. If you don't believe me, consider the grain — every plant is known by its seed.
In the land watered by the Po and the Adige, valor and courtesy used to flourish, before Frederick had his quarrel with the Church.
Now anyone can pass through there safely who is ashamed enough to avoid speaking with good people or drawing near them.
True, three old men remain in whom the old age rebukes the new, and they think God is slow to call them to a better life:
Currado da Palazzo, good Gherardo, and Guido da Castel — who is better named, in the French way, 'the honest Lombard.'
Say from now on that the Church of Rome, confounding two forms of governance in itself, falls in the mud and soils both itself and its burden."
"O my Marco," I said, "you argue well. And now I see why the sons of Levi were excluded from the inheritance.
But what Gherardo is this who, as you say, remains as a living rebuke to the barbarous age?"
"Either your speech misleads me or you're testing me," he answered. "For you speak Tuscan to me, yet seem to know nothing of good Gherardo.
I know him by no other name, unless I take it from his daughter Gaia. God be with you — I come no farther.
See the dawn already whitening through the smoke. The Angel is over there. I must go before he sees me."
So he spoke, and would hear me no more.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XVII
paragraphs: Remember, Reader, if ever a mountain fog engulfed you so that you could see no better than a mole sees through its skin —
how, when the damp, heavy vapors begin to thin out, the sun's orb weakly enters through them —
and your imagination will quickly grasp how I first glimpsed the sun again, already setting.
Matching my steps to the faithful footsteps of my Master, I came out of that cloud into rays already dead on the low shores.
O Imagination, you who steal us so completely from the outside world that a man does not notice even a thousand trumpets sounding around him —
who moves you, if the senses do not? A light moves you, formed in heaven by itself, or by a will that directs it downward.
In my imagination there appeared the trace of her impiety who changed her form into the bird that most delights in singing.
My mind was so drawn within itself that nothing from outside could be received by it.
Then into my exalted fantasy there came one crucified, his face disdainful and fierce even as he died.
Around him were the great Ahasuerus, his wife Esther, and the righteous Mordecai, who was upright in both word and deed.
And just as this image shattered of its own accord, like a bubble when the water that made it fails —
there rose up in my vision a young girl, weeping bitterly, saying: "O Queen, why did you choose in anger to be nothing?
You killed yourself so as not to lose Lavinia. But now you have lost me! I am the one who mourns, Mother — at your ruin before anyone else's."
As sleep is broken when new light suddenly strikes the closed eyelids, and it flickers and dies before fully expiring —
so this vision of mine collapsed the moment a radiance struck my face, far brighter than anything we are accustomed to.
I turned to see where I was, when a voice said, "Here is the way up" — which drove all other purposes from my mind
and made my desire so eager to see who was speaking that it will never rest until it meets that face.
But as the sun overwhelms our sight and veils its own form in its excess of brightness — so my power was insufficient here.
"This is a divine spirit who directs us upward without being asked, and who conceals himself with his own light.
He does with us as one should do with oneself. For whoever sees the need and waits to be asked already leans maliciously toward refusal.
Let us now match our feet to his invitation. Let us hurry to climb before it grows dark, for after that we cannot until the day returns."
So spoke my guide. He and I together turned our steps to a stairway. And the moment I reached the first step,
I felt near me a motion like wings, and a fanning across my face, and a voice saying: "Beati pacifici — blessed are the peacemakers, who are without sinful anger."
Already the last rays of sun, which night pursues, had risen so high above us that stars appeared on many sides.
"O my strength, why are you draining away?" I said to myself, for I felt the power of my legs give out.
We had reached the point where the stairway climbs no more, and we were motionless — like a ship that has reached the shore.
I listened briefly, to hear if there was any sound in this new circle. Then I turned to my Master and said:
"Tell me, my sweet Father — what offense is purged here in the circle where we are? Our feet may pause, but don't let your words."
And he to me: "The love of good that fell short of its duty is here restored. Here the slack oar is plied once more.
But so you may understand more clearly, turn your mind to me, and you will gather some good fruit from our delay.
Neither the Creator nor any creature, my son," he began, "was ever without love — either natural or of the mind. And you know this.
Natural love is always without error. But the other kind can err through a wrong object, or through too much or too little force.
While it is aimed at the highest good, and in lesser goods it keeps itself in check, it cannot cause sinful pleasure.
But when it twists toward evil, or pursues good with more or less zeal than it should, then the creature works against its Creator.
From this you can understand that love must be the seed within you of every virtue and of every act that deserves punishment.
Now, since love can never turn its gaze away from the well-being of the one who loves, all things are safe from hating themselves.
And since no being can be conceived as standing alone, cut off from the First Being, the desire to hate God is entirely cut off.
Therefore, if I reason well, the evil one loves must be one's neighbor's evil. And this takes three forms in your mortal clay.
There are those who hope to excel by putting their neighbor down, and who long only for his greatness to be diminished.
There are those who fear they will lose power, grace, honor, or fame because another rises, and so they grow sad and love the reverse.
And there are those whom injury seems to burn, making them hungry for revenge, so that they must plot to harm another.
This threefold love is wept for below. Now I want you to hear about the other — the love that pursues good with the wrong measure.
Everyone dimly conceives of a good in which the mind may rest, and longs for it. So each one strives to reach it.
If sluggish love draws you to look at this or to attain it, this cornice, after just repentance, punishes you for it.
There is another good that does not make a person happy. It is not true happiness — not the Good Essence that is the fruit and root of every good.
The love that surrenders too much of itself to that lesser good is lamented in the three circles above us. But how it is divided into three,
I will not say — so that you may discover it for yourself."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XVIII
paragraphs: The great Teacher had finished his argument and was looking attentively into my face to see if I appeared satisfied.
And I, goaded by a new thirst, was outwardly silent but said within: "Perhaps my too many questions are annoying him."
But that true Father, who perceived the timid wish that would not open itself, gave me the courage to speak by speaking first.
So I said: "Master, my sight is so sharpened in your light that I clearly discern whatever your words convey or describe.
Therefore I beg you, dear sweet Father, to explain love to me — the love to which you trace every good action and its opposite."
"Direct the keen eyes of your intellect toward me," he said, "and the error of the blind who would be leaders will become clear to you.
The soul, which is created ready to love, is drawn toward anything that pleases it, as soon as pleasure awakens it to action.
Your perception draws an image from some real thing and unfolds it within you, so that it makes the soul turn toward it.
And if, once turned, the soul inclines toward that thing — that inclination is love. It is a natural response, bound to you anew by pleasure.
Then, just as fire moves upward by its very nature, born to ascend to where it lasts longest in its element —
so the captive soul enters into desire, which is a spiritual movement that never rests until the beloved thing brings it joy.
Now it should be clear to you how hidden the truth is from those who declare that every love is in itself praiseworthy —
because love's object may perhaps always appear good. But not every impression is good, even if the wax is."
"Your words and my attentive mind have revealed love to me," I answered. "But that has left me more pregnant with doubt.
For if love is offered to us from outside, and the soul walks on no other foot, it deserves neither praise nor blame, whether it goes right or wrong."
And he to me: "What reason can see here, I can tell you. Beyond that, wait for Beatrice, since it is a matter of faith.
Every substantial form, distinct from matter yet united with it, carries within itself a specific power,
which is not perceptible without action and reveals itself only through its effects, as life reveals itself in a plant through its green leaves.
Therefore, where our first concepts come from, man does not know, nor where the first impulses of attraction arise —
they are in you like the instinct in a bee to make honey. And this first desire contains neither merit nor blame.
Now, so that all other desires may be gathered to this one, there is innate in you the power of judgment, which should guard the threshold of consent.
This is the principle from which your measure of merit is taken, according to whether it receives and winnows good loves from guilty ones.
Those who went deepest in reasoning understood this innate freedom, and so they bequeathed Ethics to the world.
Suppose, then, that every love kindled in you springs from necessity — the power to restrain it still lies within you.
This noble power is what Beatrice means by free will. So remember that, if she should speak of it."
The moon, rising late, almost at midnight, now made the stars seem sparser — shaped like a burning bucket.
And it ran along those paths counter to the heavens which the sun sets ablaze when someone in Rome sees it setting between Sardinia and Corsica.
That noble shade on whose account Pietola is more famous than any other Mantuan town had discharged me of my burden of questions.
So I, having received clear and plain answers, stood like a man in a drowsy reverie.
But this drowsiness was suddenly stolen from me by a crowd that had already come around behind us.
And just as the banks of the Ismenus and the Asopus once saw throngs rushing through the night whenever the Thebans had need of Bacchus —
so these souls curved their steps around that circle, driven by good will and righteous love, from what I saw of those approaching.
Soon they were upon us, because the whole great crowd was running. And two at the front cried out in tears:
"Mary hurried to the hill country, and Caesar, to subdue Ilerda, struck at Marseilles and then raced on to Spain!"
"Quick! Quick! Don't let time be lost through too little love!" cried the rest. "Let zeal for doing good refresh God's grace!"
"O people in whom sharp fervor now makes up for the delay and negligence you showed in doing good through lukewarmness —
this one who lives — and truly, I am not lying — wants to climb up when the sun next rises. So tell us where the nearest passage is."
These were my guide's words. And one of those spirits said: "Come along behind us and you'll find the opening.
We are so full of longing to keep moving that we cannot stop. So forgive us if you take our justice for rudeness.
I was the Abbot of San Zeno in Verona, under the reign of good Barbarossa, about whom Milan still speaks with sorrow.
And there is one with one foot in the grave already who will soon weep over that monastery and be sorry for having had power there —
because he put his son in place of its true pastor — his son, sick in his whole body, worse in his mind, and basely born."
Whether he said more or fell silent I don't know — he had already passed so far beyond us. But this I heard, and was glad to hold onto it.
And my guide, my help in every need, said: "Turn this way. See two of them coming, biting at slothfulness with their teeth."
At the rear they shouted: "The people for whom the sea was opened were dead before their heirs saw the Jordan!
And those who could not endure the hardship to the end with the son of Anchises offered themselves up to a life without glory."
Then, when those shades had separated from us so far that they could no longer be seen, a new thought took root within me,
from which many others, various and diverse, were born. And I drifted from one to another until, in reverie, my eyes fell shut
and meditation became dream.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XIX
paragraphs: It was the hour when the day's heat can no longer warm the cold of the moon, overcome by the earth, or perhaps by Saturn.
The hour when fortune-tellers see their Fortuna Major rise in the east before dawn, along a path that stays bright only briefly.
In my dreams, a stammering woman came to me — cross-eyed, crooked in her feet, with crippled hands and sallow skin.
I looked at her. And as the sun revives the numb limbs that the night has chilled, just so my gaze loosened her tongue
and straightened her entirely in no time, and colored her sunken face with the flush that love desires.
When her speech was thus unbound, she began to sing so beautifully that I could hardly have turned my thoughts away from her.
"I am the sweet Siren," she sang, "who leads sailors astray in mid-ocean. So full of pleasure am I to hear.
I drew Ulysses from his wandering course with my song. Whoever dwells with me rarely departs, so completely do I satisfy him."
Her mouth was not yet closed when a holy and alert Lady appeared at my side to put her to shame.
"Virgil! O Virgil! Who is this?" she said sternly. And he was drawing near, his eyes fixed on that dignified one.
She seized the other woman and tore open her clothes in front, showing me her belly. The stench that poured out woke me instantly.
I opened my eyes, and good Virgil said: "At least three times I have called you. Rise and come — let us find the entrance by which you may pass through."
I got up. Full daylight already filled all the circles of the Sacred Mountain, and we walked with the new sun at our backs.
Following behind him, I carried my forehead bowed like a man weighed down with thought, bent like the half-arch of a bridge.
Then I heard someone say, "Come — here is the passage," spoken in a manner so gentle and kind, unlike anything heard in this mortal world.
With wings spread wide like a swan's, the one who spoke thus turned us upward between the two walls of solid rock.
Then he moved his pinions and fanned us, declaring those "qui lugent" to be blessed, for their souls shall be filled with comfort.
"What ails you, that you keep staring at the ground?" my guide began to say, after we had climbed somewhat beyond the Angel.
And I: "A new vision weighs on me with such misgiving that I cannot withdraw my thoughts from it."
"Did you see that old enchantress," he said, "who alone is wept for on the terraces above us? Did you see how man is freed from her?
Let that be enough. Strike the earth with your heels. Lift your eyes to the lure that the Eternal King spins in His vast revolutions."
Just as a hawk first looks down at its feet, then turns to the falconer's call and stretches forward, drawn by the desire for food —
so I became. And so, as far as the rock splits to make way for one who climbs, I pressed on to where the circling path begins.
When I had come out upon the fifth circle, I saw people weeping, stretched face-down on the ground, all turned toward the earth.
"Adhaesit pavimento anima mea" — I heard them say with sighs so deep that the words could barely be understood.
"O chosen of God, whose sufferings are made less severe by justice and hope — direct us toward the higher stairs."
"If you have come here free from lying prostrate and wish to find the quickest way, keep your right hands always to the outside."
So the Poet asked, and so the answer came from somewhere a little ahead of us. From what was said, I guessed what was left unspoken.
I turned my eyes to my Lord's eyes, and he gave a cheerful nod of permission to what my eager look was asking for.
When I could do as I wished, I drew myself forward over that soul whose words had caught my attention.
I said: "O Spirit, in whom weeping ripens what is needed to turn to God — pause your greater care for me a moment.
Tell me: who were you, and why are all your backs turned upward? And tell me if you want me to do anything for you in the world I came from, where I still live."
And he to me: "Why heaven turns our backs to itself, you shall know. But first: scias quod ego fui successor Petri — know that I was a successor of Peter.
Between Siestri and Chiaveri flows a beautiful river, and from its name the title of my bloodline takes its height.
For barely a month and a little more I learned how heavy the great mantle weighs on one who keeps it from the mire. All other burdens seem a feather.
My conversion came late — alas! But when I was made the Roman Shepherd, I discovered that life was a lie.
I saw that even there the heart could find no rest, and in that life one could ascend no higher. So the love of this life was kindled in me.
Until that time I was a wretched soul, cut off from God, wholly given to greed. Now, as you see, I am punished for it here.
What avarice does is made plain in the purgation of these converted souls. The Mountain has no more bitter pain than this.
Just as our eyes did not lift themselves upward but stayed fastened on earthly things, so justice has here plunged them into the earth.
As avarice extinguished our love for every good, so that all right action was lost — so justice holds us in restraint here,
bound and imprisoned hand and foot. And for as long as it pleases the just Lord, we shall remain immovable and face-down."
I had fallen to my knees and was about to speak. But as I began, he sensed my reverence just from listening.
"What has bent you down like this?" he said. And I: "My conscience stung me, because of your dignity, while I was standing."
"Straighten your legs and rise, brother," he answered. "Do not err. I am a fellow-servant with you and with all the others, under one Power.
If you have ever heard that holy gospel verse which says 'neque nubent' — 'they neither marry' — you can easily understand why I say this.
Now go. I will not have you linger any longer, because your staying hinders my weeping — the weeping by which I ripen what you spoke of.
I have a granddaughter on earth named Alagia, good in herself — unless our house corrupts her by its example.
And she alone remains to me down there."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XX
paragraphs: The will struggles poorly against a better will. So, to please him and against my own wish, I drew the unsaturated sponge from the water.
I moved on, and my guide moved on, through the open spaces, keeping close to the rock the way you walk along the battlements of a wall.
For those on the other side, who drip through their eyes, drop by drop, the malady that pervades the whole world, lie too near the edge.
Cursed may you be, ancient she-wolf, who seizes more prey than all other beasts because your hunger is bottomlessly hollow!
O heavens, in whose turning some believe that conditions here below are changed — when will he come through whom she will be driven out?
We went on with slow, sparse steps, and I was listening to the shades I heard weeping and pitifully lamenting.
And by chance I heard "Sweet Mary!" cried out ahead of us amid the weeping, the way a woman does who is giving birth.
And continuing: "How poor you were is clear from that shelter where you laid down your sacred burden."
Then I heard: "O good Fabricius, you chose virtue with poverty over possessing great wealth with vice."
So pleasing were these words to me that I moved forward to learn more about the spirit from whom they seemed to come.
It was going on to speak of the generosity that Nicholas showed to the maidens, guiding their youth toward honor.
"O soul who speaks so well, tell me who you were," I said, "and why you alone renew these deserved praises.
Your words shall not go without reward, if I return to finish the short journey of this life that flies toward its end."
And he: "I'll tell you — not for any comfort I expect from earth, but because so much grace shines in you even before you are dead.
I was the root of that malignant plant which overshadows all the Christian world, so that good fruit is seldom gathered from it.
But if Douai and Ghent, Lille and Bruges had the power, vengeance would soon be taken. And this I pray of Him who judges all.
Hugh Capet was I called on earth. From me were born the Louises and the Philips by whom France has been governed in later days.
I was the son of a Parisian butcher, at a time when the ancient kings had all perished except one, who wore the gray cloth of a penitent.
I found myself grasping the reins of the realm's government, with so much new power and so many friends
that the widowed crown was placed upon the head of my own son, from whom the anointed bones of these kings descend.
So long as the great dowry of Provence had not drained my blood of all shame, my line did little worth — but at least it did no harm.
Then it began its plunder with lies and force. And afterward, for amends, it seized Ponthieu, Normandy, and Gascony.
Charles came to Italy, and for amends made a victim of Conradin. Then he thrust Thomas back to heaven — for amends.
I see a time, not very far from now, that draws forth another Charles from France, to make both himself and his family better known.
He comes unarmed, with only the lance that Judas jousted with. And he thrusts it so hard that he makes the belly of Florence burst.
From that he will gain not territory but sin and shame — all the more grievous to himself, as he counts such damage lightly.
The other, already hauled from his ship — I see him sell his daughter and haggle over her the way pirates do with female slaves.
What more can you do to us, O Avarice, now that you have drawn my blood so close to yourself that it has no care for its own flesh?
So that future and past evils may seem less, I see the fleur-de-lis enter Anagni, and Christ made captive in his own Vicar.
I see Him mocked a second time. I see the vinegar and the gall renewed. And between living thieves I see Him slain.
I see the new Pilate, so merciless that even this does not satisfy him. Without any decree, he carries his greedy sails into the Temple!
O my Lord, when shall I be made joyful by seeing the vengeance which, hidden, makes your anger sweet in its secrecy?
What I was saying about that sole bride of the Holy Ghost — which made you turn toward me for explanation —
that is the prayer ordained for us throughout the day. But when night comes, we take up the contrary sound instead.
At that time we recite the tale of Pygmalion, whose insatiable hunger for gold made him a traitor, thief, and parricide.
And the misery of avaricious Midas, whose outrageous demand was answered so that one can only laugh forever afterward.
Then everyone recalls the foolish Achan, who stole from the spoils so that the wrath of Joshua still seems to sting him here.
Then we accuse Sapphira and her husband. We praise the hooves that kicked Heliodorus. And infamy circles the whole mountain
for Polymnestor, who murdered Polydorus. At last comes the cry: 'O Crassus, tell us — you who know — what is the taste of gold?'
Sometimes we speak loud, sometimes low, according to the desire of speech that spurs us to greater or lesser pace.
But in the good that is spoken of here by day, I was not alone just now. Yet no other person nearby raised his voice."
We had already left him and were striving to cover the road as fast as our strength permitted,
when I felt the mountain tremble like something falling, and a chill seized me, like the chill that seizes a man going to his death.
Certainly Delos did not shake so violently before Latona made her nest there to give birth to the two eyes of heaven.
Then on every side a cry arose, so loud that my Master drew close to me, saying, "Do not be afraid while I am guiding you."
"Gloria in excelsis Deo" — all of them were saying, from what I could hear where it was close enough to make out the words.
We stood motionless and in suspense, just like the shepherds who first heard that song, until the trembling ceased and the hymn was finished.
Then we resumed our holy path, watching the shades that lay upon the ground, already returned to their accustomed weeping.
Never has any ignorance, if my memory does not err, assaulted me with so great a hunger to know
as I seemed to feel in that moment of reflection. Nor, in my haste, did I dare to question. Nor could I see the answer by myself.
So I went onward, timid and deep in thought.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXI
paragraphs: The natural thirst that is never quenched except by the water for whose grace the Samaritan woman begged
was tormenting me, and haste was driving me along the encumbered path behind my guide. And I was full of pity for that just punishment.
And then — just as Luke writes that Christ appeared to two travelers on the road, already risen from the tomb —
a shade appeared to us, coming from behind and gazing down upon the prostrate crowd. We were unaware of it until it spoke,
saying: "My brothers, may God give you peace." We turned at once, and Virgil gave back the proper greeting in return.
Then he said: "May the court of truth place you in peace within the blessed council — the court that banishes me to eternal exile."
"What!" said the shade, and we walked on at speed. "If you are shades whom God does not receive above, who has guided you so far up His stairs?"
My Teacher said: "If you look at the marks this one bears, which the Angel traces, you will clearly see he is destined to reign with the good.
But because she who spins both day and night had not yet drawn off for him the flax that Clotho loads and packs upon the distaff,
his soul, which is your sister and mine, could not come up alone, because it does not see the way we do.
That is why I was drawn from the wide throat of Hell to be his guide, and I shall guide him as far as my schooling can take him.
But tell us, if you know — why did the mountain shake just now, and why did everyone cry out as one, all the way down to its wet feet?"
His question hit the very eye of my desire, so that simply with the hope of an answer, my thirst became a little less fierce.
The shade began: "There is nothing in the mountain's holy order that happens without cause, and nothing foreign to its custom.
This place is free from every disturbance. What heaven receives from itself into itself can be the cause here, and nothing else.
For neither rain nor hail nor snow nor dew nor frost falls any higher than the short little stairway of three steps.
No dense clouds appear, nor thin ones, no lightning flashes, no rainbow — Thaumas's daughter, who so often shifts her region on earth.
No dry vapor rises any higher than the top of those three steps where Peter's vicar plants his feet.
Lower down it may tremble more or less. But from the wind hidden in the earth — I do not know how — up here it has never trembled.
It trembles here when any soul feels itself pure, so that it rises or moves to begin its ascent. And such a cry accompanies it.
Of purity, the will alone gives proof. The will, now wholly free to change its place, takes the soul by surprise and helps it fly.
The soul wills it from the start. But the desire — which divine justice sets upon the torment with the same force that once went toward sin — does not allow it.
And I, who have lain in this pain for five hundred years and more, only just now felt a free will toward a better place.
That is why you felt the earthquake, and why the faithful spirits praised the Lord across the mountain — may He speed them upward soon."
So he explained. And since we enjoy drinking as much as the thirst is great, I cannot say how much good his words did me.
My wise guide said: "Now I see the net that catches you here, and how you are freed, and why the earth quakes, and why you all rejoice.
Now let me know who you were. And from your words let me understand why you have been lying here for so many centuries."
"In the days when the good Titus, with the help of the supreme King, avenged the wounds from which the blood that Judas sold poured forth —
I lived on earth under the name that endures longest and most honors," the spirit replied, "greatly renowned, but not yet with faith.
My poetic voice was so sweet that Rome drew me, a Toulousan, to herself, where I earned the right to crown my brow with myrtle.
Statius, the people still call me on earth. I sang of Thebes and then of great Achilles, but I fell along the way with my second burden.
The seeds of my ardor were the sparks of that celestial flame that has set more than a thousand hearts on fire —
I mean the Aeneid. It was my mother, my nurse in poetry. Without it I would not have been worth a feather's weight.
And to have lived on earth while Virgil lived, I would gladly accept one more sun of exile than I must endure before my release."
These words made Virgil turn to me with a look that silently said: "Be silent." But the power of the will cannot do everything.
For laughter and tears follow so closely upon the feelings that give them birth that in the most honest person they least obey the will.
I only smiled, like someone giving a hint. At which the shade fell silent and gazed into my eyes, where expression dwells most clearly.
"So may you bring so great a labor to its end," it said, "tell me — why did your face just now show me the flash of a smile?"
Now I was caught between two forces. One kept me silent, the other urged me to speak. So I sighed, and I was understood.
"Speak," said my Master. "Do not be afraid of speaking. Speak out and tell him what he asks with such eagerness."
So I said: "Perhaps you are marveling, ancient spirit, at the smile I gave. But I want something even more wonderful to seize you.
This one, who guides my eyes upward, is that Virgil from whom you learned to sing of men and gods in lofty style.
If you thought my smile had any other cause, put that aside as false. Trust that it was only those words you spoke about him."
Already he was stooping to embrace my Teacher's feet. But Virgil said: "Brother, do not — for you are a shade, and a shade is what you see."
And Statius, rising: "Now you can understand the measure of love that warms me toward you — when I forget our emptiness
and treat a shadow as a solid thing."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXII
paragraphs: The Angel was already behind us — the Angel who had turned us toward the sixth circle, having erased one mark from my forehead.
He had told us that those who desire justice are "Beati" — blessed — and his voice ended it with "sitio" and nothing more.
And I, lighter than at any of the other passages, went on so effortlessly that I followed those swift spirits without any strain.
Then Virgil began: "Love that is kindled by virtue always kindles another love in return, provided its flame shows outwardly.
So from the hour that Juvenal came down among us in the Limbo of Hell and told me of your affection,
my kindness toward you has been as great as was ever felt for an unseen person. So these stairs will now seem short to me.
But tell me — and forgive me as a friend if I am letting my confidence loosen the reins too much — speak to me now as a friend:
how was it possible for avarice to find a place in your breast, given all the wisdom with which your diligence had filled you?"
These words at first made Statius smile. Then he answered: "Every word of yours is a dear sign of love to me.
Truly, things often appear that give false grounds for doubt, instead of revealing the true causes that lie hidden.
Your question shows me you believe I was a miser in the other life — perhaps because of the circle where I was.
Know then that avarice was far too distant from me. It was this extravagance that thousands of months of purgation have punished.
And had I not corrected my thinking when I heard the passage where you cry out, as if indignant at human nature:
'O cursed hunger for gold, to what do you not drive the appetites of men?' — I would now be rolling weights in the dismal jousts of Hell.
Then I understood that hands can spread their wings too wide in spending, and I repented of that as well as of my other sins.
How many shall rise on Judgment Day with cropped hair, out of ignorance that cuts off repentance for this sin, both in life and at death!
And know that the sin which directly opposes another sin dries up its green here in the same place.
Therefore, if I have been among the people who mourn avarice in order to purify myself, it happened to me because of its opposite."
"Now, when you sang of the cruel warfare of Jocasta's twofold grief," said the singer of the Bucolics,
"from what Clio accompanies you with in that poem, it does not appear that the faith without which no good works suffice had yet made you a believer.
If that is so, what sun or what candles scattered your darkness, so that you afterward set your sails to follow the Fisherman?"
And Statius to him: "You were the first to guide me toward Parnassus to drink from its springs, and the first to light my way toward God.
You did as one who walks at night, carrying his lantern behind him, which helps him not at all but makes the people following after him see clearly.
For you wrote: 'The age renews itself. Justice returns, and the primal time of man, and a new offspring descends from heaven.'
Through you I became a poet, and through you a Christian. But so you may better see my meaning, I will color it further.
Already the whole world was pregnant with the true faith, spread abroad by the messengers of the eternal kingdom.
And your words, which I just spoke of, were in harmony with the new preachers. So I took to visiting them.
They came to seem so holy to me that when Domitian persecuted them, their laments were not without my tears.
And for as long as I remained on earth, I befriended them. Their upright ways made me scorn all other sects.
And before I led the Greeks to the rivers of Thebes in my poetry, I was baptized. But out of fear I was a Christian in secret,
professing paganism for a long time. And this lukewarmness caused me to circle the fourth terrace for more than four hundred years.
You, therefore, who lifted the veil that had hidden from me the good I now speak of — while we have time to spare in our ascent —
tell me, where is our friend Terence? And Caecilius, Plautus, Varro — if you know? Tell me, are they damned, and in which district?"
"These, and Persius, and I, and many others," my Guide replied, "are with that Greek whom the Muses suckled more than any other,
in the first circle of the lightless prison. Often we speak of the mountain that forever holds our nurses.
Euripides is with us, and Antiphon, Simonides, Agathon, and many other Greeks who once crowned their brows with laurel.
There, of your own characters, one may see Antigone, Deiphyle and Argia, and Ismene, still sorrowful as of old.
There is she who showed the way to Langia. There is Tiresias's daughter, and Thetis, and Deidamia with her sisters."
Both poets now fell silent, looking around them attentively, free from the ascent and the enclosing walls.
Four handmaidens of the day had already been left behind, and the fifth was still pointing its burning horn upward at the pole,
when my guide said: "I think we should turn our right shoulders toward the edge and circle the mountain as we are accustomed to do."
So custom was our banner in that region. And we set off with less hesitation, thanks to the assent of that worthy soul.
