They went ahead, and I walked alone behind them, listening to their conversation, which gave me lessons in the art of poetry.
But soon their pleasant discourse was interrupted by a tree we found in the middle of the road, with sweet-smelling, appetizing fruit.
And just as a fir tree tapers upward from branch to branch, this one tapered downward — I think so that no one could climb it.
On the side where our path was enclosed, clear water fell from the high rock and spread itself across the leaves.
The two Poets drew near the tree, and from among the foliage a voice cried: "You shall have scarcity of this food!"
Then it said: "Mary thought more of making the wedding feast complete and honorable than of her own mouth, which now speaks for you.
And the ancient Roman women were content with water as their drink. And Daniel rejected food and won understanding.
The first age was beautiful as gold. Hunger made acorns savory, and thirst made nectar of every stream.
Honey and locusts were the food that nourished the Baptist in the wilderness. Therefore he is glorious and so greatly magnified,
as is revealed to you in the Gospel."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXIII
paragraphs: While I fixed my eyes among the green leaves like a man who wastes his life chasing after little birds,
my more-than-father said to me: "Son, come now. The time allotted to us must be better spent."
I turned my face and my steps just as quickly toward the Sages, who were talking so engagingly that the walking cost me nothing.
And then we heard a song and a lament — "Labia mea, Domine" — in a way that gave birth to both delight and grief.
"O my sweet Father, what is this I hear?" I began. And he answered: "Shades who perhaps go loosening the knot of their debt."
As thoughtful pilgrims do when they overtake strangers on the road — they turn to look but do not stop —
just so, a crowd of spirits, silent and devout, came up behind us with swifter steps, passing us and gazing at us as they went.
Each was dark and hollow in the eyes, pale in the face, and so wasted that the skin shaped itself to the very bones.
I do not think even Erysichthon could have been so withered down to the rind by famine, even when his fear of it was greatest.
I thought to myself: "These are the people who lost Jerusalem, when Mary made a meal of her own son."
Their eye sockets were like rings without their gems. Whoever reads the letters O-M-O in the human face could clearly have recognized the M.
Who would believe that the scent of an apple and the scent of water could consume them so, creating such craving, without knowing the cause?
I was still wondering what starved them so — the cause of their emaciation and wretched squalor not yet clear to me —
when from deep in the hollow of his skull, a shade turned its eyes on me and stared. Then it cried aloud: "What grace is this to me!"
I would never have known him by his looks. But in his voice was plainly revealed what his ravaged face had suppressed.
This spark reignited in me the full recognition of his altered features, and I recalled the face of Forese.
"Don't look at this dry leprosy that discolors my skin," he pleaded, "or at the lack of flesh I suffer.
But tell me the truth about yourself, and who are those two souls providing your escort? Don't hold back from speaking to me."
"That face of yours, which I once wept for dead, gives me now no lesser cause for weeping," I answered, "seeing it so changed!
But tell me, for God's sake, what strips you bare like this? Don't make me talk while I am marveling, for a man speaks badly who is full of other cravings."
And he to me: "From the eternal plan, a power falls into the water and the tree we left behind, and by it I waste away.
All these people who sing while lamenting are here re-sanctified through hunger and thirst for having followed appetite beyond all measure.
The scent from the fruit and from the water that sprays over the greenery kindles in us a craving to eat and drink.
And not once only, as we circle this ground, is our pain refreshed — I say pain, though I should say solace —
for the same desire leads us to the tree that led Christ to say 'Eli' with joy, when He freed us with His blood."
And I to him: "Forese, from the day you changed worlds for a better life, no more than five years have passed.
If the power to sin more was exhausted in you before the hour surprised you of that good sorrow that weds us back to God —
how have you come up here so quickly? I thought I would find you down below, where time repays time."
And he to me: "My Nella, with her flooding tears, has brought me so quickly to drink the sweet wormwood of these torments.
With her devout prayers and sighs she has drawn me from the slope where the dead wait, and freed me from the other circles.
So much more dear and pleasing to God is my little widow, whom I loved so much, as she is the more alone in doing good.
For the Barbagia region of Sardinia is far more modest in its women than the Barbagia where I left her.
O dear brother, what would you have me say? I can already see a future time — and this present hour will not be very old then —
when the shameless women of Florence will be forbidden from the pulpit to go about displaying their breasts and nipples.
What savages, what Saracens, ever needed spiritual or other discipline to make them cover themselves?
But if those shameless women knew what swift heaven is preparing for them, they would already have their mouths open wide to howl.
For if my foresight does not deceive me, they will be wailing before the boy who is now lulled to sleep with lullabies has grown a beard.
But brother, hide yourself from me no longer. See — not only I, but all these people are staring at the place where you block the sun."
So I said to him: "If you call to mind what you were to me and I to you, the memory will still be painful.
The one who walks ahead of me turned me from that life two days ago, when the sister of the sun over there showed herself full" — and I pointed to the sun.
"Through the deep night of the truly dead he has led me, in this real flesh that follows after him.
From there his encouragement has brought me upward, ascending and circling the mountain that straightens you whom the world made crooked.
He says he will keep me company until I am where Beatrice will be. There I must remain without him.
The one who tells me this is Virgil" — and I pointed at him — "and the other is the shade for whom just now every slope
of your realm shook, as it released him."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXIV
paragraphs: Neither the talk slowed the walking nor the walking the talk. We pressed on briskly, like a vessel driven by a strong wind.
And the shades, who looked doubly dead, stared at me from the graves of their eye sockets with wonder, aware that I was still alive.
I continued my conversation, saying: "Perhaps he climbs more slowly than he otherwise would, on account of the others.
But tell me, if you know — where is Piccarda? And tell me if I can see anyone of note among this crowd that stares at me so."
"My sister — whether she was more beautiful or more good, I cannot say — already triumphs joyfully in her crown on high Olympus."
So he said first. Then: "It is not forbidden to name each other here, since our dieting has so drained away our likeness.
This one" — and he pointed — "is Buonagiunta of Lucca. And that face beyond him, more pinched than the others,
held the holy Church in its embrace. He was from Tours, and here he purges with fasting the eels of Bolsena and the Vernaccia wine."
He named me many others one by one, and all seemed pleased to be named — I saw not a single dark look among them.
I saw Ubaldin dalla Pila biting the empty air for hunger, and Boniface, who pastured many people with his bishop's staff.
I saw Messer Marchese, who once had leisure to drink with less dryness at Forli, yet was a man who never felt satisfied.
But as someone does who looks around and then singles out one to value above the rest, I did with the one from Lucca, who seemed most eager to know me.
He was murmuring something, and I heard what sounded like "Gentucca" from the place where he felt the wound of justice that wastes them so.
"O soul," I said, "you who seem so eager to talk with me — speak so that I may hear you, and satisfy both yourself and me with your words."
"A girl is born who does not yet wear the veil," he began, "who will make my city pleasing to you, no matter how others may speak ill of it.
You will go your way with this foreknowledge. If my murmuring misled you, the real events will make it clear hereafter.
But tell me — is it really you I see here, the one who brought forth the new poetry that begins, 'Ladies who have intelligence of love'?"
And I to him: "I am one who, whenever Love inspires me, takes note, and in the manner that he dictates within, I set it down."
"O brother, now I see," he said, "the knot that held me back, and the Notary, and Guittone, short of the sweet new style I hear.
I clearly see how your pens follow closely behind the one who dictates, which certainly was not the case with ours.
And whoever sets himself to look further finds no difference between one style and the other." And as if satisfied, he fell silent.
Just as birds that winter along the Nile sometimes form themselves into a tight flock, then fly faster and stretch into a line —
so all the people there, turning their faces, quickened their steps, made light by both their leanness and their longing.
And as a man who is tired of running lets his companions go on ahead and walks, venting the panting of his chest —
so Forese let the holy flock pass by and walked with me behind them, saying: "When will I see you again?"
"I don't know how long I will live," I answered. "But my return will not be soon enough that my longing will not arrive here sooner.
Because the place where I was born to live is being stripped of good from day to day, and seems destined for wretched ruin."
"Go now," he said. "The one most guilty of it — I see him dragged at a beast's tail toward the valley where there is no repentance.
The beast goes faster with every stride, increasing until it strikes him down and leaves his body hideously mangled.
Those wheels" — and he lifted his eyes to heaven — "will not turn long before what my words cannot say further will be clear to you.
Now stay behind, for time is too precious in this kingdom, and I lose too much by walking abreast with you like this."
As a horseman sometimes bursts from a riding company at a gallop, seeking the honor of the first clash —
so Forese left us with longer strides. And I remained on the road with the two who were such mighty marshals of the world.
When he had gone so far ahead that my eyes could follow him no better than my mind could follow his words,
the laden, living boughs of another fruit tree appeared before me, not far off, since I had only just turned that way.
I saw people beneath it reaching up their hands and crying out something toward the leaves, like greedy, deluded children
who beg, while the one they beg does not answer — but holds up what they desire, to sharpen their craving, without hiding it.
Then they moved on, as if undeceived. And now we came to the great tree that refuses so many prayers and tears.
"Pass on without drawing near. Higher up stands the tree from which Eve ate, and this tree was raised from it."
So said a voice I could not see among the branches. And Virgil, Statius, and I pressed forward, crowding close to the side that rises.
"Remember," the voice said, "the accursed ones formed from cloud, who when drunk fought Theseus with their double breasts.
And remember the Jews who showed themselves soft in drinking, so that Gideon refused them as companions when he went down the hills toward Midian."
Thus, pressed close to one of the two edges, we passed on, hearing of the sins of gluttony and its miserable wages.
Then, set free upon the open road, we went a thousand steps and more in silence, each lost in his own thoughts.
"What are you three thinking about, walking along alone like this?" said a sudden voice. I started like a startled animal.
I raised my head to see who it was, and never in a furnace was glass or metal seen so red and glowing
as the one I saw, who said: "If it pleases you to climb, here you must turn. This is the way for whoever seeks peace."
His radiance had robbed me of my sight, so that I turned back toward my Teachers and walked as one who is guided by hearing alone.
And as the breeze of May, the harbinger of dawn, stirs and breathes out fragrance, pregnant with the scent of grass and flowers —
so I felt a wind strike the center of my brow, and I felt the movement of wings that breathed an odor of ambrosia.
And I heard it said: "Blessed are those whom grace so illumines that the love of taste does not kindle too great a desire in their breasts,
and who hunger always only as far as is just."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXV
paragraphs: The ascent would brook no delay now, because the sun had left its meridian circle to Taurus, and night had left its to Scorpio.
So like a man who does not linger but presses on, whatever may appear, when the sting of necessity drives him —
we entered the gap and took the stairway one before the other, so narrow that it forced us to climb in single file.
And as a little stork that lifts its wing, wanting to fly but not daring to leave the nest, and lets it droop back down —
so was I, with the desire to ask kindled and quenched by turns, getting as far as the movement of one who is about to speak.
Despite our rapid pace, my sweet father did not hold back but said: "Let fly the arrow of speech you have drawn to the barb."
With confidence I opened my mouth and began: "How can one grow thin where there is no need for nourishment?"
"If you would call to mind how Meleager wasted away with the wasting of a firebrand, this would not seem so hard to you," he said.
"And if you would think how your own image trembles in a mirror at each trembling motion, what seems difficult would seem easy.
But to fully satisfy your wish, here is Statius. I call upon him and ask that he now be the healer of your wounds."
"If I unfold to him the ways of eternal justice," Statius replied, "while you are present, let my excuse be that I can deny you nothing."
Then he began: "Son, if your mind takes in and holds these words of mine, they will be a light to you for the 'how' that puzzles you.
The purest blood, which is never drunk up by the thirsty veins and remains behind like food you clear from the table,
acquires in the heart a formative power for all the human members — the same blood that flows through the veins to become those members.
Refined further, it descends to a place better left unnamed, and from there it drops upon another's blood in the natural vessel.
There one mingles with the other — one designed to be passive, the other active, by virtue of the perfect place it springs from.
And once joined, it begins its work: first coagulating, then bringing to life what it had made solid as its material.
The active power, having become a soul like a plant's — with the difference that this is still on the way, while the plant has arrived —
then works so hard that it now moves and feels, like a sea-sponge. And then it undertakes to develop the organs whose seed it is.
Now, son, the power from the father's heart expands and extends itself, directed by nature toward all the members.
But how it goes from being animal to being human you do not yet see. This is the very point that once led a wiser man than you astray —
so far that in his teaching he separated the possible intellect from the soul, because he found no organ for it to use.
Open your breast to the truth that is coming. Know that as soon as the brain of the fetus is perfectly formed,
the First Mover turns to it with delight at such great natural artistry and breathes into it a new spirit, full of power,
which draws into its own substance whatever it finds active there, and becomes one single soul that lives, feels, and reflects upon itself.
And so that you may wonder less at my words, consider how the sun's heat becomes wine when it joins the juice that flows from the vine.
When Lachesis has no more thread to spin, the soul separates from the flesh and carries with it, in potential, both the human and the divine.
All the other faculties fall silent. But memory, intelligence, and will are far more vigorous in action than before.
Without pause, the soul falls of its own accord — marvelously — to one shore or the other. There it first learns which of its roads it must take.
As soon as that place encloses it, the formative power radiates around it, in the same form and measure as it did in the living limbs.
And just as air, when saturated with rain, adorns itself with various colors through reflected rays from elsewhere —
so the neighboring air shapes itself into the form that the soul, having come to rest, impresses upon it with its formative power.
And then, like a little flame that follows the fire wherever it moves, the new form follows the spirit.
Since from this the shade takes its appearance, it is called a shade. And from this it develops every sense, even sight.
This is why we speak and laugh. This is why we form the tears and the sighs that you may have heard upon the mountain.
The shade takes shape according to our desires and other feelings. And this is the cause of what you were wondering at."
And now we had arrived at the last of all the circles, and had turned to the right, and were intent upon a new concern.
There the embankment shoots forth flames of fire, and the cornice breathes an upward blast that drives the flames back and keeps them at bay.
So we had to walk on the open side, one by one. And I feared the fire on one side and the sheer drop on the other.
My guide said: "Along this place, one must keep the eyes on a tight rein, because it would be easy to go wrong."
"Summae Deus clementiae" — I then heard chanted from within the great burning, which made me no less eager to turn and look.
And I saw spirits walking through the flame. So I divided my gaze, looking now at my own steps, now at theirs.
After the hymn ended, they shouted aloud: "Virum non cognosco!" Then they began the hymn again softly.
When that too was done, they cried: "Diana ran to the forest and drove out Helice, who had tasted the poison of Venus!"
Then they returned to their singing. Then they called out the names of wives and husbands who were chaste, as virtue and the marriage vow demand.
And I believe this pattern sustains them for the entire time the fire burns them. With such treatment and such nourishment
the last wound of all must finally be closed.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXVI
paragraphs: While we walked on the brink like this, one before the other, the good Master kept saying: "Be careful! Let it be enough that I warn you."
The sun struck my right shoulder, and its rays were already turning the whole western sky from blue to white.
My shadow made the flames appear redder. And even this small sign, I noticed, caused many passing shades to take note.
This was what started them talking about me. They began saying to each other: "That does not seem like a phantom body!"
Then certain of them came toward me, as close as they could without stepping out of the fire where they would not be burned.
"O you who walk behind the others — not from being slower, but perhaps from reverence — answer me, who burn in thirst and fire.
Your answer is needed not by me alone. All of these thirst for it more than Ethiopians or Indians thirst for cold water.
Tell us: how is it that you make yourself a wall against the sun, as if you had not yet entered the net of death?"
So one of them addressed me. I would have revealed myself at once, had I not been distracted by a new marvel that appeared just then.
For through the middle of the burning road came people walking face-to-face with these, which held me in suspense as I stared.
I saw each group hurrying from either side, and the shades kissed one another without stopping, content with a brief greeting.
So ants, in the middle of their dark column, touch muzzle to muzzle — perhaps to scout out their route or their fortune.
No sooner is the friendly greeting over, before the first step carries them onward, than each group tries to outcry the other.
The newcomers shout: "Sodom and Gomorrah!" The others: "Pasiphae enters the cow, so that the bull may run to satisfy her lust!"
Then, like cranes that might fly in part to the Riphaean mountains and in part to the sands — these fleeing the frost, those fleeing the sun —
one group goes and the other comes, and weeping they return to their first songs and to the cry most fitting to each.
And the same ones who had entreated me drew close to me again, their faces intent on listening.
I, who had twice seen their inclination, began: "O souls who are certain of reaching a state of peace, whenever that may be —
my limbs have not remained on earth either unripe or ripened. They are here with me, with their blood and joints.
I am going up to be blind no longer. A Lady above wins this grace for me, whereby I carry my mortal body through your world.
But so may your greatest longing soon be satisfied, and the Heaven that is fullest of love and spreads widest may welcome you —
tell me, so that I may write it down, who you are, and what that crowd is that goes on its way behind your backs."
No differently is a mountain peasant bewildered, gaping and struck dumb, when rough and rustic he first enters a town —
than each shade became in its expression. But once they had shaken off their stupor — which is quickly calmed in noble hearts —
the one who had first questioned me began again: "Blessed are you, who take on freight from our borderlands for a better life!
The people who do not come with us sinned in the way that once caused Caesar, in his triumph, to hear himself called 'Queen' in mockery.
Therefore they part from us shouting 'Sodom!' — reproaching themselves, as you heard — and they add to their burning with their shame.
Our own sin was of both sexes. But because we did not observe human law, following our appetites like beasts,
we read out, to our own disgrace, when we separate, the name of her who made herself a beast within the bestial wooden frame.
Now you know our acts and what our crime was. If you would perhaps know us by name, there is no time to tell, nor could I.
But your wish to know me shall indeed be granted. I am Guido Guinizelli, and I purge myself here, having repented before the final hour."
What the two sons of Lycurgus became at the sight of their mother — that is what I became, though I did not rise so high,
the moment I heard the name of the father of me and of my betters — all who ever wrote sweet, gracious verses of love.
Without hearing or speaking, I walked a long time in thought, gazing at him, but did not draw nearer because of the fire.
When I had feasted my eyes, I offered myself entirely ready for his service, with the kind of oath that compels belief.
And he said to me: "You leave such deep and clear footprints in me, from what I hear, that Lethe cannot erase or dim them.
But if your words just now swore the truth, tell me the reason why you show in look and speech that you hold me so dear."
And I to him: "Those sweet verses of yours, which, as long as modern usage endures, will make their very ink forever precious."
"O brother," he said, "the one I point to" — and he indicated a spirit ahead — "was a better craftsman of the mother tongue.
In verses of love and romances in prose, he surpassed them all. Let the fools talk who think the one from Limoges is better.
They turn their faces to clamor rather than truth, and fix their opinions before art or reason has been heard.
So many of the ancients did with Guittone, giving him applause from cry to cry, until the truth prevailed with most.
Now, if you have such great privilege that you are allowed to enter the cloister where Christ is the abbot of the community,
say a Paternoster there for me — as much of it as we need in this world, where the power to sin no longer exists."
Then, perhaps to make room for the one behind him, he vanished into the fire like a fish diving to the bottom of the water.
I moved a little toward the spirit he had pointed out, and said that my desire was preparing an honorable place for his name.
He began to speak freely: 'Tan m'abellis vostre cortes deman, que jeu no'm puesc ni vueill a vos cobrire.
Jeu sui Arnaut, que plor e vai chantan; consiros vei la passada folor, e vei jauzen lo jorn qu'esper denan.
Ara vus prec per aquella valor, que vus condus al som de la scalina, sovenga vus a temprar ma dolor.'
Then he hid himself in the fire that purifies them.

* So pleases me your courteous request that I cannot and will not hide from you. I am Arnaut, who weep and singing go. With sorrow I see the past folly, and with joy I see the hoped-for day before me. Therefore I beg you, by that power which guides you to the summit of the stairs — remember to ease my suffering!

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXVII
paragraphs: As when the sun casts its first rays in the land where its Maker shed His blood — while the Ebro lies beneath high Libra,
and the waters of the Ganges are scorched by noon — so stood the sun. The day was departing when the glad Angel of God appeared to us.
He stood outside the flame on the edge of the path and chanted "Beati mundo corde" in a voice far more alive than ours.
Then he said: "No one goes further, holy souls, unless the fire first bites you. Enter it, and do not be deaf to the song beyond."
When we drew close he said this to us. And I became, upon hearing him, like one who is laid in the grave.
I straightened myself over my clasped hands, staring into the fire, vividly recalling the human bodies I had once seen burned.
My good guides turned toward me. Virgil said: "My son, here there may be torment, but not death.
Remember! Remember! If I guided you safely even on the back of Geryon, what shall I do now, when I am nearer to God?
Be certain: if you stood for a full thousand years in the heart of this flame, it could not singe a single hair from your head.
And if you think I am deceiving you, step close to it. Test it yourself with the hem of your garment in your own hands.
Put aside all fear now, put it aside. Turn this way and come forward in safety." And I stood still, motionless and stubborn, against my conscience.
Seeing me frozen and immovable, he said, somewhat disturbed: "Look now, son — between Beatrice and you, there is this wall."
As at the name of Thisbe the dying Pyramus opened his eyes and gazed on her, the moment the mulberry turned crimson —
just so, my stubbornness softened. I turned to my wise guide, hearing the name that forever wells up in my memory.
He shook his head and said: "Well? Shall we stay on this side?" Then he smiled, the way one smiles at a child won over by an apple.
Then he entered the fire ahead of me, asking Statius to come behind — Statius, who had walked between us for a long way.
Once inside, I would have thrown myself into molten glass to cool off, so immeasurably fierce was the burning there.
My sweet Father, to encourage me, kept talking about Beatrice as we walked, saying: "I think I can already see her eyes!"
A voice singing on the other side guided us. Attending to it alone, we emerged where the ascent began.
"Venite, benedicti Patris mei" sounded from within a splendor so bright that it overcame me, and I could not look.
"The sun departs," it added, "and night comes. Do not linger. Press your steps forward while the west is still not dark."
The path rose straight through the rock in a direction that cut off the sun's rays before me, for the sun was now low.
We had tried only a few stairs when, by the vanished shadow, my Sages and I perceived that the sun had set behind us.
And before the horizon had become one uniform expanse in all its breadth, and Night held her boundless realm,
each of us made a stair into his bed. For the nature of the mountain took from us the power to climb, though not the desire.
Just as goats who have been swift and bold on the mountaintops before they fed become passive as they ruminate,
silent in the shade while the sun is hot, watched by the herdsman leaning on his staff, tending them as he leans —
and as the shepherd, lodging out of doors, passes the night beside his quiet flock, watching that no wild beast scatter it —
such were we all three at that hour: I like the goat, and they like the herdsmen, hemmed in on both sides by the rocks.
Little could be seen of the world outside. But through that little gap I saw the stars, brighter and larger than usual.
So, ruminating and gazing at them, sleep seized me — sleep, which often knows the news before the event.
It was the hour, I think, when Cytherea, who always seems to burn with the fire of love, first beamed upon the mountain from the east.
In my dream I thought I saw a young, beautiful woman walking through a meadow, gathering flowers, and singing as she went:
"Let whoever asks know that I am Leah. I go moving my beautiful hands to make myself a garland.
To please myself at the mirror, I adorn myself here. But my sister Rachel never leaves her looking glass. She sits before it all day long.
She is as eager to see her own beautiful eyes as I am to adorn myself with my hands. Seeing satisfies her, as doing satisfies me."
And now, before the pre-dawn splendors that pilgrims find more welcome the closer to home they lodge on their return,
the darkness fled on every side, and sleep with it. I rose, seeing the great Masters already risen.
"That sweet apple which mortals go seeking through so many branches will today put your hungers to rest."
These were the words Virgil spoke to me. And never were there gifts that could compare with these in their delight.
Such longing upon longing came over me to reach the top that with every step thereafter I felt wings growing for the flight.
When the entire staircase had been run beneath us and we stood on the highest step, Virgil fixed his eyes upon me
and said: "The temporal fire and the eternal, son, you have seen. You have come to a place where I, on my own, can see no further.
By intellect and art I have brought you here. From now on, take your own pleasure as your guide. You are beyond the steep ways and the narrow.
See the sun shining on your forehead. See the grass, the flowers, the shrubs that this land produces of itself alone.
Until those beautiful eyes come rejoicing — the eyes whose weeping caused me to come to you — you may sit down or walk among them.
Expect no more word or sign from me. Your will is free, upright, and whole. It would be wrong not to follow its bidding.
Over yourself I therefore crown and mitre you."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXVIII
paragraphs: Eager now to search within and around the heavenly forest — dense and green with living trees, which softened the new daylight for my eyes —
I left the bank without further delay, crossing the level ground slowly, slowly, over the soil that breathed fragrance everywhere.
A gentle, steady breeze, with no variation in it, struck my forehead — no heavier than the touch of a soft wind.
The branches, lightly trembling, all bowed toward the side where the Holy Mountain casts its first shadow.
Yet they did not sway so far from upright that the little birds on their tops had to stop any of their arts.
Rather, with full delight they greeted the hours of early morning, singing among the leaves that bore a steady rustling accompaniment to their melodies —
such as gathers from branch to branch through the pine forest on the shore of Chiassi when Aeolus unleashes the south wind.
Already my slow steps had carried me so far into the ancient wood that I could no longer see where I had entered it.
And then a stream cut off my path, bending the grass on its banks leftward with its little waves.
All the waters on earth that are most clear would seem to hold some mixture in them, compared to this one, which hides nothing —
though it flows along with a dark, dark current under the perpetual shade, which never lets a ray of sun or moon enter.
I stopped my feet but crossed with my eyes beyond the stream, to gaze at the great variety of blossoming branches.
And there appeared to me — just as something suddenly appears that drives all other thought aside with wonder —
a lady all alone, walking along and singing, picking flower after flower from the carpet of blooms that painted her path.
"Ah, beautiful lady, you who warm yourself in the rays of love — if I may trust your looks, which are usually witnesses of the heart —
may the desire come to you to draw near to this riverbank," I said, "close enough that I can hear what you are singing.
You make me remember where and what Proserpina was in the moment when her mother lost her, and she herself lost the spring."
As a lady turns while dancing, keeping her feet close together and to the ground, barely placing one foot before the other —
so she turned toward me on the red and yellow flowers, in no other manner than a maiden who lowers her modest eyes.
And she granted my wish, drawing so near that the sweet sound reached me together with its meaning.
As soon as she was where the grasses are bathed by the waters of the beautiful stream, she granted me the favor of lifting her eyes.
I do not think so great a light shone beneath the eyelids of Venus, when she was pierced by her own son beyond his usual way!
She smiled from the other bank, holding many colors in her hands — flowers which that high land produces without seed.
Three paces of river separated us. But the Hellespont, where Xerxes crossed — still a rebuke to all human arrogance —
did not earn more hatred from Leander, surging between Sestos and Abydos, than this stream earned from me for not opening.
"You are newcomers," she began, "and perhaps because I smile in this place chosen to be the nest of human nature,
some wonder holds you marveling. But the psalm 'Delectasti' gives a light that can clear the cloud from your understanding.
And you who are in front and called to me — speak, if you wish to hear more. I came ready to answer all your questions, as far as is needed."
"The water and the sound of the forest," I said, "are fighting in me against a new belief, which I heard stated as the opposite of this."
She answered: "I will explain how the thing that makes you wonder proceeds from its cause, and clear the mist that strikes you.
The Supreme Good, who delights only in Himself, made man good and made this beautiful place as a pledge of eternal peace.
Through his own fault, man's stay here was brief. Through his own fault, he exchanged innocent laughter and sweet play for weeping and toil.
So that the disturbances caused below by the exhalations of land and water, which follow heat as far as they can,
might not wage any war upon mankind, this mountain rose toward heaven so high — and is free from them, from the gate upward.
Now, since the whole atmosphere turns in a circle with the primal motion, unless its circuit is broken somewhere,
this movement strikes upon this height, which stands entirely in the living ether — and makes the forest resound, because the trees are dense.
And the plants struck have such power that they impregnate the air with their essence, which, as it revolves, scatters it abroad.
And the earth below, according to its own nature and its climate, conceives and brings forth trees of different kinds.
Hearing this, it should no longer seem a marvel on earth when some plant takes root without any visible seed.
And you should know that this holy tableland where you stand is full of every kind of seed, and bears fruit that is never gathered there below.
The water you see does not spring from a vein replenished by vapor that the cold condenses, like a river that gains and loses flow.
It comes from a fountain, constant and sure, which by God's will regains as much as it pours out, open on two sides.
On this side it descends with the power to take away all memory of sin. On the other, it restores the memory of every good deed done.
Here it is called Lethe, and on the other side Eunoe. It does not work unless first tasted on both sides.
Its savor surpasses every other. And even though your thirst may be well slaked so that I need reveal no more to you,
I will give you a corollary as a bonus. And I do not think my words will be less dear to you if they go beyond what I promised.
Those who in ancient times sang of the Age of Gold and its happiness perhaps dreamed of this place on Parnassus.
Here the human race was innocent. Here it was always spring, with every fruit. This is the nectar of which each one speaks."
Then I turned completely around to face my Poets, and I saw that they had listened to her closing words with a smile.
Then I turned my eyes back to the beautiful lady.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXIX
paragraphs: Singing like a woman in love, she continued with the ending of her words: "Beati quorum tecta sunt peccata."
And like nymphs who used to wander alone through the forest shadows, some seeking shade, some seeking the sun —
she then moved upstream against the current, and I walked abreast of her on the other bank, matching her small steps with mine.
Between her steps and mine there were not a hundred, when the banks made an equal turn so that I was facing east.
Even then we had not gone far before the lady turned fully to me and said: "Brother, look and listen!"
And suddenly a brilliance flashed across the great forest on every side, so intense I wondered if it was lightning.
But since lightning vanishes as fast as it comes, and this kept growing brighter and brighter, I thought: "What is this?"
And a delicious melody ran through the luminous air. Holy zeal made me rebuke Eve's boldness —
for there where both earth and heaven were obedient, the woman alone, and only just created, could not bear to stay beneath any veil.
If she had stayed devoutly beneath it, I would have tasted those ineffable delights sooner and for a longer time.
While I walked enraptured among these first fruits of eternal pleasure, still hungry for more delights,
the air beneath the green branches became like a kindled fire before us, and the sweet sound was now clearly heard as singing.
O most holy Virgins! If I have ever endured hunger, cold, or sleepless nights for your sake, now necessity spurs me to claim my reward!
Now Helicon must pour forth for me, and Urania must help me with her choir, to put into verse things difficult to conceive.
A little farther on, what looked in that long intervening space like seven trees of gold appeared in outline —
but when I had come close enough that the distance no longer confused the features common to many objects,
the faculty that furnishes reason with its material recognized them as candlesticks, and in the singing I could make out "Hosanna!"
The splendid array above them flamed brighter than the moon at midnight in the middle of its month, in a clear sky.
I turned around in admiration to good Virgil, and he answered me with a look no less full of wonder.
Then I turned my face back to those high things, which were moving toward us so slowly that new brides would have outpaced them.
The lady rebuked me: "Why do you burn so with passion only for the living lights, and not look at what comes behind them?"
Then I saw people walking behind them, as if following their leaders, dressed in white — a whiteness never seen on earth.
The water on my left gleamed and reflected my left side back to me, clear as a mirror, when I looked into it.
When I had reached a spot on my bank where only the stream separated us, I stopped to see better.
I saw the flames advance, leaving the air behind them painted in their wake, so that they looked like trailing banners.
Overhead the air remained streaked with seven bands of color — the same colors that make the sun's rainbow and Diana's girdle.
These streamers stretched farther back than I could see. The outermost ones, as far as I could tell, were ten paces apart.
Beneath this beautiful canopy, twenty-four Elders came two by two, crowned with garlands of fleur-de-lis.
They all sang: "Blessed are you among the daughters of Adam, and blessed forever shall your beauty be!"
After the flowers and the tender grasses on the bank before me were cleared of that chosen company,
just as star follows star in heaven, four creatures came close behind them, each crowned with green leaves.
Each was plumed with six wings, the feathers full of eyes — the eyes of Argus, if they were living, would be such as these.
Reader, I waste no more rhymes tracing their forms, for other expenses press me so hard that I cannot be lavish here.
But read Ezekiel, who depicts them as he saw them coming from the cold region with cloud, whirlwind, and fire.
Just as you will find them in his pages, so they were here — except that in the matter of their wings, John agrees with me and differs from him.
The space between these four contained a triumphal chariot on two wheels, drawn forward by the neck of a Griffin.
The Griffin stretched both wings upward between the middle band and the three on each side, so that its flight cleaved none of them.
The wings rose so high they were lost to sight. Its limbs were gold where it was a bird, and white mixed with crimson where it was not.
Not only did Rome never gladden Africanus or Augustus with so splendid a chariot, but even the Sun's own car would be poor beside it —
that car of the Sun which swerved off course and burned, at Earth's desperate prayer, when Jove was so mysteriously just.
Three maidens came dancing in a circle at the right wheel. One was so red she would scarcely have been noticed in a fire.
The second looked as though her flesh and bones were made entirely of emerald. The third seemed like freshly fallen snow.
Now they seemed led by the white one, now by the red. And from the red one's song, the others took their pace, either slow or swift.
On the left, four others made festival, robed in purple, following the measure of one among them who had three eyes in her head.
Behind this entire company I saw two old men, unlike in dress but alike in bearing — each dignified and grave.
One appeared to be a follower of that supreme Hippocrates, whom Nature made for the creatures she loves most.
The other showed the opposite care, with a sword so sharp and gleaming that it frightened me from across the river.
Then I saw four more of humble appearance, and behind them all an old man walking alone, asleep yet with a keen face.
These seven were dressed like the first company, but wore no garlands of fleur-de-lis around their heads.
Instead, they were crowned with roses and other red flowers. At a short distance, you would have sworn flames were burning above their brows.
And when the chariot drew even with me, thunder was heard. That august company seemed forbidden to go further,
and halted there together with the leading standards.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXX
paragraphs: When the seven stars of the highest heaven — which never knew setting or rising, nor any cloud's veil but the veil of sin,
and which made everyone there aware of their duty, just as the lower seven guide the helmsman who steers toward port —
came to a halt, the truthful company that had walked between the seven lights and the Griffin turned toward the chariot as toward their peace.
And one of them, as if sent from heaven, sang "Veni, sponsa, de Libano" three times, and all the others repeated it after him.
Just as the blessed at the last summons shall rise from their graves with voices renewed, lifting up their newly clothed flesh —
so, upon that heavenly chariot, a hundred angels rose at the voice of so great an elder — ministers and messengers of eternal life.
All were saying "Benedictus qui venis!" and, scattering flowers above and all around: "Manibus, oh, date lilia plenis!"
I have seen, before now, the eastern sky all rose-colored at the start of day, with the rest of the heaven beautifully clear,
and the rising sun's face so veiled by tempering vapors that the eye could bear to look at it for a long while.
Just so, within a cloud of flowers that rose from those angelic hands and fell again, both inside and outside the chariot,
a lady appeared, olive-crowned over her white veil, dressed beneath a green mantle in the color of living flame.
And my spirit, which had been so long — so long — since it had stood trembling with awe in her presence,
without gaining more knowledge through my eyes, through a hidden power that came from her, felt the mighty force of old love.
The moment that great power struck my sight — the same power that had already pierced me through before I had left my boyhood —
I turned to my left with the trust of a little child who runs to his mother when he is frightened or hurt,
to say to Virgil: "Not a drop of blood remains in me that does not tremble. I recognize the signs of the ancient flame."
But Virgil had left us bereft of himself — Virgil, sweetest of all fathers, Virgil, to whom I had given myself for my salvation.
And not all that our first mother lost could keep my dew-cleansed cheeks from darkening again with tears.
"Dante, do not weep yet because Virgil has departed. Do not weep yet — for you must weep by another sword."
Like an admiral who goes from stern to prow to inspect the crews working in the other ships, and to cheer them on —
so, on the left side of the chariot, when I turned at the sound of my own name (which is recorded here of necessity),
I saw the Lady who had first appeared veiled beneath the angelic celebration, directing her eyes to me across the river.
Although the veil, descending from her head and encircled with Minerva's leaves, did not let her appear clearly,
she continued with a royally commanding bearing, like one who speaks while holding back the fiercest words:
"Look at me well. I am indeed Beatrice! How did you deign to approach the Mountain? Did you not know that here man finds his happiness?"
My eyes dropped to the clear fountain. But seeing myself in it, I turned to the grass — so heavy was the shame that weighed my forehead down.
As a mother seems stern to her child, so she seemed to me. For the taste of severe compassion has something bitter in it.
She fell silent. And the Angels suddenly sang, "In te, Domine, speravi" — but did not go beyond "pedes meos."
Just as the snow freezes solid among the living beams of Italy's mountain spine, packed by winds from the east,
and then, when the land that loses its shadow breathes warm, it melts and trickles through itself like a candle consumed by flame —
so I was, without a tear or sigh, before the song of those who always sing in harmony with the eternal spheres.
But when I heard in their sweet melodies a compassion for me — greater than if they had said, "Lady, why do you shame him so?" —
the ice that had frozen around my heart turned to air and water, and in anguish it burst from my chest through my mouth and eyes.
She, still standing firmly on the right side of the chariot, then directed her words to those holy beings:
"You keep your watch in the eternal day, so that neither night nor sleep can steal from you a single step the ages take upon their road.
My answer, therefore, is given with greater care, so that he who weeps over there may hear me, and so that sin and sorrow may be in equal measure.
Not only through the workings of the great wheels that direct every seed to some end, according to the stars' conjunction,
but through the abundance of heavenly graces — whose rains fall from vapors so lofty that our sight cannot approach them —
this man, in his new life, was so richly gifted in potential that every good habit would have shown admirable proof in him.
But the richer and more powerful the soil, the wilder and more savage it grows when left untilled and planted with bad seed.
For a time I sustained him with my gaze. Showing him my young eyes, I led him with me, turned in the right direction.
But as soon as I was on the threshold of my second age and I changed life, he took himself from me and gave himself to others.
When I rose from flesh to spirit and beauty and virtue increased in me, I became less dear and less pleasing to him.
He turned his steps into untrue ways, pursuing false images of good that never keep their promises.
Nor did it avail me to seek inspiration for him — through dreams and other means I called him back, but he heeded them so little.
So low he fell that all remedies for his salvation were already too short — except to show him the people of perdition.
For this I visited the gate of the dead, and to the one who has led him this far up, I carried my pleas with weeping.
God's high decree would be violated if Lethe were crossed, and if such food were tasted, without any payment
of the penitence that pours forth in tears."

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXXI
paragraphs: "O you who stand beyond the sacred river," she began, turning the sharp edge of her speech directly at me — speech that even edgewise had cut me deeply.
She continued without pause: "Say — say if this is true. To such a charge, your own confession must be added."
My faculties were in such confusion that my voice began to move but died before my lips could shape it.
She waited a moment. Then she said: "What are you thinking? Answer me. The painful memories in you have not yet been damaged by these waters."
Confusion and dismay mixed together forced a "Yes" from my mouth so faint that it took eyesight, not hearing, to make it out.
Just as a crossbow breaks when the string and the bow are drawn too tight, and the arrow strikes the target with weakened force —
so I collapsed under that heavy burden, pouring out tears and sighs in a torrent, and my voice gave out along the way.
She said to me: "In those longings of mine that led you to love the Good beyond which there is nothing to aspire to —
what ditches or what chains did you find lying across the path, that you should have stripped yourself of the hope of going forward?
And what allurements or advantages did the others show upon their faces, that you should have turned your steps toward them?"
After heaving a bitter sigh, I barely had voice enough to answer. My lips shaped the words with effort.
Weeping, I said: "The things that were present turned me aside with their false pleasure, the moment your face was hidden from me."
And she: "If you had been silent, or denied what you confess, your fault would be no less known — such is the Judge who knows it.
But when the accusation of sin comes bursting from one's own cheeks, in our court the wheel turns back against the blade.
Nevertheless, so that you may feel greater shame for your transgression, and be stronger the next time you hear the Sirens,
set aside your weeping and listen. Then you will hear how my buried flesh should have directed you in the opposite way.
Never did art or nature present to you a pleasure as great as the fair body in which I was enclosed — and that body is now scattered in the earth.
And if the greatest pleasure thus failed you through my death, what mortal thing should afterward have drawn you into desire?
You ought indeed, at the first arrow of deceptive things, to have risen up to follow me, who was no longer such.
You should not have bent your wings downward to wait for more blows — some young girl, or other vanity of such brief use.
A fledgling bird waits for two or three arrows. But before the eyes of one already fully feathered, the net is spread and the shaft shot in vain."
Like children who stand silent in their shame, eyes on the ground, aware of their fault and penitent —
so I stood. And she said: "Since you suffer pain in hearing, lift up your beard, and you will suffer greater pain in seeing."
With less resistance is a sturdy oak uprooted by a wind from its own land, or by one blowing from the deserts of North Africa,
than I raised my chin at her command. And when she demanded my face by saying "beard," I understood well the venom in her meaning.
When I lifted my face, my eyes saw that those beautiful beings had stopped strewing flowers.
And my still half-reassured eyes saw Beatrice turned toward the beast that is one person in two natures.
Beneath her veil, beyond the green bank, she seemed to surpass her former self even more than she had surpassed all others here when she was alive.
The thorn of repentance stung me so sharply then that whichever of all other things had most turned me to love it now became my greatest enemy.
Such self-knowledge pierced my heart that I was overwhelmed and fell. What I became then, she who caused it knows.
When my heart restored my outward senses, I saw the lady I had found alone standing above me, saying, "Hold me! Hold me!"
She had drawn me into the stream up to my throat, and pulling me behind her, she was gliding over the water, light as a shuttle.
When I was near the blessed shore, I heard "Asperges me" sung so sweetly that I cannot remember it, much less write it down.
The beautiful lady opened her arms wide, embraced my head, and plunged me under, where I was forced to swallow the water.
Then she drew me out and brought me, dripping, into the dance of the four beautiful ones, and each covered me with her arm.
"We are nymphs here and stars in heaven. Before Beatrice descended to the world, we were appointed as her handmaids.
We will lead you to her eyes. But the three beyond, who gaze more deeply, will sharpen yours for the joyful light within them."
So they sang. Then they led me with them to the Griffin's breast, where Beatrice stood, turned toward us.
"See that you do not spare your eyes," they said. "We have placed you before the emeralds from which Love once drew his weapons against you."
A thousand desires, hotter than flame, fastened my eyes upon those shining eyes, which remained fixed upon the Griffin.
As the sun shines in a mirror, so within her eyes the twofold creature was reflected — now with one nature, now with the other.
Think, Reader, whether I marveled when I saw the thing itself stand still, yet in its reflected image it was transforming.
While my soul, amazed and jubilant, was tasting the food that satisfies and yet makes you hunger for more,
the other three, revealing themselves to be of the highest rank in bearing, came forward, dancing to their angelic steps.
"Turn, Beatrice, O turn your holy eyes," they sang, "upon your faithful one, who has taken so many steps to see you.
In grace, do us the grace of unveiling your face to him, so that he may see the second beauty which you conceal."
O splendor of the living light eternal! Who has grown so pale beneath the shade of Parnassus, or drunk so deeply at its spring,
that his mind would not seem clouded, trying to paint you as you appeared, where the harmonious heaven was your canopy,
when you unveiled yourself in the open air?

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXXII
paragraphs: So fixed and intent were my eyes in satisfying their ten-year thirst that all my other senses had gone dead.
On this side and that they had walls of indifference — the holy smile drew them to itself with the old net.
When my gaze was forcibly turned to my left by those goddesses, because I heard them say, "Too intently!"
And that condition of the eyesight that comes from eyes just dazzled by the sun left me blind for a little while.
But when my sight adjusted to the lesser brightness — I say lesser in comparison with the greater splendor from which I had been pulled away —
I saw that the glorious host had wheeled around to the right, returning with the sun and the seven flames upon their faces.
As a squadron turns beneath its shields to save itself, wheeling with its banner, before the whole body can reverse its front —
so the soldiers of the heavenly kingdom who marched in front had entirely passed us before the chariot turned its pole.
Then the maidens returned to the wheels, and the Griffin moved his blessed burden so smoothly that not a feather ruffled.
The beautiful lady who had drawn me through the ford, and Statius and I, followed the wheel that made its turn with the smaller arc.
So we passed through the lofty forest — empty through the fault of the one who trusted the serpent — keeping time to angelic music.
Perhaps as far as three arrow-flights would carry, we had moved when Beatrice stepped down from the chariot.
I heard them all murmur, "Adam!" Then they circled a tree stripped of all flowers and foliage on every branch.
Its crown, which spread wider as it rose higher, would have been marveled at by Indians in their forests for its sheer height.
"Blessed are you, O Griffin, who do not tear with your beak these branches sweet to taste, for appetite for them once turned to evil."
So the others shouted around the mighty tree. And the twofold creature said: "Thus is the seed of all righteousness preserved."
Turning to the pole he had drawn, he brought it close to the widowed trunk and left what was of the tree bound to it.
In the same way that our earthly trees — when the great light falls, mingled with the light that shines after the celestial Fish —
begin to swell and then renew themselves, each in its own color, before the Sun harnesses his steeds beneath another constellation —
so, revealing a hue less than rose and more than violet, the tree renewed itself, whose branches had been so bare.
I never heard the hymn that those people sang — it is not sung here below — nor could I follow its melody through to the end.
If I could paint how those pitiless eyes fell asleep at the tale of Syrinx — those eyes whose long wakefulness cost them so dear —
like a painter working from a model, I would depict how I fell asleep. But let whoever can render drowsiness well do so.
So I skip to when I woke. A splendor tore the veil of sleep from me, and a voice called: "Rise! What are you doing?"
Just as Peter, John, and James were led to see the blossoming apple tree that makes the angels hungry for its fruit and keeps eternal wedding feasts in heaven —
and, overcome, came to their senses at the word that has broken deeper sleeps than theirs,
and saw their company diminished by the loss of Moses and Elijah, and their Master's robes transformed —
so I came back to myself and saw that compassionate one standing over me who had before been guide to my steps beside the river.
In complete bewilderment I said: "Where is Beatrice?" And she: "See her, sitting beneath the new-grown leaves, upon the root of the tree.
See the company that circles her. The rest are ascending behind the Griffin, with deeper, more melodious song."
Whether her words went on further I do not know, because already before my eyes was she who had shut me to all other hearing.
She sat alone on the bare ground, left there as guardian of the chariot that I had seen the two-natured beast fasten.
The seven nymphs made a ring around her, holding in their hands those lights that are proof against both north wind and south.
"You will be a dweller in this forest only briefly. And you will be with me forever — a citizen of that Rome where Christ Himself is Roman.
Therefore, for the good of the world that lives so badly, fix your eyes on the chariot. And what you see, make sure you write down when you return to earth."
So spoke Beatrice. And I, who was wholly devoted at the foot of her commands, gave my mind and eyes to wherever she directed.
Never did fire descend from a heavy cloud so swiftly, falling from the most remote region of the sky,
as I saw the bird of Jove plunge down through the tree, ripping the bark, the blossoms, and the new-grown leaves.
It struck the chariot with all its force, and the chariot reeled like a ship in a storm, tossed by waves from starboard and from larboard.
Then I saw a Fox leap into the body of the triumphal vehicle — a Fox that seemed to have fed on nothing wholesome.
But my Lady drove it to a flight as swift as its fleshless bones could carry, rebuking it for its hideous sins.
Then, by the way it had come before, I saw the Eagle descend again into the chariot's chest, and leave it feathered with its plumage.
And a voice, such as comes from a heart in mourning, issued from heaven and said: "O my little ship, how badly you are laden!"
Then the earth seemed to yawn open between the two wheels, and I saw a Dragon rise from it, driving its tail up through the chariot.
And like a wasp drawing back its sting, it pulled its venomous tail back to itself, tore away part of the floor, and went off rejoicing.
What remained, like fertile ground overtaken by weeds, was covered again with the feathers — offered perhaps with pure and kind intention —
and both wheels and the pole were re-clothed with them so quickly that a sigh keeps the lips apart for longer.
Thus transformed, the holy structure sprouted heads on its different parts — three on the pole and one at each corner.
The first three were horned like oxen, but the four at the corners had only a single horn on each forehead. A monster like this had never been seen!
Seated upon it, firm as a rock on a high mountaintop, there appeared to me a shameless whore, her eyes darting quickly around.
And as if to make sure she was not taken from him, I saw a giant standing beside her. And from time to time they kissed each other.
But because she turned her wanton, roving eye upon me, her enraged lover scourged her from head to foot.
Then, full of jealousy and fierce with rage, he loosed the monster from the tree and dragged it through the forest so far
that the forest itself became a shield between me and the whore and the strange beast.

chapters.title: Purgatorio, Canto XXXIII
paragraphs: "Deus, venerunt gentes" — alternating now three voices, now four, the maidens began a melodious psalm, weeping as they sang.
And Beatrice, sighing with compassion, listened to them with a look so altered that Mary at the foot of the cross was scarcely more changed.
But when the other virgins gave way for her to speak, she rose to her feet and answered, glowing like fire:
"Modicum, et non videbitis me; et iterum, my beloved sisters, modicum, et vos videbitis me."
Then she placed all seven ahead of her, and behind her she beckoned me, the lady, and the sage who had stayed.
So she moved on. I do not think her tenth step had touched the ground when her eyes struck mine,
and with a calm look she said: "Come closer, so that if I speak to you, you will be well placed to listen."
As soon as I was beside her as I should be, she said to me: "Brother, why do you not dare to question me, now that you are walking with me?"
As happens to those who are too reverential, speaking in the presence of superiors, unable to drag a living word to their lips —
so it was with me. Without full voice I began: "My lady, you know what I need and what is good for it."
And she to me: "I want you to shed your fear and shame from now on, and speak no longer like a man who is dreaming.
Know that the vessel the serpent broke once was and is no more. But let whoever is guilty know that God's vengeance fears no bribes.
The Eagle that left its feathers on the chariot, making it first a monster, then a prey, will not be without an heir forever.
For I see clearly, and therefore declare it, that the stars are already near, bringing a time safe from every obstacle and every barrier,
in which a Five Hundred Ten and Five, one sent by God, shall slay the thieving woman and the giant who sins with her.
And perhaps my dark prophecy, like Themis and the Sphinx, persuades you less because, in their manner, it clouds the mind.
But soon the events themselves will be the interpreters that solve this hard riddle, without the loss of flocks or crops.
Take note. And just as these words are uttered by me, so teach them to those who live that life which is a race toward death.
And keep in mind when you write them down: do not conceal what you have seen of the tree that has now been plundered twice.
Whoever robs or shatters it offends God with that act of blasphemy, for He made it holy, for His use alone.
For biting that tree, the first soul craved in pain and desire for more than five thousand years the One who punished in Himself the bite.
Your wits are asleep if they cannot see that the tree is so tall and so inverted at its crown for a special reason.
And if your vain thoughts had not been like the waters of the Elsa encrusting your mind, and their pleasure like Pyramus staining the mulberry —
from so many details alone you would have recognized, morally, God's justice in the prohibition of the tree.
But since I see your intellect turned to stone and stained with sin, so that the light of my words dazzles you —
I want you to carry my message back within you, if not in writing then at least painted — for the same reason that pilgrims bring home staffs wreathed with palm."
And I said: "As wax takes the stamp of a seal without changing its shape, so my brain is now imprinted by you.
But why does your longed-for speech soar so far beyond my sight, that the more I strain, the more I lose it?"
"So that you may recognize," she said, "the school you have been following, and see how well its teachings keep pace with my words —
and see that your way is as distant from the divine way as the earth is from the highest and swiftest heaven."
I answered her: "I do not remember ever estranging myself from you, and my conscience does not reproach me for it."
"And if you cannot remember," she answered with a smile, "then recall that just today you drank from Lethe.
And if fire may be inferred from smoke, then this forgetfulness clearly proves that your will was turned elsewhere, in error.
But from now on my words shall be plain and bare, as much as is fitting to lay them open to your unpolished sight."
And more radiant and with slower steps, the sun was holding the meridian circle, which shifts its position here and there depending on the viewer,
when the seven ladies halted — as a leader halts who goes before a troop as escort, when he finds something new upon the way —
at the edge of a pale shadow, such as the Alps cast beneath green leaves and dark branches on their cold borders.
In front of them I seemed to see the Tigris and the Euphrates issuing from a single fountain, and slowly parting, like friends, from one another.
"O light! O glory of the human race! What is this stream that unfolds here from one source and divides from itself?"
In answer to my question I was told: "Ask Matilda to tell you." And the beautiful lady replied, as one clearing herself of blame:
"This and other things I have already told him. And I am sure the waters of Lethe have not hidden them from his mind."
And Beatrice: "Perhaps a greater care, which often steals our memory, has dimmed the vision of his mind.
But see — there Eunoe rises. Lead him to it, and as you are accustomed, revive the half-dead virtue in him."
Like a gracious soul that makes no excuses but makes another's will its own the moment it is revealed,
the beautiful lady took hold of me and moved. And to Statius she said, in her womanly way: "Come with him."
If I had more space for writing, Reader, I would sing at least in part of that sweet draught that would never have sated me.
But since all the pages prepared for this second canticle are filled, the curb of art lets me go no further.
From the most holy water I returned, remade — in the manner of new trees renewed with new foliage —
pure, and ready to rise to the stars.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto I
paragraphs: The glory of the One who moves all things penetrates the universe and shines — more brightly in one part, and less in another.
I was within that heaven which receives the greatest share of His light, and there I saw things that no one returning from above has the knowledge or the power to describe.
For as our intellect draws near to its deepest desire, it plunges so far inward that memory cannot follow where it goes.
Yet whatever of that holy realm I had the power to store within my mind shall now become the subject of my song.
O great Apollo, for this final labor, make me a vessel worthy of your power — as befits the one who seeks the beloved laurel.
Until now, one peak of Parnassus has been enough for me. But now I need them both as I enter this last arena.
Enter my breast and breathe your power through me, as you did when you drew Marsyas from the sheath of his own limbs.
O divine power, if you lend yourself to me enough that I can make manifest even the shadow of that blessed realm stamped on my mind,
You will see me come to your beloved tree and crown myself with those leaves that both my theme and your inspiration will make me worthy of.
So rarely, Father, are those leaves gathered — whether for the triumph of a Caesar or a poet — such is the fault and shame of human desire,
That the Peneian foliage should bring forth joy in the joyous god of Delphi, whenever it stirs that thirst in anyone.
A small spark gives birth to a great flame. Perhaps after me, with better voices, others will pray and Cyrrha will respond.
The lamp of the world rises to mortal eyes through many different passages. But through the one that joins four circles with three crosses,
It emerges on a better course and under a better star, and tempers and stamps the wax of the world more closely to its own pattern.
That passage had made it nearly morning there and evening here, and that hemisphere was almost entirely white while the other half was dark,
When I saw Beatrice turn to face the left and gaze directly at the sun. No eagle ever fixed its eyes upon it so steadily.
And just as a second ray of light will spring from the first and rise again, like a pilgrim longing to return home,
So from her action, poured through my eyes into my imagination, I formed my own — and fixed my gaze on the sun beyond all human capacity.
Much is permitted there that is not permitted here to our mortal powers, by virtue of the place that was created as humankind's true home.
I could not look for long, but neither was it so brief that I did not see the sun spark and blaze all around, like iron drawn white-hot from the forge.
And suddenly it seemed as though day had been added to day — as if He who has the power had adorned the sky with a second sun.
Beatrice stood with her eyes fixed upon the eternal spheres, and I, lifting my gaze from above, fixed mine upon her.
Gazing at her, I was inwardly transformed — as Glaucus was when he tasted the herb that made him a god among the other gods beneath the sea.
To convey what it means to transcend the human in words is impossible. Let the example suffice for those to whom grace reserves the experience.
Whether I was only that part of me which you most recently created, O Love who governs the heavens, you know — you who lifted me with your light.
When the great wheel that you make eternal by the desire it has for you drew my attention with its harmony, which you tune and measure,
So much of the sky then seemed to blaze with the sun's flame that neither rain nor river ever spread a lake so vast.
The strangeness of the sound and the immensity of the light kindled in me a longing for their cause more acute than anything I had ever felt.
And she, who saw me as clearly as I saw myself, opened her mouth to calm my troubled mind before I could open mine to ask.
She began: "You are making yourself dull with false imagining. You cannot see what you would see if only you would shake it off.
You are not on earth, as you believe. Lightning fleeing from its proper place never flew as fast as you are now returning to yours."
If her brief words, more smiled than spoken, freed me from my first confusion, I was only the more entangled in a new one.
I said: "My great amazement was already at rest. But now I am amazed anew — how can I be rising through these bodies of light?"
At this she breathed a pitying sigh and turned her eyes toward me with the look a mother gives a child lost in fever.
And she began: "All things that exist have order among themselves. This order is the form that makes the universe resemble God.
Here the higher creatures see the footprints of the Eternal Power — the ultimate purpose for which the law I speak of was established.
Within this order, all natures are inclined, according to their different destinies, more or less near to their origin.
And so they move toward different harbors across the great sea of being, each one carried by the instinct given to it.
This instinct carries fire upward toward the moon. This is the driving force within mortal hearts. This is what binds and unites the earth.
And this bow shoots its arrows not only at creatures without intelligence, but also at those endowed with both intellect and love.
The Providence that governs all of this keeps the heaven in which the swiftest sphere revolves forever still and radiant with its light.
And there now — to that place appointed for us — the power of that bowstring carries us, which aims everything it launches at a joyful mark.
It is true that just as a work of art sometimes fails to match the artist's intention because the material is deaf to the shaping hand,
So too the creature sometimes strays from this course — for though impelled upward, it has the power to swerve in another direction,
Just as fire can be seen to fall from a cloud, if its first upward impulse is twisted earthward by some false pleasure.
You should no more marvel at your ascent, if I judge correctly, than at a stream cascading down from a high mountain to the valley floor.
The real marvel would be if, freed of every hindrance, you had remained seated below — as if a living flame on earth were to sit still and quiet."
With that, she turned her face heavenward once more.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto II
paragraphs: O you who have followed in your little boat, eager to listen, sailing in the wake of my ship that sings as it goes,
Turn back now and find your own shores again. Do not put out to the open sea, for you might lose me and find yourselves utterly lost.
The waters I am sailing have never been crossed before. Minerva fills my sails, Apollo steers my course, and nine Muses show me the way by the stars.
But you other few who lifted your minds early to the bread of angels — that food on which we live here yet never grow full —
You may indeed launch your vessel on the deep salt sea, keeping to my wake upon the water before it closes smooth again.
Those glorious heroes who sailed to Colchis were not so struck with wonder as you will be, when they saw Jason turned into a plowman.
The inborn and unending thirst for the God-shaped realm bore us upward, almost as fast as your eyes can take in the heavens.
Beatrice gazed upward, and I gazed at her. And in the time it takes an arrow to strike, fly, and leave the bowstring,
I found I had arrived at a place where something wonderful drew my sight entirely to it. And she, from whom no thought of mine could be concealed,
Turned toward me, radiant and beautiful, and said: "Fix your mind gratefully upon God, who has brought us to the first star."
It seemed to me that a luminous cloud enveloped us — dense, solid, and brilliant as a diamond struck by sunlight.
Into itself that eternal pearl received us, just as water receives a ray of light while remaining perfectly unbroken.
If I was still a body — and we cannot grasp how one dimension can contain another, as must happen when body enters body —
Then the desire should burn all the brighter in us to see that Essence in which we behold how God and our own nature were once united.
There what we now receive by faith will be seen directly — not proved by argument but self-evident, like the first truths we simply know.
I answered: "My Lady, with all the devotion I can summon, I give thanks to Him who has lifted me from the mortal world.
But tell me — what are those dark markings on this body, which make people down on earth tell that fanciful tale about Cain?"
She smiled a little and then said: "If mortal opinion goes astray where the key of the senses cannot unlock the truth,
The arrows of wonder should certainly not pierce you now. Even following the senses, you can see that reason's wings are short.
But tell me what you yourself think about it." And I replied: "What appears varied to us up here is caused, I think, by bodies being rare or dense."
And she said: "You will see your belief thoroughly drowned in error if you listen carefully to the argument I will make against it.
The eighth sphere displays many lights to you, and these can be seen to differ in both quality and quantity.
If rarity and density alone caused this, there would be only one kind of virtue in them all — distributed more or less, or equally.
Different virtues must arise from different formal principles. Your reasoning would destroy all but one of these.
Furthermore, if rarity were the cause of those dark spots, then either this planet would be thin all the way through in places,
Or else, just as fat and lean are layered in a body, so this sphere would alternate its pages of dense and thin.
If the first were true, it would show during a solar eclipse — light would shine straight through, as it does through anything translucent.
But that does not happen. So we must examine the other possibility. And if I demolish that one too, your theory falls apart entirely.
If the rarity does not go all the way through, there must be a limit where the denser material blocks further passage,
And from that boundary the light of the sun is reflected back, just as color returns from glass that has a layer of lead behind it.
Now you might argue that the sunbeam appears dimmer in those spots because it is being reflected from farther back.
Experiment can free you from this objection — experiment, which is the living spring from which the rivers of your arts all flow.
Take three mirrors. Place two at equal distance from you, and set the third farther away, between the first two, facing your eyes.
Turn toward them and have a light placed behind your back so that it illuminates all three mirrors and reflects back to you from each.
Although the image from the most distant mirror will be smaller in size, you will see that it shines with exactly equal brightness.
Now, just as the surface of snow is stripped bare by the warm touch of sunlight, losing both its whiteness and its cold,
So I will strip your intellect bare and fill it with a light so vivid it will shimmer before you.
Within the heaven of divine peace, there revolves a body whose power contains the being of everything within it.
The next heaven below — the one with so many eyes — distributes this unified being into distinct essences, contained by it yet separate from it.
The other spheres below, through their various differences, direct all the distinctions they carry within them toward their proper ends and effects.
And so the organs of the world proceed, as you can now see, from level to level. They receive from above and act upon what is below.
Pay close attention to how I come through this reasoning to the truth you seek, so that afterward you can navigate this crossing on your own.
The motion and power of the holy spheres must proceed from the blessed Intelligences that turn them, just as a hammer's craft comes from the artisan.
The heaven made beautiful by so many lights takes its imprint from the deep Intelligence that turns it, and makes that imprint into a seal.
And just as the soul within your mortal body expands through different limbs, each suited to a different faculty,
So this Intelligence unfolds its power, multiplied among the stars, while itself revolving upon its own unity.
