Each distinct virtue makes a distinct alloy with the precious body it quickens, in which — like life in you — it is bound up.
From the joyful nature it derives from, the blended virtue shines through the body, as gladness shines through a living eye.
From this comes what appears different from light to light — not from density and rarity. This is the formal principle that produces,
According to its own goodness, both the dark and the bright."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto III
paragraphs: That same Sun which had first warmed my heart with love had now revealed to me, through proof and refutation, the lovely face of truth.
And so that I might declare myself convinced and certain, as far as was fitting, I lifted my head more upright to speak.
But a vision appeared that drew me so close to itself, demanding to be seen, that I forgot what I was about to say.
As through polished and transparent glass, or through waters crystalline and undisturbed — though not so deep that the bottom is lost —
The outlines of our own faces come back to us, so faintly that a pearl on a white forehead would reach our eyes no less quickly,
Just so I saw many faces eager to speak. And I fell into the opposite error from the one that kindled love between Narcissus and the fountain.
The instant I became aware of them, I took them for reflected images and turned my eyes around to see whose faces they were.
But I saw nothing behind me, and turned forward again to look into the eyes of my sweet guide, whose holy eyes kindled with a smile.
"Do not wonder," she said to me, "that I smile at this childish thought of yours, since it does not yet trust its footing on the truth,
But turns you, as it always does, toward emptiness. These are real beings that you see, placed here for having fallen short of their vows.
Speak with them, listen, and believe. For the true light that gives them peace does not allow them to turn their feet away from it."
I turned to the soul that seemed most eager to speak, and I began, like one whom too much eagerness bewilders:
"O spirit born for blessedness, who in the rays of eternal life taste a sweetness that cannot be understood without tasting it,
It would give me joy if you would tell me your name and what became of you." And she answered readily, with laughing eyes:
"Our love never shuts its doors against a rightful wish — like the Love that wills all its court to be like itself.
I was a virgin sister in the world. And if you search your memory well, my greater beauty now will not hide me from you,
But you will recognize that I am Piccarda, placed here among these other blessed ones, myself made blessed in the slowest sphere.
All our desires, which are inflamed only by the pleasure of the Holy Spirit, rejoice in being shaped according to His design.
And this station, which seems so low, is given to us because our vows were neglected and in some part left unfulfilled."
I said to her: "In your wondrous faces there shines something divine that transforms you beyond what our first impressions can grasp.
That is why I was not quick to remember you. But what you tell me now helps me, so that recognition comes more easily.
But tell me — you who are happy here — do you desire a higher place, to see more of God or to grow closer to Him?"
She smiled a little at first, along with the other souls, then answered with such fullness of joy that she seemed to burn in the first fire of love:
"Brother, the power of charity quiets our will, making us desire only what we have and thirst for nothing more.
If we aspired to be placed higher, our desires would be at war with the will of Him who assigns us here.
You will see that such discord has no place in these spheres, if being in charity is the very condition of life here, and if you truly consider its nature.
Indeed, it is essential to this blessed existence to hold itself within the divine will, so that our own desires become one with it.
So our being stationed at different levels throughout this realm is pleasing to the whole realm, as it is to the King who makes His will our will.
And His will is our peace. It is the sea toward which everything moves — everything He creates and everything nature makes."
Then it became clear to me that everywhere in heaven is Paradise, even though the grace of the Supreme Good does not rain down in equal measure.
But just as it happens that one food satisfies while the craving for another remains, so that we accept one dish and politely decline another,
Just so, with gesture and with words, I asked her to tell me what the web was in which she had not finished plying the shuttle.
"A perfect life and high merit place above us a lady," she said, "by whose rule women in your world take the veil and habit,
So that until death they may keep vigil and sleep beside that Bridegroom who accepts every vow that love shapes to His liking.
To follow her, I fled from the world as a young girl, enclosed myself in her habit, and pledged myself to the way of her order.
Then men more accustomed to evil than to good tore me from that sweet cloister. And what my life became after that — God knows.
This other radiance that reveals itself to you on my right side, kindled with all the light of our sphere,
Understands what I say of myself, for it applies to her as well. She too was a nun, and from her head too the shadow of the sacred veil was torn.
But even when she was returned to the world against her will and against all right, she never removed the veil from her heart.
This is the splendor of the great Costanza, who from the second storm of Swabia brought forth the third and final power."
So she spoke to me, and then began to sing 'Ave Maria.' And singing, she vanished like something heavy sinking through deep water.
My sight followed her as long as it could, and when it lost her, turned to the object of its greater longing,
And fixed entirely upon Beatrice. But she blazed such lightning into my eyes that at first my vision could not bear it.
And that made me slower in forming my next question.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto IV
paragraphs: Between two dishes equally distant and equally tempting, a free man would die of hunger before he could bring either one to his mouth.
Just so a lamb would stand frozen between the jaws of two fierce wolves, fearing both alike. And just so would a dog stand paralyzed between two deer.
Therefore, if I held silent, I do not blame myself — pulled equally by my two doubts. It had to be so, and I do not take credit for it either.
I held my peace, but my desire was painted on my face, and its questioning was far more fervent than any words could have been.
Beatrice did what Daniel once did when he relieved Nebuchadnezzar of the rage that had made him unjustly cruel.
She said: "I can see clearly how you are pulled by two desires at once, so that your concern binds you up and you cannot even breathe.
You argue: if my good will remains intact, why should the violence of others reduce the measure of my merit?
Your second source of doubt is that souls seem to return to the stars after death, as Plato taught.
These are the two questions pressing equally on your mind. I will deal first with the one that has the most sting.
The highest of the Seraphim, the one most absorbed in God — Moses, Samuel, whichever John you choose, even Mary herself —
Do not have their seats in any heaven different from the spirits who just appeared to you, nor do they exist for more or fewer years.
All of them make the first circle beautiful, and all enjoy sweet life in different degrees by feeling more or less of the eternal breath.
They showed themselves here not because this sphere was assigned to them, but to give a visible sign of the celestial rank that is least exalted.
It is necessary to speak to your minds this way, since only through the senses do you grasp what the intellect then makes worthy of itself.
For this reason, Scripture bends down to your level and attributes hands and feet to God, while meaning something else entirely.
And Holy Church represents Gabriel and Michael to you in human form, along with the angel who healed Tobias.
What Plato argues in the Timaeus about the soul does not match what you see here — because it seems he actually believed what his words say.
He says the soul returns to its star, believing it was separated from there when nature first gave it as a living form.
But perhaps his doctrine differs from what his words seem to mean, and his true intention may not deserve to be dismissed.
If he means that the honor and blame of their stellar influence return to these spheres, perhaps his arrow strikes somewhere near the truth.
This principle, badly misunderstood, once led nearly the whole world astray — into worshipping Jupiter, Mercury, and Mars.
Your other doubt is less venomous, because its error could never lead you away from me.
That our divine justice should appear unjust in mortal eyes is an argument for faith, not a sign of heresy.
But since your understanding can penetrate this truth, I will satisfy your desire as you wish.
If it counts as violence only when the one who suffers does not cooperate with the one who forces, then these souls were not excused on that account.
For the will is never extinguished unless it wills to be. It acts as fire does by nature — even if violence bends it a thousand times.
Therefore, if the will yields even a little, it cooperates with the force. And these souls did yield, having the power to return to the holy place.
If their will had been as absolute as the will that held Lawrence fast on the gridiron, or that made Mucius thrust his own hand into the fire,
It would have driven them back along the path from which they were dragged, the instant they were free. But such unbreakable will is all too rare.
And if you have gathered these words as you should, the argument that would have troubled you many more times is now refuted.
But now another difficulty crosses your path — one that would exhaust you trying to solve it alone before you found the way through.
I have firmly placed in your mind that a blessed soul can never lie, because it lives in the presence of the primal Truth.
And yet you heard Piccarda say that Costanza kept her love for the veil — so she seems to contradict what I have told you.
Many times, brother, it has happened that, to escape danger, people have reluctantly done what should not have been done.
Just as Alcmaeon — entreated by his father — killed his own mother, and in trying not to lose piety became pitiless.
At this point I want you to understand that force and will can become entangled together, and when they do, the resulting wrongs cannot be excused.
The absolute will does not consent to evil. But the conditional will consents insofar as it fears, by refusing, to fall into greater harm.
So when Piccarda spoke, she meant the absolute will. And I meant the conditional will. Both of us speak the truth."
Such was the flowing of the holy river that poured from the fountain where all truth springs. And it set both my questions to rest at once.
"O beloved of the First Lover, O divine one," I said at once, "whose words flood me and warm me so that I feel more and more alive,
My own love is not deep enough to return grace for grace. Let Him who sees all and can do all respond for me.
I see clearly now that our intellect is never satisfied unless the Truth illumines it — that Truth beyond which nothing true extends.
The mind rests in that Truth as a wild beast rests in its lair, once it has reached it. And it can reach it — otherwise every desire would be in vain.
And so doubt springs up at the foot of truth like a shoot. It is nature itself that pushes us from summit to summit, ever higher.
This gives me confidence, Lady, to ask you with reverence about another truth that remains obscure to me.
I wish to know whether a person can compensate for broken vows with other good deeds, so that they do not weigh too lightly in your scales."
Beatrice looked at me with eyes so full of the sparks of love, so divine, that my strength was overcome. I turned away,
And nearly lost myself with my eyes cast down.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto V
paragraphs: "If I blaze upon you with a heat of love beyond anything seen on earth, so that I overwhelm the strength of your eyes,
Do not marvel at it. For this comes from perfected sight — which, the more clearly it sees the good, the more swiftly it moves toward it.
I can see the eternal light already shining into your intellect — that light which, once seen, kindles love forever.
And if any other thing seduces your love, it is nothing but a trace of that same light, badly understood, shining through.
You want to know whether someone can make such amends for a broken vow with other service that the soul is freed from further claim."
So Beatrice began this canto. And like one who does not break the thread of speech, she continued her holy argument:
"The greatest gift that God in His generosity made when He created — the one most closely aligned with His own goodness, the one He prizes most —
Is the freedom of the will. Every intelligent creature — all of them and only them — was and is endowed with it.
Now you will see, if you reason from this, the immense value of a vow, when it is made so that God consents when you consent.
For when the compact is sealed between God and a person, a sacrifice is made of this treasure — free will — and it is made by the will's own act.
What, then, can be offered in compensation? If you think you can put to good use what you have already given away, you would do good with stolen goods.
You are now clear on the main point. But because the Holy Church grants dispensations in these matters — which seems to contradict what I have shown you —
You must sit a while longer at the table, because the solid food you have taken needs more help for your digestion.
Open your mind to what I reveal and hold it fast. For it is not knowledge merely to hear something without retaining it.
Two things come together in the essence of a sacrifice: the substance of what is offered, and the covenant itself.
The covenant is never canceled unless it is fulfilled — and about this I have already spoken with precision above.
That is why it was required of the Hebrews to continue making offerings, though sometimes the specific thing offered could be exchanged, as you should know.
The other element — the material substance — may indeed be of a kind where no wrong is done if one thing is exchanged for another.
But let no one shift the burden on his shoulder by his own judgment, without the turning of both the white key and the yellow key.
And consider any such exchange foolish unless the replacement contains the original as four is contained in six.
Therefore, whatever has such weight in value that it tips every scale cannot be compensated by any other offering.
Let mortals never take a vow lightly. Be faithful and not reckless in making them — as Jephthah was with his first offering,
Who would have done better to say 'I was wrong' than to do worse by keeping his vow. And you will find the great leader of the Greeks equally foolish,
Over whom Iphigenia wept for her fair face, and who made both the wise and the simple weep who heard about such worship.
Christians, be more deliberate in your commitments. Do not be like a feather blown by every wind, and do not think that just any water cleanses you.
You have the Old Testament and the New, and the Shepherd of the Church to guide you. Let these be enough for your salvation.
If wicked appetite calls out for anything else, be like men and not like foolish sheep — so that the Jew among you does not mock you.
Do not be like the lamb that leaves its mother's milk and, frolicsome and silly, fights against itself for its own amusement."
So Beatrice spoke to me, just as I write it here. Then, filled with longing, she turned herself again toward that part of heaven where the world is most alive.
Her silence and her changed expression imposed silence on my eager mind, which already had new questions at the ready.
And as an arrow strikes the target before the bowstring has stopped vibrating, so we sped into the second realm.
My Lady — how joyful I saw her become as she entered the brightness of that heaven! The planet itself grew more luminous at her arrival.
And if the star itself changed and smiled, what must I have become, who am by nature mutable in every way?
As in a fishpond of pure, still water, the fish draw toward whatever drops in from outside, thinking it might be food,
So I saw more than a thousand splendors drawing toward us, and from each one came the cry: "Here is one who will increase our love!"
And as each one approached us, the soul could be seen full of bliss by the bright radiance pouring from it.
Consider, reader, if what I am beginning here went no further, how you would feel an aching need to know more.
And you will understand how eager I was to learn about their stories, the moment they became visible to my eyes.
"O soul well-born, to whom Grace grants the sight of the thrones of the eternal triumph before your mortal battle is even over,
We are kindled by the light that spreads through all of heaven. So if you wish to know about us, satisfy yourself at your pleasure."
So spoke one of those holy spirits. And Beatrice said: "Speak, speak freely, and trust them as you would trust gods."
"I can see how you nest yourself within your own light and draw it from your eyes, because they flash when you smile.
But I do not know who you are, or why you hold your station in this sphere, noble spirit — the sphere that veils itself from mortals in another's rays."
I said this toward the light that had first spoken to me. At my words, it became far more luminous than before.
Just as the sun hides itself in its own excess of light when the heat has burned away the tempering haze of the dense vapors,
So, concealed in its own greater joy and radiance, that saintly figure enclosed itself completely — and answered me,
In the manner that the following canto sings.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto VI
paragraphs: "After Constantine turned the eagle against the course of heaven — counter to the path followed by the ancient hero who wed Lavinia —
For two hundred years and more, the bird of God remained at the far edge of Europe, near the mountains from which it first took flight.
And there, beneath the shadow of its sacred wings, it governed the world, passing from hand to hand, until at last it came to rest upon mine.
I was Caesar, and I am Justinian — who, moved by the will of the Primal Love I feel, stripped from the laws all that was useless and redundant.
Before I gave myself to that work, I believed that only one nature existed in Christ, not two, and I was content with that faith.
But blessed Agapetus, who was the supreme shepherd, directed me with his words toward the true faith.
I believed him, and what he declared I now see clearly — just as you can see that every contradiction must be either false or true.
As soon as my steps fell in line with the Church, God in His grace was pleased to inspire me with this great task, and I gave myself to it entirely.
To my Belisarius I entrusted the armies. Heaven's right hand so favored him that it was a sign for me to rest from war.
Now here my answer to your first question ends. But its very nature compels me to add a sequel,
So that you may see with how little reason men act against that sacred standard — both those who claim it for themselves and those who oppose it.
Consider what great deeds made it worthy of reverence, beginning from the hour Pallas died to give it sovereignty.
You know it dwelt in Alba for three hundred years and more, until at last the three fought against three for it once again.
You know what it achieved, from the rape of the Sabine women down to Lucretia's grief, through seven kings, conquering all the neighboring peoples.
You know what it achieved when carried by the illustrious Romans against Brennus, against Pyrrhus, against all the other princes and their leagues.
From these campaigns, Torquatus, Quinctius — named for his unkempt hair — the Decii and the Fabii all received the fame I gladly preserve.
It struck down the pride of the Arabs who followed Hannibal across the Alpine ridges — the Po, from which you descend.
Under it, while still young men, Scipio and Pompey triumphed. And to the hill beneath which you were born, it showed a bitter face.
Then, near the time when heaven willed to bring the whole world to its serene order, Caesar took it up by the will of Rome.
What it achieved from the Var to the Rhine was witnessed by the Isere, the Saone, the Seine, and every valley fed by the Rhone.
What it achieved after leaving Ravenna and leaping the Rubicon was a flight so swift that neither tongue nor pen could follow it.
It wheeled its legions toward Spain, then toward Durazzo, and struck Pharsalia so hard that the pain was felt as far as the hot Nile.
It saw Antandros and the Simois again, where it first set out, and the place where Hector lies. Then it roused itself — badly for Ptolemy.
From there it fell like lightning upon Juba, then wheeled again toward your West, where it heard the Pompeian trumpet.
For what it did under the next standard-bearer, Brutus and Cassius howl together in Hell, and Modena and Perugia were left in grief.
The sorrowful Cleopatra still weeps because of it — she who, fleeing before it, took sudden black death from the serpent.
With Augustus it ran to the shore of the Red Sea. With him it set the world in such deep peace that the temple of Janus was closed.
But all that the standard I speak of achieved before, and would achieve afterward, throughout the mortal realm beneath it,
Becomes pale and dim in appearance if it is seen in the hand of the third Caesar with a clear eye and a pure heart.
For the living Justice that inspires me granted it, in the hand of the one I speak of, the glory of exacting vengeance for His wrath.
Now mark well what I tell you next. Later, it marched with Titus to take vengeance upon the vengeance for the ancient sin.
And when the Lombard tooth bit into Holy Church, Charlemagne came victoriously to her rescue under those same wings.
Now you can judge for yourself the kind of people I accused before, and judge their crimes — which are the cause of all your miseries.
One faction sets the golden lilies against the sacred standard; the other claims it for a party. It is hard to say which sins more gravely.
Let the Ghibellines carry on their scheming under some other banner. This one is always ill-served by anyone who separates it from justice.
And let this new Charles not strike it down — he and his Guelfs — but let him fear the talons that have stripped the hide from a far nobler lion.
Many times already, sons have wept for their father's sin. Let him not believe that God will trade His coat of arms for the lilies.
This little planet adorns itself with good spirits who were active in their lives so that fame and honor would follow after them.
And when desires ascend in that direction, straying from the true path, the rays of genuine love must rise less vividly.
But the proportion between our reward and what we deserve is part of our joy, because we see our wages as neither too little nor too great.
In this way, living Justice sweetens our love so perfectly that it can never bend toward any wrong.
Different voices make sweet harmonies together. Just so, the different stations in our life here create sweet harmony among these spheres.
And within the compass of this present pearl shines the light of Romeo, whose great and noble work was repaid with treachery.
But the Provencals who plotted against him have not had the last laugh. Those who make the good deeds of others into their own injury walk a bitter road.
Raymond Berenger had four daughters, each one of them a queen. Romeo accomplished this for him — a poor man, a pilgrim.
And then malicious words persuaded the count to summon this honest man to render his accounts — the man who had returned him seven and five for every ten.
So Romeo departed, poor and old. And if the world could know the heart he carried, begging his bread from door to door,
Though it praises him well enough already, it would praise him far more."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto VII
paragraphs: "Hosanna, holy God of hosts, who with your radiance illumine from above the blessed fires of these kingdoms!"
Singing thus, returning to its melody, this being upon which a double light was doubled began to sing.
And this soul and all the others entered their dance, and like swift-darting sparks, veiled themselves from me with sudden distance.
I stood in doubt, saying within myself, "Tell her, tell her" — saying "Tell my Lady," who quenches my thirst with her sweet outpourings.
And yet that reverence which masters all of me at the mere sound of 'Be' and 'ice' bowed me down again like one who drowses.
Beatrice did not let me stay that way for long. She began, lighting me with a smile that would make a man happy even in fire:
"According to my unerring judgment, you are puzzling over how a just vengeance could justly be avenged.
But I will quickly untangle your mind. Listen carefully, for my words will make you a gift of great doctrine.
By refusing to accept the curb placed on his will for his own good, that man who was never born — Adam — in damning himself, damned all his descendants.
Because of this, the human race lay sick for many centuries in terrible error, until it pleased the Word of God to descend
To where the nature that had estranged itself from its own Maker was joined to Him in one person, by the sole act of His eternal love.
Now fix your sight on what I say next. This human nature, when it was united to its Maker, was pure and good, just as it was when first created.
But on its own — by itself — it had been cast out of Paradise, because it strayed from the way of truth and from its proper life.
Therefore, the punishment the cross inflicted — measured against the nature that was assumed — was more just than any penalty ever imposed.
And yet it was also the greatest injustice ever committed, considering the Person who suffered it — He in whom that human nature was contained.
And so from one single act, opposite results were born. One death was pleasing both to God and to the Jews. At it the earth shook and the heavens opened.
It should no longer seem difficult to you now, when it is said that a just vengeance was afterward justly avenged by a just court.
But now I see your mind tangled from thought to thought in a knot from which it longs to free itself.
You are thinking: 'I understand what I hear. But it remains hidden from me why God chose this way and only this way for our redemption.'
This decree lies buried, brother, from the eyes of everyone whose nature has not yet matured in the flame of love.
But since many gaze long at this question and see little, I will explain why this way was the most worthy.
Divine Goodness, which rejects all envy from itself, burns so brightly within that it unfolds the eternal beauties.
Whatever flows directly from this Goodness has no end, for once it sets its seal, the imprint is never removed.
Whatever rains down from it directly is entirely free, because it is not subject to the power of created things.
The more closely a thing resembles this Goodness, the more it pleases God. For the sacred fire that illumines all things blazes brightest in what most resembles Him.
The human creature was blessed with all these gifts. And if even one of them fails, it must fall from its nobility.
Sin alone strips that nobility away, making the creature unlike the Highest Good, so that its light shines less in him.
And he never regains his dignity unless he fills the void left by sin with fitting penalties for unlawful pleasure.
Your nature, when it sinned entirely in its first root, was separated from these dignities just as it was separated from Paradise.
And if you consider the matter carefully, they could never be recovered by any path unless one of these two fords were crossed:
Either God, by His mercy alone, forgave the debt — or humankind, by its own act, made satisfaction for its folly.
Now fix your eyes within the abyss of eternal counsel, and follow my words as closely as you can.
Humankind, within its own limits, could never have made satisfaction — for it could never descend in humble obedience as far as it had risen in disobedient pride.
And this is the reason why humans were excluded from the power to make amends by themselves.
Therefore it was necessary for God to restore humanity to its full life by His own ways — by one way, or by both together.
But because an act is all the more prized the more it reveals the goodness of the heart from which it springs,
The divine Goodness that imprints itself upon the world was pleased to use all its ways to raise you up again.
Between the first day and the final night, there has never been and never will be a deed so lofty and magnificent by either one of those two paths.
For God was more generous in giving Himself so that humanity might rise than if He had simply pardoned on His own.
And every other means would have fallen short of justice, had the Son of God not humbled Himself to become flesh.
Now, to satisfy your every wish, I must go back and clarify one point, so that you may see it as clearly as I do.
You say: 'I see water, I see fire, I see air and earth, and all their mixtures, come to corruption and endure only briefly.
Yet these too were created things. And if what I said before is true, they should be immune to corruption.'
Brother, the angels and the pure country where you now are may be called fully created in their complete being.
But the elements you named, and all the things made from their mixtures, are given their form by created powers.
Created was the matter they contain. Created was the shaping virtue in the stars that revolve around them.
The life of every animal and plant is drawn from compounds with potential, by the ray and motion of the holy lights.
But your life is breathed directly by the Supreme Goodness, which so fills it with love for itself that it desires God ever after.
And from this you can further deduce your resurrection, if you think again about how human flesh was made
At the time when both the first parents were created."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto VIII
paragraphs: The world once believed, to its peril, that the lovely Cyprian goddess radiated the madness of love as she turned in the third epicycle.
And so the ancient peoples, caught in their ancient error, paid her honor not only with sacrifices and votive cries,
But also honored Dione as her mother and Cupid as her son, and told how he had sat in Dido's lap.
From her — the goddess with whom my song begins — they took the name of the star that courts the sun, now trailing behind it, now racing ahead.
I was not aware of our ascent into it. But that we had arrived, my Lady's growing beauty gave me full assurance.
And as within a flame a spark is seen, and as within one voice another voice can be heard — one holding steady, the other coming and going —
So within that light I saw other lights moving in a circle, faster or slower, in proportion, I think, to the depth of their inner vision.
Never from a cold cloud did winds descend, whether visible or invisible, so swiftly that they would not seem sluggish and hampered
To anyone who had seen those divine lights come toward us, leaving the great rotation that began among the highest Seraphim.
And from those nearest the front came the sound of "Hosanna!" — so beautiful that never since have I been free of the desire to hear it again.
Then one drew nearer to us, and alone it began: "We are all ready for your pleasure, that you may take joy in us.
We circle with the celestial Princes — one orbit, one turning, one thirst — those to whom you once said in the world,
'You who by intellect move the third heaven.' And we are so full of love that, to give you pleasure, a moment of stillness will be no less sweet."
After my eyes had offered themselves reverently to my Lady, and she had made them content and certain of themselves,
They turned back to the light that had promised so much. And "Who are you?" was my voice, stamped with deep affection.
Oh, how that light grew and how much more radiant it became with the new joy that was added to its joys the moment I spoke!
Thus transformed, it said to me: "The world possessed me only a short time below. Had it been longer, much evil that came to pass would not have been.
My gladness hides me from you, shining around me and concealing me — like a silkworm wrapped within its own cocoon.
You loved me deeply, and you had good reason. For had I lived longer, I would have shown you more than just the leaves of my affection.
That left bank which is bathed by the Rhone after it joins the Sorgue was waiting for me to become its lord in due time.
And so was that horn of Italy studded with the towns of Bari, Gaeta, and Catona, where the Tronto and the Verde empty into the sea.
Already the crown of that realm watered by the Danube, after it leaves the German lands, was shining on my brow.
And beautiful Sicily, darkened between Pachino and Peloro along the gulf that suffers most from the east wind,
Not by Typhon's doing but by rising sulfur, would still have awaited its rightful kings through me — descended from Charles and Rudolph —
If bad government, which always embitters subject peoples, had not driven Palermo to cry out 'Death! Death!'
And if my brother could have foreseen this, he would flee from the greedy poverty of Catalonia before it could torment him.
For truly some provision must be made — by him or by another — so that no more cargo is loaded onto his already overburdened ship.
His nature, which descended from a generous line only to become miserly, would need the kind of soldiers who do not care about filling their chests."
"Because I believe, my lord, that the deep joy your speech pours into me is seen by you as clearly as I see it myself, there where every good thing begins and ends,
It is all the more welcome to me. And I hold this dear as well — that you perceive it by looking into God.
You have made me glad. Now make this clear to me as well, since your words have stirred me to doubt: how can bitter fruit come from sweet seed?"
This I asked him. And he answered: "If I can show you one truth, you will be facing what you now have at your back.
The Good that turns and satisfies the entire realm you are ascending through makes its providence a living force within these vast celestial bodies.
And not only are the natures of things foreseen in the mind that is perfect in itself — they are foreseen together with their preservation.
For whatever this bow releases falls toward a foreseen end, aimed like a shaft directed at its mark.
If this were not so, the heaven through which you travel would produce its effects so chaotically that they would not be works of art but wreckage.
And that cannot be, unless the Intelligences that move these stars are deficient — and unless the First Intelligence that made them is deficient too.
Shall I make this truth still clearer for you?" And I said: "No, there is no need. For I can see that it is impossible for nature to fall short in what is essential."
He continued: "Now tell me — would it be worse for humans on earth if they were not citizens of communities?" "Yes," I answered. "And here I ask for no proof."
"And can they live in communities if people do not live differently for different functions? Not if your master Aristotle writes truly."
By this chain of reasoning he arrived at this point, then concluded: "Therefore the roots of your different capacities must themselves be diverse.
And so one person is born a Solon, another a Xerxes, another a Melchisedec, and another the one who lost his son while flying through the air.
The revolving nature of the heavens, which is a seal pressed into mortal wax, performs its art well — but it does not distinguish one household from another.
That is why Esau differs from Jacob in the seed, and why Quirinus comes from a father so lowly that he is credited to Mars.
A child's begotten nature would always follow the path of its parents, if divine Providence were not triumphant.
Now what was behind you is before you. But so that you know I take pleasure in your company, I will wrap you in one more truth.
When nature encounters fortune that is discordant with it — like any seed planted outside its proper region — the result is always poor.
And if the world below would only pay attention to the foundation that nature lays, and follow it, its people would thrive.
But instead you force into the religious life someone born to wield the sword, and make a king of one who should be preaching.
And so your steps wander far from the true road."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto IX
paragraphs: After your Charles had enlightened me, beautiful Clemence, he told me of the treacheries that his descendants would suffer.
But he said: "Be still, and let the years turn." So all I can say is that rightful grief shall follow upon the wrongs done to you.
And already the life of that holy light had turned itself back to the Sun that fills it — as toward that good which is sufficient for all things.
Ah, deceived souls! Godless creatures! You turn your hearts away from such goodness and aim your minds at empty vanities!
And now another of those splendors approached me, signaling its desire to please me by shining more brightly outward.
The eyes of Beatrice, fixed upon me as before, gave me the dear assurance that my wish to speak was welcome.
"Bring swift satisfaction to my longing, blessed spirit!" I said. "Give me proof that what I think can be reflected in you."
At this, the light — still new to me — spoke from its depths, where it had been singing before, with the delight of one eager to do good:
"In that region of corrupt Italy that lies between Rialto and the sources of the Brenta and the Piave,
There rises a hill — not very high — from which a torch once descended and laid waste to the whole region.
Both I and that torch were born from one root. My name was Cunizza, and I shine here because the splendor of this star overcame me.
But I gladly forgive myself the cause of my lot, and it does not grieve me — though this might seem hard for your common people to understand.
Of this brilliant and precious jewel nearest to me in our heaven, great fame endures. And before that fame dies out,
This hundredth year shall be multiplied five times over. See whether a person ought to make himself excellent, so that the first life may leave another behind!
But the current rabble penned between the Adige and the Tagliamento gives this no thought — nor repents, even after being scourged.
But soon it will come to pass that Padua will stain the marsh waters that bathe Vicenza, because its people are so stubborn against duty.
And where the Sile and the Cagnano meet, one man lords it over all and walks with his head held high — though even now the net is being woven to catch him.
And Feltro shall weep for the crime of its impious bishop — a crime so monstrous that no one ever entered Malta's prison for anything like it.
The vat that could hold all the blood the Ferrarese will shed would be enormous, and weary would be the one who tried to weigh it ounce by ounce.
This generous priest will make a gift of it all to prove himself a loyal partisan. And such gifts will suit the customs of that land.
Above us there are mirrors — you call them Thrones — from which God in His judgment shines down upon us. That is why we speak as we do."
Here she fell silent and seemed to turn her attention elsewhere, rejoining the wheel she had been part of before.
The other joy, already known to me, became so radiant in my sight that it was like a fine ruby struck by the sun.
Up there, joy produces radiance, just as a smile does here below. But down in Hell, the soul's darkness deepens outwardly as the mind grows sad.
"God sees all things, and your sight rests in Him, blessed spirit," I said, "so that no act of will can ever be hidden from you.
Your voice, then — which gladdens heaven forever with the singing of those holy fires who make a cowl of their six wings —
Why does it not satisfy my longing? I would not wait for you to ask, if I could see into you as you can see into me."
"The greatest of all the world's valleys," it began at once, "that vast body of water — excepting only the sea that encircles the earth —
Stretches so far between its opposing shores against the sun's path that it makes its meridian where before it made its horizon.
I dwelt on that valley's shore between the Ebro and the Magra, which with its short course divides the Tuscan from the Genoese.
Nearly the same sunset and sunrise are shared by Bougie and the city I came from, whose blood once made its harbor steam.
The people who knew my name called me Folco. And now this heaven is stamped by me, as I was once stamped by it.
For the daughter of Belus never burned more fiercely — wronging both Sichaeus and Creusa — than I did, so long as it suited my youthful hair.
Nor did the woman of Rhodope who was betrayed by Demophoon, nor Hercules when he had locked Iole in his heart.
Yet here we do not repent. We smile — not at the sin, which does not return to memory, but at the Power that ordered and foresaw all things.
Here we behold the art that adorns creation with so much love, and we see the good through which the world above governs the world below.
But so that you may carry away every wish that was born in you within this sphere, I must say more.
You want to know who is inside this light that sparkles so near me, like a sunbeam glancing off clear water.
Know, then, that within it rests Rahab. And being joined to our order, she seals it at its highest rank.
Into this heaven — where the shadow cast by your earth comes to its point — she was taken up before any other soul, as a trophy of Christ's triumph.
It was entirely fitting to leave her in some heaven as a palm of victory — won by Him with both palms of His hands nailed to the cross.
She earned it because she aided the first glorious campaign of Joshua in the Holy Land — a place that barely stirs the Pope's memory.
Your city, which was planted by the one who first turned his back on his Maker, and whose envy is so bitterly lamented,
Produces and scatters the accursed flower that has led both sheep and lambs astray, since it has turned the shepherd into a wolf.
For this the Gospels and the great Doctors of the Church are abandoned. Only the Decretals are studied — as the worn margins of their pages show.
On these the Pope and Cardinals fix all their attention. Their thoughts never reach Nazareth, where Gabriel once spread his wings.
But the Vatican, and all the other chosen parts of Rome that have been a cemetery for the soldiers who followed Peter,
Shall soon be freed from this adultery."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto X
paragraphs: Gazing upon His Son with all the Love that each of them eternally breathes forth, the Primal and unspeakable Power
Made everything that revolves before the mind or eye with such perfect order that no one can behold it without delighting in Him.
Lift up your eyes with me, then, reader, straight to that part of the heavens where one motion crosses the other,
And there begin to contemplate with joy the art of the Master who loves it so deeply within Himself that His eye never turns from it.
See how the oblique circle branches off from that point — the zodiac that carries the planets — to answer the needs of the world that calls upon them.
If their pathway were not tilted at that angle, much of heaven's power would be wasted, and nearly every capacity on earth would be dead.
And if the departure from the straight line were greater or less, much would be lacking in the world's order, both above and below.
Stay now upon your bench, reader, and keep thinking about what I have set before you, and you will find delight before weariness.
I have laid the table for you. Now feed yourself, for the subject I have been made to write about claims all my attention.
The greatest minister of nature — the sun, who stamps the world with heaven's power and measures time for us with his light —
Joined with that part of the sky I just described, was spiraling along those paths where each day he shows himself a little earlier.
And I was with him. But I was no more conscious of our ascent than a person is conscious of a first thought before it arrives.
It is Beatrice who leads the way from good to better so instantaneously that her action cannot be measured by time.
How luminous she must have been in herself! And what I found within the sun — apparent not by color but by light alone —
I could not describe even if I summoned all my genius, art, and practice. But believe it is so, and long to see it for yourself.
And if our imagination is too humble for such heights, it is no wonder — for no eye has ever gone beyond the sun.
Such, in this place, was the fourth family of the Exalted Father, who satisfies them always, showing them how He breathes forth and how He begets.
And Beatrice began: "Give thanks, give thanks to the Sun of angels, who by His grace has raised you to this visible sun!"
Never was a mortal heart so disposed to worship, or so ready to give itself to God with its whole gratitude,
As I became at those words. And so entirely was my love absorbed in Him that Beatrice was eclipsed in my forgetting.
But she was not displeased. She smiled at it so brightly that the splendor of her laughing eyes split my focused mind into many things at once.
I saw many vivid and triumphant lights arrange themselves around us in a circle, sweeter in their singing than brilliant in their glow.
Just so we sometimes see the moon's daughter Latona girdled with a halo when the air is heavy enough to hold the thread that forms her ring.
In the court of Heaven from which I return, there are many jewels so beautiful and precious that they cannot be carried out of that realm.
And the singing of those lights was one such jewel. If you do not take wings and fly up there, you may wait for news of it from the mute.
After those burning suns had circled around us three times, like stars revolving near the fixed poles,
They seemed like ladies who have not left the dance but pause, listening in silence until they have caught the thread of a new melody.
And from within one of them I heard a voice begin: "Since the ray of grace — by which true love is kindled and which then grows by loving —
Shines in you so multiplied that it leads you upward by this stairway where no one descends without climbing it again,
Whoever refused to pour the wine of his knowledge into your thirst would be no more free than water that refuses to flow to the sea.
You wish to know what flowers make up this garland that circles with delight the beautiful Lady who strengthens you for heaven.
I was one of the lambs in the holy flock that Dominic leads along a path where they grow fat if they do not stray.
The one nearest to me on my right was my brother and my master: Albert of Cologne. And I am Thomas of Aquinas.
If you wish to know all the rest, follow my words with your eyes, moving upward along this blessed garland.
The next light shines from the smile of Gratian, who served both the ecclesiastical and the civil courts in a way that pleased Paradise.
The next one adorning our choir was Peter Lombard, who, like the poor widow, offered his treasure to Holy Church.
The fifth light — the most beautiful among us — breathes from such love that the whole world below hungers for news of it.
Within it is the lofty mind into which such deep wisdom was placed that, if the truth is true, no second ever rose to equal it.
Next you see the light of that candle who, in the flesh below, saw most deeply into the nature and ministry of angels.
In that other small light smiles the advocate of the Christian ages, whose eloquence provided Augustine with his rhetoric.
Now, if your mind's eye is following from light to light as I praise them, you are already thirsty for the eighth.
Within it, rejoicing in the sight of every good, is the sainted soul who exposes the world's deceit to anyone who listens well.
The body from which it was driven out lies in Cieldauro. And from martyrdom and exile, that soul came to this peace.
See, flaming farther on, the ardent spirits of Isidore, of Bede, and of Richard, who in contemplation was more than a man.
This one, from which your gaze now returns to me, is the light of a spirit for whom, in his grave meditations, death seemed to come too slowly.
It is the eternal light of Siger, who, lecturing in the Street of Straw, proved uncomfortable truths by rigorous logic."
Then, like a clock that calls us at the hour when the Bride of God rises for matins to sing to her Bridegroom so He may love her,
In which one part pulls another and pushes it, chiming ting! ting! with a note so sweet that it swells the well-disposed spirit with love,
Just so I saw that glorious wheel begin to turn, and voice answered voice in harmonies and sweetness beyond all comprehension,
Save only in that place where joy is made eternal.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XI
paragraphs: O senseless strivings of mortal men! How flawed are the arguments that make you beat your wings in downward flight!
One was chasing after law, another after medical maxims. One was pursuing the priesthood, another aiming to rule by force or cunning.
One was busy with theft, another with politics. One was entangled in the pleasures of the flesh until exhaustion, and another simply gave himself to idleness.
While I, set free from all these things, was high above with Beatrice in the heavens, received with such surpassing glory!
When each of those lights had returned to the point in the circle where it had stood before, it halted — motionless as a candle in its holder.
And from within the radiance that had first spoken to me, I heard it begin again, smiling as it grew still more luminous:
"Just as I am kindled by its ray, so, looking into the Eternal Light, I can perceive the cause of your thoughts.
You are in doubt and wish me to re-explain my words in language so broad and plain that they become clear to your understanding.
You need clarity on two points: where I said earlier, 'where one grows fat,' and where I said, 'no second ever rose.' Here we must distinguish carefully.
The Providence that governs the world with counsel so deep that every created eye is defeated before it reaches the bottom,
So that the bride of Him who with a great cry espoused her with His sacred blood might go toward her Beloved,
Confident in herself and more faithful to Him — ordained two princes for her benefit, to be her guides on either side.
One was all seraphic in his burning love. The other, through his wisdom, was a splendor on earth of cherubic light.
I will speak of one, for in praising either, both are praised, since their labors served the same end.
Between the Tupino and the stream that falls from the hill chosen by blessed Ubaldo, a fertile slope hangs from a high mountain.
From it, Perugia feels both cold and heat through its Porta Sole, while behind it Gualdo and Nocera groan beneath their heavy yoke.
From that slope, at the point where it breaks most steeply, a sun rose upon the world — just as our own sun sometimes rises from the Ganges.
Therefore, let anyone who speaks of that place not call it Ascesi, which would say too little, but Orient — if they wish to speak truly.
He had not yet traveled far from his rising before the earth began to feel some comfort from his mighty power.
For while still young, he drew his father's anger for the sake of a certain Lady, to whom — as to Death itself — no one willingly opens the door of pleasure.
And before his bishop's spiritual court, and in the presence of his father, he was united to her. And from that day forward, he loved her more ardently with each passing day.
She, bereft of her first husband, had been scorned and ignored for eleven hundred years and more, waiting without a suitor until he came.
It did not help that she was found unmoved beside Amyclas at the voice of him who terrified the whole world.
Nor did it help that she was so constant and fearless that, when Mary stayed below, she mounted the cross with Christ.
But lest I proceed too darkly — take Francis and Poverty as the two lovers I have been describing.
Their harmony and their joyful faces, their love, their wonder, and their tender gazes became the cause of holy thoughts in others.
So much so that the venerable Bernard was the first to strip his feet bare. He ran after such great peace and, even running, thought himself too slow.
O unknown riches! O true goodness! Giles goes barefoot, Sylvester goes barefoot, following the bridegroom — so much does the bride delight them!
Then that father and master set forth — he and his Lady and the family that was already tying on the humble cord.
No cowardice of heart weighed down his brow at being the son of Pietro Bernardone, nor at appearing marvelously despised.
But with royal resolve he revealed his hard determination to Pope Innocent, and from him received the first seal upon his Order.
After the mendicant people following him grew in number — this man whose wondrous life would be better sung in the glory of heaven —
The holy purpose of this great shepherd was crowned a second time through Pope Honorius, by the Eternal Spirit.
And when, driven by his thirst for martyrdom, he preached Christ to the proud Sultan and to those who came after him,
And found the people too unripe for conversion, rather than linger there in vain, returned to harvest the fruit of Italian soil,
On the rough crag between the Tiber and the Arno, he received from Christ the final seal — the stigmata, which his body bore for two full years.
When He who had chosen Francis for such great good was pleased to draw him upward to the reward he had earned through his humility,
To his brothers, as his rightful heirs, Francis commended his most beloved Lady — Poverty — and commanded them to love her faithfully.
And from her embrace, his illustrious soul chose to depart, returning to its kingdom. And for his body, he wanted no other bier than the bare ground.
Now consider what kind of man was worthy to be his companion, to steer the bark of Peter on the high seas and keep it on its proper course.
And that man was our patriarch Dominic. Whoever follows where he leads can see that the cargo is good.
But his flock has grown so greedy for new pastures that it is impossible they do not scatter across far-flung fields.
And the farther his sheep wander from him, remote and wayward, the emptier of milk they are when they return to the fold.
True, some of them stay close to the shepherd, fearing the harm of straying. But they are so few that it takes very little cloth to cut their hoods.
Now, if my words have not been unclear, if your hearing has been attentive, and if you call to mind what I have said,
Your wish will be partly satisfied. For you will see how the plant is being chipped away, and you will understand the reproach contained in the words,
'Where one grows fat, if one does not stray.'"

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XII
paragraphs: The moment that blessed flame had finished speaking its final word, the holy millstone began to turn,
And had not yet completed its full revolution before a second ring of lights enclosed it, matching motion to motion and song to song.
That song surpassed our Muses and our Sirens in those sweet trumpets as much as a first light surpasses its own reflection.
And as two parallel rainbows of the same color are stretched across a thin cloud when Juno sends her handmaid,
The outer one born from the inner, like the voice of that wandering nymph whom love consumed as the sun consumes the mist,
And they make the people here on earth, through the covenant God made with Noah, know that the world will never again be drowned in flood,
Just so those two garlands of everlasting roses encircled us, and the outer ring answered to the inner.
After the dance and the great celebration — of singing and of lights blazing tenderly and joyously, radiance answering radiance —
All stopped together, at one moment and with one accord, like eyes that must open and close together as the will directs them.
And from the heart of one of the new lights there came a voice that made me turn toward it like a compass needle to the star.
It began: "The love that makes me beautiful draws me to speak about the other leader, who is praised so well here on behalf of mine.
It is right that where one is named, the other should be brought in too, so that — as they fought side by side — their glory may shine together.
The army of Christ, which had cost so dearly to rearm, was moving behind its standard, slow, uncertain, and few in number,
When the Emperor who reigns forever came to the aid of His endangered host — through grace alone, not because it was deserving.
And, as was said, He sent two champions to His Bride, at whose deeds and words the scattered people were drawn back together.
In that region where the sweet west wind rises to open the new leaves with which Europe clothes herself afresh,
Not far from the beating of the waves, behind which the sun, in its long journey, sometimes hides itself from every mortal eye,
Sits the fortunate town of Calahorra, under the protection of the mighty shield on which the lion is both subject and sovereign.
There was born the passionate lover of the Christian faith — the consecrated champion, kind to his own and fierce against his enemies.
And when his mind was created, it was so filled with living power that it made his mother prophetic while he was still in the womb.
As soon as the betrothal was complete between him and the Faith at the holy font, where they endowed each other with mutual salvation,
The woman who had given consent for him in that rite saw in a dream the wondrous fruit that would come from him and from his heirs.
And so that he might be understood as he truly was, a spirit went forth from heaven to name him with the possessive of the One to whom he wholly belonged.
Dominic was his name. And I speak of him as the laborer whom Christ chose to help Him in His garden.
He truly appeared as Christ's messenger and servant. For the first love that manifested in him was for the first counsel Christ ever gave.
Many times his nurse found him silent and awake upon the bare ground, as though he were saying, 'This is what I came for.'
O Felix, truly your name means happy, his father! O Joanna, truly his mother — if her name, interpreted, means what they say!
Not for the sake of the world people labor for now, following Ostiense and Taddeo, but driven by hunger for the true bread of heaven,
He became so great a teacher in a short time that he began to go about the vineyard — which withers quickly if the keeper is faithless.
And from the papal See — which once was kinder to the righteous poor, not through any fault of its own but through the one who sits there now and degenerates —
He asked not for permission to keep two or three out of six, not for the revenue of the first vacancy, not for the tithes belonging to God's poor.
No — he asked for permission to fight against the straying world for the sake of the seed from which these twenty-four plants surrounding you have grown.
Then, armed with both doctrine and determination, and with apostolic authority, he moved like a torrent bursting from a high mountain spring.
And his force struck hardest among the heretical thickets, wherever the resistance was the greatest.
From him, many streams branched out, watering the Catholic garden so that its plantings stand more green and alive.
If such was one wheel of the chariot in which Holy Church defended herself and won its civic battle in the field,
Then the excellence of the other wheel — the one Thomas spoke of so graciously before I came — should be fully clear to you.
But the track carved by the outermost rim of that wheel has been abandoned, so that mold now grows where there was once a firm crust.
His family, which once walked straight ahead with their feet in his footprints, have turned around so completely that they set the toe where the heel should be.
And soon the harvest of this bad husbandry will be evident, when the weeds complain that the granary has been taken from them.
Still, I grant that anyone who searches our book leaf by leaf would find some page that reads, 'I am what I have always been.'
But that page will not come from Casale or from Acquasparta — places that send men to the written rule who either evade it or squeeze it too tight.
I am Bonaventure of Bagnoregio, who in great offices always put the lesser considerations last.
Here are Illuminato and Augustino, who were among the first barefoot beggars and, taking the cord, became friends of God.
Hugh of Saint Victor is among them here, and Peter Mangiatore, and Peter of Spain, whose twelve volumes still shine in the world below.
Nathan the prophet, and the great Chrysostom, and Anselm, and Donatus, who was pleased to set his hand to the first of the liberal arts.
Here is Rabanus, and beside me here shines the Calabrian Abbot Joachim, who was endowed with the spirit of prophecy.
The ardent courtesy and the wise words of Brother Thomas have moved me to celebrate so great a champion,
And with me, they have moved this whole company."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XIII
paragraphs: Let anyone who wishes to grasp what I now saw picture this, and hold the image steady in their mind like a rock while I speak.
Imagine the fifteen stars that enliven the sky in their various regions with a light so strong it pierces through every thickness of the air.
Imagine the Great Bear, for which the vault of heaven suffices night and day, so that it never vanishes as it turns around the pole.
Imagine the mouth of the horn that begins at the tip of the axis around which the outermost sphere revolves.
Now picture all of these forming two constellations in the sky, like the one Ariadne made at the moment she felt the chill of death.
And imagine one shining within the other, both wheeling in such a way that one moves forward while the other moves backward.
And you will have some faint foreshadowing of the true constellation and the double dance that circled around the point where I stood.
For it exceeds our experience as much as the swiftest heaven outstrips the sluggish current of the Chiana.
There they sang not of Bacchus, not of Apollo, but of three Persons in one divine nature, and of the divine and human united in one Person.
The singing and the dancing completed their measure, and those holy lights turned their attention to us, growing happier as they passed from one care to the next.
Then the silence among those harmonious saints was broken by the light in which the wondrous life of God's own beggar had been told to me.
It said: "Now that one sheaf has been threshed and its grain stored away, sweet love invites me to beat out the other.
You believe that into the breast from which the rib was drawn to form the beautiful face whose taste has cost the whole world so dearly,
And into the breast that, pierced by the lance, made such satisfaction for the past and future that it outweighs the balance of all sin,
Whatever light is permitted for human nature to possess was entirely poured in by the same Power that created both of them.
And so you wonder at what I said before, when I declared that the good contained within the fifth light had no equal.
Now open your eyes to my answer, and you will see that your belief and my words meet in the truth like the center of a circle.
Everything that dies and everything that does not die is nothing but the reflection of the Idea that our Lord, through His love, brings into being.
For that living Light which flows from its source so fully that it neither separates from Him nor from the Love that joins them as three,
Through its own goodness gathers its rays into nine subsistences, as if into mirrors — while itself remaining eternally One.
From there it descends to the lowest potencies, step by step from act to act, until it produces only brief contingent things.
And by these contingent things I mean the things that the heavens generate through their motion, with or without seed.
Neither their wax nor what stamps it remains constant. And therefore, beneath the ideal seal, the light shines through more in some and less in others.
This is why the same kind of tree bears better and worse fruit, and why you are born with different temperaments.
If the wax were perfectly tempered and the heavens were at the peak of their power, the full brilliance of the seal would shine through.
But nature always delivers it somewhat deficient — working like an artist who has the skill of the craft but whose hand trembles.
Yet when the burning Love and the clear Vision of the Primal Power itself arrange and stamp the form, absolute perfection is achieved.
In this way the earth was once made worthy of complete animal perfection. In this way the Virgin was made to conceive.
So I approve your opinion: that human nature has never been, and never will be, what it was in those two individuals.
Now, if I went no further, 'Then in what way was he without equal?' would be your very first question.
But to make clear what is not yet clear, consider who he was and what moved him to ask, when he was told, 'Make your request.'
I have spoken clearly enough for you to see that he was a king who asked for wisdom — so that he might be a king sufficient to his task.
He did not ask to know how many angelic movers exist above, or whether a necessary premise combined with a contingent one can produce a necessary conclusion,
Or whether there can be a first self-generating motion, or whether a triangle can be inscribed in a semicircle without having a right angle.
So if you consider this, along with everything I have said, the kingly prudence at which my arrow is aimed is that matchless seeing I spoke of.
And if you turn clear eyes to the word 'rose,' you will see it refers only to kings — of whom there are many, but the good ones are rare.
Take what I said with this distinction, and it will be perfectly consistent with your belief about the first father, Adam, and about our Delight, Christ.
And let this always weigh upon your feet like lead, making you slow — like a tired man — to say either 'yes' or 'no' to things you do not see clearly.
For very low among the fools ranks the one who affirms or denies without making distinctions, in either case alike.
Because it often happens that a hasty opinion bends in the wrong direction, and then emotion binds the intellect.
Far worse than uselessly does one set out from shore who fishes for truth without the proper skill — for he returns worse off than when he left.
And clear proof of this in the world are Parmenides, Melissus, Bryson, and many others who went forward without knowing where.
So too did Sabellius and Arius, and those fools who were like swords to Scripture, distorting its straight meaning.
Let people not be too confident in their judgments — like one who counts the grain in a field before it is ripe.
For I have seen the thornbush look harsh and stubborn all winter long, only to bear the rose upon its crown in spring.
And I have seen a ship sail straight and swift across the entire sea, only to sink at the very mouth of the harbor.
Let neither Dame Bertha nor Ser Martin suppose, when they see one man steal and another make an offering, that they are seeing them as divine judgment sees them.
For the one may yet rise, and the other may yet fall."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XIV
paragraphs: From center to rim, from rim to center, the water in a round basin moves — depending on whether it is struck from without or within.
This comparison dropped suddenly into my mind at the moment when the glorious voice of Thomas fell silent,
Because of the resemblance born between his words and those of Beatrice, who was pleased to begin after him:
"This man needs — though he does not tell you so, neither with his voice nor even in his thought — to reach the root of yet another truth.
Tell him whether the light that blossoms from your being will remain with you eternally, exactly as it is now.
And if it does remain, explain how, after you are made visible again in the flesh, it can avoid overwhelming your sight."
As those who dance in a ring are sometimes moved by a surge of greater joy to raise their voices and quicken their steps,
So, at that devout and eager prayer, the holy circles showed new joy in their turning and in their marvelous song.
Whoever grieves that we die here so that we may live above has never tasted the refreshment of the eternal rain.
The One and Two and Three who lives forever, and forever reigns in Three and Two and One — uncircumscribed, yet circumscribing all —
Was chanted three separate times by each of those spirits, with a melody that would be a just reward for any merit.
And in the most divine radiance of the smaller ring, I heard a gentle voice — perhaps like the angel's voice to Mary —
Answer: "As long as the celebration of Paradise endures, just so long will our love radiate this garment of light around us.
Its brightness is proportioned to our ardor, our ardor to our vision, and our vision is as great as the grace it has received beyond its own deserving.
When our glorified and sanctified flesh is taken up again, our persons will be more pleasing for being finally complete.
And so the free light that the Supreme Good grants us will increase — the light that makes us fit to see Him.
From that, our vision must increase; from that, the ardor kindled by the vision must increase; from that, the radiance poured forth by the ardor must increase.
But as a coal that produces a flame, yet outshines it with its white glow so that its own form remains visible,
So this radiance that already wraps us now will be surpassed in brightness by the flesh that the earth still covers.
Nor will so great a light have power to tire us, for the organs of the body will be made strong enough for everything that can bring us joy."
So quick and eager to say 'Amen!' were both the first and second chorus that they showed plainly how they longed for their dead bodies —
Perhaps not only for themselves, but for their mothers, their fathers, and for all who were dear to them before they became these eternal flames.
And behold — all around, beyond what was already shining, a new brightness arose of equal radiance, like the horizon growing light.
And as at the first approach of evening, new points of light begin to appear in the sky so that the sight half believes and half doubts what it sees,
So it seemed to me that I began to perceive new beings there, forming a ring outside the other two circles.
O true sparkling of the Holy Spirit! How suddenly and searingly bright it blazed before my eyes, so that they could not endure it!
But Beatrice revealed herself to me so beautiful and smiling that it must be left among those sights my memory cannot follow.
From this my eyes regained the strength to raise themselves, and I saw that I had been transported — alone with my Lady — to a higher state of blessedness.
That I had risen higher, the star's intensely red glow told me clearly, burning more fiercely than was its custom.
With all my heart, and in that language which is the same for all, I made a burnt offering to God fitting for this new grace.
And the fire of my sacrifice was not yet spent within my breast before I knew the offering had been accepted and favored.
For with such splendor, and so red, lights appeared within two rays that I cried out, "O Helios, who adorns them so!"
As the Milky Way, marked out between the poles of the universe, gleams white — so white it makes the wisest wonder at its cause —
So those rays, arranged in constellation, formed the venerable sign of the cross deep within that star — the sign that the joining of four quadrants makes.
Here memory outstrips my skill. For that cross flashed forth Christ so vividly that I can find no worthy comparison.
But whoever takes up his cross and follows Christ will yet forgive me for what I leave unsaid, when he sees that white blaze lightning with Christ.
From arm to arm, and from foot to head, lights were moving, sparkling brilliantly as they met and passed one another.
Just so we see here on earth, straight and slanting, swift and slow, changing their appearance, long and short — the motes of matter that move through the beam of light
That sometimes streaks across the shade people contrive with skill and ingenuity to protect themselves.
And as a viol and a harp, strung in harmony with many strings, make a sweet chiming to one who cannot catch the tune,
So from the lights that appeared to me there, a melody gathered along that cross which held me rapt, though I could not follow the hymn.
I could tell it was a song of high praise, for the words "Arise" and "Conquer" came to me like fragments heard by one who only half understands.
And I was so moved by love there that, until that moment, nothing had ever bound me with such sweet chains.
Perhaps my words seem too bold — setting aside the pleasure of those beautiful eyes in which my every longing finds its rest as I gaze into them.
But whoever considers that the living seals of all beauty grow more powerful the higher they ascend, and that I had not yet turned to those eyes,
Can excuse me for what I accuse myself of to justify myself — and see that I speak the truth. For that holy delight is not excluded here,
Since it grows purer as it rises.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XV
paragraphs: A generous will — in which the love that breathes rightly always reveals itself, just as selfish desire reveals itself in a will turned to evil —
Imposed silence on that sweet lyre and stilled the sacred strings that the hand of heaven loosens and draws tight.
How can those beings be deaf to righteous prayers, who, in order to give me the desire to ask, fell silent with one accord?
It is right that he should grieve without end who, for the love of what does not last, strips himself forever of this love.
As through the still and cloudless evening sky, a sudden streak of fire will sometimes shoot, drawing the eye that was resting quietly,
And it seems like a star changing its place — except that from the spot where it ignited, nothing is lost, and the flash itself is brief —
So, from the arm that stretches to the right, a star ran down to the foot of that cross along the constellation shining there.
Nor did the jewel leave its ribbon. Along the radial line it moved, like fire burning behind an alabaster screen.
With equal tenderness, the shade of Anchises reached out — if our greatest Muse deserves belief — when in Elysium he recognized his son.
"O blood of mine! O grace of God poured out beyond all measure! To whom was heaven's gate ever thrown open twice, as it is for you?"
So spoke that light. And I gave it my full attention. Then I turned my face to my Lady, and on both sides I was struck with wonder.
For within her eyes burned such a smile that I thought my own had reached the very floor of my grace and of my Paradise.
Then the spirit — a joy to hear and to behold — added things to his opening words that were too deep for my understanding.
Not by choice did he hide his meaning from me — it was by necessity, for his thoughts were set above the mark of mortal minds.
But when the bow of his burning love had slackened enough that his words descended to the target of our intellect,
The first thing I understood was this: "Blessed be You, Three-in-One, who show such favor to my descendant!"
And he continued: "A long and welcome hunger, drawn from reading the great volume where white and black are never changed,
You have relieved for me, my son, within this light in which I speak to you — thanks to her who gave you wings for this high flight.
You believe that your thought flows to me from the Primal Thought, just as from the number one, if it is known, both five and six ray forth.
And so you do not ask me who I am, or why I appear more joyful to you than any other spirit in this festive throng.
You believe correctly. For both the greater and the lesser souls in this life gaze into that mirror in which thought is displayed before it is even thought.
But so that the sacred love in which I keep vigil with perpetual sight, and which makes me ache with sweet longing, may be better fulfilled,
Let your own voice — confident, bold, and joyful — ring out your will, ring out your desire, for my answer is already decreed."
I turned to Beatrice, and she heard before I spoke, granting me a sign that made the wings of my desire grow.
Then I began: "The moment the First Equality appeared to you, love and understanding became equal within each of you,
For in that Sun which illuminated and warmed you with its heat and light, these two are so perfectly balanced that all comparisons fall short.
But in mortals, will and the power to express it — for reasons clear to you — are feathered with very different wings.
And so I, who am mortal, feel this inequality within myself, and therefore it is only with my heart that I thank you for your fatherly welcome.
I do beg you truly, living topaz set in this precious jewel — satisfy me with your name."
"O leaf of mine, in whom I took delight even while only awaiting you — I was your root." So he began his answer.
Then he said: "The one from whom your family takes its surname, who for a hundred years and more has circled the first ledge of the mountain,
Was my son, and he was your great-grandfather. It is fitting that you should shorten his long labor with your works.
Florence, within the ancient circle of walls from which she still receives the tierce and nones, lived in peace, modest and temperate.
She had no golden chains, no crowns, no embroidered gowns, no sash that was more striking to see than the person wearing it.
A daughter's birth did not yet fill her father with dread, for the bride-price and the wedding age had not yet swung to either extreme.
There were no houses empty of families. Sardanapalus had not yet arrived to show what could be done in the bedchamber.
Your Uccellatoio had not yet surpassed your Montemalo — which, as it has been surpassed in its rise, shall be surpassed in its fall.
Bellincion Berti I saw go belted in leather and bone, and his wife come away from the mirror without a painted face.
I saw the lords of Nerli and Vecchietti content with plain, unlined leather, and their wives content with spindle and thread.
O fortunate women! Each one was certain of her burial place. None yet had been abandoned in her bed because of France.
One kept watch over the cradle, using that baby-talk that first delights new fathers and mothers.
Another, drawing the thread from the distaff, would tell her family stories of the Trojans, of Fiesole, and of Rome.
A Cianghella or a Lapo Salterello would have been as much a marvel then as Cincinnatus or Cornelia would be today.
To so peaceful, so beautiful a life among citizens, to so loyal a community, to so sweet a dwelling place,
Mary gave me — called upon with loud cries in her labor pains — and in your ancient Baptistery I became both a Christian and Cacciaguida.
Moronto and Eliseo were my brothers. My wife came to me from the valley of the Po, and from her came your family surname.
Then I followed Emperor Conrad, and he girded me with his knighthood, so greatly did I rise in his good graces through my deeds.
