With him I marched against the wickedness of that law whose people usurp your rightful heritage through the fault of the shepherds.
There, by that foul race, I was released from the deceitful world whose love corrupts so many souls.
And from martyrdom I came to this peace."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XVI
paragraphs: O our poor nobility of blood! If you make people boast of you down here, where our desires grow weak and weary,
It will never be a marvel to me. For even there, where appetite is not corrupted — in heaven itself — I boasted of you!
Truly you are a cloak that quickly shortens, so that unless we add to you day by day, time goes around you with his shears.
With the formal 'you' — which Rome first permitted, though her people are less faithful to it now — I once again began to speak.
At which Beatrice, standing somewhat apart, smiled and appeared like the lady-in-waiting who coughed at the first recorded slip of Guinevere.
And I began: "You are my ancestor. You give me all the boldness to speak. You lift me so high that I am more than myself.
So many streams of gladness fill my mind that it takes joy in itself, marveling that it can contain all this without bursting.
Tell me then, my cherished ancestral root — who were your ancestors? And what were the years that were recorded in your boyhood?
Tell me about the sheepfold of Saint John — how large it was, and who among its people were worthy of the highest seats."
As a coal quickens to flame at the breath of wind, so I saw that light grow more resplendent at my words of praise.
And as it grew more beautiful to my eyes, it spoke to me in a voice sweeter and more tender — though not in this modern dialect:
"From the 'Ave' of the Annunciation to the birth in which my mother — now a saint — was lightened of the burden that was me,
This planet of Mars had returned to its Lion five hundred and eighty times, to rekindle itself beneath its paw.
My ancestors and I had our birthplace where the runner in your annual race first enters the last ward of the city.
Let this suffice about my forebears. Who they were and where they came from — silence is more fitting than speech.
All those fit to bear arms who lived at that time between the shrine of Mars and the Baptist numbered one fifth of those living there today.
But the citizenry — which is now mixed with blood from Campi, Certaldo, and Figghine — was pure even in the humblest craftsman.
Oh, how much better it would be to have those people I speak of as neighbors, and to set your boundary at Galluzzo and Trespiano,
Than to have them inside the city walls, enduring the stench of the yokel from Aguglione and the one from Signa who already has sharp eyes for swindling.
If the people who degenerate most in all the world had not been a stepmother to Caesar, but had been kind as a mother to her son,
Some who play the Florentine now, trading and dealing, would have gone back to Semifonte, where their grandfathers begged for bread.
The Counts would still be at Montemurlo, the Cerchi in the parish of Acone, and perhaps the Buondelmonti still in Valdigrieve.
The mixing of populations has always been the source of a city's sickness, just as too much food is the source of sickness in the body.
And a blind bull plunges more headlong than a blind lamb. And one sword often cuts better and more than five.
If you look at Luni and Urbisaglia, see how they have perished — and how Chiusi and Sinigaglia are wasting away after them.
Then to hear how families exhaust themselves will seem neither new nor hard to you, since even cities come to an end.
All your works have their mortality, just as you do. But in some it is hidden because they last a long time, while your lives are short.
And as the turning of the moon covers and uncovers the shores without pause, so fortune does with Florence.
So it should not seem a marvel — what I am about to tell you of the great Florentines whose fame is buried in the past.
I saw the Ughi, the Catellini, the Filippi, the Greci, the Ormanni, and the Alberichi — illustrious citizens even in their decline.
And I saw, as ancient as they were mighty, the families of della Sannella and dell'Arca, and the Soldanieri, Ardinghi, and Bostichi.
Near to the gate now burdened with a new treachery of such weight that it will soon be cast overboard from the ship,
Lived the Ravignani, from whom Count Guido descended, and whoever has since taken the great name of Bellincione.
He of della Pressa already knew the art of governing, and already Galigaio had gilded hilt and pommel in his house.
Already great was the Column of Vair, the Sacchetti, Giuochi, Fifanti, and Barucci, and the Galli, and those who blush for the false bushel.
The stock from which the Calfucci sprang was already great, and the Sizii and the Arrigucci had already been chosen for the highest civic seats.
Oh, how great I saw those families who have been ruined by their own pride! And the Golden Balls — how they made Florence bloom with all their mighty deeds!
So too did the ancestors of those who, whenever your bishop's seat is vacant, grow fat by lingering in the consistory.
The insolent clan that turns like a dragon on anyone who flees, but becomes gentle as a lamb to whoever shows his teeth — or his purse —
Was already rising, though from humble roots. And it displeased Ubertino Donato that his father-in-law had made him their kinsman.
Caponsacco had already come down from Fiesole into the marketplace, and Giuda and Infangato were already good citizens.
I will tell you something incredible but true: people entered the small city through a gate that took its name from the della Pera family!
Everyone who bears the beautiful coat of arms of the great baron whose memory and name are kept alive on the feast of Saint Thomas
Received knighthood and privilege from him — though today, one who trims those arms with a border allies himself with the common people.
The Gualterotti and the Importuni were already there. And the Borgo would still be quieter if they had not been fed with new neighbors.
The house from which your grief was born — through the righteous anger that brought death among you and ended your joyful life —
Was honored in itself and in its companions. O Buondelmonte, in what an evil hour you fled that marriage at another's urging!
Many who are sad today would be rejoicing if God had drowned you in the Ema the first time you came to the city.
But it was fated that the broken statue that guards the bridge should provide Florence with a sacrifice in her last hour of peace.
With all these families, and others beside them, I saw Florence in such profound repose that she had no cause for weeping.
With all these families I saw her people so just and glorious that the lily was never hung reversed upon the lance,
Nor was it ever turned from white to red by civic strife."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XVII
paragraphs: As Phaethon came to Clymene to be made certain of what he had heard spoken against him — the one who still makes fathers wary with their children —
Just so was I, and so I was perceived to be, both by Beatrice and by the holy light that had first shifted its position for my sake.
Therefore my Lady said to me: "Send forth the flame of your desire so that it issues clearly stamped with the impression of your will.
Not that our knowledge is made greater by your speech, but so that you may grow accustomed to declaring your thirst, so that we may give you drink."
"O my beloved root, you who raise yourself so high that — just as earthly minds perceive that no triangle can contain two obtuse angles —
You see contingent things before they exist, by fixing your eyes upon that point in which all times are present.
While I traveled with Virgil, both on the mountain that heals souls and when descending into the dead world,
Heavy words were spoken to me about my future life. Though I feel myself foursquare against the blows of fortune.
For this reason my wish would be satisfied to hear what fate approaches me, since an arrow that is foreseen arrives more slowly."
So I spoke to that same light that had spoken to me before. And as Beatrice wished, my own will was made clear.
Not in the ambiguous language that trapped the foolish people of old, before the Lamb of God who takes away sins was slain,
But in clear words and precise speech, that fatherly love replied — hidden and revealed within its own smile:
"Contingency, which does not extend beyond the pages of your material world, is entirely depicted in the eternal vision.
Yet it takes no necessity from that — any more than a ship moving downstream takes necessity from the eye that mirrors its passage.
From that eternal sight, as sweet harmony reaches the ear from an organ, there comes before my eyes the time that is preparing for you.
As Hippolytus was driven from Athens by his false and cruel stepmother, so you must depart from Florence.
This is already willed, already being sought. And soon it will be accomplished by the one who schemes for it there, where Christ is bought and sold every day.
The blame will be heaped on the injured party, as usual, by the public outcry. But the vengeance will bear witness to the truth that dispenses it.
You will leave behind everything you love most dearly. And this is the arrow that the bow of exile shoots first.
You will learn how salty another man's bread tastes, and how hard a path it is to climb and descend another man's stairs.
And what will weigh most heavily on your shoulders will be the wretched and foolish company with whom you will fall into that valley.
For they will become entirely ungrateful, mad, and godless toward you. But soon after, it will be their brows, not yours, that turn scarlet with shame.
Their own actions will be proof enough of their brutishness. It will be well for you to have made a party of yourself alone.
Your first refuge and your first inn will be the courtesy of the great Lombard who bears the sacred bird upon the ladder.
He will look upon you with such generous regard that between the two of you, the giving and the asking will reverse their usual order.
With him you will see one who at birth was so strongly marked by this star of Mars that his achievements will be remarkable.
The world does not yet know him because of his young age — these spheres have revolved only nine years around him so far.
But before the Gascon deceives the noble Henry, some sparks of his virtue will appear in his indifference to money and to toil.
His magnificence will become so widely recognized that even his enemies will be unable to keep silent about it.
Place your hope in him and in his generosity. Through him, many people will be transformed — the rich made poor and the beggars made wealthy.
And you will carry written in your mind things about him" — and here he told me things incredible to those who will be present to see them.
Then he added: "Son, these are the commentaries on what was said to you along the way. These are the traps hidden behind only a few turns of the years.
Yet I would not have you envy your neighbors, for your life will reach far beyond the punishment of their treacheries."
When that sainted soul showed by its silence that it had finished weaving the weft into the warp I had stretched out for it,
I began again, like a man who yearns for counsel in his uncertainty from one who sees clearly, wills rightly, and loves:
"I see well, my father, how time spurs toward me, ready to deal me such a blow as falls heaviest on the one who is least prepared.
Therefore it is wise to arm myself with foresight, so that if the dearest place is taken from me, I may not lose the others through my writings.
Down through the world of endless bitterness, and over the mountain from whose beautiful summit the eyes of my Lady lifted me,
And afterward through heaven, from light to light, I have learned things that, if I tell them again, will have a bitter taste for many.
And if I am a timid friend to truth, I fear I will lose my life among those who will call this time 'the old days.'"
The light in which my treasure was smiling — the treasure I had found there — flashed at first like a golden mirror in the sun.
Then it replied: "A conscience clouded by its own shame or another's will indeed find your words bitter.
But nonetheless, cast aside all falsehood and make your whole vision known. Let them scratch wherever the itch is.
For if your words are bitter at first taste, they will leave behind a vital nourishment once they are digested.
This cry of yours will do as the wind does — it strikes hardest against the highest peaks. And that is no small proof of honor.
For this reason, within these spheres, upon the mountain, and in the valley of sorrow, only souls known to fame have been shown to you.
Because the listener's mind does not rest upon, nor place its trust in, an example whose roots are unknown and hidden,
Or for any other reason that is not self-evident."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XVIII
paragraphs: Now that blessed soul was rejoicing alone in its own words, and I was savoring mine — tempering the bitter with the sweet.
And the Lady who was leading me to God said: "Shift your thoughts. Consider that I am near the One who lifts the weight of every wrong."
I turned to the loving voice of my comfort, and what love I saw then, burning in those holy eyes, I must leave unspoken here.
Not only because I distrust my language, but because my memory cannot climb so far above itself unless another hand guides it.
This much I can say about that moment: gazing at her again, my affection was freed from every other longing.
While the eternal joy that shone directly upon Beatrice satisfied me from her fair face with its reflected radiance,
She conquered me with the light of a smile and said: "Turn around and listen. Paradise is not only in my eyes."
Just as here on earth we sometimes read affection in a person's face, when it is so strong that it absorbs the whole soul,
So, by the blazing of the holy radiance to which I turned, I recognized in it the desire to speak to me further.
And it began: "In this fifth resting place upon the tree that lives from its summit, always bearing fruit and never losing a leaf,
There are blessed spirits who, before they came to heaven, were of such great renown below that any Muse would be enriched by them.
Look now at the arms of the cross. Whomever I name will flash across it as lightning does within a cloud."
I saw a splendor drawn across the cross at the naming of Joshua — and it happened even as the name was spoken, the deed came before the word.
And at the name of the great Maccabee, I saw another light spin and revolve, and gladness was the whip that drove that top.
Likewise for Charlemagne and for Roland, my gaze followed two of them attentively, as the eye follows its falcon in flight.
Then William of Orange, Renouard, Duke Godfrey, and Robert Guiscard drew my sight along that cross.
Then the soul that had been speaking to me moved and mingled with the other lights, showing what a great artist it was among the singers of heaven.
I turned to my right to see in Beatrice, whether by word or gesture, what I should do next.
And I saw her eyes so translucent, so full of joy, that her face surpassed every other expression of beauty, even its most recent.
And just as a man who does good day after day becomes aware, by feeling greater delight, that his virtue is growing,
So I became aware that my circling arc through heaven had grown wider, when I saw that miracle adorned still more.
And as the change in a pale woman's face is swift and visible when the weight of blushes lifts from her,
So it was with my eyes when I turned and found myself within the white and temperate star — the sixth, Jupiter, which had drawn me to itself.
Within that torch of Jove I saw the sparkling of the love that dwelt there spelling out our language before my eyes.
And as birds rising from a riverbank, as if in celebration over their feeding, form themselves into flocks — now round, now long —
So within those lights the holy creatures sang as they flew, and in their formations they shaped themselves into the letters D, then I, then L.
First they moved in rhythm to their own song. Then, having formed each letter, they paused briefly and fell silent.
O divine Pegasea, you who give genius its glory and its long life, as genius gives glory to cities and kingdoms,
Illuminate me with your power so that I can render their figures as I perceived them! Let your might be apparent in these brief verses.
They displayed themselves, then, in five times seven vowels and consonants. And I noted the parts as they appeared, spoken to me.
'Diligite justitiam' — 'Love justice' — were the first words depicted. 'Qui judicatis terram' — 'you who judge the earth' — were the last.
Then they stayed arranged within the M of the fifth word, so that Jupiter seemed to be silver inlaid with gold.
And I saw other lights descend to the crown of the M and settle there, singing of the Good that draws them to itself.
Then, as when you strike burning logs and countless sparks fly upward — the kind from which fools try to read their fortunes —
More than a thousand lights seemed to rise from there, some higher, some less, just as the Sun that kindles them allotted.
And when each had settled into its place, the head and neck of an eagle stood shaped by that fire inlaid upon the letter.
He who paints there needs no guide. He Himself is the guide. And from Him comes the power that gives form to every nest.
The other blessed spirits, who had seemed content at first to form a lily crowning the M, with a slight motion completed the design.
O gentle star! How many and how brilliant were the gems that showed me our justice is the work of the heaven you adorn!
Therefore I pray the Mind in which your motion and your power begin — look to the place from which the smoke rises that corrupts your rays!
So that once more it may grow angry at the buying and selling in the temple whose walls were built with miracles and blood!
O host of heaven, whom I contemplate — pray for those on earth who have all gone astray, following the bad example!
Once the custom was to wage war with swords. But now it is waged by withholding here and there the bread that the merciful Father denies to no one.
But you who write only to cancel — remember that Peter and Paul, who died for this vineyard you are devastating, are still alive!
Well may you say: "My desire is so fixed upon the one who chose to live alone and was dragged to martyrdom through a dance,
That I know neither the Fisherman nor Paul."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XIX
paragraphs: Before me, with its wings spread wide, appeared the beautiful image that those interwoven souls made jubilant in their sweet delight.
Each soul appeared as a little ruby in which the ray of the sun burned so fiercely that it was reflected straight into my eyes.
And what I must now describe, no voice has ever reported, no ink has ever written, no imagination has ever grasped.
For I saw the beak speak, and I heard it — and it uttered 'I' and 'my' with its voice, when in its thought it was 'we' and 'our.'
And it began: "Because I was just and merciful, I am exalted here to this glory that cannot be surpassed by any desire.
And on earth I left behind a memory such that the evil-minded praise it there but do not follow its example."
Just as a single warmth is felt from many coals, so from many loves a single voice issued from that image.
And I replied: "O everlasting flowers of the eternal joy, who make all your manifold fragrances seem to me like one,
By breathing out, break within me the great fast that has held me hungry for so long, since I have found no food for it on earth.
I know well that if divine Justice makes its mirror in another realm of heaven, yours perceives it without any veil.
You know how intently I prepare myself to listen. And you know the question that has been so old a fast within me."
Like a falcon freed from its hood, moving its head and clapping its wings to show desire and make itself fine,
So I saw that standard — woven from the praises of divine grace — become animated, with songs known only to those who rejoice there.
Then it began: "He who turned His compass upon the outer boundary of the world, and within it devised so much, both hidden and revealed,
Could not stamp the imprint of His power upon the entire universe without His Word remaining in infinite excess.
And this is proved by the fact that the first proud being — the highest of all creatures — fell unripe for having refused to wait for light.
From this it follows that every lesser nature is too small a vessel for that good which is without limit and measures itself only by itself.
Therefore our vision — which must be but one ray of the intelligence with which all things are filled —
Cannot be so powerful by its own nature that it does not perceive its origin far beyond anything it can see.
And so the vision your world receives penetrates eternal justice as the eye penetrates the ocean —
Which, though it can see the bottom near the shore, cannot perceive it on the open deep. Yet the bottom is there — it is simply hidden by the depth.
There is no light except from that serenity which is never overcast. Everything else is darkness — either the shadow of the flesh, or its poison.
Now the cavern has been opened wide for you — the one that hid the living justice you questioned so insistently.
For you said: 'A man is born on the banks of the Indus, where no one can speak of Christ, no one can read, no one can write.'
And all his inclinations and his deeds are good, as far as human reason can see — without sin in his life or in his words.
He dies unbaptized and without faith. Where is the justice that condemns him? Where is his fault if he does not believe?'
Now who are you, to sit upon the bench and judge from a thousand miles away, with a sight that barely spans a hand?
Truly, for the one who tries to reason closely with me — if Scripture were not set above you, there would be marvelous grounds for doubt.
O earthbound creatures! O dull minds! The Primal Will, which is goodness itself, has never moved from itself, the Supreme Good.
Only what accords with that Will is just. No created good draws that Will to itself — rather, that Will, by shining forth, creates the good."
Just as a stork circles above her nest after feeding her young, and the one who has been fed looks up at her,
So I raised my brow, and so that blessed image became — beating its wings, driven by so many counsels.
Wheeling around, it sang and said: "As my songs are to you, who cannot understand them, such is the eternal judgment to you mortals."
Then those luminous splendors of the Holy Spirit grew still, though remaining within the standard that made the Romans reverend to the world.
It spoke again: "To this kingdom no one ever ascended who did not have faith in Christ — either before or after He was nailed to the tree.
But look — many cry 'Christ! Christ!' who at the Judgment will be far less close to Him than some who never knew Christ.
Such Christians the Ethiopian will condemn when the two companies are divided — one forever rich, the other forever poor.
What will the Persians say to your kings when they see that book opened in which all their disgraces are recorded?
There will be seen, among the deeds of Albert, the one that will soon set the pen in motion — the deed that will make the kingdom of Prague a desert.
There will be seen the grief he brings to the Seine by debasing the coinage — he who will die from the charge of a wild boar.
There will be seen the pride that breeds such thirst it drives the Scot and the Englishman mad, so that neither can stay within his own borders.
There will be seen the luxury and soft living of the king of Spain and the king of Bohemia, who never knew valor and never wished for it.
There will be seen the Cripple of Jerusalem, his goodness marked with a single 'I' while his vices fill an 'M.'
There will be seen the greed and cowardice of the one who guards the Island of Fire, where Anchises ended his long life.
And to show how contemptible he is, his record will be written in cramped abbreviations that note much in little space.
And the foul deeds of an uncle and a brother will be revealed — men who dishonored so famous a nation and two crowns.
And the king of Portugal and the king of Norway will be known there, and the king of Rascia, who debased the coin of Venice to his ruin.
O happy Hungary, if she refuses to be wronged further! And happy Navarre, if she arms herself with the mountains that surround her!
And as a foretaste of this, let all believe that Nicosia and Famagosta already cry and rage because of their own beast,
Who will not leave the side of all the others."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XX
paragraphs: When the one who illumines the whole world sinks so far below our hemisphere that daylight is consumed on every side,
The sky, which before was lit by the sun alone, suddenly reveals itself again through many lights, in one of which it is most splendid.
And this act of heaven came into my mind when the standard of the world and of its leaders fell silent in its blessed beak.
For all those living lights, shining far more brilliantly now, began songs that have since slipped and fallen from my memory.
O sweet Love, who cloaks yourself in a smile — how ardent you appeared in those sparks that held only the breath of holy thoughts!
After the precious and pellucid crystals with which the sixth light I beheld was jeweled imposed silence on their angelic chimes,
I seemed to hear the murmuring of a river running clear from rock to rock, revealing the abundance of its mountain source.
And as a sound takes shape upon the neck of a lute, and as wind takes form at the vent of a rustic pipe where it enters,
Just so, free of any delay, that murmuring of the eagle rose up along its neck, as if the neck were hollow.
There it became a voice and issued from the beak, formed into words of the kind that the heart was waiting for, where I inscribed them.
"The part of me that sees and bears the sun in mortal eagles," it began, "must now be gazed upon steadily.
For of the fires that make my figure, those from which the eye sparkles in my head are the supreme among all their ranks.
The one who shines in the center as the pupil was once the singer of the Holy Spirit, who carried the ark from city to city.
Now he knows the merit of his song, insofar as it was the result of his own will, by the reward that matches it.
Of the five that form an arc upon my brow, the one nearest to my beak consoled the poor widow for her son.
Now he knows how dearly it costs not to follow Christ, by his experience of this sweet life and of its opposite.
And the next one along the upper arc I describe was the one who delayed his own death through true repentance.
Now he knows that eternal judgment is not altered when a worthy prayer on earth makes tomorrow's event happen today.
The next one — with the best of intentions that bore the worst of fruit — made himself a Greek along with the shepherd and with the laws, by ceding Rome to him.
Now he knows how the evil that sprang from his good deed does not harm him, even though the world was destroyed by it.
And the one you see on the downward arc was William, whom that land mourns which weeps for Charles and Frederick still alive.
Now he knows how heaven is enamored of a righteous king, and he makes it visible still by the radiance of his glow.
Who down in your erring world would believe that Ripheus the Trojan was the fifth of the holy lights in this arc?
Now he knows much of divine grace that the world cannot see, even though his own sight cannot reach the bottom."
Like a lark that soars into the air, first singing, then falling silent, satisfied by the last sweetness of its song,
Such seemed to me the image of the seal of the Eternal Pleasure, by whose will each thing becomes what it is.
And though I was to my doubt there like glass through which color shines, it could not endure the waiting in silence.
But from my mouth it pressed the words "What things are these?" by its own weight. At which I saw a great feast of sparkling lights.
Then, with its eye still more enkindled, the blessed standard answered me, to keep me from remaining suspended in my wonder:
"I see that you believe these things because I say them, but you do not see the how. So though they are believed, they remain hidden.
You are like one who knows a thing by name but cannot see its quiddity — its essence — unless another reveals it.
'Regnum coelorum' — the kingdom of heaven — suffers the force of burning love and of living hope, which conquers the divine will.
Not as man conquers man. It lets itself be conquered because it wills to be — and, conquered, conquers with its own benevolence.
The first life on the brow and the fifth astonish you because you see the region of the angels painted with them.
They did not leave their bodies as pagans, as you think, but as Christians — with firm faith, one in the feet that were to suffer, the other in the feet that had already suffered.
For one came back to his bones from Hell — where no one ever returns to righteous will — and this was the reward of living hope.
Of living hope, which gave power to the prayers made to God to raise him up, so that his will might be moved.
The glorious soul I speak of, returning briefly to the flesh, believed in Him who had the power to help him.
And believing, was kindled into such a fire of true love that at his second death he was worthy to enter this celebration.
The other, through a grace that wells from so deep a spring that no creature's eye has ever reached its source,
Set all his love below upon righteousness. And so, from grace to grace, God opened his eyes to our future redemption.
He believed in it, and from that day could not endure the stench of paganism, and rebuked the perverted peoples for it.
Those three ladies you saw at the right wheel of the chariot served as his baptism, more than a thousand years before there was any baptism.
O predestination, how remote is your root from the vision of those who cannot see the First Cause entire!
And you mortals, hold yourselves back from judging. For we, who see God, do not yet know all those who are elect.
And this incompleteness is sweet to us, because our good is refined in this good — that what God wills, we also will."
So from that divine image, to clear the blur of my short sight, a sweet medicine was given to me.
And as an accomplished citharist accompanies a good singer with the trembling of the strings, giving the song still greater pleasure,
So, while it spoke, I remember that I saw both those blessed lights,
Like eyes blinking in harmony, move their little flames in time with the words.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XXI
paragraphs: Already my eyes were fastened once more on my Lady's face, and with them my mind, withdrawn from every other thought.
And she did not smile, but said: "If I were to smile, you would become what Semele became when she was turned to ashes.
Because my beauty, which kindles more brightly the higher we ascend the stairs of the eternal palace, as you have seen,
Would be so resplendent, if it were not tempered, that all your mortal power would be like a leaf crushed by lightning.
We have been raised to the seventh splendor, which beneath the burning Lion's breast now radiates downward, mingled with his strength.
Fix the attention of your eyes behind your mind, and make your eyes a mirror for the figure that will appear to you in this one."
Whoever could know what a feast my sight was making in that blessed face, when I turned to a different care,
Would understand how welcome it was to obey my heavenly guide, by weighing one pleasure against the other.
Within the crystal sphere that bears the name of its beloved ruler — Saturn, under whom all wickedness lay dead —
Colored like gold gleaming in the sun, I saw a stairway rising to such a height that my eye could not follow it.
And I saw so many splendors descending along its steps that I thought every light in heaven had been poured out there.
And as is the natural custom of rooks at daybreak, they stir themselves to warm their cold feathers.
Then some fly off without returning, others come back to where they started, and others wheel about, staying near home.
Such, it appeared to me, was the manner of those sparklings that came together as soon as they struck a certain step.
And the one that stopped nearest to us became so bright that I said in my mind: 'I can clearly see the love you are showing me.'
But she, from whom I await the how and when of speech and silence, stands still. And so, against my desire, I do well not to ask.
Then she, who saw my silence in the sight of Him who sees everything, said to me: "Let your warm desire loose."
And I began: "No merit of my own makes me worthy of your answer. But for the sake of her who permits me to ask,
O blessed soul, who remains hidden within your happiness, make known to me the reason that draws you so near to my side.
And tell me why the sweet symphony of Paradise is silent in this sphere, when through all the others below it sounds so devoutly."
"Your hearing is mortal, like your sight," came the answer. "They do not sing here for the same reason that Beatrice has not smiled.
I have descended this far along the holy stairway only to welcome you — with words and with the light that wraps me.
Nor was it greater love that made me swifter, for love burns as much and more up there, as the flaming you see makes clear.
But the deep charity that makes us prompt servants of the counsel governing the world assigns us here, as you observe."
"I see well, O sacred lamp," I said, "how free love in this court suffices to carry out eternal Providence.
But what is hard for me to grasp is this: why were you alone, out of all your companions, predestined to this role?"
I had not reached my final word before the light made its center a spinning axis, whirling itself around like a swift millstone.
Then the love within it answered: "A divine light is directed upon me, piercing through the radiance in which I am enfolded.
Its power, joined with my sight, lifts me so far above myself that I can see the Supreme Essence from which it flows.
From this comes the joy with which I blaze. For I make the brightness of my flame equal to the clarity of my sight.
But even the purest soul in heaven — the seraph whose eye is most fixed upon God — could not satisfy this question of yours.
Because what you ask sinks so deep into the abyss of the eternal decree that it is cut off from every created sight.
And when you return to the mortal world, carry this back: let it no longer presume to direct its steps toward such a goal.
The mind that shines here still smokes down on earth. Consider, then: how can it do below what it cannot even when heaven takes it up?"
His words set such a limit on me that I abandoned the question and confined myself to asking humbly who he was.
"Between two shores of Italy rise cliffs, not far from your own birthplace, so high that the thunder rumbles far below them.
They form a ridge called Catria, beneath which a hermitage is consecrated — once devoted solely to worship."
So began his third speech. Then continuing: "There I became so steadfast in the service of God
That, feeding only on olive juice, I passed through heat and frost lightly, content in contemplative thoughts.
That cloister used to yield abundantly to these heavens. But now it has become so empty that the truth must soon be revealed.
In that place I was Peter Damian. And I was Peter the Sinner in the house of Our Lady on the Adriatic shore.
Little of mortal life remained to me when I was called and dragged to the cardinal's hat — which passes from bad to worse.
Cephas came barefoot and lean, and the great Vessel of the Holy Spirit came the same way, taking food at any inn.
But today's shepherds need someone to prop them up on either side, someone to lead them — so heavy are they — and someone to hold their trains.
They cover their horses with their cloaks, so that two beasts walk beneath one hide. O Patience, how much you endure!"
At this voice I saw many little flames descending from step to step, spinning as they went, and each revolution made them more beautiful.
They gathered around this one and stood still, and let out a cry of such tremendous volume that nothing here could match it.
Nor could I make out the words — the thunder of it overwhelmed me.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XXII
paragraphs: Overwhelmed with shock, I turned to my guide like a little child who always runs to the place where he feels most safe.
And she, like a mother who quickly comforts her pale and breathless boy with the voice that always reassures him,
Said to me: "Do you not know you are in heaven? Do you not know that all of heaven is holy, and that what happens here comes from righteous passion?
You can now imagine how the singing would have transformed you, and how my smile — since even this cry has shaken you so deeply.
If you had understood the prayers within that cry, you would already know the vengeance that you will witness before you die.
The sword of heaven strikes neither in haste nor tardily, though it may seem so to the one who waits for it in fear or in longing.
But turn now toward the others, for you will see illustrious spirits if you direct your gaze as I tell you."
I turned my eyes as she wished, and saw a hundred tiny spheres that embellished one another with their interwoven light.
I stood like a man who holds back the sharp point of his desire, not daring to ask for fear of presuming too much.
And now the largest and most luminous of those pearls came forward to satisfy my desire concerning it.
Then from within it I heard: "If you could see the charity that burns among us as I see it, your thoughts would already have been expressed.
But so that by waiting you do not arrive late at the lofty goal, I will answer the very thought you are too cautious to speak.
That mountain on whose slope Cassino stands was once frequented at its summit by a deluded and wayward people.
And I am the one who first carried up there the name of Him who brought to earth the truth that lifts us so high.
And such abundant grace shone upon me that I drew all the surrounding towns away from the godless worship that had seduced the world.
These other flames were all contemplative men, kindled by the warmth that makes holy flowers and fruits spring forth.
Here is Macarius, here is Romualdus, here are my brothers who kept their feet within the cloister and held a steadfast heart."
And I said to him: "The affection you show in speaking with me, and the good will I see and note in all your glowing,
Have so expanded my confidence — as the sun opens a rose until it unfolds as far as it can —
That I pray you, father, and beg you to assure me: may I receive enough grace to see you with your face unveiled?"
He replied: "Brother, your high desire will be fulfilled in the uttermost sphere, where all desires are fulfilled — mine included.
There, every desire is perfect, ripe, and complete. In that sphere alone, every part is where it has always been.
For that sphere is not in space, nor does it turn on poles. And our stairway reaches up to it — which is why it vanishes from your sight.
All the way to that height, the patriarch Jacob saw it stretching its upper part, that time when it appeared to him so crowded with angels.
But now, no one lifts his feet from the earth to climb it. And my Rule survives below only as wasted paper.
The walls that used to house an abbey have become dens of robbers, and the cowls are sacks filled with rotten meal.
But even heavy usury does not offend God as grievously as that fruit which drives the hearts of monks insane.
For whatever the Church holds in keeping is for the people who ask in God's name — not for one's relatives or for something worse.
The flesh of mortals is so very soft that a good beginning on earth does not last long enough for the oak to grow from the sprouting to the acorn.
Peter began his community with neither gold nor silver. I began mine with prayer and fasting. And Francis began his with humility.
And if you look at how each one began, and then see where it has ended up, you will see the white turned into brown.
Truly, the Jordan flowing backward and the sea parting when God willed it were more wondrous sights than any rescue coming here."
So he spoke to me, and then withdrew to his band. The band closed ranks, and then like a whirlwind they were all swept upward.
My gentle Lady urged me after them up that stairway with just a single sign — so much did her power overcome my nature.
And never down here, where we go up and down by natural law, was any motion so swift that it could compare with the speed of my wings.
Reader, as I hope to return to that devout triumph — for whose sake I often weep and beat my breast over my sins —
You would not have thrust your finger into fire and drawn it out again before I saw the sign that follows Taurus, and was within it.
O glorious stars! O light impregnated with mighty power, from which I acknowledge all my genius, whatever it may be.
With you, the sun was rising and setting — the father of all mortal life — when I first breathed the air of Tuscany.
And then, when grace was freely given to me to enter the high wheel that turns you, your region was assigned to me.
To you my soul devoutly sighs at this hour, that it may acquire the strength for the stern passage that draws it to itself.
"You are so near to the final salvation," Beatrice began, "that your eyes ought now to be clear and sharp.
And therefore, before you go further in, look down once more and see how vast a world you have already set beneath your feet,
So that your heart may present itself as joyful as it can to the triumphant throng that comes rejoicing through this rounded heaven."
I turned my sight back through all seven spheres, and saw this globe of ours — and smiled at its shabby appearance.
And I approve as best the opinion that counts it least. Whoever turns his mind to other things may truly be called just.
I saw the daughter of Latona shining without that shadow which had once led me to believe she was partly rare, partly dense.
I endured the sight of your son, Hyperion — the sun — and saw how Maia and Dione move around and near him.
From there I saw the temperate light of Jove between his father Saturn and his son Mars, and clearly perceived the changes they make in their positions.
And all seven were revealed to me — how great they are, how swift, and how far apart they are in their dwelling places.
The little threshing floor that makes us so proud, turning beneath the eternal Twins, was all laid bare before me from mountain peak to harbor.
Then to those beautiful eyes I turned my own.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XXIII
paragraphs: As a bird among the beloved leaves, quiet upon the nest of her sweet brood throughout the night that hides all things from us,
Who, eager to see their longed-for faces and to find the food with which to feed them — a labor that is welcome to her love —
Goes ahead of the dawn to an open branch, and waits for the sun with burning longing, gazing intently the moment light begins to break:
Just so my Lady stood, upright and alert, turned toward that region of the sky beneath which the sun shows less haste.
And seeing her so rapt and yearning, I became like one who desires something and, while hoping, is consoled.
But the time was brief between one 'when' and the other — between my waiting and my seeing the sky grow brighter and brighter.
And Beatrice cried out: "Behold the hosts of Christ's triumphal march, and all the fruit harvested by the turning of these spheres!"
Her face seemed to me entirely on fire, and her eyes were so full of ecstasy that I must pass on without describing them.
As in clear nights of the full moon, Trivia smiles among the eternal nymphs who paint the sky across all its depths,
So I saw, above thousands upon thousands of lights, one Sun that kindled them all — just as our own sun kindles the stars above.
And through that living light the luminous Presence shone so intensely clear into my eyes that I could not endure it.
O Beatrice, sweet and gentle guide! She said to me: "What overwhelms you is a power from which nothing can shield itself.
There dwell the wisdom and the omnipotence that opened the roads between heaven and earth — the roads so long desired."
As fire bursts from a cloud, expanding until it cannot be contained and plunges down against its nature to the ground,
So my mind, feasting on those wonders, outgrew itself and poured beyond its bounds — and what it became, it cannot remember.
"Open your eyes and look at what I am. You have seen such things that you are now strong enough to bear my smile."
I was like someone who still carries the feeling of a forgotten vision, struggling in vain to bring it back to mind,
When I heard that invitation — so worthy of gratitude that it will never be erased from the book that records the past.
If all the tongues that Polyhymnia and her sisters made most rich with their delicious milk were sounding now to help me,
They would not reach a thousandth of the truth in singing of that holy smile and how it lit up her holy face.
And so, in representing Paradise, the sacred poem must leap across the gap, like a traveler who finds the road cut off.
But whoever considers the weight of the theme and the mortal shoulder bearing it should not blame that shoulder if it trembles.
This is no passage for a little boat — this course my daring prow is cutting through — nor for a helmsman who would spare himself.
"Why does my face so captivate you that you do not turn to the beautiful garden blossoming beneath the rays of Christ?
There is the Rose in which the Word Divine became flesh. There are the lilies whose fragrance showed the way."
So spoke Beatrice. And I, wholly obedient to her counsel, surrendered myself once more to the battle of my overwhelmed sight.
As my eyes have sometimes seen a meadow of flowers, covered in shadow, suddenly lit by a beam of sunlight streaming through a broken cloud,
So I saw multitudes of splendors illuminated from above by burning rays, though I could not see the source of the radiance.
O benign Power that stamps them so! You raised yourself higher to give my eyes more room, for they were not yet strong enough.
The name of that beautiful flower which I invoke morning and evening utterly captivated my soul, compelling me to gaze upon the greatest fire.
And when both my eyes had taken in the splendor and the magnitude of that living star — which excels there as it excelled here below —
A little torch descended through the sky, shaped in a circle like a crown, and girdled and wheeled about her.
Whatever melody sounds sweetest on earth and most draws the soul to itself would seem like a thunderclap from a torn cloud
Compared to the sound of that lyre which crowned the beautiful sapphire — she who gives the brightest heaven its sapphire hue.
"I am the angelic Love who circles round the sublime joy that breathes from the womb that was the dwelling place of our Desire.
And I shall circle, Lady of Heaven, as long as you follow your Son and make the highest sphere more divine by entering it."
Thus the circling melody sealed itself. And all the other lights made the name of Mary resound.
The royal mantle of all the spheres of this world — the one most fervent and alive with the breath and the works of God —
Had its inner border stretched so far above us that from where I stood, its outline had not yet appeared to me.
Therefore my eyes did not have the power to follow the crowned flame as it rose upward toward its own seed.
And as a baby who has just nursed reaches its arms up toward its mother, moved by an impulse that flames outward,
So each of those white gleams reached upward with its peak, revealing to me the depth of their love for Mary.
Then they stayed there in my sight, singing 'Regina coeli' with such sweetness that the delight has never left me.
Oh, what abundance is stored in those rich coffers — those souls who were good farmers for the sowing here below!
There they live and feast upon the treasure that was won through tears in the exile of Babylon, where gold was left behind.
There he triumphs — beneath the lofty Son of God and Mary, in His victory, together with the old and new councils —
He who holds the keys to such glory.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XXIV
paragraphs: "O company chosen for the great feast of the blessed Lamb, who feeds you so that your desire is always full,
If by the grace of God this man is given a foretaste of what falls from your table before death sets his time,
Consider his immense longing and refresh him a little. You drink forever from the fountain that feeds his thought."
So spoke Beatrice. And those blessed souls transformed themselves into spheres upon fixed poles, blazing intensely like comets.
And as the wheels in a clockwork turn so that the first seems motionless to the observer while the last seems to fly,
So those circling dances, moving at different speeds, gave me the measure of their blessedness — whether swift or slow.
From the one I judged most beautiful, I saw a fire emerge so radiant that it left none brighter behind.
Three times it circled around Beatrice with a song so divine that my imagination cannot repeat it to me.
So my pen leaps past it and I do not write it down. For such subtle folds defeat our imagination, let alone our speech.
"O my holy sister, who implores us with such devotion — by your ardent love you draw me from that beautiful sphere!"
After it stopped, the blessed fire directed its breath toward my Lady, speaking as I have described.
And she said: "O eternal light of the great man to whom our Lord gave the keys he carried down from this wondrous joy,
Examine this one on matters light and grave, as you see fit, concerning the Faith by which you walked upon the sea.
Whether he loves well, hopes well, and believes — this is not hidden from you, for your sight reaches the place where everything is seen.
But since this kingdom has gained its citizens through the true Faith, it is fitting that he have the chance to speak of it, to glorify it."
As a student arms himself and does not speak until the master proposes the question — ready to argue it, not to settle it —
So I armed myself with every argument while she spoke, to be ready for such an examiner and such a profession of faith.
"Speak, good Christian! Declare yourself. What is Faith?" At this I raised my brow toward the light from which these words had breathed.
Then I turned to Beatrice, and she gave me swift signals to pour forth the water from my inner fountain.
"May the grace that permits me to make confession to the great centurion," I began, "make all my thoughts find clear expression!"
And I continued: "As the truthful pen of your dear brother wrote, Father — he who with you set Rome on the right path —
Faith is the substance of things hoped for and the evidence of things not seen. And this seems to me its essential nature."
Then I heard: "You understand correctly — if you also understand why he placed it first among substances, then among evidences."
And I replied: "The deep truths that reveal themselves to me here are so hidden from all eyes below
That their existence there rests only in belief. And upon that belief, high hope is founded — which is why faith has the nature of substance.
And from this belief we must reason without any other proof. Which is why it has the nature of evidence."
Then I heard: "If everything acquired below through teaching were understood this clearly, no sophist would find room to maneuver."
So breathed that kindled love. Then it added: "The alloy and weight of this coin have been examined well enough.
But tell me: do you have it in your purse?" And I answered: "Yes — so shining and so round that there is no doubt about its stamp."
Then from the deep light that was shining there came the words: "This precious jewel, on which every virtue is founded —
Where did you get it?" And I replied: "The abundant outpouring of the Holy Spirit, spread upon the ancient and new scriptures,
Is a proof so sharp that, compared with it, every other demonstration seems blunt to me."
Then I heard: "The ancient premise and the new, which you find so conclusive — why do you take them as the word of God?"
And I answered: "The proof that reveals the truth to me lies in the works that followed — works for which Nature never heated iron nor struck an anvil."
The reply came: "Tell me — who assures you those works actually happened? The very thing that needs to be proved — nothing else confirms it."
"If the world was converted to Christianity without miracles," I said, "then that itself is such a miracle that the others are not a hundredth part of it.
For you entered the field poor and fasting, to sow there the good plant that was once a vine and has now become a thorn."
When this was done, the high and holy court resounded through the spheres, singing 'We praise one God!' in the melody that is chanted there above.
And that Baron who had led me thus from branch to branch, examining me until we approached the outermost leaves,
Began again: "The grace that courts your intellect has opened your mouth, up to this point, as it should be opened.
I approve what came forth. But now you must declare what you believe, and from what source your belief was given to you."
"O holy father, spirit who now sees what you once believed so firmly that you outran younger feet to reach the tomb,"
I began, "you wish me here to express the form of my ready belief, and you also ask the reason for it.
And I answer: I believe in one God, sole and eternal, who moves all the heavens with love and desire, Himself unmoved.
And for this faith I have not only proofs from physics and metaphysics, but it is given to me also by the truth that rains down from this place,
Through Moses, through the Prophets and the Psalms, through the Gospel, and through you who wrote after the fiery Spirit made you holy.
And I believe in three eternal Persons — these I believe to be one essence, so one and so threefold that they sustain both 'are' and 'is.'
With this profound divine condition that I am now touching on, the Gospel teaching stamps my mind again and again.
This is the beginning, this is the spark that afterward expands into a living flame and shines within me like a star in heaven."
As a master who hears news that pleases him immediately embraces his servant, rejoicing in the good report the moment the man falls silent,
So, singing its blessing, the apostolic light circled me three times after I fell silent — at whose command
I had spoken, and in my speaking I had pleased him so.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XXV
paragraphs: If it ever comes to pass that this sacred poem — to which both heaven and earth have set their hand, and which has made me lean for many years —
Overcomes the cruelty that bars me from the fair sheepfold where I slept as a lamb, an enemy to the wolves that prey upon it,
Then with a different voice and different fleece I shall return as a poet, and at my baptismal font I shall take the laurel crown.
Because I entered into the faith that makes souls known to God, and then Peter, for its sake, encircled my brow.
Then a light moved toward us from the band that had produced the first fruits Christ left behind among his vicars.
And my Lady, full of joy, said to me: "Look! Look! Behold the baron for whose sake people make their pilgrimage to Galicia!"
As when a dove alights near its companion and both pour out their affection, circling and cooing around each other,
So I saw one great prince glorified by the other with mutual greetings of welcome, praising the feast that is enjoyed up there.
But when their congratulations were complete, each one stood still before me in silence, so incandescent that it overwhelmed my sight.
Then Beatrice said with a smile: "Illustrious soul, by whom the generous gifts of our great basilica were recorded,
Make Hope resound at this height. You know that you embody it as often as Jesus showed greater clarity to the three."
"Lift up your head and take heart. For what comes here from the mortal world must ripen in our radiance."
This encouragement came to me from the second flame. And so I raised my eyes to the mountains that had bent them down before with too much weight.
"Since, through His grace, our Emperor wills that you should come face to face with His counts in His most secret chamber before you die,
So that, having seen the truth of this court, you may strengthen Hope in yourself and in others — Hope, which rightly kindles love below —
Tell what it is, and how your mind flowers with it, and from what source it came to you." So the second light continued.
And the compassionate Lady who had guided the feathers of my wings for this high flight answered before I could:
"The Church Militant has no child with greater hope than this one, as is written in that Sun which lights our entire company.
Therefore he is permitted to come from Egypt to see Jerusalem before his time of warfare is complete.
The two remaining points — asked not for the sake of knowledge but so that he may report how much this virtue pleases you —
I leave to him. He will not find them difficult or a cause for boasting. Let him answer them, and may the grace of God assist him."
Like a student who follows his teacher, ready and willing in the subject he knows, so that his skill may be displayed,
I said: "Hope is the certain expectation of future glory — the effect of divine grace and of merit that precedes it.
This light comes to me from many stars. But the one who first instilled it in my heart was the supreme singer of the supreme Lord.
'Let them hope in you,' he says in his divine song, 'who know your name.' And who does not know God's name, if they share my faith?
You then added to his instilling with your own, in your Epistle, so that I am full and rain your rain upon others."
While I was speaking, within the living breast of that fire an effulgence quivered — sudden and constant, like lightning.
Then it breathed: "The love with which I still burn for the virtue that followed me all the way to the palm branch and the end of the battlefield
Wills that I speak to you — since you take delight in her. And it is pleasing to me that you tell what Hope promises you."
And I answered: "The ancient Scriptures and the new establish the target, and that target shows it to me, for all the souls God has made His friends.
Isaiah says that each one shall be clothed in his own land with a double garment — and his own land is this blissful life.
And your brother, even more explicitly, where he writes of the white robes, makes this revelation clear to us."
And as I finished these words, from above us came the sound of 'Sperent in te' — 'Let them hope in you' — to which all the dancing circles responded.
Then one light among them grew so bright that if Cancer held such a gem, winter would have a month of unbroken day.
And as a graceful maiden rises, steps forward, and joins the dance — only to honor the bride, not from any failing in herself —
Just so I saw that brightened splendor approach the two who were turning in a wheel, as befitted their ardent love.
It entered into the song and the dance. And my Lady kept her eyes fixed upon them, like a bride, silent and still.
"This is the one who lay upon the breast of our Pelican. And this is the one chosen from the cross for the great office."
So spoke my Lady. But her gaze did not shift from its steady focus, either before or after her words.
Like a man who stares, straining to see the sun when it begins to be eclipsed, and who, by the act of seeing, becomes blind,
So I became before that last flame, while a voice said: "Why do you dazzle yourself trying to see something that has no existence here?
My body is earth in the earth, and there it shall remain with all the others, until our number matches the eternal purpose.
With both garments in the blessed cloister, the only lights that have ascended are the two you see. And this you shall carry back to your world."
At these words the flaming circle fell still, together with the sweet intermingling of sound made by that threefold breath.
As oars that were beating the water all at once are suspended at the sound of a whistle, to escape from danger or fatigue.
Ah, how deeply I was troubled when I turned to look at Beatrice and could not see her — even though I was
Right at her side, in the Happy World!

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XXVI
paragraphs: While I stood anxious over my quenched sight, a breath issued from the blazing flame that had quenched it, drawing my attention.
It said: "While you recover the power of sight that you consumed by gazing at me, it is well that you compensate for it with speech.
Begin, then, and declare what your soul aims at. And know for certain that your sight is only dazzled, not destroyed,
Because the Lady who guides you through this divine realm has in her look the same power that the hand of Ananias had."
I said: "As it pleases her, sooner or later, let healing come to these eyes that were the gates through which she entered with the fire that burns in me forever.
The Good that satisfies this court is the Alpha and the Omega of all the writing that love reads to me, whether softly or aloud."
The same voice that had taken from me the terror of my sudden blindness prompted me in my thoughts to speak further.
It said: "Truly, you must sift with a finer sieve. You must tell me who aimed your bow at such a target."
And I answered: "By philosophical arguments and by the authority that descends from here, such love must stamp itself upon me.
For the Good, insofar as it is good, the moment it is understood, kindles love — and all the more, the more goodness it contains.
Therefore, toward that Essence whose goodness is such that every good found outside it is nothing but a ray of its own light,
The mind of everyone who discerns the truth on which this proof is founded must be moved in love, more than toward anything else.
This truth is revealed to my intellect by the one who demonstrates to me the primal love of all the eternal beings.
It is revealed by the voice of the truthful Author, who says to Moses, speaking of Himself: 'I will make all my goodness pass before you.'
And you reveal it too, at the opening of your sublime Gospel, which proclaims this mystery to earth more loudly than any other herald."
And I heard: "By human reasoning and by the authorities in harmony with it, your highest love looks to God.
But tell me further: do you feel other cords drawing you toward Him, so that you may declare how many teeth this love bites with?"
The holy intention of Christ's eagle was not hidden from me. I could see well where he was leading my profession of love.
So I began again: "All those things whose bite can make the heart turn to God have worked together to create my love.
The existence of the world and my own existence, the death He bore so that I might live, and what every believer hopes for as I do,
Together with the living knowledge I have described, have drawn me from the sea of twisted love and placed me on the shore of the love that is straight and true.
The leaves that cover with green the entire garden of the Eternal Gardener — I love them in proportion to the good that He has given them."
The moment I fell silent, a song of supreme sweetness rang through heaven, and my Lady joined the rest in crying, "Holy! Holy! Holy!"
And as a sharp light wakes a sleeper, because the spirit of sight races through the layers that the light penetrates, membrane after membrane,
And the one who is roused flinches at what he sees, so mindless is his sudden waking — until his judgment comes to help him,
So from my eyes Beatrice chased away every last speck with the beam of her own, which shone from more than a thousand miles away.
And then I saw more clearly than before. And almost stunned, I asked about a fourth light that I saw among us.
And my Lady said: "Within those rays, the first soul that the First Power ever created gazes with love upon its maker."
As a branch that bends its crown when the wind passes over it, and then springs back upright by the very force that raises it,
So I did while she was speaking, struck with wonder. And then a desire to speak, which burned within me, restored my confidence.
And I began: "O fruit who alone were created ripe — ancient father, to whom every bride is both daughter and daughter-in-law —
As devoutly as I can, I beg you: speak to me. You see my wish. To hear you sooner, I do not speak it."
Sometimes an animal will stir beneath a covering so that its movement makes the wrapping follow, revealing what it feels inside.
In the same way, that first soul showed me through its covering of light how joyfully it came to give me pleasure.
Then it breathed: "Without your telling me, I discern your wish better than you can see the things you hold most certain.
For I see it in the truthful mirror that makes itself a perfect reflection of all other things, while nothing can make itself a perfect reflection of it.
You wish to know how long ago God placed me in the high garden where she prepared you for this long stairway.
And how long it was a delight to my eyes, and the true cause of the great wrath, and the language I created and used.
Now, my son, the tasting of the tree was not in itself the cause of so great an exile, but only the act of overstepping the boundary.
In the place from which your Lady sent Virgil, I longed for this assembly four thousand three hundred and two revolutions of the sun.
And I saw it return to all the constellations along its path nine hundred and thirty times while I lived on earth.
The language I spoke was entirely extinct long before the people of Nimrod attempted their unfinishable work.
For no product of human reason has ever been lasting, because of the influence of the heavens, which changes human tastes.
It is natural for humans to speak, but whether in this way or that, nature lets you do as you please.
Before I descended to the anguish of Hell, 'I' was the name on earth for the Supreme Good, from whom comes the joy that clothes me.
Later it was called 'El.' And that is fitting, for the usage of mortals is like a leaf on a branch — one goes and another comes.
On the mountain that rises highest from the sea, my life — pure and then disgraced — lasted from the first hour to the hour that follows the sixth,
When the sun changes quadrant.

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XXVII
paragraphs: "Glory to the Father, to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit" — all of Paradise began to sing, and the sweetness of it intoxicated me.
What I saw seemed to me a smile of the universe, so that my rapture entered through both hearing and sight.
O joy! O gladness beyond words! O life made whole with love and peace! O riches held without desire!
Before my eyes those four torches stood blazing, and the one that had first approached me began to grow more vivid.
And it became in appearance like Jupiter would if he and Mars were birds and exchanged their plumage with each other.
The Providence that there assigns to each its role had imposed silence on the blessed chorus on every side,
When I heard: "Do not wonder that I change color. For as I speak, you will see all these change color too.
The one who on earth usurps my place — my place, my place, which in the sight of the Son of God stands vacant —
Has made of my burial ground a sewer of blood and filth, which satisfies the Fallen One who fell from up here."
With that color which the opposing sun paints on a cloud at evening and at dawn, I saw the whole of heaven become suffused.
And as a virtuous woman who is sure of herself yet grows timid merely hearing another's shame,
So Beatrice changed in her appearance. And such an eclipse, I believe, there was in heaven when the Supreme Power suffered on the cross.
Then his words continued, in a voice so altered from its former tone that his appearance had not changed more than his speech:
"The Bride of Christ was not nourished on my blood, and the blood of Linus and of Cletus, to be used for the acquisition of gold.
It was to acquire this joyful life that Sixtus and Pius, Callixtus and Urban, shed their blood after much weeping.
It was never our intention that part of the Christian people should sit on the right hand of our successors, and part on the left.
Nor that the keys entrusted to me should become the emblem on a standard raised against the baptized.
Nor that I should become the figure on a seal for sold and lying privileges — at which I often blush and flash with anger.
In the clothing of shepherds, rapacious wolves can be seen from up here in all the pastures. O defense of God, why do you still lie idle?
Cahorsines and Gascons are preparing to drink our blood. O fair beginning, to what a vile ending must you fall!
But the high Providence that once saved Rome and its glory for the world through Scipio will bring swift aid, as I conceive.
And you, my son, who will return below again because of your mortal weight — open your mouth and do not hide what I do not hide."
Just as our air sends down flakes of frozen vapor when the horn of the Goat in heaven touches the sun,
So I saw the sky adorned as those triumphant vapors rose upward — they who had lingered there with us.
My sight was following their forms, and followed until the distance between us grew too great to let it penetrate further.
Then my Lady, seeing me freed from straining upward, said to me: "Cast your sight downward and see how far you have revolved."
I saw that since the first time I had looked down, I had moved through the entire arc from the middle to the end of the first clime.
So that I saw, beyond Cadiz, the mad crossing of Ulysses, and on this side, nearly the shore where Europa made herself a sweet burden.
And more of this little threshing floor would have been revealed to me, but the sun beneath my feet had moved on, a sign or more ahead.
My enamored mind, which always courts my Lady, was burning more than ever to bring my eyes back to her.
And if nature or art has ever made a lure to catch the eye and thus possess the mind — whether in human flesh or in portraits of it —
All of them together would seem as nothing beside the divine pleasure that shone upon me when I turned to her smiling face.
And the power that her gaze bestowed upon me plucked me from the fair nest of Leda and launched me into the swiftest heaven.
Its parts, most alive and lofty, are so uniform that I cannot say which one Beatrice chose as my place within it.
But she, who saw my desire, began — smiling so radiantly that God Himself seemed to rejoice in her face:
"The nature of the universe, which holds the center still and moves all the rest around it, begins here as from its starting point.
And this heaven has no other 'where' than the mind of God, in which the love that spins it is kindled, and the power that it rains down.
Light and love enclose it in one circle, as it encloses the others. And only He who girds it understands that girding.
Its motion is not measured by another's, but all the others are measured by this one — as ten is measured by its half and its fifth.
And how time can have its roots in such a vessel and its leaves in all the others, should now be clear to you.
O greed, you who plunge mortals so deep beneath you that none has the power to lift his eyes above your waves!
The will blossoms well enough in human beings, but the endless rain turns the sound plums into rotten ones.
Faith and innocence are found only in little children. Then each of them runs away before the cheeks grow bearded.
One who still lisps observes the fasts but later, once his tongue is free, devours any food in any month.
And one who, while he stammers, loves and listens to his mother, once his speech has become fluent, longs to see her buried.
So the fair daughter of him who brings the morning and leaves the evening turns black in the white skin of her first appearance.
And you, lest you marvel at this, consider that on earth there is no one who governs. And therefore the human family goes astray.
But before January slips entirely out of winter through that hundredth part you all neglect down there,
These lofty spheres shall roar so loud that the storm long awaited will turn the fleet around, setting prow where stern now points.
And true fruit shall follow upon the blossom."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XXVIII
paragraphs: After she who fills my mind with Paradise had spoken the truth against the present life of wretched mortals,
Just as in a mirror a torch lit behind a person can be seen before it comes into his sight or thought,
And he turns around to see whether the glass has told the truth, and finds that it matches the reality as perfectly as a song matches its measure,
So my memory recalls that I did the same, gazing into those beautiful eyes from which Love had fashioned the noose to catch me.
And when I turned, and my own eyes were met by what appears within that sphere whenever one gazes intently upon its rotation,
I saw a Point that radiated a light so sharp that the eye on which it blazes must close against its piercing fire.
And whatever star appears smallest from here would seem a moon if placed beside it, as one star is placed beside another.
Perhaps as near as a halo appears to encircle the light that paints it, when the vapor carrying it is at its densest,
At such a distance around that Point a circle of fire was spinning so fast that it would have outstripped the swiftest motion in the universe.
And this was surrounded by another ring, and that by a third, and the third by a fourth, the fourth by a fifth, and the fifth by a sixth.
Beyond that followed the seventh, already so wide that the messenger of Juno, if made complete, would be too narrow to contain it.
So too the eighth and the ninth. And each one moved more slowly according to how far its number was from the first.
And the one with the least distance from the pure Spark had the clearest flame, because, I believe, it partakes most deeply of that Spark's truth.
My Lady, who saw me deep in suspense and uncertainty, said: "From that Point hang the heavens and all nature.
Look at the circle nearest to it, and know that its motion is so swift because of the burning love by which it is pierced."
And I to her: "If the universe were ordered in the same arrangement I see in these wheels, what has been set before me would satisfy me.
But in the world of sense, the spheres can be seen to be more divine the farther they are from the center.
And so, if my desire is to find its end in this wondrous and angelic temple that has only love and light as its boundary,
I need to hear still further why the model and the copy do not go by the same plan — for by myself, I contemplate this in vain."
"It is no marvel if your fingers are unequal to this knot, since no one has ever tried to untie it, and it has grown so tight."
So spoke my Lady. Then she said: "Take what I tell you, if you wish to satisfy your hunger, and sharpen your wits upon it.
The material spheres are wide or narrow according to the greater or lesser virtue that is spread through all their parts.
Greater goodness intends a greater blessing, and a greater body contains a greater blessing, if all its parts are equally perfect.
Therefore this sphere, which sweeps along with it the rest of the universe, corresponds to the circle that loves and knows the most.
So if you draw your measure around the virtue, not the appearance, of the substances that appear to you as circles,
You will see a marvelous correspondence of greater to larger and of smaller to less, in each heaven to its Intelligence."
As the hemisphere of air remains splendid and serene when Boreas blows from his gentler cheek,
And the haze that had obscured it is cleared and dissolved, so that the sky smiles at us with the beauties of its every region,
So I was cleared when my Lady provided me with her luminous answer. And the truth was seen as clearly as a star in heaven.
And when her words came to a stop, the circles sparked — as iron does when it boils — and every spark kept spinning with its ring.
Their sparks were more numerous than the doubling of a chessboard, square upon square — more than all the grains on every square combined.
I heard Hosanna sung from choir to choir to that fixed Point which holds them, and will forever hold them, in the 'where' they have always been.
And she, who saw the questions in my thoughts, said: "The first circles have shown you the Seraphim and the Cherubim.
They follow their bonds so swiftly in order to resemble the Point as much as they can, and they can as much as their vision is exalted.
Those other loves that circle around them are called Thrones of the divine aspect — and with them the first triad is complete.
And you should know that all of them find their bliss in proportion to how deeply their sight penetrates the Truth in which every intellect finds rest.
From this it can be seen that blessedness is founded on the act of seeing, not on the act of loving — which comes after.
And the measure of their sight is merit, which is born of grace and of good will. And so the progression goes from grade to grade.
The second triad, which flowers thus in this eternal springtime that no autumnal Ram can strip of its leaves,
Perpetually sings Hosanna with three melodies sounding through the three orders of joy with which that triad is woven.
In that hierarchy are the three divinities: first Dominions, then Virtues, and the third are Powers.
Then, in the two penultimate dances, the Principalities and Archangels wheel. The last is all of angelic play.
These orders all gaze upward, and their downward influence is such that all are drawn and all draw toward God.
And Dionysius set himself with such desire to contemplate these orders that he named and distinguished them just as I do.
But Gregory afterward departed from him. And so, the moment he opened his eyes in this heaven, he laughed at himself.
And if a mortal on earth declared a truth so hidden, do not wonder — for the one who saw it here above revealed it to him,
Along with much more of the truth about these circles."

chapters.title: Paradiso, Canto XXIX
paragraphs: When both children of Latona, covered by the Ram and by the Scales, make the horizon their belt at the same instant,
As long as the zenith holds them balanced — until one and the other, changing hemispheres, are freed from that belt —
For just that long, her face lit with a smile, Beatrice kept silent, gazing at the Point that had overcome me.
Then she began: "I tell, not ask, what you wish to hear, for I have seen it where every 'where' and every 'when' converge to a single point.
Not to gain any good for Himself — which is impossible — but so that His splendor, shining back, could say 'I am,'
In His eternity, beyond all time, beyond every other limit, as it pleased Him, the Eternal Love opened into new loves.
Nor did He lie as if asleep before this. For neither 'before' nor 'after' applied to God's moving over these waters.
Form and matter, joined and separate, came into being that had no flaw, like three arrows shot from a three-stringed bow.
And as in glass, in amber, or in crystal a ray of light shines so that there is no interval between its coming and its being complete,
So the threefold creation was flashed into being by its Lord all at once, without any distinction in its beginning.
